title: Modeling Checklist
text:
This checklist helps turn a criminological question into a simple model. The goal is not to force every topic into mathematics. The goal is to make assumptions explicit.
A model should clarify actors, choices, information, incentives, timing, and expected outcomes.

title: Modeling Checklist
text:
The basic modelling chain





flowchart TD
    A[Research problem] --> B[Actors]
    B --> C[Choices]
    C --> D[Information]
    D --> E[Payoffs and constraints]
    E --> F[Timing]
    F --> G[Solution or prediction]
    G --> H[Interpretation]
    H --> I[Evidence and limitations]






A weak model skips steps. A strong model makes each step visible.

title: Modeling Checklist
text:
Step 1: Define the problem
Start with the behaviour or institution you want to explain.
Examples:

Why do some victims not report crime?
How does monitoring affect rule-breaking?
Why do co-offenders cooperate?
How do police allocate patrols?
Why do defendants accept plea bargains?
How does cybercrime scale across platforms?

Write the problem in one sentence:
I want to explain why [actor] chooses [action] under [condition].

title: Modeling Checklist
Modeling Checklist
text:
Step 3: Define choices
Each actor needs a choice set.
Examples:



Actor
Possible choices




offender
offend / not offend


police
inspect / not inspect


victim
report / not report


prosecutor
charge / dismiss / bargain


defendant
accept plea / reject plea


co-offender
cooperate / betray


regulator
audit / not audit


platform
moderate / ignore / report



Keep the first version small. A two-action model is often enough to clarify the mechanism.

title: Modeling Checklist
Modeling Checklist
Modeling Checklist
text:
Step 6: Choose timing
Timing determines the model type.





flowchart TD
    A[Timing] --> B[Simultaneous]
    A --> C[Sequential]
    A --> D[Repeated]
    A --> E[Networked]

    B --> B1[Normal-form game]
    C --> C1[Extensive-form game]
    D --> D1[Repeated game]
    E --> E1[Network model]






Examples:

Offender and police choose simultaneously: inspection game.
Offender acts, victim reports, police respond: sequential game.
Community and police interact repeatedly: repeated trust game.
Offending spreads through peers: network model.

title: Modeling Checklist
section: Step 7: Choose the solution concept or prediction
text:
Step 7: Choose the solution concept or prediction
The solution concept depends on the model.



Model type
Typical solution or prediction




One-person choice model
optimal action


Simultaneous game
Nash equilibrium


Sequential game
backward induction or subgame perfection


Incomplete-information game
Bayesian reasoning


Repeated game
cooperation, punishment, reputation


Network model
diffusion, centrality, clustering


Empirical prediction model
validation and error analysis



Not every model needs a formal equilibrium. Sometimes the purpose is to clarify a mechanism or generate testable predictions.

title: Modeling Checklist
text:
Step 8: Interpret the result
A model result should be translated back into criminological language.
For example, if the model says:
offending falls when detection probability rises
then interpret:

Do actors perceive detection risk?
Is enforcement evenly distributed?
Does crime displace?
Does trust change?
Does recorded crime rise because detection rises?
What are the unintended consequences?

Interpretation prevents the model from becoming detached from reality.

title: Modeling Checklist
text:
Step 9: Connect to evidence
Every model should suggest observable implications.





flowchart LR
    A[Model prediction] --> B[Observable implication]
    B --> C[Data source]
    C --> D[Evidence]
    D --> E[Revise model]






For example:







Model claim
Observable implication




deterrence works through perceived risk
perceived risk should change before behaviour changes


trust affects reporting
low-trust groups should report less, holding victimization constant


peer effects matter
behaviour should cluster through social ties


stigma affects reoffending
formal contact should affect later opportunity


displacement occurs
crime should move across place, time, target, or method

title: Modeling Checklist
text:
Example: reporting model
Problem:
Why might victims not report crime?
Actors:

victim;
police or institution.

Victim choices:

report;
do not report.

Information:

expected police response;
perceived cost of reporting;
trust in institution;
fear of retaliation;
seriousness of harm.

Payoffs:
report if expected benefit of reporting > expected cost of reporting
Mechanism:





flowchart LR
    A[Victimization] --> B[Expected benefit of reporting]
    C[Cost, fear, stigma] --> D[Reporting decision]
    B --> D
    E[Institutional trust] --> D
    D --> F[Recorded or hidden crime]






Prediction:

higher trust should increase reporting;
higher stigma or retaliation risk should reduce reporting;
recorded crime may rise if reporting increases.

title: Modeling Checklist
text:
Example: inspection game
Problem:
How does monitoring affect rule-breaking?
Actors:

potential offender;
authority.

Choices:

offender: offend or comply;
authority: inspect or not inspect.

Information:

offender may not know whether inspection occurs;
authority may not know whether offending occurs.

Payoffs:

offending gives gain if undetected;
inspection is costly;
punishment reduces payoff if detected.

Mechanism:





flowchart LR
    A[Inspection probability] --> B[Expected punishment]
    B --> C[Offending incentive]
    C --> D[Observed offending]
    A --> E[Detection and recorded crime]






Prediction:

higher perceived inspection risk should reduce offending;
higher inspection may increase recorded crime in the short run;
offenders may adapt if monitoring is predictable.

title: Modeling Checklist
text:
Common mistakes

1. Including too many actors
Start simple. Add actors only when they change the mechanism.


2. Making choices vague
Choices should be specific enough to analyse.


3. Ignoring information
Strategic behaviour depends heavily on what actors know or believe.


4. Treating payoffs as only money
Status, fear, legitimacy, shame, and time may matter.


5. Confusing model outcome with data
The model may predict true offending, while the data may measure recorded crime.


6. Jumping from model to policy
Policy requires evidence, implementation, ethics, and institutional feasibility.

title: Modeling Checklist
text:
Checklist
Use this checklist before writing a model page:

What is the behaviour or institution being explained?
Who are the actors?
What choices do they have?
What does each actor know?
What is uncertain?
What beliefs matter?
What does each actor value?
What are the constraints?
What is the timing?
Is the interaction one-shot, repeated, or networked?
What solution concept or prediction is appropriate?
What observable implication follows?
What data could test or illustrate the prediction?
What does the model ignore?
What policy implication is safe to draw?

title: Organized Crime
text:
Organized crime involves coordinated illegal activity that is structured, repeated, and often protected by reputation, violence, corruption, secrecy, or governance. It may involve illicit markets, extortion, trafficking, fraud, protection, smuggling, cybercrime, or control over territory and networks.
The key feature is organization under illegality. Since illegal agreements cannot rely on ordinary courts, organized crime often develops alternative enforcement mechanisms.

title: Organized Crime
text:
Basic mechanism map





flowchart TD
    A[Organized Crime] --> B[Illicit coordination]
    A --> C[Governance]
    A --> D[Violence or threat]
    A --> E[Corruption]
    A --> F[Market structure]

    B --> B1[Roles]
    B --> B2[Networks]
    B --> B3[Repeated exchange]

    C --> C1[Dispute resolution]
    C --> C2[Rule enforcement]

    D --> D1[Reputation]
    D --> D2[Intimidation]

    E --> E1[Protection]
    E --> E2[Information leakage]

    F --> F1[Demand]
    F --> F2[Supply chains]
    F --> F3[Risk premium]






Organized crime is not just “crime by groups.” It is crime where coordination, enforcement, and continuity matter.

title: Organized Crime
text:
Core mechanisms

Illegal governance
Organized groups may provide enforcement, protection, dispute resolution, and contract discipline in illegal markets.


Reputation
Reputation can substitute for legal enforcement. A group may maintain a reputation for violence or reliability to control behaviour.


Violence
Violence can be used to punish betrayal, deter rivals, discipline members, intimidate witnesses, or regulate markets.


Corruption
Corruption reduces enforcement risk, provides information, protects markets, or allows illegal activity to operate under legal cover.


Network resilience
Organized crime may survive enforcement because roles and ties can shift. Removing one actor may not destroy the structure.

title: Organized Crime
text:
Measurement issues
Organized crime is difficult to observe.



Issue
Why it matters




Hidden structure
membership and hierarchy are often unknown


Witness intimidation
reporting and cooperation may be suppressed


Corruption
institutional data may be compromised


Market secrecy
transactions are hidden


Network adaptation
groups reorganize after enforcement


Legal ambiguity
some activities mix legal and illegal businesses



Data often come from investigations, prosecutions, intelligence, interviews, seizures, or network reconstruction. Each source is partial.

title: Organized Crime
text:
Repeated exchange model
Illegal markets face a problem: participants cannot use ordinary legal contract enforcement.
Repeated interaction can partly solve this.





flowchart LR
    A[Illegal exchange] --> B{Can parties trust each other?}
    B -->|No| C[High betrayal risk]
    B -->|Yes| D[Repeated cooperation]
    D --> E[Reputation]
    E --> F[Future business]
    C --> G[Violence or enforcement]
    G --> E






The same mechanism that supports cooperation within the group can also produce violence against outsiders or defectors.

title: Organized Crime
text:
Corruption as protection
Corruption can be modelled as an exchange between criminal actors and officials.





flowchart TD
    A[Criminal group] --> B[Payment or favour]
    B --> C[Corrupt official]
    C --> D[Protection, information, or non-enforcement]
    D --> E[Lower expected punishment]
    E --> F[Illicit market stability]






Corruption changes expected costs and can make illegal markets more durable.

title: Organized Crime
text:
Policy trade-offs








Policy
Mechanism
Possible limitation




Arrest leaders
disrupts hierarchy
may create succession violence


Asset seizure
reduces resources
groups may hide assets


Anti-corruption enforcement
raises protection cost
politically difficult


Witness protection
increases cooperation
expensive and trust-dependent


Market disruption
raises transaction cost
may displace activity


Network targeting
attacks central nodes
network may adapt

title: Organized Crime
text:
Organized crime and violence
Violence may increase when markets are unstable. Strong groups may reduce visible violence by governing markets, while fragmented competition may increase conflict.
This creates a difficult policy issue:





flowchart LR
    A[Enforcement pressure] --> B[Market disruption]
    B --> C[Power vacuum]
    C --> D[Rival competition]
    D --> E[Violence risk]






This does not mean enforcement is bad. It means enforcement can have transitional effects that should be anticipated.

title: Organized Crime
text:
Common mistakes

1. Treating organized crime as a fixed hierarchy
Some groups are hierarchical, but others are networked, flexible, or project-based.


2. Ignoring governance
Organized crime may provide illegal order, not only disorder.


3. Treating violence as random
Violence may serve strategic functions such as discipline, reputation, and market control.


4. Ignoring corruption
Corruption can be central to durability.


5. Assuming removal of leaders ends the organization
Networks may adapt after leadership removal.

title: Organized Crime
text:
Checklist for analysing organized crime

What activity or market is being organized?
What roles exist?
How are agreements enforced?
What role does violence play?
What role does corruption play?
Is the structure hierarchical or networked?
How does the group manage betrayal?
How is the activity measured?
What happens if enforcement disrupts the group?
What unintended effects may follow?

title: Property Crime
text:
Property crime involves taking, damaging, entering, or interfering with property. It includes theft, burglary, vehicle crime, robbery with property motives, vandalism, shoplifting, and fraud-like low-level acquisition offences.
Property crime is especially useful for studying opportunity, target selection, guardianship, routine activity, and displacement.

title: Property Crime
text:
Basic mechanism map





flowchart TD
    A[Property Crime] --> B[Motivation]
    A --> C[Opportunity]
    A --> D[Target]
    A --> E[Guardianship]
    A --> F[Market or disposal]

    B --> B1[Need or gain]
    B --> B2[Peer influence]
    B --> B3[Low perceived risk]

    C --> C1[Access]
    C --> C2[Timing]
    C --> C3[Location]

    D --> D1[Value]
    D --> D2[Visibility]
    D --> D3[Portability]

    E --> E1[People nearby]
    E --> E2[Locks and alarms]
    E --> E3[Surveillance]

    F --> F1[Resale]
    F --> F2[Informal markets]
    F --> F3[Online platforms]






The key idea is that property crime often depends less on deep motivation and more on the immediate structure of opportunity.

title: Property Crime
text:
Routine activity logic
Routine activity theory argues that crime becomes more likely when three elements converge:

a motivated offender;
a suitable target;
absence of capable guardianship.






flowchart LR
    A[Motivated offender] --> D[Crime event]
    B[Suitable target] --> D
    C[Weak guardianship] --> D






This framework is especially useful for burglary, theft, vehicle crime, and shoplifting.

title: Property Crime
Property Crime
Property Crime
text:
Measurement issues
Property crime has several measurement problems.







Issue
Why it matters




Insurance incentives
some incidents are reported mainly for claims


Low-value offences
small losses may not be reported


Business reporting
firms may record losses internally rather than report


Repeat victimization
one location or person may experience many events


Classification
theft, burglary, robbery, and fraud may be separated legally


Online resale
stolen property markets may be hard to observe



Recorded property crime can fall because offending falls, but also because reporting falls or insurance behaviour changes.

title: Property Crime
text:
A simple target-selection model
A property offender may choose among possible targets by comparing expected gain and expected cost.
A simple expression is:
\[
\text{Expected payoff}
=
\text{value of target}
-
\Pr(\text{caught}) \times \text{sanction}
-
\text{effort cost}.
\]
The offender chooses the target with the highest expected payoff.





flowchart LR
    A[Target value] --> D[Expected payoff]
    B[Detection risk] --> D
    C[Effort cost] --> D
    D --> E[Target choice]
    E --> F[Crime concentration]






This model explains why crime can cluster around attractive targets and weakly guarded places.

title: Property Crime
text:
Displacement
Property crime interventions often raise the issue of displacement.
If one target becomes harder, offending may move to:

another place;
another time;
another target;
another method;
another offence type.






flowchart TD
    A[Intervention] --> B[Target becomes harder]
    B --> C{Offender adapts?}
    C -->|No| D[Crime reduction]
    C -->|Yes| E[Displacement]
    E --> F[Place]
    E --> G[Time]
    E --> H[Target]
    E --> I[Method]






Displacement is possible, but not automatic. Some interventions reduce crime without full displacement because offenders do not always find equally attractive alternatives.

title: Property Crime
text:
Policy trade-offs








Policy
Mechanism
Possible risk




Better locks
increases effort cost
benefits depend on adoption


CCTV
increases detection risk
may shift crime elsewhere


Street lighting
increases guardianship
effect varies by context


Hotspot patrol
increases perceived risk
may affect trust


Product marking
lowers resale value
requires market checks


Platform monitoring
disrupts stolen-goods markets
privacy and enforcement concerns

title: Property Crime
text:
Common mistakes

1. Treating property crime as purely economic
Material gain matters, but peer influence, drug markets, habit, status, and opportunity may also matter.


2. Ignoring target suitability
Not all targets are equally attractive or accessible.


3. Assuming displacement is complete
Offenders may not perfectly substitute to other targets.


4. Treating recorded crime as true crime
Reporting varies by value, insurance, trust, and victim type.


5. Ignoring repeat victimization
Some people, firms, or places are victimized repeatedly.

title: Property Crime
text:
Checklist for analysing property crime

What kind of property crime is being studied?
What is the target?
What makes the target suitable?
What guardianship exists?
What is the expected gain?
What is the perceived risk?
How is the crime reported and recorded?
Is repeat victimization present?
Could displacement occur?
What policy mechanism is being used?

title: Violent Crime
text:
Violent crime involves the use, threat, or attempted use of physical force. It includes behaviours such as assault, robbery, homicide, domestic violence, sexual violence, and group-based violence. These behaviours differ greatly in motive, severity, setting, and institutional response, so violent crime should not be treated as one simple category.
A useful analysis of violent crime usually connects individual factors, situational triggers, social context, weapons, institutions, and measurement.

title: Violent Crime
text:
Basic mechanism map





flowchart TD
    A[Violent crime] --> B[Individual factors]
    A --> C[Situational triggers]
    A --> D[Social environment]
    A --> E[Institutional context]

    B --> B1[Impulsivity]
    B --> B2[Trauma or victimization]
    B --> B3[Substance use]

    C --> C1[Conflict]
    C --> C2[Status threat]
    C --> C3[Weapon availability]

    D --> D1[Peer audience]
    D --> D2[Retaliation norms]
    D --> D3[Low trust]

    E --> E1[Policing]
    E --> E2[Reporting]
    E --> E3[Protection and support]






Violence often occurs when several mechanisms combine. A conflict may escalate because of intoxication, peer pressure, weapon access, low trust in authorities, and expectations of retaliation.

title: Violent Crime
text:
Core mechanisms

Conflict escalation
Many violent events begin as disputes. The key question is why a dispute becomes physical. Escalation may depend on emotion, perceived disrespect, alcohol, audience effects, weapon availability, or fear of appearing weak.


Retaliation
Violence can become self-reinforcing when one act creates pressure for revenge. Retaliation is especially important when formal institutions are not trusted to resolve disputes.


Status and identity
In some contexts, violence functions as a way to defend reputation, masculinity, group identity, or status. The payoff is not only material. It may include respect, fear, belonging, or avoidance of humiliation.


Opportunity and guardianship
Violence is also situational. Some settings create more opportunities for violence because of crowding, alcohol, weak guardianship, or repeated contact between conflicting groups.


Coercive control
Domestic and intimate partner violence cannot be understood only as isolated incidents. In many cases, violence is part of a broader pattern of control, fear, dependency, surveillance, and isolation.

title: Violent Crime
text:
Measurement issues
Violent crime is not measured perfectly.







Issue
Why it matters




Underreporting
Many violent events, especially domestic and sexual violence, are not reported


Severity variation
The same legal category may include very different levels of harm


Recording practices
Police classification can change recorded trends


Victim-offender relationship
Stranger violence and domestic violence have different mechanisms


Hospital data
Medical records may capture injuries that police data miss


Fear and trauma
Harm may persist beyond the physical event



A rise in recorded violent crime may reflect more violence, better reporting, changed recording rules, or greater institutional attention.

title: Violent Crime
text:
A simple retaliation model
Violence can be modelled as a repeated interaction where failure to retaliate may reduce status, while retaliation creates future risk.





flowchart LR
    A[Initial conflict] --> B[Perceived disrespect or harm]
    B --> C{Retaliate?}
    C -->|Yes| D[Immediate status or revenge payoff]
    C -->|No| E[Possible loss of status]
    D --> F[Future retaliation risk]
    E --> G[Conflict may fade]






The policy implication is that reducing violence may require changing the expected payoff from retaliation, creating safe alternatives, and increasing trust in non-violent dispute resolution.

title: Violent Crime
Violent Crime
text:
Policy trade-offs








Policy
Possible benefit
Possible risk




Increased patrol
higher guardianship and deterrence
reduced trust if aggressive or unequal


Focused deterrence
targets high-risk conflicts
depends on legitimacy and implementation


Weapon restrictions
reduces lethality
displacement to other methods possible


Victim support
increases safety and reporting
requires trust and access


Mediation
reduces retaliation
may be inappropriate for coercive abuse


Rehabilitation
addresses behaviour and trauma
slow and resource-intensive

title: Violent Crime
text:
Common mistakes

1. Treating all violence as the same
Domestic violence, street violence, robbery, homicide, and group conflict may involve different mechanisms.


2. Ignoring the victim-offender relationship
Violence between strangers differs from violence between intimate partners, family members, peers, or rivals.


3. Treating violence as purely impulsive
Some violence is impulsive, but some is strategic, retaliatory, coercive, or reputation-based.


4. Ignoring reporting
Recorded violent crime may change because reporting changes.


5. Ignoring institutions
Trust in police and courts can shape whether people report, seek help, retaliate, or remain silent.

title: Violent Crime
text:
Checklist for analysing violent crime

What type of violence is being studied?
Who is involved?
What is the relationship between victim and offender?
What situational trigger is present?
Is the violence expressive, instrumental, retaliatory, coercive, or mixed?
What role do peers, weapons, alcohol, or place play?
How is the violence measured?
What institutional response is available?
What policy mechanism is being proposed?
What unintended consequences are possible?

title: Cybercrime
text:
Cybercrime refers to offences that use digital systems as targets, tools, environments, or markets. It includes hacking, malware, phishing, online fraud, identity theft, ransomware, platform abuse, data theft, harassment, and illicit online marketplaces.
Cybercrime is not one mechanism. It is a domain shaped by scale, anonymity, automation, weak attribution, platform design, and cross-border enforcement problems.

title: Cybercrime
text:
Basic mechanism map





flowchart TD
    A[Cybercrime] --> B[Technical opportunity]
    A --> C[Anonymity and attribution]
    A --> D[Automation and scale]
    A --> E[Human vulnerability]
    A --> F[Platform and market structure]

    B --> B1[Software weakness]
    B --> B2[Credential exposure]

    C --> C1[Hidden identity]
    C --> C2[Cross-border actors]

    D --> D1[Mass attempts]
    D --> D2[Low marginal cost]

    E --> E1[Phishing]
    E --> E2[Social engineering]

    F --> F1[Online markets]
    F --> F2[Platform rules]
    F --> F3[Data economies]






The distinctive feature of cybercrime is that one actor can target many victims at low marginal cost.

title: Cybercrime
text:
Core mechanisms

Automation
Digital tools allow repeated attempts at scale. A fraud attempt with a very low success rate may still be profitable if the cost per attempt is tiny.


Anonymity and weak attribution
Cyber offenders can hide identity, location, or responsibility. This reduces expected detection and complicates enforcement.


Social engineering
Many cybercrimes exploit human behaviour rather than only technical weaknesses. Phishing, romance scams, and impersonation attacks rely on trust, urgency, fear, or confusion.


Platform dependency
Cybercrime often occurs through platforms, payment systems, social media, marketplaces, cloud services, or messaging apps. Platform rules shape opportunity.


Cross-border enforcement
Victims, offenders, servers, financial intermediaries, and platforms may be in different jurisdictions.

title: Cybercrime
text:
Measurement issues
Cybercrime is hard to measure.







Issue
Why it matters




Underreporting
victims may feel shame or see reporting as useless


Misclassification
incidents may be recorded as fraud, harassment, or data breach


Private handling
firms may resolve incidents internally


Cross-border cases
jurisdiction complicates recording


Rapid change
offence methods evolve quickly


Technical uncertainty
victims may not know how the offence occurred



Recorded cybercrime usually captures only part of the problem.

title: Cybercrime
text:
Attacker-defender logic
Cybercrime can be represented as an attacker-defender game.





flowchart LR
    A[Defender chooses security level] --> B[Attacker observes or infers weakness]
    B --> C[Attacker chooses target or method]
    C --> D{Attack succeeds?}
    D -->|Yes| E[Loss to victim]
    D -->|No| F[Attack cost or failure]
    E --> G[Defender updates security]
    F --> G






The strategic point is adaptation. Defenders harden systems, attackers search for weaker targets or new methods.

title: Cybercrime
text:
Phishing as persuasion
Phishing can be understood as manipulative communication.





flowchart TD
    A[Attacker sends message] --> B[Victim interprets credibility]
    B --> C{Trust message?}
    C -->|Yes| D[Click, pay, or reveal credentials]
    C -->|No| E[Ignore or report]
    D --> F[Loss or account compromise]






The message works when it changes beliefs or triggers action before verification.

title: Cybercrime
text:
Policy trade-offs








Policy
Mechanism
Possible limitation




Security education
reduces human vulnerability
training fatigue


Multi-factor authentication
reduces credential misuse
adoption and usability issues


Platform moderation
disrupts abuse at scale
false positives and evasion


Incident reporting rules
improves visibility
firms may under-disclose


International cooperation
improves enforcement
slow and politically difficult


Payment tracing
disrupts monetization
offenders adapt to alternatives

title: Cybercrime
text:
Cybercrime and displacement
Cyber offenders adapt quickly. Removing one method may shift activity to another.





flowchart LR
    A[Security improvement] --> B[Original attack becomes harder]
    B --> C[Attacker adapts]
    C --> D[New target]
    C --> E[New method]
    C --> F[New platform]






This does not mean prevention is useless. It means policy should consider adaptation.

title: Cybercrime
text:
Common mistakes

1. Treating cybercrime as purely technical
Many cybercrimes exploit psychology, trust, institutions, and markets.


2. Ignoring scale
Low success rates can still be profitable at large scale.


3. Treating victims as careless
Cybercrime often involves sophisticated manipulation and structural vulnerability.


4. Ignoring platforms
Platforms shape opportunity, visibility, reporting, and enforcement.


5. Ignoring cross-border enforcement
Jurisdiction is often central to the problem.

title: Cybercrime
text:
Checklist for analysing cybercrime

Is the digital system the target, tool, environment, or market?
What is the offender trying to gain?
Is the mechanism technical, psychological, economic, or mixed?
What makes the target vulnerable?
How does anonymity or attribution matter?
Is automation or scale important?
Which platform or intermediary is involved?
How is the incident measured?
What intervention changes the offender’s expected payoff?
How might offenders adapt?

title: Criminology Foundations
text:
Foundations clarify the basic objects of criminological analysis: crime, deviance, harm, law, measurement, reporting, units of analysis, and explanation. These concepts matter because criminology often studies events that are partly hidden, socially interpreted, and institutionally recorded.
The goal of this section is to make the primitives clear before moving to mechanisms, institutions, models, or policy.

title: Criminology Foundations
text:
Why foundations matter
In criminology, the object being studied is rarely simple. A recorded crime is not only an event. It is also the result of reporting, classification, policing, and legal definition.





flowchart LR
    A[Social behaviour] --> B[Legal definition]
    B --> C[Crime event]
    C --> D[Reporting]
    D --> E[Recording]
    E --> F[Official statistics]
    F --> G[Research interpretation]






This means a criminological claim usually depends on both social reality and measurement process.
For example, a rise in recorded crime may reflect:

more actual offending;
more reporting;
changes in policing;
changes in legal classification;
changes in recording standards;
greater visibility of certain groups or places.

title: Criminology Foundations
text:
Main foundation pages



Key Definitions
Core concepts such as crime, deviance, harm, law, social control, criminalization, victimization, and recorded crime.
Open →




Units of Analysis
How criminological explanations change when the unit is an individual, event, place, group, network, institution, or society.
Open →

title: Criminology Foundations
text:
Crime, deviance, and harm
A behaviour can be harmful without being criminal. A behaviour can be criminal without being treated as equally harmful in practice. A behaviour can also be deviant without being illegal.
These distinctions are important.








Concept
Basic meaning
Example question




Crime
Behaviour prohibited by criminal law
What does the law define as punishable?


Deviance
Behaviour violating social norms
What does society label as unacceptable?


Harm
Damage to persons, groups, or institutions
Who is injured or made worse off?


Criminalization
Process of making behaviour criminal
Why is this behaviour treated as a criminal matter?


Social control
Formal or informal regulation of behaviour
Who enforces norms, and how?



Criminology often studies the relationship among these categories rather than assuming they are identical.

title: Criminology Foundations
Criminology Foundations
text:
Units of analysis
Criminological research can focus on different units.







Unit
Typical question




Individual
Why does this person offend, desist, report, or comply?


Event
Why did this crime happen here and now?


Place
Why are some places crime hotspots?


Group
How do peers, gangs, or organizations shape behaviour?


Network
How do ties transmit information, opportunity, or trust?


Institution
How do police, courts, prisons, or regulators act?


Society
How do inequality, culture, law, and state capacity shape crime?



A theory that works at one level may not automatically work at another. For example, a theory of individual offending is not the same as a theory of neighbourhood crime rates.

title: Criminology Foundations
text:
From concept to measurement
A good empirical study must connect the concept being discussed to the variable being measured.





flowchart LR
    A[Concept] --> B[Operational definition]
    B --> C[Measurement]
    C --> D[Data]
    D --> E[Inference]






For example:

“fear of crime” may be measured by survey responses;
“police activity” may be measured by stops, arrests, patrol time, or spending;
“violence” may be measured by hospital admissions, police records, or victimization data;
“trust” may be measured by survey items, reporting behaviour, or cooperation.

Each measurement choice captures something slightly different.

title: Criminology Foundations
text:
Explanation versus description
Description answers:

What is happening?

Explanation asks:

Why is it happening?

A descriptive claim might say that burglary is concentrated in certain areas. An explanatory claim asks why those areas experience more burglary: opportunity, guardianship, poverty, housing structure, policing, social networks, or reporting practices.





flowchart TD
    A[Observed pattern] --> B[Description]
    A --> C[Possible explanations]
    C --> D[Mechanism]
    D --> E[Testable implication]
    E --> F[Evidence]






The move from pattern to mechanism is where theory becomes important.

title: Criminology Foundations
text:
Causation and mechanism
A mechanism is a process that connects cause and effect.
For example:
poverty → stress and opportunity constraints → illegal income strategies
or:
low institutional trust → lower reporting → lower recorded crime
or:
increased guardianship → fewer suitable opportunities → lower burglary
A mechanism should make clear:

what changes;
who responds;
why they respond;
what outcome follows;
what evidence would support or challenge the explanation.

title: Criminology Foundations
text:
Common measurement problems

1. Underreporting
Many crimes are never reported to authorities. This is especially important for domestic abuse, sexual violence, fraud, drug offences, and crimes involving distrust of police.


2. Recording variation
Even reported events may not be recorded consistently across time, place, or institution.


3. Detection bias
Some crimes are found only when institutions search for them. Drug offences, tax violations, and regulatory offences often depend heavily on enforcement intensity.


4. Classification changes
Legal or administrative changes can alter crime categories without any real change in behaviour.


5. Visibility bias
Highly visible populations and places may appear more criminal because they are more closely monitored.


6. Ecological fallacy
Patterns at the group or area level should not be automatically applied to individuals.

title: Criminology Foundations
text:
Checklist for foundation-level analysis
Before using a criminological claim, ask:

What is being defined as crime?
Is the issue crime, deviance, harm, or criminalization?
What is the unit of analysis?
Is the evidence about true crime or recorded crime?
What measurement process produced the data?
What mechanism is being proposed?
What alternative explanations are possible?
Does the claim confuse description with causation?
Are institutions part of the measurement process?
What would count as contrary evidence?

title: Criminology Notes
text:
The basic analytical chain
A useful criminological explanation usually connects context, mechanism, behaviour, measurement, and response.





flowchart LR
    A[Social or institutional context] --> B[Mechanism]
    B --> C[Behaviour]
    C --> D[Observed data]
    D --> E[Interpretation]
    E --> F[Policy response]






This chain also shows where mistakes can occur. A change in recorded crime may reflect a change in actual offending, reporting, detection, classification, or enforcement intensity.

title: Criminology Notes
text:
Crime as behaviour and record
One of the most important distinctions in criminology is the difference between true crime and recorded crime.
True crime refers to events that actually occur. Recorded crime refers to events that appear in official data.
These are not the same.





flowchart TD
    A[Crime event occurs] --> B{Victim or witness reports?}
    B -->|No| C[Hidden crime]
    B -->|Yes| D{Police record the event?}
    D -->|No| E[Unrecorded reported event]
    D -->|Yes| F[Recorded crime]
    F --> G[Official statistics]






This distinction matters because many empirical claims rely on recorded data. A rise in recorded crime may mean more offending, better reporting, changed police practice, or changed classification.

title: Criminology Notes
text:
Mechanisms before labels
A theory is most useful when it identifies a mechanism.
For example:







Theory family
Possible mechanism




Deterrence
Sanctions change expected costs


Routine activity
Crime occurs when opportunity, target, and weak guardianship coincide


Self-control
Impulsivity affects sensitivity to immediate reward


Social learning
Behaviour spreads through peers and reinforcement


Labeling
Official reaction changes identity and opportunity


Legitimacy
Perceived fairness affects willingness to comply


Life-course theory
Turning points change constraints and attachments



The same crime type can involve several mechanisms at once. Violent crime may involve self-control, retaliation, peer norms, alcohol, weapon access, and weak guardianship.

title: Criminology Notes
Criminology Notes
text:
Why models are useful
Models do not replace empirical evidence or qualitative interpretation. They help clarify assumptions.
A model can show:

who the actors are;
what choices they face;
what information they have;
what incentives matter;
what outcome should be expected;
what would change under a policy intervention.






flowchart TD
    A[Criminological question] --> B[Identify actors]
    B --> C[Specify choices]
    C --> D[Specify information]
    D --> E[Specify payoffs or incentives]
    E --> F[Derive prediction]
    F --> G[Compare with evidence]






This is especially useful when the same policy may have different effects depending on reporting, deterrence, displacement, trust, and institutional response.

title: Criminology Notes
text:
Example: deterrence as a mechanism
A simple deterrence argument says that offending becomes less attractive when expected punishment increases.
Expected punishment can be written roughly as
\[
\text{Expected punishment}
=
\Pr(\text{caught}) \times \text{sanction severity}.
\]
A deterrence policy may increase either the probability of detection or the severity of punishment.
But the mechanism is not automatic. The effect depends on whether potential offenders perceive the risk, whether they are responsive to future consequences, whether opportunities remain available, and whether enforcement is legitimate.
This is why a simple model should be paired with institutional and behavioural interpretation.

title: Criminology Notes
text:
Example: reporting and trust
Recorded crime depends partly on reporting. Reporting depends partly on trust.





flowchart LR
    A[Crime or victimization] --> B{Report to authorities?}
    B -->|Yes| C[Case enters official data]
    B -->|No| D[Hidden from official data]
    E[Trust in institutions] --> B
    F[Expected benefit of reporting] --> B
    G[Expected cost or stigma] --> B






This means recorded crime can rise even when true crime does not rise, if victims become more willing to report. It can also fall even when true crime does not fall, if trust declines.

title: Criminology Notes
text:
Common mistakes

1. Treating recorded crime as true crime
Official statistics are valuable, but they are shaped by reporting, recording, policing, and classification.


2. Naming a theory without explaining the mechanism
A label is not an explanation. The mechanism should show how one thing produces another.


3. Ignoring institutions
Crime policy works through institutions, and institutions have incentives, constraints, and errors.


4. Assuming punishment works mechanically
Deterrence depends on perceived risk, responsiveness, legitimacy, and available alternatives.


5. Ignoring displacement
An intervention may move crime across time, space, target, method, or offence type.


6. Separating theory and measurement
The way crime is measured affects the conclusions that can be drawn from evidence.

title: Criminology Notes
section: How these notes connect to the rest of the site
text:
How these notes connect to the rest of the site
Criminology connects naturally with game theory and psychology.
Game theory helps analyse enforcement, inspection, reporting, bargaining, cooperation, and strategic adaptation.
Psychology helps analyse impulse, identity, emotion, trauma, social cognition, moral judgement, and compliance.
Foundations help keep the reasoning clear: optimization for incentives, probability for uncertainty, dynamic reasoning for future consequences, and networks for social structure.

title: Criminology Models
text:
Models are simplified representations of criminological mechanisms. They help make assumptions explicit: who acts, what they choose, what they know, what they value, and how institutions respond.
The purpose of this section is not to make criminology artificially mathematical. The purpose is to use models as disciplined thinking tools.

title: Criminology Models
text:
Why use models?
A model helps answer questions such as:

Who are the actors?
What choices are available?
What information does each actor have?
What incentives or constraints matter?
What outcome should we expect?
What would change under a different policy?






flowchart LR
    A[Criminological problem] --> B[Actors]
    B --> C[Choices]
    C --> D[Information]
    D --> E[Payoffs or constraints]
    E --> F[Prediction]
    F --> G[Evidence or policy test]






A good model is not a full description of the world. It is a controlled way to isolate a mechanism.

title: Criminology Models
text:
Map of criminology models





flowchart TD
    A[Criminology Models] --> B[Inspection Games]
    A --> C[Reporting and Trust]
    A --> D[Co-offending Games]
    A --> E[Network Crime]
    A --> F[Plea Bargaining]
    A --> G[Allocation Dynamics]

    B --> B1[Monitoring]
    B --> B2[Deterrence]
    B --> B3[Detection risk]

    C --> C1[Victim or witness decision]
    C --> C2[Institutional trust]
    C --> C3[Recorded crime]

    D --> D1[Coordination]
    D --> D2[Betrayal risk]
    D --> D3[Group offending]

    E --> E1[Diffusion]
    E --> E2[Peer effects]
    E --> E3[Central actors]

    F --> F1[Asymmetric information]
    F --> F2[Trial risk]
    F --> F3[Bargaining]

    G --> G1[Hotspots]
    G --> G2[Resource allocation]
    G --> G3[Displacement]






These models connect directly to mechanisms. Deterrence can be modelled as inspection. Reporting can be modelled as cooperation under trust. Co-offending can be modelled as coordination. Crime diffusion can be modelled through networks.

text:
Model pages



Inspection Games
Models of monitoring, deterrence, enforcement, detection risk, and strategic adaptation between rule-breakers and authorities.
Open →

Open →

title: Criminology Models
text:
From mechanism to model
A mechanism explains a process. A model formalises the process enough to examine its implications.





flowchart TD
    A[Mechanism] --> B[Choose actors]
    B --> C[Define actions]
    C --> D[Define information]
    D --> E[Define payoffs]
    E --> F[Choose timing]
    F --> G[Choose solution concept]
    G --> H[Derive prediction]
    H --> I[Interpret criminologically]






For example, deterrence as a mechanism can become an inspection game:
authority chooses monitor/not monitor
individual chooses offend/not offend
payoffs depend on gain, punishment, monitoring cost, and detection probability
This model can then ask how behaviour changes when monitoring becomes cheaper, punishment becomes harsher, or detection becomes more likely.

title: Criminology Models
text:
Matching models to questions







Research question
Useful model




How does monitoring affect offending?
Inspection game


Why do victims report or stay silent?
Reporting and trust model


Why do offenders cooperate with one another?
Co-offending game


How does crime spread through groups?
Network crime model


Why do defendants accept plea deals?
Plea bargaining model


How should police allocate scarce resources?
Allocation dynamics model



The model should be chosen because it fits the mechanism, not because it looks sophisticated.

title: Criminology Models
text:
Actors and choices
Every model begins by identifying actors and choices.
Examples:








Model
Actors
Choices




Inspection game
offender, authority
offend/comply; inspect/not inspect


Reporting model
victim/witness, police
report/not report; respond/not respond


Co-offending game
potential co-offenders
join/not join; cooperate/betray


Plea bargaining
prosecutor, defendant
offer/accept/reject; trial/settle


Network model
connected individuals
offend, transmit information, recruit, withdraw


Allocation model
enforcement agency, offenders
allocate patrols; move, offend, avoid



A model is unclear if the actors and choices are unclear.

title: Criminology Models
Criminology Models
Criminology Models
text:
Timing
Timing determines the logic of the model.





flowchart TD
    A[Choose timing] --> B[Simultaneous]
    A --> C[Sequential]
    A --> D[Repeated]
    A --> E[Networked or dynamic]

    B --> B1[Nash equilibrium]
    C --> C1[Backward induction or SPE]
    D --> D1[Reputation and punishment]
    E --> E1[Diffusion and feedback]






For example, deterrence may look different if police move first, offenders move first, or both adapt over time.

title: Criminology Models
text:
Interpretation
The final step is interpretation. A model result should be translated back into criminological language.
A model may produce a result like:
\[
\Pr(\text{offend}) \text{ decreases when } \Pr(\text{detection}) \text{ increases}.
\]
But the interpretation should ask:

Do people perceive detection risk accurately?
Which groups are most affected?
Does enforcement change reporting?
Does crime move elsewhere?
Does legitimacy rise or fall?
Are there unintended consequences?

Without interpretation, a model is only algebra.

title: Criminology Models
text:
Common mistakes

1. Adding too many features too early
A useful first model should be simple. Add complexity only when it clarifies the mechanism.


2. Forgetting the unit of analysis
A model of individual offending is not the same as a model of neighbourhood crime rates.


3. Treating payoffs as purely monetary
Status, fear, shame, addiction, trust, and identity may matter.


4. Ignoring institutions
Police, courts, prisons, regulators, and communities are strategic actors too.


5. Ignoring measurement
A model may predict true crime, but the available data may measure recorded crime.


6. Treating model results as automatic policy advice
A model clarifies one mechanism. Policy requires institutional, empirical, and ethical interpretation.

title: Criminology Models
section: Checklist for building a criminology model
text:
Checklist for building a criminology model

What crime, behaviour, or institution is being studied?
Who are the actors?
What choices do they have?
What information does each actor have?
What are the payoffs, constraints, or motivations?
What is the timing?
Is the interaction one-shot, repeated, or networked?
What solution concept is appropriate?
What prediction does the model produce?
What measurement problem might affect evidence?
What would the model miss?
What policy implication, if any, follows?

title: Plea bargaining (asymmetric information)
text:
Plea bargaining is bargaining under uncertainty: - prosecutor offers a plea sentence, - defendant accepts or goes to trial, - trial outcomes are uncertain and costly.
A core theme is selection into trial.

title: Plea bargaining (asymmetric information)
text:
Plea bargaining is bargaining under uncertainty: - prosecutor offers a plea sentence, - defendant accepts or goes to trial, - trial outcomes are uncertain and costly.
A core theme is selection into trial.

title: Plea bargaining (asymmetric information)
text:
Canonical setup (two types)
Defendant type \(\theta\in\{L,H\}\) with prior \(\Pr(H)=\pi\). Type affects conviction probability: \(0<p_L<p_H<1\).
Trial sentence if convicted: \(T>0\).
Plea offer: \(x\).
Trial costs: prosecutor \(c_P>0\), defendant \(c_D>0\).
Defendant accepts iff: \[
x \le p_\theta T + c_D.
\]

title: Plea bargaining (asymmetric information)
text:
Screening pattern (one offer)
To induce \(H\) accept and \(L\) reject: \[
x \in (p_L T + c_D,\; p_H T + c_D].
\]
Expected payoff to prosecutor under this policy: - Type \(H\): \(x\) - Type \(L\) (trial): \(p_L T - c_P\)
So: \[
\pi x + (1-\pi)(p_L T - c_P).
\]

title: Plea bargaining (asymmetric information)
text:
Predictions (qualitative)

Higher \(c_D\) increases plea acceptance.
Higher \(c_P\) increases reliance on pleas.
Stronger evidence (higher \(p_\theta\)) increases acceptance.

title: Network crime (diffusion and strategic complements)
text: Network models study how behavior depends on peers and connections: learning, diffusion, and strategic complementarities.

title: Network crime (diffusion and strategic complements)
text: Network models study how behavior depends on peers and connections: learning, diffusion, and strategic complementarities.

title: Network crime (diffusion and strategic complements)
text:
Canonical linear-quadratic network game
Agent \(i\) chooses \(x_i\ge 0\) and: \[
u_i(x)= a_i x_i - \frac{1}{2}x_i^2 + \beta x_i \sum_j g_{ij}x_j.
\]
Best response: \[
x_i = a_i + \beta \sum_j g_{ij}x_j.
\]
Vector form: \[
x = (I-\beta G)^{-1}a
\] when invertible.

title: Network crime (diffusion and strategic complements)
text:
Predictions (qualitative)

shocks to incentives propagate through a network multiplier
targeting central nodes has outsized effects
strong complements generate clustering and persistence

title: Network crime (diffusion and strategic complements)
text:
Connections

Mechanisms

Social interactions & networks
Inequality & social trust (shifts \(a_i\))
Opportunity & routine activity (local environment enters \(a_i\))



Institutions

Policing (targeting, disruption)
Corrections (network disruption and reentry)



Models

title: Network crime (diffusion and strategic complements)
text:
Later-on analysis
Add enforcement targeted by network position; add diffusion dynamics; add endogenous network formation/sorting.

title: Life-course dynamics (onset and desistance)
text:
NoteStylized facts this mechanism aims to match




Offending often shows strong age patterns: onset, persistence, and eventual desistance for many individuals.
Turning points (school, work, relationships) and system contact can change trajectories.

title: Life-course dynamics (onset and desistance)
text:
NoteStylized facts this mechanism aims to match




Offending often shows strong age patterns: onset, persistence, and eventual desistance for many individuals.
Turning points (school, work, relationships) and system contact can change trajectories.

title: Life-course dynamics (onset and desistance)
text:
Mechanism (core idea)
Life-course criminology emphasizes that offending is dynamic: - people’s constraints, opportunities, and social ties evolve; - past behavior can affect future options (e.g., stigma, skill loss); - interventions can have different short-run vs long-run effects.
A theory-first approach treats these as state variables.

title: Life-course dynamics (onset and desistance)
text:
Canonical modeling primitives

A) States and transitions
Let state \(x_t\) capture employability, social ties, addiction, stigma, etc. Choices (crime vs no crime) affect: - immediate payoff, - transition of \(x_{t+1}\).


B) Dynamic incentives

“crime today” may increase short-run payoff but worsen future states (stigma, incarceration).
“no crime” may build human capital or relationships, improving future payoffs.



C) Heterogeneity
Different types (impulsive vs patient; high-skill vs low-skill) create persistence and concentration.

title: Life-course dynamics (onset and desistance)
text:
Predictions (qualitative)

Policies that raise short-run costs (sanctions) can deter some behavior but may increase long-run crime if they worsen future states (e.g., incarceration reduces future legal options).
Interventions that improve transitions (training, reentry support) can shift long-run equilibria even if short-run deterrence is unchanged.
Stigma channels can create “path dependence”: early system contact changes the trajectory.

title: Life-course dynamics (onset and desistance)
text:
What would count as evidence? (conceptual)
Evidence often aims to distinguish: - selection (who gets system contact) vs causal impact (contact changes the person), - short-run incapacitation vs long-run dynamic effects.

title: Life-course dynamics (onset and desistance)
text:
Later-on analysis (model links)

Dynamic games / Markov decision models fit naturally here.
Courts/corrections pages will connect: punishment policies affect state transitions.
“Labeling & stigma” is a specific mechanism that often lives inside life-course dynamics.

title: Inequality, deprivation & social trust
text:
NoteStylized facts this mechanism aims to match




Violence and disorder often co-move with deprivation and low social trust (interpretations differ across theories).
Communities with stronger informal social control tend to sustain lower levels of violence and fear.

title: Inequality, deprivation & social trust
text:
NoteStylized facts this mechanism aims to match




Violence and disorder often co-move with deprivation and low social trust (interpretations differ across theories).
Communities with stronger informal social control tend to sustain lower levels of violence and fear.

title: Inequality, deprivation & social trust
text:
Mechanism (core idea)
This mechanism family links macro social conditions to micro behavior through: - outside options (returns to legal work vs illegal gain), - social trust / social capital (willingness to cooperate and enforce norms), - collective efficacy (informal guardianship and community capacity), - stress/strain (pressure and constraints that affect choices).
In theory-first notes, it’s useful to treat inequality/deprivation not as a single cause but as a bundle of parameter shifts affecting incentives and cooperation.

title: Inequality, deprivation & social trust
text:
Canonical modeling primitives

A) Opportunity cost and outside options

legal income option \(w\) vs illegal gain \(b\)
unemployment or low wages reduce \(w\), raising relative attractiveness of crime



B) Trust and collective action

community cooperation increases detection probability \(q\) (through reporting/witnessing)
social capital reduces coordination costs of informal prevention



C) Equilibrium feedback

low trust reduces reporting → lower detection → higher crime → further erosion of trust This can generate multiple equilibria (high-trust/low-crime vs low-trust/high-crime).

title: Inequality, deprivation & social trust
text:
Predictions (qualitative)

Lower outside options (\(w\) down) increase participation in illegal activity when deterrence is unchanged.
Lower trust reduces cooperation and reporting, potentially lowering recorded crime in the short run but raising incidence in the long run.
If trust enters detection, policies that improve legitimacy can shift the system to a different equilibrium.

title: Inequality, deprivation & social trust
section: What would count as evidence? (conceptual, not a full review)
text:
What would count as evidence? (conceptual, not a full review)
To support this mechanism, studies typically look for variation in: - labor-market shocks (outside options), - interventions that change community trust/collective efficacy, - exogenous changes in reporting or guardianship.
The main caution is separating behavior from recorded outcomes when reporting changes.

title: Inequality, deprivation & social trust
text:
Later-on analysis (model links)

Inspection/deterrence: inequality shifts \(w\) and \(b\) (returns), and trust shifts \(q\).
Reporting & legitimacy: trust directly enters reporting decisions.
Network effects: deprivation can interact with peer complementarities, amplifying clustering.

title: Incentives & deterrence
text:
Mechanism (core idea)
Potential offenders compare expected benefits of offending with expected costs: - probability of detection, - severity of sanction, - opportunity costs (legal work, stigma, future).
In academic work this is often called rational choice or deterrence logic. It does not imply perfect rationality; it is a modeling language for incentives.

title: Incentives & deterrence
section: Canonical model: a simple inspection game
text:
Canonical model: a simple inspection game

Story
A shop owner chooses how intensively to monitor (e.g., cameras/guards). A potential offender chooses whether to steal.


Players and actions

Offender chooses: Crime (\(C\)) or No crime (\(N\)).
Enforcer chooses: Inspect (\(I\)) or Not inspect (\(\bar I\)).



Payoffs (reduced form)
Let: - offender benefit from crime be \(b>0\) if not caught, - sanction (net cost) be \(s>0\) if caught, - inspection cost be \(k>0\) to the enforcer, - harm from a successful crime be \(h>0\) to the enforcer.
Payoffs: - If offender chooses \(N\): offender gets \(0\); enforcer gets \(0\) (regardless of inspection). - If offender chooses \(C\): - if \(I\): offender is caught → payoff \(-s\); enforcer payoff \(-k\) (prevents harm) - if \(\bar I\): offender succeeds → payoff \(b\); enforcer payoff \(-h\)
So the normal-form game is:
\[
\begin{array}{c|cc}
& I & \bar I\\ \hline
C & (-s,\,-k) & (b,\,-h)\\
N & (0,\,0) & (0,\,0)
\end{array}
\]

title: Incentives & deterrence
text:
Solved example (mixed-strategy equilibrium)

Problem
Find the mixed-strategy Nash equilibrium (inspection probability and crime probability).


Solution
Let the enforcer inspect with probability \(q\) and the offender commit crime with probability \(p\).
Step 1 (offender indifference condition).
Offender’s expected payoff from \(C\): \[
\mathbb{E}[u_O(C)] = q(-s) + (1-q)b = b - q(b+s).
\] Offender’s payoff from \(N\) is \(0\).
In a mixed equilibrium where offender randomizes, set: \[
b - q(b+s)=0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad q^*=\frac{b}{b+s}.
\]
Step 2 (enforcer indifference condition).
Enforcer’s expected payoff from \(I\): \[
\mathbb{E}[u_E(I)] = p(-k) + (1-p)0 = -pk.
\] From \(\bar I\): \[
\mathbb{E}[u_E(\bar I)] = p(-h) + (1-p)0 = -ph.
\] In a mixed equilibrium where enforcer randomizes, set: \[
-pk = -ph \quad \Rightarrow \quad k=h.
\]
This shows an important fact: with this payoff structure, a true interior mixed equilibrium exists only when \(k=h\). Otherwise, the enforcer has a strict preference: - If \(k<h\): inspection is cheaper than expected harm → enforcer prefers inspect. - If \(k>h\): inspection is too costly → enforcer prefers not inspect.


Interpreting the equilibrium cases

If \(k<h\) (inspection relatively effective/cheap): enforcer chooses \(I\), offender chooses \(N\) if \(-s<0\) (always). Crime is deterred.
If \(k>h\) (inspection expensive/ineffective): enforcer chooses \(\bar I\), offender chooses \(C\) if \(b>0\) (always). Crime occurs.

Takeaway: even in a tiny model, deterrence depends on the enforcement cost–harm tradeoff.

title: Incentives & deterrence
text:
Comparative statics (predictions)

Increasing sanction \(s\) reduces the inspection probability needed to deter crime because \(q^*=\frac{b}{b+s}\) decreases in \(s\).
Increasing benefit \(b\) makes deterrence harder (raises \(q^*\)).
Increasing harm \(h\) makes inspection more attractive; increasing cost \(k\) makes it less attractive.

title: Incentives & deterrence
text:
Later-on analysis (where criminology becomes richer)

Adaptation/substitution: offenders can switch targets, locations, or tactics → model multiple actions and substitution.

Endogenous detection: detection probability depends on offender effort and police allocation (dynamic).

Reporting & legitimacy: observed crime depends on victim reporting and trust.

Heterogeneity: different types (opportunistic vs persistent offenders) generate concentration.

title: Self-control and present bias (behavioral microfoundations)
text:
NoteStylized facts this mechanism aims to match




Some offending appears impulsive or myopic rather than forward-looking.
Short-run temptations and situational triggers can matter even when long-run costs are large.

title: Self-control and present bias (behavioral microfoundations)
text:
NoteStylized facts this mechanism aims to match




Some offending appears impulsive or myopic rather than forward-looking.
Short-run temptations and situational triggers can matter even when long-run costs are large.

title: Self-control and present bias (behavioral microfoundations)
text:
Mechanism (core idea)
Behavioral approaches model departures from fully forward-looking choice: - present bias (overweight immediate payoff), - limited attention to detection risk, - self-control constraints.
This does not replace incentive-based models; it changes how incentives are processed.

title: Self-control and present bias (behavioral microfoundations)
text:
Canonical modeling primitives

A) Present-biased utility
A simple representation: - immediate gain from crime is weighted heavily relative to future costs - sanction \(s\) that arrives later is discounted more than “standard” exponential discounting would imply


B) Attention and perceived risk
Perceived detection probability \(\tilde q\) may differ from objective \(q\) due to salience, experience, and misinformation.


C) Commitment and environment
Guardianship/opportunity changes can serve as “commitment devices” by reducing temptations.

title: Self-control and present bias (behavioral microfoundations)
text:
Predictions (qualitative)

Increasing sanction severity may have weaker deterrent effects when behavior is present-biased (especially if punishment is delayed or uncertain).
Making detection risk salient and immediate can matter more than increasing severity.
Situational prevention (reducing opportunities) can be effective even without changing preferences.

title: Self-control and present bias (behavioral microfoundations)
text:
What would count as evidence? (conceptual)
Studies often focus on: - timing of consequences (immediate vs delayed), - salience interventions (visibility of police, warnings), - measures of impulsivity/self-control correlated with offending.

title: Self-control and present bias (behavioral microfoundations)
text:
Later-on analysis (model links)

Combine with deterrence: replace \(q\) by perceived \(\tilde q\), or change discounting of \(s\).
Combine with opportunity: changes in environment affect temptation and attention.
Dynamic models: repeated experiences update perceived risk and behavior.

title: Institutions
text:
Institutions shape how crime is defined, detected, processed, punished, prevented, and recorded. In criminology, institutions are not only background conditions. They are strategic actors with incentives, constraints, errors, legitimacy problems, and information limits.
This section focuses on policing, courts, corrections, and the broader institutional chain connecting crime events to official responses.

title: Institutions
text:
Why institutions matter
A crime event does not automatically become a criminal justice outcome. It must pass through many institutional stages.





flowchart LR
    A[Crime or alleged crime] --> B[Reporting or detection]
    B --> C[Police response]
    C --> D[Investigation]
    D --> E[Charging decision]
    E --> F[Court process]
    F --> G[Sentence or dismissal]
    G --> H[Correctional or community supervision]
    H --> I[Long-term consequences]






Each stage involves discretion. Each stage can create error, inequality, delay, deterrence, legitimacy, or distrust.

title: Institutions
text:
Main institution pages



Policing
Police as detection, enforcement, order maintenance, service provision, and legitimacy-producing institutions.
Open →




Courts
Courts as institutions of adjudication, bargaining, legal classification, procedural fairness, and case processing.
Open →




Corrections
Prisons, probation, parole, rehabilitation, incapacitation, reentry, stigma, and long-term institutional effects.

title: Institutions
text:
The institutional chain
A useful way to analyse institutions is to follow the case pathway.





flowchart TD
    A[Event] --> B{Observed?}
    B -->|No| C[No institutional case]
    B -->|Yes| D{Reported or detected?}
    D -->|No| E[Hidden from system]
    D -->|Yes| F[Police contact]
    F --> G{Recorded?}
    G -->|No| H[No official crime record]
    G -->|Yes| I[Official record]
    I --> J{Suspect identified?}
    J -->|No| K[Unsolved case]
    J -->|Yes| L[Charge or diversion decision]
    L --> M[Court or settlement process]
    M --> N[Outcome]






This chain shows why official criminal justice data are institutionally produced. They are not pure measurements of social behaviour.

title: Institutions
text:
Institutions as strategic actors
Institutions respond to incentives and constraints.
Police may respond to crime rates, public pressure, budgets, political priorities, legal rules, performance targets, and community relations.
Courts may respond to caseload pressure, evidence quality, plea bargaining incentives, procedural rules, and sentencing guidelines.
Correctional systems may respond to capacity, public safety claims, rehabilitation goals, labour constraints, and political pressure.





flowchart LR
    A[Institutional constraints] --> B[Institutional incentives]
    B --> C[Discretionary decisions]
    C --> D[Observed justice outcomes]
    D --> E[Public trust or distrust]
    E --> B






The feedback loop matters. Institutional action changes public trust, and public trust changes reporting, cooperation, compliance, and legitimacy.

title: Institutions
Institutions
text:
Courts
Courts process cases under uncertainty.
Key questions include:

How strong is the evidence?
What is the expected trial outcome?
What are the costs of delay?
What are the incentives to accept a plea?
How does procedural fairness affect legitimacy?
How do sentencing rules shape bargaining?

Court outcomes are not only legal outcomes. They are also negotiated outcomes produced under institutional pressure.





flowchart LR
    A[Evidence strength] --> B[Charging and bargaining]
    C[Trial risk] --> B
    D[Caseload pressure] --> B
    E[Legal rights and procedure] --> B
    B --> F[Case outcome]

title: Institutions
text:
Corrections
Corrections include prisons, probation, parole, rehabilitation, and reentry.
Correctional institutions can produce different mechanisms:







Mechanism
Possible effect




Incapacitation
prevents offending during custody


Deterrence
discourages future offending through expected punishment


Rehabilitation
changes skills, constraints, or behaviour


Stigma
reduces future opportunity


Network exposure
connects people to criminogenic networks


Reentry support
reduces barriers after release



Correctional policy therefore involves trade-offs. A sanction can reduce crime through incapacitation while increasing future risk through stigma or disrupted employment.

title: Institutions
text:
Legitimacy and institutional trust
Institutions do not only change incentives. They also shape whether people view law as rightful.
Legitimacy matters because voluntary compliance and cooperation are partly trust-based.





flowchart TD
    A[Procedural fairness] --> B[Institutional legitimacy]
    B --> C[Trust]
    C --> D[Reporting and cooperation]
    C --> E[Voluntary compliance]
    D --> F[Institutional effectiveness]
    E --> F






When legitimacy falls, institutions may need more coercion to produce the same behavioural outcome. That can further reduce trust.

title: Institutions
text:
Institutional errors
Criminal justice institutions face several kinds of error.







Error type
Meaning




False positive
treating an innocent person as guilty


False negative
failing to detect or sanction actual wrongdoing


Classification error
recording an event under the wrong category


Discretionary bias
unequal treatment across people or places


Process error
delay, lost evidence, weak procedure, or inconsistent decision-making



Institutional analysis should ask where errors enter the chain and who bears their cost.

title: Institutions
text:
Policy questions
Institutional policy should be analysed through mechanisms.
Examples:







Policy
Mechanism to examine




Hotspot policing
concentration of patrol and deterrence


Body-worn cameras
accountability, evidence, and behaviour change


Procedural justice training
legitimacy and cooperation


Sentencing reform
deterrence, incapacitation, proportionality, prison population


Diversion
reduced stigma and alternative intervention


Reentry programmes
employment, housing, support, and desistance



The key question is not simply whether a policy is “tough” or “soft.” The key question is what mechanism it activates and what consequences it produces.

title: Institutions
text:
Common mistakes

1. Treating institutions as neutral recording devices
Institutions shape the data they produce.


2. Ignoring discretion
Rules matter, but discretionary interpretation and implementation also matter.


3. Equating more enforcement with less crime
More enforcement may increase detection and recorded crime, change displacement, or reduce trust.


4. Ignoring legitimacy
Compliance is not only produced by fear of punishment.


5. Treating punishment as one mechanism
Punishment can deter, incapacitate, stigmatize, rehabilitate, or destabilize.


6. Ignoring feedback
Institutional action changes future behaviour, cooperation, reporting, and trust.

title: Institutions
text:
Checklist for institutional analysis

Which institution is acting?
What choices does it have?
What information does it observe?
What incentives and constraints does it face?
Where does discretion enter?
What errors are possible?
How does the institution affect recorded data?
How does it affect trust and legitimacy?
What feedback effects may follow?
Which groups bear the costs and benefits?

title: Policing
text:
This page treats policing as an institution with: - objectives (harm reduction, clearance, legitimacy), - constraints (budget, staffing, information), - strategic interactions (offender adaptation, community cooperation).
The aim is an academic map of how policing is analyzed, not a program-evaluation catalogue.

title: Policing
text:
This page treats policing as an institution with: - objectives (harm reduction, clearance, legitimacy), - constraints (budget, staffing, information), - strategic interactions (offender adaptation, community cooperation).
The aim is an academic map of how policing is analyzed, not a program-evaluation catalogue.

title: Policing
text:
Core research questions

How does police presence/effort change incidence vs recorded outcomes (reporting/recording)?
How should scarce resources be allocated across places and times (hotspots, patrol allocation)?
How does legitimacy affect cooperation (reporting, witnessing), and thereby detection?

title: Policing
text:
Institutional primitives (what to model)

A) Capacity and allocation
Policing is constrained: effort must be allocated across: - locations (hotspots vs non-hotspots), - time (day/night; weekends), - tasks (patrol vs investigation).


B) Information and targeting
Police learn from: - calls for service (endogenous reporting), - observed incidents, - intelligence, - past allocation outcomes.


C) Performance measures and incentives
Observed metrics may include: - recorded crime rates, - arrests/clearance rates, - response times, - complaints.
These metrics can shape agency behavior (sometimes away from welfare-maximizing choices).

title: Policing
text:
Strategic responses (equilibrium thinking)

Offender adaptation
Policies can trigger substitution: - location displacement, - temporal displacement, - target substitution, - tactic substitution.


Community cooperation
Reporting and witness cooperation are endogenous and depend on: - expected responsiveness, - perceived fairness, - fear of retaliation, - legitimacy.

title: Policing
text:
Canonical modeling approaches

Inspection/deterrence (monitoring vs offending)

Spatial equilibrium (offenders choose locations; police allocate patrol)

Dynamic allocation (learning, belief-updating, capacity constraints)

Reporting & trust (victims decide to report; police decide effort; offenders anticipate)

title: Policing
text:
Later-on analysis
A theory-first program often treats policing as a player with: - budget constraint, - allocation decision, - outcome function (detection/harm), - legitimacy/cooperation channel.

title: Stylized facts
text:
This page lists stylized facts: recurring empirical regularities widely discussed in criminology and related social-science literatures.
They are not meant as a complete empirical review, but as constraints for theory: mechanisms and models should be able to reproduce (at least qualitatively) these patterns.
A recurring caution: many “crime facts” depend on measurement (reporting, enforcement, recording practices). When relevant, the fact is stated as a pattern about recorded crime, victimization, or behavior.

title: Stylized facts
text:
This page lists stylized facts: recurring empirical regularities widely discussed in criminology and related social-science literatures.
They are not meant as a complete empirical review, but as constraints for theory: mechanisms and models should be able to reproduce (at least qualitatively) these patterns.
A recurring caution: many “crime facts” depend on measurement (reporting, enforcement, recording practices). When relevant, the fact is stated as a pattern about recorded crime, victimization, or behavior.

title: Stylized facts
text:
1) Concentration in people and places

A small share of people account for a large share of offending (repeat offending / persistence).
Theory implication: heterogeneity and dynamics (states, types, or learning) matter.
Crime concentrates spatially (hotspots: small areas produce disproportionate incidents).
Theory implication: opportunity and guardianship are place-specific; equilibrium responses can relocate activity.

(Links that will eventually connect) - Opportunity / routine activity → notes/mechanisms/opportunity-routine.qmd - Policing allocation / hotspots → notes/institutions/policing.qmd

title: Stylized facts
section: 2) Recorded crime is not the same as incidence
text:
2) Recorded crime is not the same as incidence

Not all victimization is reported, and reporting varies by offense type, victim characteristics, and trust in institutions.
Theory implication: include a reporting stage; observed data may reflect participation constraints.
Enforcement is selective: arrest/case data reflect policing choices and capacity, not just offending.
Theory implication: strategic interaction can change observables even when underlying behavior changes less.

(Links) - Legitimacy & compliance → notes/mechanisms/legitimacy-compliance.qmd - Reporting & trust model → notes/models/reporting-trust.qmd

title: Stylized facts
text:
3) Opportunity and routine predict timing

Crime risk often shifts with routine activity patterns (crowding, guardianship, mobility, visibility).
Theory implication: “technology of opportunity” matters; policies can change opportunity without changing preferences.

(Links) - Opportunity / routine activity → notes/mechanisms/opportunity-routine.qmd

title: Stylized facts
section: 4) Sanctions: detection vs severity (and strategic adaptation)
text:
4) Sanctions: detection vs severity (and strategic adaptation)

The deterrent effect of punishment is often discussed as depending on both probability of detection and severity of sanction; in practice, offenders may adapt (switch targets, tactics, locations, or timing).
Theory implication: model deterrence as a game (inspection/monitoring) and allow substitution across actions.

(Links) - Incentives & deterrence → notes/mechanisms/incentives-deterrence.qmd - Inspection games → notes/models/inspection-games.qmd

title: Stylized facts
text:
5) Social interactions and networks matter

Offending can be socially embedded: co-offending, peer effects, clustering within networks, diffusion of tactics.
Theory implication: strategic complements, learning, and partner choice can generate clustering and persistence.

(Links) - Social interactions → notes/mechanisms/social-interactions.qmd - Co-offending games → notes/models/co-offending-games.qmd - Network crime → notes/models/network-crime.qmd

title: Stylized facts
section: 6) Inequality, deprivation, and trust appear repeatedly
text:
6) Inequality, deprivation, and trust appear repeatedly

Many literatures link violence and disorder to deprivation, inequality, and low social trust/collective efficacy (interpretations differ across theories).
Theory implication: these factors can enter as outside options, returns to legitimate work, enforcement cooperation, or social capital.

(Links) - Inequality & trust → notes/mechanisms/inequality-trust.qmd

title: Stylized facts
text:
7) Life-course dynamics: onset and desistance

Offending is often described as following a life-course pattern (onset, persistence, desistance), with strong roles for transitions (schooling, work, relationships) and system contact (stigma).
Theory implication: dynamic incentives and state dependence; consider reputational/stigma channels.

(Links) - Life-course dynamics → notes/mechanisms/life-course.qmd

title: Stylized facts
section: 8) Institutions are strategic actors, not passive rules
text:
8) Institutions are strategic actors, not passive rules

Policing, courts, and corrections have objectives, constraints, and incentives; policy changes can produce equilibrium responses (by offenders, victims, and agencies).
Theory implication: model institutions as players with limited capacity and endogenous targeting.

(Links) - Policing → notes/institutions/policing.qmd - Courts / bargaining → notes/institutions/courts.qmd - Corrections → notes/institutions/corrections.qmd - Allocation dynamics → notes/models/allocation-dynamics.qmd
