text:
Minimal “theory constraints” (what your models should be able to explain)
A theory-first criminology note set is especially strong if it can generate: - concentration (people/places), - substitution/adaptation under enforcement, - the role of reporting and legitimacy, - network clustering/co-offending, - dynamics (persistence and desistance).

title: Game Theory Notes
text:
Game theory studies situations in which outcomes depend not only on one person’s choice, but also on the choices, beliefs, and incentives of others. It is useful whenever behaviour is strategic: each player asks not only “What should I do?”, but also “What will others do, what do they believe, and how will they respond?”
The aim of these notes is not to turn every social situation into a mathematical puzzle. It is to build a disciplined language for thinking about interdependence: conflict, cooperation, credibility, information, bargaining, punishment, trust, and reputation.

title: Game Theory Notes
text:
The basic idea
A decision problem becomes a game when one person’s payoff depends on another person’s action. In an ordinary optimization problem, the decision-maker chooses the best action against a fixed environment. In a game, the “environment” also thinks, chooses, reacts, and sometimes tries to anticipate you.





flowchart LR
    A[Ordinary choice] --> B[Choose best action against fixed conditions]
    C[Strategic choice] --> D[Choose best action while anticipating others]
    D --> E[Others are also anticipating you]
    E --> F[Equilibrium reasoning]






This is why game theory is central to economics, politics, law, criminology, psychology, and everyday social life. Prices, contracts, promises, threats, negotiations, norms, crime, trust, and communication often depend on strategic interaction.

title: Game Theory Notes
text:
How the field fits together
The diagram below gives a simple map of the main branches of game theory.





flowchart TD
    A[Game Theory] --> B[Static Games]
    A --> C[Dynamic Games]
    A --> D[Bayesian Games]
    A --> E[Repeated Games]
    A --> F[Communication Games]

    B --> B1[Normal Form]
    B --> B2[Best Responses]
    B --> B3[Nash Equilibrium]

    C --> C1[Extensive Form]
    C --> C2[Backward Induction]
    C --> C3[Subgame Perfect Equilibrium]

    D --> D1[Types]
    D --> D2[Beliefs]
    D --> D3[Bayesian Nash Equilibrium]

    E --> E1[Reputation]
    E --> E2[Punishment]
    E --> E3[Cooperation over Time]

    F --> F1[Cheap Talk]
    F --> F2[Signaling]
    F --> F3[Screening]






The point of the map is not to memorise labels. It is to see how each part of the subject changes one modelling ingredient: timing, information, repetition, or communication.

title: Game Theory Notes
text:
Basic ingredients of a game
A game normally specifies four objects:

Players: the decision-makers.
Strategies: the complete plans available to each player.
Information: what each player knows when they choose.
Payoffs: how each player ranks the possible outcomes.

A simple normal-form game can be written as
\[
G = \langle N, (S_i)_{i \in N}, (u_i)_{i \in N} \rangle,
\]
where \(N\) is the set of players, \(S_i\) is player \(i\)’s strategy set, and \(u_i\) is player \(i\)’s payoff function.
For a strategy profile \(s=(s_1,\ldots,s_n)\), player \(i\)’s payoff is written as
\[
u_i(s_i,s_{-i}),
\]
where \(s_i\) is player \(i\)’s own strategy and \(s_{-i}\) denotes the strategies chosen by everyone else.

title: Game Theory Notes
text:
The modelling workflow
A useful way to study a game is to move from primitives to solution concept in a fixed order.





flowchart TD
    A[Identify players] --> B[Specify actions or strategies]
    B --> C[Specify information]
    C --> D[Write payoffs]
    D --> E[Identify timing]
    E --> F[Choose solution concept]
    F --> G[Solve for equilibrium]
    G --> H[Interpret behaviour]
    H --> I[Check comparative statics]






This workflow prevents a common mistake: solving for an equilibrium before the game itself has been clearly defined.

title: Game Theory Notes
text:
Best responses
The most basic object in game theory is the best response. Given the strategies of others, player \(i\) chooses a strategy that maximizes their payoff:
\[
BR_i(s_{-i}) \in \arg\max_{s_i \in S_i} u_i(s_i,s_{-i}).
\]
The best response idea is simple but powerful. It says that a player’s action should be judged relative to what they believe others are doing.
For example, if a firm believes its competitor will set a low price, its best response may be to set a low price too. If it believes the competitor will set a high price, its best response may change. Strategic behaviour is therefore conditional behaviour.

title: Game Theory Notes
text:
Nash equilibrium
A Nash equilibrium is a strategy profile in which every player is choosing a best response to the strategies of the others. Formally, a strategy profile \(s^* = (s_1^*, \ldots, s_n^*)\) is a Nash equilibrium if, for every player \(i\),
\[
u_i(s_i^*, s_{-i}^*) \geq u_i(s_i, s_{-i}^*)
\quad \text{for all } s_i \in S_i.
\]
The key idea is mutual optimality: no player wants to deviate alone, taking the others’ strategies as given.
A Nash equilibrium does not necessarily mean that the outcome is socially good, fair, efficient, or morally desirable. It only means that no individual player has a unilateral incentive to change their strategy.
This distinction is important. A bad outcome can be stable if each player is individually responding optimally to the incentives they face.

title: Game Theory Notes
text:
Static games
In a static game, players choose actions without observing the current actions of others. The standard representation is the normal form, usually shown as a payoff matrix.
Static games are useful for studying:

price competition
public goods contribution
coordination problems
one-shot conflict
voting or participation decisions
inspection and enforcement problems

The main solution concept is usually Nash equilibrium.
See: Normal-form games.

title: Game Theory Notes
text:
Dynamic games
In a dynamic game, timing matters. Players move in sequence, observe earlier actions, or make plans that unfold over time.
Dynamic games introduce a new question: credibility.
A player may announce a threat or promise, but the announcement matters only if it is optimal to carry it out when the time comes. This is why dynamic games often require stronger solution concepts than ordinary Nash equilibrium.
The standard method in finite perfect-information games is backward induction: solve from the end of the game back to the beginning.





flowchart TD
    A[Look at the final decision nodes] --> B[Find the last mover's optimal action]
    B --> C[Replace the continuation with payoffs]
    C --> D[Move one step backward]
    D --> E[Find the previous player's optimal action]
    E --> F[Continue until the initial node]
    F --> G[Obtain subgame perfect equilibrium]






See: Extensive-form games and Dynamic reasoning.

title: Game Theory Notes
text:
Bayesian games
A Bayesian game introduces incomplete information. A player may not know another player’s type, payoff, cost, ability, preference, or intention.
Instead of knowing the whole game directly, players hold beliefs over possible types. These beliefs become part of strategic reasoning.
A Bayesian game usually includes:

a set of players
a set of possible types for each player
a prior belief over types
strategy sets conditional on type
payoffs that may depend on type

The central solution concept is Bayesian Nash equilibrium, where each type of each player chooses a best response given beliefs and other players’ type-contingent strategies.
See: Bayesian games, Bayesian Nash equilibrium, and Probability.

title: Game Theory Notes
text:
Repeated games
A repeated game studies what happens when the same strategic situation occurs more than once. Repetition changes incentives because current actions can affect future behaviour.
Cooperation may be sustained not because players are kind, but because deviation today can trigger punishment tomorrow.
The basic repeated-game logic is:





flowchart LR
    A[Current action] --> B[Observed by others]
    B --> C[Changes future beliefs or strategies]
    C --> D[Future reward or punishment]
    D --> E[Current incentive]






Repeated games are useful for studying:

cooperation
reputation
collusion
trust
social norms
long-term relationships
informal enforcement

See: Repeated games.

title: Game Theory Notes
text:
Communication games
Communication becomes strategic when one player has information and another player must decide whether to believe, ignore, or interpret the message.
There are several important cases:







Type
Main idea




Cheap talk
Messages are costless and non-binding


Signaling
Messages or actions may be costly and informative


Screening
The uninformed side designs choices to reveal information


Mechanism design
The designer structures incentives to elicit behaviour or information



A central question is whether information can be transmitted when players’ interests are not perfectly aligned.
See: Cheap talk, Signaling, and Screening & mechanism design.

title: Game Theory Notes
text:
Equilibrium concepts
Different games require different equilibrium concepts. The choice of equilibrium concept depends on what the model needs to discipline.








Situation
Typical solution concept
What it disciplines




Simultaneous choice
Nash equilibrium
Mutual best responses


Sequential choice
Subgame perfect equilibrium
Credibility and sequential rationality


Incomplete information
Bayesian Nash equilibrium
Type-contingent optimality


Dynamic incomplete information
Perfect Bayesian / sequential equilibrium
Beliefs and sequential rationality


Robustness to small mistakes
Trembling-hand perfect equilibrium
Stability under perturbations


Correlated recommendations
Correlated equilibrium
Obedience to signals


Strategic reasoning without equilibrium
Rationalizability
Survival of best-response reasoning



See: Equilibrium concepts.

title: Game Theory Notes
text:
Efficiency and welfare
Equilibrium analysis is not the same as welfare analysis. A game may have an equilibrium that is inefficient.
A classic example is the prisoners’ dilemma. Each player has an individual incentive to defect, but mutual defection makes both players worse off than mutual cooperation.
This creates one of the central themes of game theory:

individually rational behaviour can produce collectively undesirable outcomes.

The tension between private incentives and collective welfare appears in public goods problems, arms races, price wars, overuse of common resources, and many forms of institutional failure.

title: Game Theory Notes
text:
Common modelling mistakes

1. Confusing actions and strategies
An action is a move at one decision point. A strategy is a complete plan. In dynamic games, a strategy must say what the player would do at every relevant information set, even after histories that do not occur in equilibrium.


2. Solving before defining the game
Before solving, specify players, strategies, information, timing, and payoffs. Many errors come from unclear primitives.


3. Treating equilibrium as moral approval
An equilibrium is a stability concept, not a claim that the outcome is good.


4. Ignoring off-path behaviour
In dynamic games, what players would do after unreached histories can affect whether threats and promises are credible.


5. Forgetting beliefs
In Bayesian and signaling games, actions cannot be understood without beliefs. What matters is not only what is true, but what players infer from what they observe.

title: Game Theory Notes
text:
How to read these notes
A good reading order is:

Start with Optimization, especially argmax and best responses.
Read Probability, especially belief updating.
Read Normal-form games.
Read Nash equilibrium.
Move to Extensive-form games and Subgame perfect equilibrium.
Then read Bayesian games, Repeated games, and Cheap talk.

title: Screening and Mechanism Design
text:
Screening and mechanism design study how an uninformed party can structure choices, contracts, rules, or menus to induce informed parties to reveal information or choose desirable actions.
In signaling, the informed side moves to reveal information.
In screening, the uninformed side designs the environment.

title: Screening and Mechanism Design
text:
Basic idea
Screening begins with private information.
The uninformed side cannot directly observe type, so it offers a menu of choices. Different types may self-select into different options.





flowchart LR
    A[Private types] --> B[Designer offers menu]
    B --> C[Types choose options]
    C --> D[Choices reveal information]
    D --> E[Allocation or contract]






The menu works only if each type prefers the option intended for that type.

title: Screening and Mechanism Design
text:
Screening versus signaling








Feature
Signaling
Screening




Who has private information?
sender / informed agent
agent / informed side


Who moves to reveal information?
informed side
uninformed designer creates menu


Main object
signal
menu or mechanism


Key condition
incentive-compatible signaling
self-selection



Examples:

signaling: worker chooses education to reveal ability;
screening: employer offers contracts to separate worker types.

title: Screening and Mechanism Design
text:
Types and menus
Suppose there are two types:
\[
\theta \in \{H,L\}.
\]
The designer offers a menu:
\[
(x_H,t_H), (x_L,t_L).
\]
Each type chooses one option.
A separating menu induces:
\[
H \text{ chooses } (x_H,t_H),
\]
and
\[
L \text{ chooses } (x_L,t_L).
\]

title: Screening and Mechanism Design
text:
Incentive compatibility
Incentive compatibility means each type prefers the option designed for that type.
For type \(H\):
\[
U_H(x_H,t_H) \geq U_H(x_L,t_L).
\]
For type \(L\):
\[
U_L(x_L,t_L) \geq U_L(x_H,t_H).
\]
These are self-selection constraints.





flowchart TD
    A[Menu offered] --> B[High type compares options]
    A --> C[Low type compares options]
    B --> D{High chooses high option?}
    C --> E{Low chooses low option?}
    D --> F[Incentive compatibility]
    E --> F

title: Screening and Mechanism Design
text:
Participation constraints
Participation constraints ensure each type prefers participating to opting out.
For type \(\theta\):
\[
U_\theta(\text{assigned option}) \geq \bar U_\theta.
\]
Here \(\bar U_\theta\) is the outside option.
A contract may separate types but still fail if some type refuses to participate.

title: Screening and Mechanism Design
Screening and Mechanism Design
text:
Insurance screening example
An insurer may not know whether a customer is high-risk or low-risk.
It can offer a menu:

high premium, full coverage;
low premium, partial coverage.

Different risk types may select different contracts.





flowchart LR
    A[Insurer offers contract menu] --> B[High-risk customer]
    A --> C[Low-risk customer]
    B --> D[Chooses more coverage]
    C --> E[Chooses less coverage]
    D --> F[Information revealed by choice]
    E --> F






The menu screens types through self-selection.

title: Screening and Mechanism Design
text:
Mechanism design
Mechanism design asks a broader question:

How should rules be designed so that self-interested agents produce a desired outcome?

A mechanism specifies:

messages or reports agents can send;
how reports determine allocations;
how transfers or payoffs are assigned.






flowchart TD
    A[Designer objective] --> B[Choose mechanism]
    B --> C[Agents report or choose]
    C --> D[Outcome rule]
    D --> E[Incentives determine behaviour]
    E --> F[Implemented outcome]






Mechanism design is sometimes called reverse game theory because we start with the desired outcome and design the game.

title: Screening and Mechanism Design
text:
Revelation principle
The revelation principle says, roughly:

if an outcome can be implemented by some mechanism, it can often be implemented by a direct mechanism where agents truthfully report their types.

This does not mean people are naturally truthful. It means the mechanism can be designed so that truth-telling is incentive compatible.
A direct mechanism asks agents to report types:
\[
\hat\theta_i.
\]
Truthful reporting requires:
\[
\theta_i \text{ reports } \theta_i
\]
to be optimal.

title: Screening and Mechanism Design
text:
Incentive compatibility in direct mechanisms
A direct mechanism is incentive compatible if every type prefers truthful reporting.
For type \(\theta\):
\[
U_\theta(\text{outcome after reporting } \theta)
\geq
U_\theta(\text{outcome after reporting } \hat\theta)
\]
for all possible misreports \(\hat\theta\).
This is the same self-selection idea expressed through reports.

title: Screening and Mechanism Design
text:
Applications
Screening and mechanism design appear in:



Domain
Example




insurance
separating high-risk and low-risk customers


labour
contracts for different ability or effort types


regulation
inducing firms to reveal costs


auctions
allocating goods to high-valuation bidders


public goods
eliciting willingness to pay


taxation
designing incentives under private income or effort


criminal justice
plea bargains under private evidence or risk


platforms
rules that induce reporting or moderation

title: Screening and Mechanism Design
Screening and Mechanism Design
text:
Common mistakes

1. Confusing screening with signaling
Screening is designed by the uninformed side. Signaling is chosen by the informed side.


2. Forgetting participation constraints
A menu must be acceptable, not only separating.


3. Ignoring incentive compatibility
A proposed menu fails if types want to imitate each other.


4. Assuming truth-telling without mechanism design
Truthful reporting must be made optimal.


5. Treating the revelation principle as behavioural honesty
The revelation principle is a design result, not a psychological claim.

title: Screening and Mechanism Design
text:
Checklist
When analysing screening or mechanism design, ask:

Who has private information?
Who designs the menu or mechanism?
What are the possible types?
What options are offered?
What is each type supposed to choose?
Are incentive compatibility constraints satisfied?
Are participation constraints satisfied?
What outcome does the designer want?
Can truthful reporting be made optimal?
What information is revealed by choices?

title: Cheap Talk
text:
Cheap talk is communication that is costless, non-binding, and directly payoff-irrelevant. A sender sends a message, and a receiver chooses an action after hearing it.
The central question is:
Cheap talk is important because many real interactions involve advice, promises, claims, warnings, recommendations, excuses, and persuasion without formal commitment.

title: Cheap Talk
text:
Basic structure
A cheap-talk game usually has three stages:

Nature determines the sender’s private information.
The sender sends a costless message.
The receiver observes the message and chooses an action.






flowchart LR
    A[Nature chooses state or type] --> B[Sender observes information]
    B --> C[Sender sends costless message]
    C --> D[Receiver observes message]
    D --> E[Receiver chooses action]
    E --> F[Payoffs realized]






The message has no direct payoff effect. It matters only if it changes the receiver’s belief and action.

title: Cheap Talk
text:
Why cheap talk is puzzling
If messages are free, why would anyone believe them?
A sender may want to manipulate the receiver. If the receiver knows this, the receiver may ignore the message. If messages are ignored, communication becomes uninformative.
This creates the basic cheap-talk tension:





flowchart LR
    A[Sender has private information] --> B[Sender may benefit from influencing receiver]
    B --> C[Receiver anticipates bias]
    C --> D[Receiver may discount or ignore message]
    D --> E[Communication may collapse]






Cheap talk is therefore not automatically informative.

title: Cheap Talk
Cheap Talk
text:
Messages
Messages are often written as:
\[
m \in M.
\]
A sender’s strategy maps information into messages.
If the sender observes state \(\theta\), a messaging strategy is:
\[
\sigma_S(\theta) \in M.
\]
The receiver’s strategy maps messages into actions:
\[
\sigma_R(m) \in A.
\]
A cheap-talk equilibrium specifies both a sender messaging rule and a receiver response rule.

title: Cheap Talk
text:
Beliefs
After hearing message \(m\), the receiver forms a belief about the state:
\[
\mu(\theta \mid m).
\]
If message \(m\) is sent with positive probability in equilibrium, beliefs are updated using Bayes’ rule:
\[
\mu(\theta \mid m)
=
\frac{
\Pr(m\mid \theta)\Pr(\theta)
}{
\sum_{\theta'}\Pr(m\mid \theta')\Pr(\theta')
}.
\]
The receiver then chooses an action that maximizes expected payoff given this posterior belief.





flowchart LR
    A[Message] --> B[Receiver posterior belief]
    B --> C[Expected payoff from each action]
    C --> D[Receiver best response]

title: Cheap Talk
text:
Informative and uninformative communication
Cheap talk may be:



Type
Meaning




Fully revealing
different states induce different messages


Partially revealing
messages reveal coarse information


Babbling
messages reveal no information


Pooling
multiple types send the same message


Separating
different types send different messages



A babbling equilibrium always exists in many cheap-talk games: the sender’s message is ignored, so the sender has no reason to choose one message over another.

title: Cheap Talk
text:
Babbling equilibrium
In a babbling equilibrium:

all types of sender send messages that do not affect beliefs;
the receiver ignores the message;
the receiver chooses the action optimal under the prior.






flowchart LR
    A[Sender sends message] --> B[Receiver ignores message]
    B --> C[Receiver uses prior belief]
    C --> D[Receiver chooses prior-optimal action]






Babbling is uninformative communication. It is strategically stable because messages do not change the receiver’s action.

title: Cheap Talk
section: When can cheap talk be informative?
text:
When can cheap talk be informative?
Cheap talk can be informative when sender and receiver interests are sufficiently aligned.
If the sender benefits when the receiver chooses an action close to the truth, then the sender may have an incentive to communicate honestly or partially honestly.
If the sender always wants the receiver to choose a higher action than the receiver would prefer, full truth-telling may fail, but coarse communication may still be possible.





flowchart TD
    A[Preference alignment] --> B{High enough?}
    B -->|Yes| C[Informative communication possible]
    B -->|No| D[Babbling or very coarse communication]






The degree of conflict shapes how much information can be transmitted.

title: Cheap Talk
text:
Bias
A common cheap-talk model has a sender who is biased relative to the receiver.
For example, the receiver wants to choose action \(a\) close to state \(\theta\):
\[
u_R(a,\theta)=-(a-\theta)^2.
\]
The sender wants the receiver’s action to be shifted upward by bias \(b\):
\[
u_S(a,\theta)=-(a-(\theta+b))^2.
\]
If \(b=0\), preferences are aligned.
If \(b>0\), the sender wants a higher action than the receiver would choose under full information.
The larger the bias, the harder informative communication becomes.

title: Cheap Talk
text:
Partition equilibria
In some cheap-talk games, equilibrium communication partitions the state space.
The sender does not reveal the exact state. Instead, the sender sends a message indicating that the state lies in a range.





flowchart LR
    A[Low states] --> D[Message 1]
    B[Middle states] --> E[Message 2]
    C[High states] --> F[Message 3]
    D --> G[Receiver chooses action for interval]
    E --> H[Receiver chooses action for interval]
    F --> I[Receiver chooses action for interval]






This is partial information transmission.

title: Cheap Talk
Cheap Talk
text:
Cheap talk versus signaling
Cheap talk differs from signaling.








Feature
Cheap talk
Signaling




Message/action cost
costless
often costly


Direct payoff effect
none
may affect payoffs directly


Information source
strategic message
costly action or signal


Credibility
from incentives and equilibrium
often from differential costs



Cheap talk can be credible only through aligned incentives or equilibrium structure. Signaling can be credible because different types face different costs or benefits from sending signals.

title: Cheap Talk
text:
Common mistakes

1. Assuming costless messages are always meaningless
Cheap talk can be informative when incentives are sufficiently aligned.


2. Assuming messages are automatically truthful
Cheap talk requires incentive compatibility. Truthful messages must be optimal for the sender.


3. Ignoring receiver beliefs
Messages matter only through beliefs and receiver actions.


4. Confusing babbling with no communication
Babbling may involve messages, but messages carry no information.


5. Treating off-path beliefs as irrelevant
Unexpected messages may affect whether a proposed equilibrium is plausible.

title: Cheap Talk
text:
Checklist
When analysing a cheap-talk game, ask:

What does the sender know?
What does the receiver need to decide?
What messages are available?
Are messages costly or binding?
What are the sender’s preferences?
What are the receiver’s preferences?
Are preferences aligned or biased?
How does each message change beliefs?
What is the receiver’s best response to each belief?
Is the sender willing to send the proposed message?

title: Signaling
text:
Signaling games study situations where an informed sender takes an action that may reveal private information to an uninformed receiver.
Unlike cheap talk, a signal often has a cost or direct payoff consequence. This cost can make the signal credible when different types face different costs or benefits.

title: Signaling
text:
Basic structure
A signaling game usually has this timing:

Nature chooses the sender’s type.
The sender observes their own type.
The sender chooses a signal.
The receiver observes the signal.
The receiver forms a belief and chooses an action.
Payoffs are realized.






flowchart LR
    A[Nature chooses type] --> B[Sender observes type]
    B --> C[Sender chooses signal]
    C --> D[Receiver observes signal]
    D --> E[Receiver updates belief]
    E --> F[Receiver chooses action]
    F --> G[Payoffs realized]






Signaling is dynamic and involves incomplete information, so it usually requires belief-based equilibrium concepts such as perfect Bayesian equilibrium.

title: Signaling
Signaling
text:
Types and signals
Let the sender’s type be:
\[
\theta \in \Theta.
\]
Let the sender choose signal:
\[
s \in S.
\]
The receiver observes \(s\) but not \(\theta\).
The receiver forms belief:
\[
\mu(\theta \mid s).
\]
Then the receiver chooses action:
\[
a \in A.
\]
A signaling equilibrium specifies:

sender signal choices for each type;
receiver beliefs after each signal;
receiver actions after each signal.

title: Signaling
text:
Separating equilibrium
In a separating equilibrium, different types choose different signals.





flowchart TD
    A[High type] --> B[Signal H]
    C[Low type] --> D[Signal L]
    B --> E[Receiver believes high type]
    D --> F[Receiver believes low type]






Separating equilibria transmit information. The receiver can infer the sender’s type from the observed signal.

title: Signaling
text:
Pooling equilibrium
In a pooling equilibrium, different types choose the same signal.





flowchart TD
    A[High type] --> C[Same signal]
    B[Low type] --> C
    C --> D[Receiver cannot distinguish types]
    D --> E[Receiver uses pooled belief]






Pooling equilibria transmit less information. The receiver’s belief after the pooled signal is based on the prior or equilibrium mixture.

title: Signaling
text:
Semi-separating equilibrium
In a semi-separating equilibrium, at least one type randomizes, or the signal only partly reveals type.





flowchart LR
    A[Types] --> B[Signals partly overlap]
    B --> C[Receiver updates beliefs partially]
    C --> D[Receiver response depends on posterior]






Semi-separating equilibria are common when incentives are close or when full separation is too costly.

title: Signaling
text:
Costly signals
A signal can be credible when it is less costly for one type than another.
For example, suppose education is easier for high-ability workers than low-ability workers. Then high education may signal high ability if low-ability workers find it too costly to imitate.
The logic is:





flowchart TD
    A[High type] --> B[Low cost of signal]
    C[Low type] --> D[High cost of signal]
    B --> E[High type sends signal]
    D --> F[Low type does not imitate]
    E --> G[Signal becomes credible]






This is the single-crossing intuition.

title: Signaling
text:
Incentive compatibility
A separating equilibrium requires incentive compatibility.
Each type must prefer the signal assigned to that type over imitating another type.
For high type \(H\) and low type \(L\), a separating equilibrium may require:
\[
U_H(s_H,a_H) \geq U_H(s_L,a_L),
\]
and
\[
U_L(s_L,a_L) \geq U_L(s_H,a_H).
\]
The first condition says the high type does not want to mimic the low type.
The second says the low type does not want to mimic the high type.

title: Signaling
text:
Receiver beliefs
Receiver beliefs must be consistent with observed signals on the equilibrium path.
If signal \(s_H\) is sent only by high type in equilibrium, then:
\[
\mu(H\mid s_H)=1.
\]
If signal \(s_L\) is sent only by low type, then:
\[
\mu(L\mid s_L)=1.
\]
If both types send the same signal, the receiver’s posterior is the prior conditional on pooling.
Off-path beliefs are more delicate and can affect equilibrium plausibility.

title: Signaling
Signaling
text:
Signaling versus human capital
Education can be interpreted in two ways.



Interpretation
Main idea




Human capital
education increases productivity


Signaling
education reveals productivity or ability



Real education may do both. The model separates the mechanisms.

title: Signaling
text:
Signaling and social behaviour
Signaling is not only economic.
Examples:








Domain
Signal
Possible type being inferred




politics
costly commitment
ideological seriousness


crime
retaliation
toughness or willingness to punish


organizations
compliance programme
responsibility or legal caution


relationships
apology
remorse or sincerity


markets
warranty
product quality


academia
credential
ability or training



The key question is always whether the signal is incentive-compatible.

title: Signaling
text:
Cheap talk versus signaling








Feature
Cheap talk
Signaling




Cost
costless
often costly


Direct payoff effect
none
may directly affect payoff


Credibility source
preference alignment
differential cost or incentive


Main issue
can messages be informative?
can actions reveal type?



Cheap talk can reveal information without cost if preferences are aligned. Signaling can reveal information even with conflict if imitation is too costly.

title: Signaling
text:
Common mistakes

1. Treating every observable action as a signal
An action is a signal only if it changes beliefs about hidden information.


2. Ignoring signal cost
If imitation is costless, separation may fail.


3. Forgetting receiver beliefs
The receiver’s action depends on posterior beliefs.


4. Assuming separating equilibrium always exists
Separation requires incentive compatibility.


5. Confusing signaling with productivity
A signal may reveal ability without causing ability.


6. Ignoring off-path beliefs
Unexpected signals can support or undermine equilibria.

title: Signaling
text:
Checklist
When analysing a signaling game, ask:

What is the sender’s private type?
What signal can the sender choose?
Does the signal have a cost?
Does the cost differ by type?
What does the receiver observe?
What beliefs does the receiver form?
What action does the receiver choose?
Is the proposed equilibrium separating, pooling, or semi-separating?
Are incentive compatibility conditions satisfied?
Are off-path beliefs reasonable?

title: Evolutionary games & learning
text: Evolutionary game theory studies strategy change over time via selection, imitation, or learning. Instead of fully rational choice each period, strategy shares evolve.

title: Evolutionary games & learning
text: Evolutionary game theory studies strategy change over time via selection, imitation, or learning. Instead of fully rational choice each period, strategy shares evolve.

title: Evolutionary games & learning
text:
What’s special

Focus shifts from equilibrium as a static concept to stability under dynamics.
Key objects: ESS (evolutionarily stable strategy), replicator dynamics, learning rules.
Useful when players are boundedly rational or populations adapt.

title: Evolutionary games & learning
text:
One example (replicator dynamics, 2 strategies)
Let the population share using strategy 1 be \(x\in[0,1]\). If payoffs are \(\pi_1(x)\) and \(\pi_2(x)\), replicator dynamics are:
\[
\dot{x} = x(1-x)\bigl(\pi_1(x)-\pi_2(x)\bigr).
\]
Intuition: the share of a strategy grows when it performs better than the alternative. Fixed points correspond to states where neither strategy has a payoff advantage.

title: Evolutionary games & learning
text:
Story
In a large community, newcomers copy behaviors that seem to “work.” Strategies that perform better spread. Nobody solves the game explicitly, yet population patterns evolve.

title: Evolutionary games & learning
text:
Model

Strategies are held by a population
Relative payoff determines growth
Dynamics describe how shares change

title: Evolutionary games & learning
text:
Dynamics (replicator)
Let \(x\) be the share playing strategy 1, payoffs \(\pi_1(x)\) and \(\pi_2(x)\): \[
\dot{x}=x(1-x)\bigl(\pi_1(x)-\pi_2(x)\bigr).
\]

title: Evolutionary games & learning
text:
Equilibrium / stability (what to look for)

Rest points satisfy \(\dot{x}=0\) (often \(x=0\), \(x=1\), or where \(\pi_1(x)=\pi_2(x)\)).
Stability depends on whether nearby deviations push \(x\) back or away.

title: Evolutionary games & learning
text:
Later-on analysis

ESS: a refinement capturing robustness to mutant invasions.
Learning rules: fictitious play, reinforcement learning, best-response dynamics.
Link to Nash: some dynamics converge to Nash in certain classes of games, but not always.

title: Global games / equilibrium selection
text: Global games study equilibrium selection in coordination games by adding small private noise to information about fundamentals.

title: Global games / equilibrium selection
text: Global games study equilibrium selection in coordination games by adding small private noise to information about fundamentals.

title: Global games / equilibrium selection
text:
What’s special

Many coordination games have multiple equilibria (good/bad outcomes).
Tiny informational frictions can select a unique equilibrium.
Provides a disciplined way to talk about “which equilibrium happens” without arbitrary refinements.

title: Global games / equilibrium selection
text:
One example (currency-attack intuition)
A government defends a peg if fundamentals are strong; speculators attack if they expect others to attack.
Each speculator observes a noisy signal of the fundamental. If signals are slightly noisy, an equilibrium often takes a threshold form: attack if your signal is below a cutoff. The cutoff is pinned down endogenously, yielding a unique prediction.

title: Global games / equilibrium selection
text:
Story
A bank can survive if depositors stay calm, but fails if too many withdraw. Everyone hears rumors, each slightly noisy. If you expect others to run, running is rational; if you expect calm, staying is rational. Multiple equilibria appear.
Global games add tiny private noise and often recover a single “threshold” prediction.

title: Global games / equilibrium selection
text:
Model

Fundamental \(\theta\) (bank strength)
Private signal: \(x_i=\theta+\varepsilon_i\)
Action: withdraw or stay
Payoffs depend on the fraction withdrawing

title: Global games / equilibrium selection
text:
Equilibrium (threshold form, idea)
A typical global-games prediction is: - withdraw iff \(x_i \le x^*\)
The cutoff \(x^*\) solves an indifference condition at which a depositor is just willing to withdraw.

title: Global games / equilibrium selection
text:
Later-on analysis

Selection: small noise breaks multiplicity and selects one equilibrium.
Policy: transparency and information disclosure can move the cutoff.
Related models: currency attacks, coordination failures, debt rollovers.

title: Extensive-form Games
text:
Extensive-form games represent strategic interaction over time. They show who moves when, what each player observes, what actions are available, and what payoffs follow from each possible path.
The extensive form is especially useful for studying sequential decisions, credibility, threats, promises, commitment, entry deterrence, bargaining, signalling, and institutional processes.

title: Extensive-form Games
text:
Why extensive form matters
A normal-form game lists strategies and payoffs. An extensive-form game shows the structure of play.





flowchart LR
    A[Normal form] --> B[Strategies and payoffs]
    C[Extensive form] --> D[Timing]
    C --> E[Observation]
    C --> F[Histories]
    C --> G[Credibility]






This matters because timing can change the strategic result. If one player moves first and another responds, the second player’s credible response shapes the first player’s decision.

title: Extensive-form Games
text:
Basic components
An extensive-form game usually includes:



Component
Meaning




Players
who makes decisions


Nodes
points where a decision or event occurs


Root
the initial node


Branches
available actions


Terminal nodes
endpoints of the game


Payoffs
outcomes assigned at terminal nodes


Information sets
what a player can distinguish when choosing


Strategies
complete plans for every possible decision point



The game tree is the visual representation of these objects.

title: Extensive-form Games
text:
A simple game tree





flowchart TD
    A[Player 1] -->|Enter| B[Player 2]
    A -->|Stay Out| C[Payoffs: 0,2]
    B -->|Fight| D[Payoffs: -1,-1]
    B -->|Accommodate| E[Payoffs: 2,1]






This tree says:

Player 1 chooses whether to enter.
If Player 1 stays out, the game ends.
If Player 1 enters, Player 2 chooses whether to fight or accommodate.
Payoffs are assigned at the terminal nodes.

title: Extensive-form Games
text:
Histories
A history is a sequence of actions that has occurred so far.
In the entry game above, after Player 1 chooses Enter, the history is:
\[
h = \text{Enter}.
\]
After Player 1 chooses Stay Out, the game ends.
Histories matter because strategies in dynamic games are contingent plans. A player may choose different actions after different histories.

title: Extensive-form Games
text:
Strategies in extensive-form games
A strategy is not just one action. It is a complete plan.
If Player 2 moves only after entry, then Player 2’s strategy must specify what to do after entry:
\[
s_2(\text{Enter}) \in \{\text{Fight},\text{Accommodate}\}.
\]
In more complex games, a strategy must specify what the player would do at every information set where they may be called to move.
This is one of the most common sources of confusion in dynamic games.





flowchart TD
    A[Dynamic strategy] --> B[Action after history 1]
    A --> C[Action after history 2]
    A --> D[Action after history 3]
    B --> E[Complete contingent plan]
    C --> E
    D --> E

title: Extensive-form Games
text:
Perfect information
A game has perfect information if every player observes all previous actions before choosing.
Chess is a classic example. Each player observes the whole history of moves.
In perfect-information games, decision nodes are not grouped into non-trivial information sets. Players know exactly where they are in the tree.

title: Extensive-form Games
text:
Imperfect information
A game has imperfect information if a player does not know exactly which node they are at when choosing.
This is represented by an information set.
For example, if Player 2 cannot observe whether Player 1 chose \(A\) or \(B\), then Player 2’s two decision nodes are in the same information set.





flowchart TD
    A[Player 1] -->|A| B[Player 2 node 1]
    A -->|B| C[Player 2 node 2]
    B -. same information set .- C
    B -->|L| D[Outcome]
    B -->|R| E[Outcome]
    C -->|L| F[Outcome]
    C -->|R| G[Outcome]






The dotted connection means Player 2 cannot distinguish the two nodes.

title: Extensive-form Games
text:
Backward induction
In finite games with perfect information, backward induction solves the game from the end to the beginning.





flowchart TD
    A[Start at final decision nodes] --> B[Choose last mover's optimal action]
    B --> C[Replace continuation with payoff]
    C --> D[Move one step backward]
    D --> E[Choose previous player's optimal action]
    E --> F[Repeat until root]
    F --> G[Predicted path]






Backward induction is the natural method for extensive-form games because earlier players anticipate later rational behaviour.

title: Extensive-form Games
text:
Credible threats
A threat is credible only if the player would actually want to carry it out when the time comes.
In the entry game, suppose Player 2 threatens to fight if Player 1 enters. If fighting gives Player 2 a lower payoff than accommodating after entry, then the threat is not credible.





flowchart LR
    A[Threat announced] --> B{Optimal later?}
    B -->|Yes| C[Credible threat]
    B -->|No| D[Non-credible threat]
    D --> E[Should not deter in SPE]






This is why Nash equilibrium alone may be too weak for dynamic games.

title: Extensive-form Games
text:
Subgames
A subgame is a part of the game that begins at a decision node and contains all future actions from that node onward.
A subgame must not cut across an information set.
Subgames matter because a dynamic equilibrium should prescribe optimal behaviour after every possible history.





flowchart TD
    A[Whole game] --> B[Subgame after history 1]
    A --> C[Subgame after history 2]
    B --> D[Continuation equilibrium]
    C --> E[Continuation equilibrium]






This leads to subgame perfect equilibrium.

title: Extensive-form Games
text:
Normal form versus extensive form
Every finite extensive-form game can be represented in normal form by listing each player’s complete strategies.
However, this conversion often hides timing.








Representation
Strength
Limitation




Extensive form
shows timing and information
can be visually large


Normal form
shows all strategy profiles and payoffs
hides credibility and sequence



For dynamic games, extensive form is usually better for reasoning.

title: Extensive-form Games
text:
Example: entry deterrence
Suppose an entrant decides whether to enter a market. If it enters, the incumbent chooses whether to fight or accommodate.





flowchart TD
    A[Entrant] -->|Stay Out| B[0,2]
    A -->|Enter| C[Incumbent]
    C -->|Fight| D[-1,-1]
    C -->|Accommodate| E[2,1]






Solve by backward induction:

If entry occurs, the incumbent compares Fight and Accommodate.
The incumbent prefers Accommodate because \(1>-1\).
The entrant anticipates Accommodate.
The entrant compares Enter, giving \(2\), with Stay Out, giving \(0\).
The entrant enters.

The subgame perfect outcome is:
\[
(\text{Enter}, \text{Accommodate}).
\]

title: Extensive-form Games
text:
Dynamic games with chance
Some extensive-form games include nature. Nature represents random events.
For example, nature may choose a player’s type before the player acts.





flowchart TD
    A[Nature] -->|High type| B[Sender H]
    A -->|Low type| C[Sender L]
    B --> D[Message]
    C --> E[Message]
    D --> F[Receiver response]
    E --> F






This structure appears in signaling games and Bayesian extensive-form games.

title: Extensive-form Games
text:
Strategies and off-path behaviour
In an extensive-form game, a strategy must specify what to do even after histories that do not occur in equilibrium.
These histories are called off-path.
Off-path behaviour matters because it can support or undermine threats and promises.
For example, if entry does not occur in equilibrium, the incumbent’s planned response after entry is still part of the strategy.

title: Extensive-form Games
text:
Common mistakes

1. Solving from the root first
For finite perfect-information games, solve from the end backward.


2. Confusing action and strategy
A strategy is a complete plan, not just the action taken on the equilibrium path.


3. Ignoring off-path actions
Dynamic equilibrium requires behaviour after possible histories, even if they are not reached.


4. Treating all Nash equilibria as credible
Some Nash equilibria rely on non-credible threats.


5. Cutting across information sets
A subgame cannot begin inside an information set.

title: Extensive-form Games
text:
Checklist
When analysing an extensive-form game, ask:

Who moves first?
Who moves later?
What does each player observe?
What are the histories?
What are the terminal payoffs?
What are each player’s strategies?
Are there information sets?
Are there proper subgames?
What does backward induction predict?
Are threats and promises credible?

title: Bargaining
text: Bargaining models how parties negotiate over surplus (price, wage, division of a pie), often with disagreement or delay.

title: Bargaining
text: Bargaining models how parties negotiate over surplus (price, wage, division of a pie), often with disagreement or delay.

title: Bargaining
text:
What’s special

Timing and outside options shape outcomes.
With discounting, delay is costly → early agreement is attractive.
Incomplete information introduces screening and strategic delay.

title: Bargaining
text:
One example (alternating-offers, intuition)
Two players bargain over splitting 1. In each round, one proposes a split; the other accepts or rejects. If rejected, bargaining continues next round with discount factor \(\delta\).
Backward induction in the infinite-horizon model yields immediate agreement: the proposer offers the responder just enough to make them indifferent between accepting now vs rejecting and waiting. More patient players (higher \(\delta\)) obtain better terms.

title: Bargaining
text:
Story
Two coauthors must decide authorship order before tomorrow’s submission deadline. Delay is costly: missing the deadline reduces the paper’s impact. One proposes a split; the other can accept or reject. If rejected, the other proposes next round.

title: Bargaining
text:
Model

Pie size: 1
Alternating offers
Common discount factor: \(\delta\in(0,1)\)
Solution concept: subgame perfect equilibrium

title: Bargaining
text:
Equilibrium (Rubinstein alternating offers, symmetric discounting)
In the infinite-horizon alternating-offers model with the same discount factor \(\delta\) for both players, the unique SPE split is:

First proposer receives: \[
\frac{1}{1+\delta}
\]
Responder receives: \[
\frac{\delta}{1+\delta}.
\]

Intuition: rejecting means you become proposer next round, but you discount the future by \(\delta\).

title: Bargaining
text:
Later-on analysis

Asymmetric patience: if one player has higher \(\delta\), they get a larger share.
Outside options: disagreement payoffs shift the split.
Incomplete information: can generate delay, signaling, and “toughness” reputations.

title: Correlated equilibrium
text:
A correlated equilibrium (CE) allows players to condition their actions on a shared signal (a recommendation from a mediator). The signal can correlate players’ actions.
A distribution over action profiles is a CE if, when a player receives a recommendation, they have no incentive to deviate given they believe others follow their recommendations.

title: Correlated equilibrium
text:
A correlated equilibrium (CE) allows players to condition their actions on a shared signal (a recommendation from a mediator). The signal can correlate players’ actions.
A distribution over action profiles is a CE if, when a player receives a recommendation, they have no incentive to deviate given they believe others follow their recommendations.

title: Correlated equilibrium
text:
Where it shows up

Normal-form games
Information and mediation (recommendation systems)
Mechanism design / persuasion / traffic routing interpretations
Computational game theory (CE is often easier to compute than NE)

title: Correlated equilibrium
text:
How to solve (recipe)

Choose a distribution over action profiles (a “correlation device”).
For each player and each recommended action, write the no-deviation (obedience) constraints:

expected payoff from following ≥ expected payoff from deviating.

If all obedience constraints hold, the distribution is a correlated equilibrium.

title: Correlated equilibrium
section: Solved example (a simple CE that improves outcomes)
text:
Solved example (a simple CE that improves outcomes)

Problem (context + question)
Two drivers choose routes: \(A\) or \(B\). If both choose the same route, there is congestion and each gets 0. If they choose different routes, each gets 1.
Payoffs: - If actions differ: payoff 1 each - If same: payoff 0 each
Question: Construct a correlated equilibrium that achieves expected payoff 1 for each driver.


Solution
Consider a mediator who flips a fair coin and privately recommends: - with probability 1/2: recommend (Driver 1: A, Driver 2: B) - with probability 1/2: recommend (Driver 1: B, Driver 2: A)
So the induced distribution puts probability 1/2 on (A,B) and 1/2 on (B,A).
Step 1: Check obedience for Driver 1 - If Driver 1 is told “A”, they infer Driver 2 was told “B”, so following yields payoff 1. Deviating to “B” would match Driver 2 and yield 0. - If Driver 1 is told “B”, symmetric: follow yields 1; deviating yields 0.
So Driver 1 never wants to deviate. Same for Driver 2.
Result: This recommendation device is a correlated equilibrium with payoff 1 for each.


Takeaway
CE allows coordination using signals, often improving welfare relative to uncoordinated play.

title: Correlated equilibrium
text:
Later-on analysis

Every Nash equilibrium induces a correlated equilibrium (as a special case), but CE can be larger.
CE is closely related to “obedience constraints” in mechanism design.
If you ever do computation: CE can be found via linear programming in finite games.

title: Equilibrium Concepts
text:
Equilibrium concepts describe what it means for behaviour to be stable in a strategic setting. Different games require different notions of stability: simultaneous games need mutual best responses; dynamic games need credible continuation behaviour; incomplete-information games need beliefs; and communication games need consistency between messages, beliefs, and incentives.
The purpose of this page is to give a map of the main equilibrium concepts used across the notes.

title: Equilibrium Concepts
text:
The basic question
Every equilibrium concept answers some version of the same question:

Given what everyone else is doing, believing, or expecting, does each player have a reason to change their behaviour?

The details depend on the model. In a static game, the issue is whether anyone wants to deviate from their chosen action. In a dynamic game, we also ask whether future threats and promises are credible. In a Bayesian game, we ask whether each type of each player is acting optimally given beliefs.

title: Equilibrium Concepts
text:
A map of equilibrium concepts





flowchart TD
    A[Equilibrium Concepts] --> B[Nash Equilibrium]
    A --> C[Bayesian Nash Equilibrium]
    A --> D[Subgame Perfect Equilibrium]
    A --> E[Dynamic Incomplete Information]
    A --> F[Refinements]
    A --> G[Alternative Notions]

    B --> B1[Mutual best responses]

    C --> C1[Types]
    C --> C2[Beliefs over types]

    D --> D1[Sequential rationality]
    D --> D2[Credible threats]

    E --> E1[Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium]
    E --> E2[Sequential Equilibrium]

    F --> F1[Trembling-hand Perfect]
    F --> F2[Proper Equilibrium]

    G --> G1[Correlated Equilibrium]
    G --> G2[Rationalizability]
    G --> G3[Babbling Equilibrium]






The map is not a strict hierarchy. Some concepts are designed for different kinds of games, while others are refinements that rule out implausible equilibria.

title: Equilibrium Concepts
text:
Core equilibrium concepts



Nash Equilibrium
The basic equilibrium concept for strategic interaction. Each player chooses a best response to the strategies of the others.
Open →




Subgame Perfect Equilibrium
A refinement of Nash equilibrium for dynamic games. It requires optimal behaviour after every possible history.
Open →




Bayesian Nash Equilibrium
The basic equilibrium concept for games with incomplete information. Each type chooses optimally given beliefs about other players’ types.
Open →




Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium
A dynamic incomplete-information concept combining sequential rationality with belief updating.
Open →




Sequential Equilibrium
A stronger dynamic incomplete-information concept based on sequential rationality and consistent beliefs.
Open →




Equilibrium Cheat Sheet
A compact comparison of the main concepts and when to use them.
Open →

title: Equilibrium Concepts
text:
Refinements and related notions



Trembling-hand Perfect Equilibrium
Rules out equilibria that are not robust to small mistakes.
Open →




Proper Equilibrium
A stronger refinement where more costly mistakes are much less likely than less costly mistakes.
Open →




Correlated Equilibrium
Allows players to condition actions on signals from a common recommendation device.
Open →




Rationalizability
Keeps strategies that can survive iterative best-response reasoning, without requiring a full equilibrium.
Open →




Babbling Equilibrium
A cheap-talk equilibrium in which messages carry no information and are ignored by the receiver.
Open →

title: Equilibrium Concepts
text:
From basic equilibrium to refinements
A useful way to understand refinements is to ask what problem each concept tries to fix.





flowchart LR
    A[Nash Equilibrium] --> B[Problem: non-credible threats]
    B --> C[Subgame Perfect Equilibrium]

    C --> D[Problem: beliefs after unexpected moves]
    D --> E[Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium]

    E --> F[Problem: belief consistency]
    F --> G[Sequential Equilibrium]

    A --> H[Problem: fragile equilibria]
    H --> I[Trembling-hand Perfect Equilibrium]
    I --> J[Proper Equilibrium]






Nash equilibrium is the starting point. Refinements add extra discipline when the basic idea of mutual best response is not enough.

title: Equilibrium Concepts
text:
Choosing the right concept





flowchart TD
    A[What kind of game is it?] --> B[Simultaneous and complete information]
    A --> C[Sequential and complete information]
    A --> D[Static incomplete information]
    A --> E[Dynamic incomplete information]
    A --> F[Cheap talk or communication]
    A --> G[Recommendation device or mediated play]

    B --> B1[Nash Equilibrium]
    C --> C1[Subgame Perfect Equilibrium]
    D --> D1[Bayesian Nash Equilibrium]
    E --> E1[Perfect Bayesian or Sequential Equilibrium]
    F --> F1[Informative or Babbling Equilibrium]
    G --> G1[Correlated Equilibrium]






This decision tree is only a guide. In actual modelling, the right solution concept depends on what the model needs to explain.

title: Equilibrium Concepts
text:
Comparison table









Concept
Used for
Core requirement
Main issue addressed




Nash equilibrium
Static games
Mutual best responses
Strategic stability


Subgame perfect equilibrium
Dynamic complete-information games
Nash equilibrium in every subgame
Credibility


Bayesian Nash equilibrium
Static incomplete-information games
Type-contingent best responses
Private information


Perfect Bayesian equilibrium
Dynamic incomplete-information games
Sequential rationality and beliefs
Off-path inference


Sequential equilibrium
Dynamic incomplete-information games
Sequential rationality and consistent beliefs
Stronger belief discipline


Trembling-hand perfect equilibrium
Strategic-form games
Robustness to small mistakes
Fragile equilibria


Proper equilibrium
Strategic-form games
Costlier mistakes are less likely
Stronger mistake discipline


Correlated equilibrium
Games with recommendations
Obedience to signals
Coordination through information


Rationalizability
Strategic reasoning
Survival under best-response reasoning
Reasoning without full equilibrium


Babbling equilibrium
Cheap-talk games
Messages ignored by receiver
No information transmission

title: Equilibrium Concepts
text:
Why equilibrium is not enough
An equilibrium can be stable but undesirable. It can also be mathematically valid but behaviourally implausible. This is why equilibrium analysis usually needs interpretation.
When reading an equilibrium result, ask:

What incentives make this behaviour stable?
What beliefs support the behaviour?
Are threats and promises credible?
Is the equilibrium efficient or inefficient?
Are there multiple equilibria?
Would the result survive small changes in assumptions?

These questions matter because equilibrium is a tool for explanation, not a guarantee of realism.

title: Equilibrium Concepts
text:
Suggested reading order
If you are reading this section for the first time, a good order is:

Nash equilibrium
Subgame perfect equilibrium
Bayesian Nash equilibrium

Sequential equilibrium
Trembling-hand perfect equilibrium
Proper equilibrium
Correlated equilibrium
Rationalizability

title: Rationalizability
text:
Rationalizability predicts which actions can be justified as best responses to some beliefs about others’ actions, assuming everyone is rational and this is common knowledge.
It often corresponds to iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies (IESDS). (With weak dominance, elimination order can matter, so newcomers usually start with strict dominance.)

title: Rationalizability
text:
Rationalizability predicts which actions can be justified as best responses to some beliefs about others’ actions, assuming everyone is rational and this is common knowledge.
It often corresponds to iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies (IESDS). (With weak dominance, elimination order can matter, so newcomers usually start with strict dominance.)

title: Rationalizability
text:
Where it shows up

Normal-form games when you want predictions weaker than Nash
Settings with equilibrium multiplicity (rationalizability gives a set of plausible actions)
As a foundation for epistemic game theory

title: Rationalizability
section: How to solve (recipe: iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies)
text:
How to solve (recipe: iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies)

Identify strictly dominated actions for any player and remove them.
Recompute dominance in the reduced game.
Repeat until no more strictly dominated actions remain.
The remaining actions are rationalizable.

title: Rationalizability
text:
Solved example (iterated deletion)

Problem (context + question)
Player 1 actions: \(U, M, D\). Player 2 actions: \(L, R\). Payoffs to player 1 are:
\[
\begin{array}{c|cc}
& L & R\\ \hline
U & 3 & 0\\
M & 2 & 1\\
D & 1 & 0
\end{array}
\]
Assume player 2’s payoffs are irrelevant for this exercise.
Question: Which actions of player 1 are rationalizable by iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies?


Solution
Compare player 1 actions:

Does \(D\) get strictly dominated by \(M\)?

Against \(L\): \(u_1(M)=2 > u_1(D)=1\)
Against \(R\): \(u_1(M)=1 > u_1(D)=0\) Yes: \(M\) strictly dominates \(D\).


So eliminate \(D\).
Now remaining actions for player 1: \(U\) and \(M\). - Does \(U\) strictly dominate \(M\)? No: - Against \(L\): \(U=3 > M=2\) - Against \(R\): \(U=0 < M=1\) - Does \(M\) strictly dominate \(U\)? No, same reason.
Result: The rationalizable actions for player 1 are \(\{U, M\}\).


Takeaway
Rationalizability removes clearly irrational actions but may still leave multiple plausible choices.

title: Rationalizability
text:
Later-on analysis

Nash equilibrium is a stronger prediction than rationalizability.
In some games, iterated strict dominance leads to a unique outcome (then it’s very powerful).
With weak dominance, elimination can depend on order; if you include it, add a warning section.

title: Proper equilibrium
text:
A proper equilibrium is a refinement of trembling-hand perfection. It assumes players can make mistakes, but very bad mistakes are much less likely than slightly bad ones.
Intuition: if an action yields a much lower payoff than another, the chance you mistakenly choose it should be much smaller.

title: Proper equilibrium
text:
A proper equilibrium is a refinement of trembling-hand perfection. It assumes players can make mistakes, but very bad mistakes are much less likely than slightly bad ones.
Intuition: if an action yields a much lower payoff than another, the chance you mistakenly choose it should be much smaller.

title: Proper equilibrium
text:
Where it shows up

Normal-form games with multiple perfect equilibria
Equilibrium selection arguments based on “plausible mistakes”
Advanced micro/game theory refinements

title: Proper equilibrium
text:
How to solve (recipe)

Start from candidate equilibria (usually Nash / perfect).
Compare payoffs of different deviations.
Impose the idea: probability of a worse deviation is tiny relative to a better deviation.
Check whether the equilibrium can be supported as the limit of such “proper” trembles.

(For most newcomer notes, the key is the intuition, not the full formal definition.)

title: Proper equilibrium
text:
Solved example (intuition with unequal mistakes)

Problem (context + question)
Player 1 is choosing between three actions \(A,B,C\) against a fixed opponent strategy. Payoffs to player 1 are:

\(u_1(A)=10\) (best)
\(u_1(B)=9\) (slightly worse)
\(u_1(C)=0\) (much worse)

Question: Under the “proper” idea of trembles, which mistake is more plausible: choosing \(B\) or choosing \(C\)?


Solution
Proper equilibrium assumes that when players tremble: - they might mistakenly choose \(B\) instead of \(A\) with small probability, - but choosing \(C\) (which is drastically worse) should be far less likely than choosing \(B\).
So “proper trembles” treat worse errors as exponentially rarer than mild errors.
Result: A proper refinement would allow small probability on \(B\) but push the probability on \(C\) to be negligible relative to \(B\) as trembles vanish.


Check
This matches the guiding principle: the likelihood of mistakes respects payoff ranking and payoff gaps.


Takeaway
Proper equilibrium captures “bounded rationality with common sense”: huge blunders are rarer than small slips.

title: Proper equilibrium
text:
Later-on analysis

Proper equilibrium ⟹ trembling-hand perfect ⟹ Nash (in finite games).
In practice, proper equilibrium is used when you want a sharper selection than perfection provides.
If you later want a fully formal statement, we can add it as an appendix section.

title: Sequential Equilibrium
text:
Sequential equilibrium is a refinement for dynamic games with incomplete information. It strengthens perfect Bayesian equilibrium by requiring strategies to be sequentially rational and beliefs to be consistent as limits of fully mixed strategies.
The central idea is:

title: Sequential Equilibrium
text:
Why sequential equilibrium matters
Perfect Bayesian equilibrium requires sequential rationality and Bayes’ rule where possible. But off-path beliefs may still be too flexible.
Sequential equilibrium adds stronger discipline to beliefs.





flowchart LR
    A[PBE] --> B[Sequential rationality]
    A --> C[Beliefs]
    C --> D[Off-path freedom]
    D --> E[Sequential equilibrium adds consistency]






This makes sequential equilibrium useful when off-path beliefs matter.

title: Sequential Equilibrium
text:
Assessment
A sequential equilibrium is defined as an assessment:
\[
(\sigma,\mu),
\]
where:



Object
Meaning




\(\sigma\)
strategy profile


\(\mu\)
system of beliefs



The assessment must satisfy:

sequential rationality;
consistency.

title: Sequential Equilibrium
text:
Sequential rationality
Sequential rationality means every player chooses optimally at every information set, given beliefs and continuation strategies.
For each information set, the prescribed strategy must maximize expected continuation payoff.





flowchart LR
    A[Information set] --> B[Belief over nodes]
    B --> C[Expected continuation payoff]
    C --> D[Optimal action]






This is similar to PBE.

title: Sequential Equilibrium
text:
Consistency
Consistency is the stronger belief requirement.
Beliefs should be obtainable as limits of beliefs generated by completely mixed strategy profiles.
A completely mixed strategy assigns positive probability to every action. This ensures every information set is reached with positive probability, so Bayes’ rule can be applied everywhere.
Then we take a limit as trembles go to zero.





flowchart TD
    A[Completely mixed strategies] --> B[Every information set reached]
    B --> C[Bayes' rule applies everywhere]
    C --> D[Generate beliefs]
    D --> E[Take limit]
    E --> F[Consistent beliefs]






This prevents arbitrary off-path beliefs that cannot be justified by small mistakes.

title: Sequential Equilibrium
text:
Sequential equilibrium versus PBE








Concept
Sequential rationality
Belief requirement




PBE
yes
Bayes’ rule on path; off-path beliefs often flexible


Sequential equilibrium
yes
beliefs must be consistent limits of fully mixed strategies



Every sequential equilibrium is generally a PBE, but not every PBE is sequential.

title: Sequential Equilibrium
text:
Why completely mixed strategies?
If every action has positive probability, then every information set can be reached.
That means beliefs can always be computed by Bayes’ rule.
The idea is that even if an action is not supposed to occur in equilibrium, it could occur as a small mistake or tremble.
Beliefs after unexpected actions should be consistent with the relative likelihood of such mistakes.

title: Sequential Equilibrium
text:
Example intuition
Suppose a receiver observes an unexpected signal.
PBE may allow many possible beliefs after that signal.
Sequential equilibrium asks:

If the unexpected signal occurred because of very small mistakes, which type would be more likely to make that mistake?

This gives off-path beliefs more structure.

title: Sequential Equilibrium
text:
Relation to trembling-hand perfection
Both sequential equilibrium and trembling-hand perfection use the idea of small mistakes, but in different ways.







Concept
Main object




Trembling-hand perfect equilibrium
robustness of strategies to small mistakes


Sequential equilibrium
consistency of beliefs and sequential rationality


Proper equilibrium
relative likelihood of more costly mistakes



Sequential equilibrium is especially designed for extensive-form games with imperfect information.

title: Sequential Equilibrium
text:
Beliefs at information sets
In an extensive-form game, an information set may contain several decision nodes.
A belief assigns probabilities to these nodes.
For example, if information set \(I\) contains nodes \(x\) and \(y\), beliefs may be:
\[
\mu(x\mid I)=0.6,
\]
and
\[
\mu(y\mid I)=0.4.
\]
The player’s optimal action depends on expected payoff under these beliefs.

title: Sequential Equilibrium
text:
Sequential equilibrium in signaling
In a signaling game, sequential equilibrium can restrict off-path beliefs after unexpected signals.
For example, in a pooling equilibrium, both types send the same signal. If the receiver observes an unexpected signal, PBE may allow arbitrary beliefs. Sequential equilibrium asks whether those beliefs can be justified by small probabilities of each type deviating.





flowchart LR
    A[Pooling signal observed normally] --> B[Receiver uses pooled belief]
    C[Unexpected signal] --> D[Need off-path belief]
    D --> E[Sequential consistency restricts belief]

title: Sequential Equilibrium
text:
Why it is stronger
Sequential equilibrium is stronger because it connects beliefs to possible trembles.
It rules out some equilibria that rely on unreasonable beliefs after unexpected events.
However, it can also be more technically demanding than PBE.

title: Sequential Equilibrium
text:
Common mistakes

1. Treating sequential equilibrium as the same as PBE
Sequential equilibrium has a stronger consistency requirement.


2. Ignoring beliefs
Sequential equilibrium is an assessment: strategies plus beliefs.


3. Thinking consistency means only Bayes’ rule on path
Consistency also disciplines off-path beliefs through limits.


4. Forgetting sequential rationality
Beliefs alone are not enough. Actions must be optimal given beliefs.


5. Confusing trembles with actual behaviour
Trembles are a refinement device, not necessarily a literal behavioural claim.

title: Sequential Equilibrium
text:
Checklist
When checking sequential equilibrium, ask:

What is the strategy profile?
What beliefs are assigned at each information set?
Are strategies sequentially rational given beliefs?
Can beliefs be generated by fully mixed strategies?
Do those fully mixed strategies converge to the proposed strategy?
Do the induced beliefs converge to the proposed beliefs?
Are off-path beliefs justified by this limiting process?
Is the assessment also a PBE?
What equilibria are ruled out by consistency?
Is the refinement substantively important in this model?

title: Nash Equilibrium
text:
Nash equilibrium is the basic solution concept of non-cooperative game theory. It describes a strategy profile in which every player is choosing a best response to the strategies of the others.
The central idea is:

title: Nash Equilibrium
text:
The definition
Let
\[
G=\langle N,(S_i)_{i\in N},(u_i)_{i\in N}\rangle
\]
be a normal-form game.
A strategy profile
\[
s^*=(s_1^*,\ldots,s_n^*)
\]
is a Nash equilibrium if, for every player \(i\),
\[
u_i(s_i^*,s_{-i}^*)
\geq
u_i(s_i,s_{-i}^*)
\quad
\text{for all } s_i\in S_i.
\]
This means that \(s_i^*\) solves player \(i\)’s optimization problem given the strategies of the other players.
Equivalently,
\[
s_i^* \in BR_i(s_{-i}^*)
\quad
\text{for every } i.
\]

title: Nash Equilibrium
text:
Intuition
A Nash equilibrium is a state of mutual best response.





flowchart LR
    A[Player 1 best responds to Player 2] --> C[Nash equilibrium]
    B[Player 2 best responds to Player 1] --> C
    C --> D[No unilateral profitable deviation]






The equilibrium is stable in a specific sense: if everyone expects the equilibrium strategies, no single player wants to change their own strategy.

title: Nash Equilibrium
section: What Nash equilibrium does and does not say

title: Nash Equilibrium
text:
Best-response method
To find a Nash equilibrium, find mutual best responses.





flowchart TD
    A[Write the game] --> B[Find each player's best responses]
    B --> C[Look for mutual best responses]
    C --> D[Identify Nash equilibria]
    D --> E[Interpret stability and welfare]






In a payoff matrix, a pure-strategy Nash equilibrium is a cell where each player’s chosen strategy is a best response to the other player’s chosen strategy.

title: Nash Equilibrium
text:
Example: coordination game
Consider this game:




Player 2: L
Player 2: R




Player 1: U
\((2,2)\)
\((0,0)\)


Player 1: D
\((0,0)\)
\((1,1)\)



If Player 2 chooses \(L\), Player 1 prefers \(U\).
If Player 2 chooses \(R\), Player 1 prefers \(D\).
If Player 1 chooses \(U\), Player 2 prefers \(L\).
If Player 1 chooses \(D\), Player 2 prefers \(R\).
Therefore, there are two Nash equilibria:
\[
(U,L)
\]
and
\[
(D,R).
\]
This shows that Nash equilibrium may not be unique.

title: Nash Equilibrium
text:
Example: prisoners’ dilemma
In a prisoners’ dilemma, each player has an individual incentive to defect, even though both would be better off if both cooperated.
The usual ranking is:
\[
T > R > P > S,
\]
where:



Symbol
Meaning




\(T\)
temptation payoff from defecting while the other cooperates


\(R\)
reward from mutual cooperation


\(P\)
punishment from mutual defection


\(S\)
sucker payoff from cooperating while the other defects



The Nash equilibrium is mutual defection.
This outcome is stable because no player wants to cooperate unilaterally. But it is inefficient because both players would prefer mutual cooperation.





flowchart LR
    A[Individual incentive to defect] --> B[Mutual defection]
    B --> C[Nash equilibrium]
    C --> D[Collectively worse than mutual cooperation]

title: Nash Equilibrium
Nash Equilibrium
text:
Mixed-strategy Nash equilibrium
A Nash equilibrium may involve mixed strategies.
A mixed strategy is a probability distribution over pure strategies.
In a mixed-strategy equilibrium, each player must be willing to randomize among the pure strategies used with positive probability.
This means the player must be indifferent among those pure strategies.
For example, if Player 1 mixes between \(U\) and \(D\), then
\[
U_1(U,\sigma_2)=U_1(D,\sigma_2).
\]
If one pure strategy gave a strictly higher expected payoff, Player 1 would not randomize.

title: Nash Equilibrium
text:
Indifference principle
The indifference principle is often used to solve mixed equilibria.





flowchart TD
    A[Player mixes between actions] --> B[Each used action must give same expected payoff]
    B --> C[Set expected payoffs equal]
    C --> D[Solve for opponent's mixing probability]






This can feel strange at first. When solving for Player 2’s mixing probability, we often use Player 1’s indifference condition. Player 2 randomizes in a way that makes Player 1 willing to mix.

title: Nash Equilibrium
section: Nash equilibrium as a fixed point
text:
Nash equilibrium as a fixed point
Nash equilibrium can be understood as a fixed point of the best-response correspondence.
Let \(BR(s)\) be the set of best-response profiles to \(s\). A Nash equilibrium satisfies
\[
s^* \in BR(s^*).
\]
This means that if everyone best responds to \(s^*\), the resulting strategy profile can still be \(s^*\).





flowchart LR
    A[Strategy profile s] --> B[Best-response correspondence]
    B --> C[Best responses BR s]
    C --> D{Contains s?}
    D -->|Yes| E[Nash equilibrium]
    D -->|No| F[Not equilibrium]






This connection explains why fixed-point theorems are used to prove equilibrium existence.

title: Nash Equilibrium
text:
Existence
Every finite game has at least one Nash equilibrium in mixed strategies.
This does not mean every finite game has a pure-strategy equilibrium.
For example, matching pennies has no pure-strategy Nash equilibrium, but it has a mixed-strategy equilibrium.
The existence result relies on allowing players to randomize.

title: Nash Equilibrium
Nash Equilibrium
text:
Nash equilibrium in dynamic games
Nash equilibrium can be applied to dynamic games by treating strategies as complete contingent plans.
However, Nash equilibrium alone may allow non-credible threats.
This is why dynamic games often use stronger concepts such as subgame perfect equilibrium.
Example:
A player threatens to punish later, but when later arrives, punishment is costly and irrational.
Nash equilibrium may not rule this out unless the threat is tested inside the relevant subgame.

title: Nash Equilibrium
text:
Common mistakes

1. Thinking Nash equilibrium means the best outcome
Nash equilibrium is about stability, not welfare.


2. Forgetting unilateral deviation
Nash equilibrium checks whether one player can improve by deviating alone, holding others fixed.


3. Ignoring mixed strategies
A game with no pure equilibrium may still have a mixed equilibrium.


4. Confusing best response with dominant strategy
A best response depends on what others do. A dominant strategy is best no matter what others do.


5. Treating multiple equilibria as a contradiction
Multiple equilibria mean several outcomes are strategically stable.


6. Using Nash equilibrium when timing matters
For dynamic games, check whether subgame perfection or another refinement is needed.

title: Nash Equilibrium
text:
Checklist for finding Nash equilibrium

Identify players.
List strategies.
Write payoffs.
For each opponent strategy, find each player’s best response.
Mark mutual best responses.
Check if any player can profitably deviate alone.
If no pure equilibrium exists, check mixed strategies.
If multiple equilibria exist, interpret the selection problem.
Check whether the equilibrium is efficient.
If the game is dynamic, ask whether the equilibrium is credible.
