title: Convexity
text:
Convexity is a way of describing shape. It is important in optimization, probability, game theory, and equilibrium existence because convex objects behave well under mixtures.
The central idea is simple:

title: Convexity
text:
Convex sets
A set \(X\) is convex if for any two points \(x,y \in X\) and any \(\alpha \in [0,1]\),
\[
\alpha x + (1-\alpha)y \in X.
\]
This means the line segment between \(x\) and \(y\) stays inside \(X\).





flowchart LR
    A[Point x in set] --> C[Mixture alpha x plus 1 minus alpha y]
    B[Point y in set] --> C
    C --> D{Still in the set?}
    D -->|Yes| E[Convex set]
    D -->|No| F[Not convex]






Convexity is useful because it allows interpolation, mixing, and averaging without leaving the feasible set.

title: Convexity
text:
Simple examples

Convex example
The interval
\[
[0,1]
\]
is convex. If \(x,y \in [0,1]\), then any weighted average of \(x\) and \(y\) is also in \([0,1]\).


Non-convex example
The set
\[
[0,1] \cup [2,3]
\]
is not convex.
For example, \(1\) and \(2\) are in the set, but their average is
\[
\frac{1+2}{2}=1.5,
\]
which is not in the set.

title: Convexity
text:
Convex combinations
A convex combination of points \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) is
\[
\sum_{k=1}^n \alpha_k x_k,
\]
where
\[
\alpha_k \geq 0
\]
for all \(k\), and
\[
\sum_{k=1}^n \alpha_k=1.
\]
The weights behave like probabilities.
This is why convexity appears naturally in mixed strategies, expectations, and probability distributions.





flowchart LR
    A[Weights are nonnegative] --> C[Convex combination]
    B[Weights sum to one] --> C
    C --> D[Weighted average]

title: Convexity
text:
Convexity and probability
A probability distribution is a convex combination.
If outcome \(x_k\) occurs with probability \(p_k\), then the expected value is
\[
\mathbb{E}[X]=\sum_k p_k x_k.
\]
The probabilities satisfy
\[
p_k \geq 0
\]
and
\[
\sum_k p_k = 1.
\]
So expectation is a weighted average.
This is why convexity is closely connected to probability and mixed strategies.

title: Convexity
text:
Mixed strategies
In game theory, a mixed strategy is a probability distribution over pure strategies.
If a player has actions \(A\) and \(B\), then a mixed strategy can be written as
\[
\sigma = (p,1-p),
\]
where
\[
p \in [0,1].
\]
The set of possible mixed strategies is convex. If one mixed strategy assigns probability \(p\) to \(A\), and another assigns probability \(q\) to \(A\), then a mixture of those mixed strategies assigns probability
\[
\alpha p+(1-\alpha)q
\]
to \(A\).
This remains a valid probability.





flowchart TD
    A[Pure strategies] --> B[Probability distributions over them]
    B --> C[Mixed strategy space]
    C --> D[Convex set]
    D --> E[Fixed-point existence arguments]






Convexity of mixed-strategy spaces is one reason finite games have mixed-strategy equilibria.

title: Convexity
text:
Convex functions
A function \(f\) is convex if for all \(x,y\) and \(\alpha \in [0,1]\),
\[
f(\alpha x+(1-\alpha)y)
\leq
\alpha f(x)+(1-\alpha)f(y).
\]
The graph of a convex function lies below the chord between any two points.
A standard example is
\[
f(x)=x^2.
\]
Convex functions are important in minimization problems.

title: Convexity
text:
Concave functions
A function \(f\) is concave if
\[
f(\alpha x+(1-\alpha)y)
\geq
\alpha f(x)+(1-\alpha)f(y).
\]
The graph of a concave function lies above the chord between any two points.
A standard example is
\[
f(x)=\log x.
\]
Concave functions are important in maximization problems.

title: Convexity
text:
Convexity and optimization
Convexity makes optimization easier.
For maximization, concavity is especially useful. If the objective function is concave and the feasible set is convex, then local optima are global optima.





flowchart LR
    A[Convex feasible set] --> C[Well-behaved optimization]
    B[Concave objective for maximization] --> C
    C --> D[Local optimum is global]
    D --> E[Clear comparative statics]






This matters because many economic models rely on maximization.

title: Convexity
text:
First-order conditions and concavity
Suppose \(f\) is differentiable and concave. If an interior point \(x^*\) satisfies
\[
f'(x^*)=0,
\]
then \(x^*\) is a global maximum.
If \(f\) is strictly concave, then the maximum is unique.
This is stronger than the ordinary second-order check because concavity gives global structure.

title: Convexity
text:
Quasi-concavity
A function is quasi-concave if its upper contour sets are convex.
The upper contour set at level \(c\) is
\[
\{x: f(x)\geq c\}.
\]
Quasi-concavity is useful because it captures single-peakedness or convex preferences without requiring full concavity.
In economics, quasi-concavity often appears in consumer theory and game theory because it helps ensure well-behaved best responses.

title: Convexity
text:
Convexity and best responses
In game theory, convexity helps with equilibrium existence.
A typical existence argument needs:

compact strategy spaces;
convex strategy spaces;
continuous payoff functions;
quasi-concave payoff functions in own strategy.

These conditions help ensure that best responses exist and are well behaved.





flowchart TD
    A[Convex strategy spaces] --> B[Well-behaved best responses]
    C[Continuous payoffs] --> B
    D[Quasi-concavity in own strategy] --> B
    B --> E[Fixed-point theorem applies]
    E --> F[Equilibrium exists]

title: Convexity
text:
Convexity and mixtures
Convexity is also useful conceptually.
A mixture between two strategies, beliefs, policies, or outcomes can be meaningful only if the mixture remains inside the relevant set.
Examples:



Object
Why convexity matters




mixed strategies
probabilities over pure actions


beliefs
probabilities over states


feasible policies
combinations of policy instruments


consumption bundles
mixtures of goods


expected payoffs
probability-weighted values


correlated recommendations
distributions over action profiles

title: Convexity
text:
Common mistakes

1. Confusing convex sets and convex functions
A set is convex if mixtures of points stay inside the set. A function is convex if its graph satisfies a shape condition.


2. Forgetting the weights must sum to one
A convex combination requires nonnegative weights that add to one.


3. Using convex when concave is needed
For maximization, concavity is usually the helpful property. For minimization, convexity is usually helpful.


4. Assuming every feasible set is convex
Some real choices are discrete or non-convex.


5. Treating local conditions as global without curvature
First-order conditions alone do not guarantee a global optimum unless additional structure such as concavity is present.

title: Convexity
text:
Checklist
When convexity appears, ask:

Is the object a set or a function?
If it is a set, do mixtures stay inside?
If it is a function, is it convex or concave?
Are weights nonnegative and do they sum to one?
Is the feasible set convex?
Is the objective concave for maximization?
Are best responses well behaved?
Is convexity being used for optimization, probability, or equilibrium existence?
Are there discrete choices that break convexity?
What substantive interpretation does the mixture have?

title: Information & beliefs (measure-lite)
text:
In Bayesian and information economics, “information” is usually represented by what events a player can distinguish.
There are two common (equivalent) ways to think about it:

Information partition (finite case): a player observes which cell of a partition they are in.
\(\sigma\)-algebra (general case): the collection of events the player can condition on.

You almost never need heavy measure theory for standard game theory notes—just the intuition.

title: Information & beliefs (measure-lite)
text:
In Bayesian and information economics, “information” is usually represented by what events a player can distinguish.
There are two common (equivalent) ways to think about it:

Information partition (finite case): a player observes which cell of a partition they are in.
\(\sigma\)-algebra (general case): the collection of events the player can condition on.

You almost never need heavy measure theory for standard game theory notes—just the intuition.

title: Information & beliefs (measure-lite)
text:
\(\sigma\)-algebra (concept only)
Let \(\Omega\) be the set of possible states of the world.
A \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\mathcal{F}\) is a collection of subsets of \(\Omega\) (events) such that:

\(\Omega \in \mathcal{F}\)

If \(A \in \mathcal{F}\) then \(A^c \in \mathcal{F}\)

If \(A_1, A_2, \dots \in \mathcal{F}\) then \(\bigcup_{k=1}^\infty A_k \in \mathcal{F}\)

Intuition. \(\mathcal{F}\) lists the events you are able to talk about (and condition on).
Coarser \(\mathcal{F}\) = less information.

Finite shortcut (partition view)
If \(\Omega\) is finite and a player’s information is a partition \[
\Pi = \{C_1,\dots,C_m\},
\] then the player can distinguish only which cell \(C_j\) contains the true state.
The corresponding \(\sigma\)-algebra is “all unions of cells of \(\Pi\)”.

title: Information & beliefs (measure-lite)
section: Conditional expectation as “best prediction given information”
text:
Conditional expectation as “best prediction given information”
Given an integrable random variable \(X\) (e.g., payoff-relevant quantity) and an information set \(\mathcal{G}\subseteq\mathcal{F}\), the conditional expectation \(\mathbb{E}[X\mid \mathcal{G}]\) is the random variable that represents the best mean-squared prediction of \(X\) using only information in \(\mathcal{G}\).
Projection idea (intuition). Think of \(\mathbb{E}[X\mid \mathcal{G}]\) as projecting \(X\) onto the space of \(\mathcal{G}\)-measurable variables (things you can compute using the information you have).

title: Information & beliefs (measure-lite)
section: Example: conditional expectation with a partition
text:
Example: conditional expectation with a partition
Let the state space be \[
\Omega=\{\omega_1,\omega_2,\omega_3,\omega_4\},
\qquad
\mathbb{P}(\omega_k)=\tfrac14 \text{ for each }k.
\]
Let \[
X(\omega_1)=0,\;X(\omega_2)=2,\;X(\omega_3)=4,\;X(\omega_4)=6.
\]
Suppose the player only observes whether the state is in \[
C_1=\{\omega_1,\omega_2\}\quad\text{or}\quad C_2=\{\omega_3,\omega_4\}.
\]
That information corresponds to a partition \(\Pi=\{C_1,C_2\}\) (and a \(\sigma\)-algebra generated by it).
Then the conditional expectation is constant on each cell:

On \(C_1\): \[
\mathbb{E}[X\mid C_1]
=\frac{X(\omega_1)+X(\omega_2)}{2}
=\frac{0+2}{2}=1.
\]
On \(C_2\): \[
\mathbb{E}[X\mid C_2]
=\frac{X(\omega_3)+X(\omega_4)}{2}
=\frac{4+6}{2}=5.
\]

So \(\mathbb{E}[X\mid \mathcal{G}]\) takes value \(1\) if you learn “cell \(C_1\)”, and value \(5\) if you learn “cell \(C_2\)”.
Game theory interpretation. This is exactly what beliefs do: you map what you observed to an updated expectation of payoff-relevant quantities.

title: Information & beliefs (measure-lite)
text:
Common knowledge (concept)
An event \(E\) is common knowledge if: - everyone knows \(E\), - everyone knows that everyone knows \(E\), - everyone knows that everyone knows that everyone knows \(E\), - and so on indefinitely.
Intuition. Common knowledge is what makes coordination possible (or impossible). It is stronger than “everyone knows”.

Iterated beliefs (one-line idea)
In Bayesian games, strategies can depend on: - beliefs about types, - beliefs about others’ beliefs, - higher-order beliefs.
Often you don’t compute these explicitly; you just need to know they exist and that equilibrium concepts impose consistency.

title: Information & beliefs (measure-lite)
text:
Practical takeaway
For most game theory work: - partitions are enough to model information, - conditional expectation captures “best prediction given what you know”, - common knowledge / higher-order beliefs matter conceptually for coordination and equilibrium.

title: Foundations
text:
The foundations section collects the mathematical and conceptual tools used across the site. These pages are not separate from the substantive notes. They are the background machinery behind game theory, criminology models, psychology overlaps, and rationality under uncertainty.
The aim is practical: each foundation page should help explain how to read, build, or interpret a model.

title: Foundations
text:
Map of the foundations section





flowchart TD
    A[Foundations] --> B[Optimization]

The core idea is that formal models usually combine several foundations at once. A Bayesian game, for example, uses probability for beliefs, optimization for best responses, and fixed-point reasoning for equilibrium.

title: Foundations
text:
How these tools connect
Many models can be read as a chain:





flowchart LR
    A[Model primitives] --> B[Choice problem]
    B --> C[Optimization]
    C --> D[Best response]
    D --> E[Equilibrium condition]

For models with uncertainty, the chain becomes:





flowchart LR
    A[Uncertain state or type] --> B[Prior belief]
    B --> C[Signal or action]
    C --> D[Posterior belief]

For dynamic models, the chain becomes:





flowchart LR
    A[History] --> B[Continuation game]
    B --> C[Continuation payoff]
    C --> D[Credible action]
    D --> E[Current incentive]






These diagrams are deliberately simple. Their purpose is to show that formal reasoning usually follows a small number of repeatable patterns.

title: Foundations
text:
Suggested reading order
If you are reading the site from the beginning, use this order:

Optimization
Probability

Fixed points
Convexity
Linear algebra

This order works because optimization and probability appear almost everywhere. Dynamic reasoning becomes important once timing matters. Fixed points, convexity, and linear algebra become more important when the models become more abstract.

title: Foundations
text:
Foundations for game theory
Game theory uses all of these tools.







Foundation
Use in game theory




Optimization
Best responses and payoff maximization


Probability

Dynamic reasoning

Existence of equilibrium

A Nash equilibrium can be understood as a fixed point of best-response reasoning. A Bayesian equilibrium combines optimization with beliefs. A dynamic equilibrium combines optimization with histories and continuation values.

title: Foundations
text:
Foundations for criminology
The same tools also appear in criminology.







Foundation
Use in criminology

Choice under incentives, sanctions, and opportunity

Risk, detection, reporting, and uncertainty

deterrence, retaliation, reputation, and life-course processes

social norms and stable patterns of behaviour

trade-offs in policy design and resource allocation

networks, transitions, and population-level systems



The goal is not to reduce crime to equations. The goal is to make assumptions visible and to understand how mechanisms generate predictions.

section: How to use the foundation pages
text:
How to use the foundation pages
Each foundation page should be read with three questions:

What problem does this tool solve?
Where does it appear in a model?
What mistake does it help prevent?

For example, optimization prevents vague claims about “choosing well.” Probability prevents vague claims about “uncertainty.” Dynamic reasoning prevents vague claims about “future threats.” Fixed points prevent vague claims about “stable outcomes.”

title: Foundations
text:
Common mistakes

1. Treating foundations as detached mathematics
The tools are useful because they organise substantive arguments. They should be connected to models and examples.


2. Memorising formulas without knowing the role
A formula matters because it does something in an argument: maximizes, updates, compares, verifies, or predicts.


3. Skipping assumptions
Most formal results depend on assumptions such as differentiability, concavity, complete information, common knowledge, or finite action spaces.


4. Ignoring interpretation
A mathematical solution is not the end of the analysis. The final step is to explain what the result means.

title: Linear Algebra
text:
Linear algebra is the language of vectors, matrices, systems, and transformations. It appears in game theory, statistics, networks, Markov processes, mixed strategies, and models with many interacting parts.
This page gives the basic ideas needed for reading the notes.

title: Linear Algebra
text:
Why linear algebra matters
Many objects in social science can be represented as lists of numbers.
Examples:

a mixed strategy;
a belief over states;
a payoff vector;
a network adjacency matrix;
a transition matrix;
a feature vector in data analysis;
a system of equations.






flowchart TD
    A[Linear Algebra] --> B[Vectors]
    A --> C[Matrices]
    A --> D[Systems of equations]
    A --> E[Transformations]
    A --> F[Networks and transitions]

    B --> B1[Strategies]
    B --> B2[Beliefs]
    B --> B3[Payoffs]

    C --> C1[Games]
    C --> C2[Networks]
    C --> C3[Data]

    F --> F1[Markov chains]
    F --> F2[Diffusion]






The point is not to make everything abstract. The point is to organize many related numbers cleanly.

title: Linear Algebra
text:
Vectors
A vector is an ordered list of numbers.
For example,
\[
x=
\begin{pmatrix}
2\\
5\\
1
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
A vector can represent a point, a bundle, a strategy, a belief, or a collection of variables.
In game theory, a mixed strategy over three actions may be written as
\[
\sigma=
\begin{pmatrix}
0.2\\
0.5\\
0.3
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The entries are probabilities, so they are nonnegative and sum to one.

title: Linear Algebra
text:
Vector addition
If
\[
x=
\begin{pmatrix}
x_1\\
x_2
\end{pmatrix}
\quad
\text{and}
\quad
y=
\begin{pmatrix}
y_1\\
y_2
\end{pmatrix},
\]
then
\[
x+y=
\begin{pmatrix}
x_1+y_1\\
x_2+y_2
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Vector addition is component-by-component.

title: Linear Algebra
text:
Scalar multiplication
If \(\alpha\) is a number and
\[
x=
\begin{pmatrix}
x_1\\
x_2
\end{pmatrix},
\]
then
\[
\alpha x=
\begin{pmatrix}
\alpha x_1\\
\alpha x_2
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
This is important for convex combinations:
\[
\alpha x+(1-\alpha)y.
\]

title: Linear Algebra
text:
Dot product
The dot product of two vectors is
\[
x \cdot y
=
\sum_{k=1}^{n}x_k y_k.
\]
For example,
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
1\\
2\\
3
\end{pmatrix}
\cdot
\begin{pmatrix}
4\\
5\\
6
\end{pmatrix}
=
1\cdot 4+2\cdot 5+3\cdot 6
=
32.
\]
In probability, expected value can be written as a dot product:
\[
\mathbb{E}[X]=p \cdot x.
\]
where \(p\) is a probability vector and \(x\) is an outcome vector.

title: Linear Algebra
Linear Algebra
text:
Matrix-vector multiplication
If
\[
A=
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & 2\\
3 & 4
\end{pmatrix}
\quad
\text{and}
\quad
x=
\begin{pmatrix}
5\\
6
\end{pmatrix},
\]
then
\[
Ax=
\begin{pmatrix}
1\cdot5+2\cdot6\\
3\cdot5+4\cdot6
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
17\\
39
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Matrix multiplication combines rows of the matrix with the vector.





flowchart LR
    A[Matrix] --> C[Transformation]
    B[Vector input] --> C
    C --> D[Vector output]

title: Linear Algebra
text:
Systems of equations
A linear system can be written as
\[
Ax=b.
\]
For example:
\[
\begin{cases}
x+y=5,\\
2x-y=1.
\end{cases}
\]
This can be written as
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & 1\\
2 & -1
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
x\\
y
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
5\\
1
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Linear algebra gives compact methods for solving such systems.

title: Linear Algebra
text:
Payoff matrices
A normal-form game can be represented with payoff matrices.
For example, if Player 1 has two actions and Player 2 has two actions, Player 1’s payoffs can be written as
\[
U_1=
\begin{pmatrix}
u_1(A,L) & u_1(A,R)\\
u_1(B,L) & u_1(B,R)
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Player 2 has a corresponding payoff matrix.
If Player 1 uses mixed strategy \(p\) and Player 2 uses mixed strategy \(q\), expected payoffs can be computed using matrix notation.

title: Linear Algebra
text:
Expected payoff with matrices
Suppose Player 1’s payoff matrix is \(U_1\). Let \(p\) be Player 1’s mixed strategy vector and \(q\) be Player 2’s mixed strategy vector.
Then Player 1’s expected payoff can be written as
\[
p^\top U_1 q.
\]
This expression means:

Player 1 randomizes according to \(p\);
Player 2 randomizes according to \(q\);
the payoff matrix assigns payoffs to action pairs;
the expression averages over all possible action pairs.






flowchart LR
    A[Player 1 mixed strategy p] --> D[Expected payoff]
    B[Payoff matrix U] --> D
    C[Player 2 mixed strategy q] --> D

title: Linear Algebra
text:
Probability vectors
A probability vector has nonnegative entries that sum to one.
For example,
\[
p=
\begin{pmatrix}
0.1\\
0.6\\
0.3
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
This can represent beliefs over three states:
\[
\theta_1,\theta_2,\theta_3.
\]
A Bayesian update changes the probability vector after observing evidence.

title: Linear Algebra
text:
Transition matrices
A transition matrix describes movement between states.
For example,
\[
P=
\begin{pmatrix}
0.8 & 0.2\\
0.3 & 0.7
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
If the current state distribution is
\[
v_t=
\begin{pmatrix}
0.5\\
0.5
\end{pmatrix},
\]
then the next state distribution can be written as
\[
v_{t+1}=P^\top v_t
\]
or with the alternative row-vector convention,
\[
v_{t+1}=v_t P.
\]
The convention should always be made clear.
Transition matrices are useful for learning, Markov chains, population dynamics, and repeated processes.

title: Linear Algebra
text:
Networks and adjacency matrices
A network can be represented by an adjacency matrix.
If there are three people, an adjacency matrix might be
\[
A=
\begin{pmatrix}
0 & 1 & 1\\
1 & 0 & 0\\
1 & 0 & 0
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
A value of 1 means a tie exists. A value of 0 means no tie exists.
Networks can represent:

friendship;
communication;
co-offending;
trade;
influence;
information flow;
institutional links.






flowchart TD
    A[Social network] --> B[Adjacency matrix]
    B --> C[Centrality]
    B --> D[Diffusion]
    B --> E[Clusters]

title: Linear Algebra
text:
Eigenvectors and steady states
An eigenvector of a matrix \(A\) is a nonzero vector \(v\) such that
\[
Av=\lambda v.
\]
The matrix changes the length of the vector but not its direction.
Eigenvectors appear in:

network centrality;
Markov-chain steady states;
dynamic systems;
principal components;
stability analysis.

A steady-state distribution in a Markov process often satisfies
\[
\pi P = \pi.
\]
This is also a fixed-point condition.

title: Linear Algebra
text:
Linear algebra and fixed points
Some fixed points can be written as linear equations.
For example,
\[
x = Ax.
\]
This can be rewritten as
\[
(I-A)x=0.
\]
This connects linear algebra to equilibrium, steady states, and dynamic systems.

title: Linear Algebra
text:
Common mistakes

1. Ignoring dimensions
Matrix multiplication only works when dimensions match.


2. Confusing rows and columns
Always check whether vectors are written as row vectors or column vectors.


3. Treating matrices as just tables
Matrices can represent transformations, not only stored numbers.


4. Forgetting probability constraints
A probability vector must have nonnegative entries that sum to one.


5. Confusing adjacency with intensity
A network matrix may record whether a tie exists or how strong the tie is. These are different.

title: Linear Algebra
text:
Checklist
When using linear algebra, ask:

What does the vector represent?
What does the matrix represent?
Are dimensions compatible?
Are entries numbers, probabilities, payoffs, or ties?
Is the vector a row or column?
Is the matrix transforming a vector or storing data?
Are probability constraints satisfied?
Does the system describe a static relation or dynamic transition?
Is there a fixed point or steady state?
What is the substantive interpretation?

title: Margins of Rationality
text:
Core theme
Many social situations have the same underlying structure:





flowchart LR

    B --> C[Choices]
    C --> D[Strategic interaction]

The site studies this loop from different angles: formal models, criminological mechanisms, psychological processes, and institutional settings.

title: Margins of Rationality
Psychopathology
text:
Psychopathology (often taught as abnormal psychology) studies patterns of suffering and impairment: - how symptoms cluster, - what mechanisms maintain them, - how context and development shape them, - what interventions tend to work (at a high level).
This page is non-diagnostic: it does not teach you to label people or self-diagnose. It is a mechanism map useful for understanding behavior, stigma, and institutions.
A good stance: > Many clinical patterns are loops: cognition + emotion + behavior + reinforcement + social context.

title: Psychopathology
text:
1) Models and levels of explanation

Categorical vs dimensional views

Categorical: disorders as distinct boxes (useful for services and communication).
Dimensional: symptoms vary continuously (often closer to reality).

Practical note: comorbidity is common because dimensions overlap.


Stress–vulnerability (diathesis–stress) model
Outcomes depend on interaction between: - vulnerabilities (traits, history, biology), - stressors (acute shocks, chronic strain), - protective factors (support, routines, safety).
Prediction pattern: reducing chronic stress and increasing stability can reduce symptoms even without “changing personality.”

title: Psychopathology
text:
2) Anxiety-related patterns (mechanism lens)

Threat appraisal and intolerance of uncertainty
Anxiety often involves: - overestimating threat probability or cost, - treating uncertainty as unacceptable, - hypervigilance to threat cues.


Avoidance learning loop
A common maintaining loop: - cue → anxiety → avoidance → immediate relief → stronger avoidance
Prediction patterns - anxiety persists when avoidance prevents corrective learning. - graded exposure can weaken anxiety over time by generating prediction errors.

title: Psychopathology
text:
3) Depressive patterns (mechanism lens)

Reward processing and withdrawal
Depressive patterns often include: - low energy, - reduced reward sensitivity (anhedonia), - withdrawal from activities and people.


Rumination and negative retrieval
Rumination captures attention and biases memory retrieval toward negative material.
A common loop: - low mood → withdrawal/rumination → fewer rewards + more negative retrieval → lower mood
Prediction patterns - structured activity (behavioral activation) can interrupt withdrawal loops. - sleep stabilization can reduce emotional volatility and improve control.

title: Psychopathology
text:
4) Trauma-related patterns (mechanism lens)
After extreme stress, some people develop: - intrusive memories, - hypervigilance, - avoidance of reminders, - emotion numbing, - sleep disruption.
Mechanism sketch: - emotion-tagged memory + threat sensitization + avoidance learning
Prediction patterns - unpredictable cues maintain hypervigilance. - environments that feel unsafe sustain symptoms. - strong stigma increases concealment and reduces help-seeking.

title: Psychopathology
text:
5) Obsessions, compulsions, and checking loops
Compulsive patterns often resemble: - intrusive thought → distress → ritual/checking → temporary relief → stronger ritual
Prediction patterns - reducing reassurance/checking can be difficult short-run but improves long-run via learning. - stress increases urges and habit dominance.
(Links strongly to your Addiction & compulsion page.)

title: Psychopathology
text:
6) Substance use and dual reinforcement
Substance use can be maintained by: - positive reinforcement (pleasure), - negative reinforcement (relief from stress/withdrawal).
Prediction patterns - stress spikes predict relapse risk. - cue exposure predicts craving independent of “motivation.”

title: Psychopathology
text:
7) Psychosis-spectrum concepts (high-level, cautious)
Some symptom patterns involve: - unusual beliefs or interpretations, - altered salience (neutral events feel meaningful), - disruptions in reality testing.
Important stance: these are not “just irrationality.” They can be understood as altered inference under extreme uncertainty, stress, or biological vulnerability.
Prediction patterns - sleep disruption and stress can worsen symptoms. - supportive, predictable environments can reduce distress even if beliefs do not fully change.

title: Psychopathology
text:
8) Personality pathology (conceptual lens)
Rather than labels, focus on: - chronic maladaptive interpersonal patterns, - emotion regulation instability, - rigid scripts and attribution styles, - threat sensitivity and distrust.
Prediction pattern: stable relationships, clear boundaries, and predictable feedback reduce escalation cycles.

title: Psychopathology
section: 9) Stigma, shame, and concealment (social context matters)
text:
9) Stigma, shame, and concealment (social context matters)
Stigma changes the symptom trajectory by: - reducing disclosure and help-seeking, - increasing shame and isolation, - increasing stress and avoidance.
Prediction pattern: increasing safe disclosure pathways increases treatment access and reduces harmful loops.

title: Psychopathology
text:
10) Treatment families (high-level map, non-clinical)
This is a conceptual map of common approaches:

CBT-family: change thoughts/behaviors; exposure; skills (mechanism: learning + reappraisal)
Behavioral activation: rebuild reward loops (mechanism: reinforcement)
Skills-based regulation approaches: distress tolerance, emotion regulation (mechanism: control + reappraisal)
Interpersonal/systemic approaches: relationship patterns and roles (mechanism: scripts + repair)
Medication: modulates underlying physiology (mechanism: arousal/mood systems; varies by condition)

Pitfall: assuming “one treatment fits all.” Match mechanism to loop.

title: Psychopathology
text:
A reusable psychopathology analysis template
When reading about a condition or case, specify:

Symptom dimension(s): threat, reward, control, sleep, social trust

Maintaining loop: avoidance loop? withdrawal loop? compulsion loop?

Context: stressors, safety, support, stigma

Development: when did it start and what reinforced it?

Intervention lever: exposure, activation, skills, environment change, support

Prediction: what would break the loop first?

title: Psychopathology
text:
Canonical examples (stubs you can expand)

Example A: Panic–avoidance cycle

bodily cue interpreted as threat,
panic rises,
avoidance and safety behaviors increase,
sensitivity increases.

Mechanisms: threat appraisal + avoidance learning


Example B: Depression withdrawal loop

low mood reduces action,
fewer rewarding experiences occur,
mood drops further.

Mechanisms: reduced reinforcement + rumination + sleep disruption

Overlaps: institutions (access, legitimacy), criminology (stress/trauma exposure), policy design (stigma and measurement artifacts)

title: Development
text:
Development is about how psychological mechanisms change across the life course: - cognitive capacity and control, - learning styles and sensitivity to reward/punishment, - social reasoning and identity, - emotion regulation and stress reactivity.
This page is a mechanism map you can reuse when thinking about age, cohorts, schooling, family, and peer environments.

title: Development
text:
A practical stance
Instead of treating “age” as a label, treat it as a bundle of changing parameters:

capacity (attention, working memory, executive control)
experience (learned scripts, habits, domain knowledge)
motivation (goals, identity, status)
context (family, school/work, peers, institutions)
plasticity (how quickly learning happens; sensitivity to feedback)

title: Development
section: Mechanism 1: Executive function and self-control develop (then decline later)
text:
Mechanism 1: Executive function and self-control develop (then decline later)
Self-control is strongly linked to: - attention regulation, - inhibition, - planning, - working memory.
In many people: - executive control increases through childhood/adolescence into early adulthood, - then can decline later with aging, depending on health and context.
Prediction patterns - impulsive choices are more common when executive control is still developing, especially under stress. - structure and routines help when control capacity is limited. - environments with strong cues and temptations amplify control differences.

title: Development
section: Mechanism 2: Reward sensitivity and novelty seeking
text:
Mechanism 2: Reward sensitivity and novelty seeking
Many adolescent/young-adult environments involve: - heightened sensitivity to social reward, - stronger status incentives, - stronger novelty seeking.
This is not only “immaturity”; it can be adaptive for exploration, but risky under certain environments.
Prediction patterns - peer presence increases risk-taking more for younger individuals than older adults. - interventions that change social reward (status, approval) can be more effective than purely informational warnings.

title: Development
section: Mechanism 3: Social cognition and identity formation
text:
Mechanism 3: Social cognition and identity formation
Social cognition becomes more sophisticated over time, but identity pressures also rise: - belonging and status needs can dominate, - group norms become highly salient.
Prediction patterns - identity threats amplify motivated reasoning and conformity. - in-group messengers and identity-safe framing matter more in identity-sensitive periods.

title: Development
section: Mechanism 4: Learning and habit formation across stages
text:
Mechanism 4: Learning and habit formation across stages
People learn through reinforcement, imitation, instruction, and practice. But: - early experiences can set durable scripts (“what relationships are like,” “what authority is like”), - repeated environments create habits that persist even after beliefs change.
Prediction patterns - early consistent feedback shapes stable expectations (trust vs threat). - inconsistent or unpredictable environments increase vigilance and short-horizon choice. - habit change is harder when environments remain cue-rich.

title: Development
section: Mechanism 5: Family, peers, and institutions as developmental environments
text:
Mechanism 5: Family, peers, and institutions as developmental environments
Development is not only “inside the person”; it is shaped by: - parenting styles and family stability, - peer networks and norms, - school/work structures, - exposure to stress and safety, - institutional legitimacy and fairness.
Prediction patterns - stable, predictable environments support long-horizon planning and emotion regulation. - chronic threat environments increase vigilance, distrust, and reactive responses.

title: Development
text:
Mechanism 6: Sensitive periods and plasticity (high-level)
Some skills and patterns are easier to shape during windows when: - learning rates are high, - scripts are not yet rigid, - identity is still forming.
Prediction patterns - early interventions can have high returns when they change routines and peer norms. - later change is still possible, but often requires environment redesign and sustained practice.

title: Development
text:
A reusable development analysis template
When age or life stage matters, specify:

Which capacity is changing? (control, attention, social cognition, reward sensitivity)

Which environment dominates? (family, peers, school/work, institutions)

What feedback loops exist? (reward, punishment, reputation, stigma)

What is the predicted direction? (more exploration? more conformity? more threat sensitivity?)

Which intervention lever fits the stage? (structure, peer norms, identity, commitment, support)

title: Development
text:
Connections

Foundations: cognition, learning, self-control, emotion & motivation, social cognition
Topics: norms & groups, relationships, sleep & stress
Overlaps: institutions (schools, justice systems), criminology (peer effects, life-course patterns, hot states)

title: Biases & heuristics
text:
Biases are systematic patterns in judgment and choice. A useful framing:
This page is organized as mechanism → prediction rather than a long list.

title: Biases & heuristics
text:
Two categories that prevent confusion

Judgment vs choice

Judgment biases: errors in beliefs (probabilities, frequencies, causal stories).
Choice biases: shifts in preferences or decisions due to framing, defaults, and context.

A pattern can be both.


Bias vs noise

Bias: systematic direction (predictable).
Noise: randomness (unpredictable variability).

Reducing noise is often easier than “removing” bias.

title: Biases & heuristics
text:
Mechanism 1: Availability (retrieval-driven judgment)
People judge frequency/risk by what comes to mind easily.
Prediction patterns - vivid events feel more common than they are, - recent events dominate risk perception, - repeated exposure increases perceived truth (“familiarity = credibility”).
Common pitfall: interpreting availability as “irrational” when the environment is genuinely changing (recency may be informative).

title: Biases & heuristics
text:
Mechanism 2: Representativeness (pattern-matching)
People assess likelihood by similarity to a stereotype or prototype.
Prediction patterns - base rates are neglected when similarity cues are strong, - small samples are treated as representative (overconfidence), - people see “streaks” in randomness.
Testable intervention: making base rates salient reduces the effect.

title: Biases & heuristics
text:
Mechanism 3: Anchoring (starting-point dependence)
Numerical judgments are pulled toward an initial value, even if arbitrary.
Prediction patterns - first numbers in negotiation or estimation shape outcomes, - adjustments are insufficient, especially under time pressure.
Intervention: generate your own anchor first, or force multiple independent estimates.

title: Biases & heuristics
text:
Mechanism 4: Framing (representation changes choice)
Equivalent descriptions can change the perceived problem.
Prediction patterns - gains vs losses change risk-taking, - “per 100 people” vs “percentage” changes intuitions, - order and grouping of options change perceived attractiveness.
Practical note: framing is often more about attention and categorization than deep preference change.

title: Biases & heuristics
text:
Mechanism 5: Confirmation and asymmetric skepticism
People search for evidence that supports what they already think, and scrutinize opposing evidence more harshly.
Prediction patterns - polarization increases with identity-relevant topics, - mixed evidence leads to stronger prior beliefs (biased assimilation), - people become more confident after consuming selective information.
Intervention: force consideration of strong counterarguments; pre-commit to what evidence would change your mind.

title: Biases & heuristics
text:
Mechanism 6: Overconfidence and miscalibration
People often overestimate accuracy and underestimate uncertainty.
Prediction patterns - too-narrow confidence intervals, - “illusion of control” in noisy environments, - planning fallacy (systematic underestimation of time/cost).
Intervention: reference class forecasting (use similar past projects as priors).

title: Biases & heuristics
section: Mechanism 7: Status quo, defaults, and friction
text:
Mechanism 7: Status quo, defaults, and friction
Doing nothing is often a decision rule.
Prediction patterns - defaults dominate choices when attention is scarce, - small “hassle costs” change behavior a lot, - opt-in vs opt-out designs shift participation dramatically.
Interpretation: not necessarily preference; often an attention/effort allocation outcome.

title: Biases & heuristics
section: Mechanism 8: Affect and arousal (emotion as a driver)
text:
Mechanism 8: Affect and arousal (emotion as a driver)
Feelings shape what seems risky, urgent, or morally acceptable.
Prediction patterns - fear increases threat sensitivity and avoidance, - anger increases punitive choices and perceived intentionality, - stress increases habit reliance and narrows attention.
Links: this connects directly to Emotion & motivation.

title: Biases & heuristics
text:
A compact “bias debugging” checklist
When you see a bias-like pattern, ask: 1) Attention: what information is salient vs hidden? 2) Memory: what examples come to mind? 3) Computation: is the task too complex for working memory? 4) Feedback: is learning noisy, delayed, or selective? 5) Identity/emotion: is the topic threatening or status-relevant? 6) Choice architecture: are defaults/friction doing the work?
If changing (1), (3), or (5) changes behavior, it’s likely not a stable preference.

title: Biases & heuristics
text:
Connections to other pages

Cognition: biases often come from attention, memory, and representation limits.
Decision-making: biases shape both judgment and choice.
Social cognition: identity and norms amplify confirmation and attribution patterns.
Criminology: measurement, reporting, and enforcement contexts interact with bias and salience.

title: Personality
text:
Personality is about stable individual differences in how people think, feel, and behave across time and situations.
A clean stance for notes: - People differ (traits are real and predictive), - Situations matter (context can amplify or suppress traits), - The interesting part is person × situation.

title: Personality
text:
What personality is (in practice)
Personality is typically measured using: - questionnaires (self-report), - informant reports, - behavioral tasks, - digital traces (with caution).
Traits are not “destiny,” but they are: - moderately stable, - meaningfully predictive, - useful for explaining heterogeneity.

title: Personality
text:
The Big Five (high-level map)
A common organizing framework uses five broad dimensions:

Openness: curiosity, imagination, preference for novelty/complexity
Conscientiousness: self-control, planning, persistence, reliability
Extraversion: social energy, assertiveness, positive affect
Agreeableness: cooperation, empathy, conflict avoidance
Neuroticism (emotional instability): sensitivity to threat, negative affect

These are not the only model, but they’re a practical baseline.
Prediction pattern: these traits correlate with typical life outcomes (health behaviors, relationship stability, work patterns), but effects depend strongly on environment.

title: Personality
section: Traits vs states vs skills (avoid a common confusion)
text:
Traits vs states vs skills (avoid a common confusion)

Trait: stable tendency (baseline).
State: temporary condition (stress, fatigue, mood).
Skill: learned capability (self-regulation strategies, social skills).

A person can have: - low baseline self-control (trait), - but strong self-regulation skills (skill), - and still fail under extreme stress (state).

title: Personality
text:
Person × situation: why “traits sometimes disappear”
Behavior is shaped by: - trait tendencies, - incentives and constraints, - norms and roles, - salience and emotional state.
Two environments can produce different behavior from the same person: - in one setting, the trait is expressed, - in another, it’s suppressed by norms or constraints.
Prediction pattern: strong situations (strict rules, high surveillance, high stakes) reduce observed personality differences.

title: Personality
text:
Mechanisms: how personality “shows up”
Traits influence behavior through: - attention (what cues you notice), - interpretation (what stories you tell about events), - emotion (how strongly you react), - habits (default routines), - social strategy (approach/avoid conflict, seek status, seek belonging).
This keeps personality from being “just labels.”

title: Personality
text:
Conscientiousness as the workhorse trait (often)
Conscientiousness is especially linked to: - long-run planning, - persistence, - reliability, - lower impulsivity.
Prediction pattern: in many domains, conscientiousness moderates the impact of present bias and temptation.
Interventions note: skills + environment often outperform “changing the trait.” Examples: - reminders, checklists, friction reduction, - commitment devices, - predictable routines.

title: Personality
section: Dark-side traits and antisocial patterns (careful framing)
text:
Dark-side traits and antisocial patterns (careful framing)
Some personality patterns are associated with: - low empathy, - impulsivity, - antagonism, - thrill-seeking, - manipulativeness.
Use caution: - avoid moralizing labels as explanations, - specify mechanisms (emotion regulation, threat perception, reinforcement history), - distinguish trait disposition from situational triggers.

title: Personality
text:
Measurement cautions (methods-minded)

Self-report is sensitive to self-image and social desirability.
Traits can be distorted by current mood/state.
Cross-cultural measurement invariance matters (same questions may not mean the same thing).

Rule of thumb: treat trait measures as informative but noisy; triangulate when possible.

title: Personality
text:
A reusable explanation template
When using personality in an explanation:

Which trait dimension is relevant?

Which mechanism connects the trait to behavior (attention, emotion, habit, strategy)?

What situation features amplify/suppress expression (rules, monitoring, threat, incentives)?

What prediction follows (who changes behavior under which intervention)?

title: Personality
text:
Connections

Decision-making: personality affects risk tolerance, patience, and self-control expression.
Emotion & motivation: neuroticism relates to threat sensitivity; extraversion relates to positive affect and approach.
Social cognition: agreeableness affects trust and conflict interpretation.
Criminology: trait heterogeneity matters (impulsivity, self-control, antagonism), but should be modeled alongside environment and institutions.

title: Educational psychology
text:
Note



Common UG elective; also a core pillar in many PG tracks (education, learning sciences, educational measurement).

title: Educational psychology
text:
What it is
Educational psychology studies how people learn in real instructional settings, and how we can design environments that reliably produce learning and development. It sits between basic psychology (memory, attention, motivation) and applied decisions (curriculum, assessment, classroom climate, policy).
A useful working split is: - Learning mechanisms: what changes in the learner (knowledge, skills, habits, beliefs). - Instructional design: how tasks, explanations, practice, and feedback shape those changes. - Motivation + context: why learners engage (or avoid), and how classrooms and institutions amplify or block learning. - Measurement: how we infer learning and compare approaches without fooling ourselves.
Links you’ll likely use a lot: - Learning - Measurement - Methods - Motivation & goals - Development - How to study

title: Educational psychology
text:
Core questions

1) What counts as learning?
A simple but strict definition: learning is a durable change in capability (not just a temporary performance bump). This is why short-term “looks good in class” effects can vanish when tested after delay, under transfer, or without cues.


2) Why do smart students fail to learn?
Often it’s not raw ability. Common culprits are: - shallow processing (recognition mistaken for recall), - poor practice scheduling (cramming), - miscalibrated confidence, - attention/working-memory overload, - low expectancy/value or high perceived cost.


3) What is the teacher (or system) optimizing?
Sometimes it’s grades or coverage, not retention or transfer. Edu-psych tries to align incentives and measurement with the actual learning objective.

title: Educational psychology
text:
Learning frameworks used in education

Behaviorist (instruction as shaping)
Reinforcement and practice matter. In modern form this shows up as: - deliberate practice routines, - immediate feedback for procedural skills, - structured scaffolding for early competence.


Cognitive / information-processing (instruction as memory engineering)
The classroom is a pipeline from attention → working memory → long-term memory. Design implications: reduce noise, structure explanations, provide guided practice, and space retrieval.


Social-cognitive (learning as modeling + self-efficacy)
Students learn by observing others and by beliefs about capability (self-efficacy). This connects strongly to: - teacher expectations, - peer effects, - identity and belonging, - attribution patterns after failure.


Constructivist / sociocultural (learning as meaning-making in context)
Knowledge is built through activity and interaction; language and tools matter. This frames: - inquiry-based learning (done well vs done vaguely), - collaborative learning, - zone of proximal development / scaffolding.

title: Educational psychology
text:
Instructional design and cognitive load
A practical lens is: “How much of the student’s limited processing is spent on the target idea vs avoidable friction?”
Typical design levers: - Worked examples → fading (start with full solutions, gradually remove steps). - Segmenting (break complex explanations into chunks). - Dual coding / modality (use words + diagrams thoughtfully, not as decoration). - Retrieval practice (testing as learning, not only evaluation). - Spacing + interleaving (timing and mixture of practice).
If you want the short bridge to your study page: - Retrieval + spacing are the “highest ROI” habits for most academic learning → see How to study.

title: Educational psychology
text:
Motivation, goals, and engagement
Motivation can be treated as a choice under constraints: “Is effort worth it right now?” A common decomposition is:
[ - . ]
Where: - Expectancy: “If I try, can I succeed?” - Value: “Does this matter to me?” - Cost: time, anxiety, effort, opportunity cost, ego threat.
This connects to: - mastery vs performance goal orientations, - self-determination (autonomy/competence/relatedness), - growth mindset vs fixed beliefs (best treated as beliefs + learning design, not slogans), - feedback framing (information vs judgment).
See: Motivation & goals, Self-control.

title: Educational psychology
text:
Assessment and measurement
Assessment is not just grading; it is information that shapes behavior.
Key splits: - Formative: feedback to improve learning during the process. - Summative: certification / selection. - Criterion-referenced vs norm-referenced: “did you meet a standard?” vs “where are you relative to others?”
Measurement pitfalls that show up constantly: - teaching to the test can be good (if the test matches the construct) or destructive (if the test measures a narrow proxy), - reliability vs validity tradeoffs, - short-term performance inflation (especially when items mirror practice too closely), - fairness and differential item functioning across groups.
See: Measurement.

title: Educational psychology
text:
Individual differences and support
Educational psychology also covers why the same instruction produces different outcomes: - prior knowledge and skill prerequisites, - language background, - attention / executive function constraints, - anxiety and stress, - special educational needs / disability accommodations, - home environment and resource constraints.
This overlaps with: - Mental health - Sleep & stress - Development

title: Educational psychology
text:
Classroom climate, relationships, and discipline
Learning is social. The “hidden curriculum” includes norms, identity signals, and trust.
Core ingredients: - psychological safety to ask questions, - teacher–student relationship quality, - norms around effort and help-seeking, - predictable routines and fair discipline, - peer effects (both academic and behavioral).
(If you want the institutional angle later, this ties nicely to your overlaps pages on institutions and policy.)

title: Educational psychology
text:
Evidence: what counts as “works”?
Edu-psych is full of interventions that sound right but fail under replication or scale. A useful hierarchy: - theory → mechanism → measurable intermediate outcomes → durable learning → transfer → real-world outcomes.
Methods you’ll see often: - classroom RCTs with cluster randomization, - quasi-experiments (policy changes, cutoff rules), - longitudinal models (growth curves), - meta-analysis (with all the usual publication-bias worries).
See: Methods.

title: Educational psychology
text:
Common traps and myths

“Learning styles” as matching instruction to a fixed style (weak evidence; the better move is varied representations + retrieval).
Confusing engagement with learning (fun ≠ retention).
Overvaluing immediate fluency (easy processing today can mean weak memory tomorrow).
Treating motivation as a pure personality trait rather than a design + context outcome.

title: Educational psychology
section: A practical checklist for building a course or self-study plan
text:
A practical checklist for building a course or self-study plan

Define the learning targets as capabilities (what can the learner do).
Design practice that forces retrieval, not recognition.
Space practice over weeks; revisit core ideas repeatedly.
Use feedback that diagnoses errors (not just “right/wrong”).
Measure learning after delay and under transfer tasks.
Keep costs low: reduce friction, anxiety triggers, and pointless complexity.

title: Educational psychology
text:
Suggested anchors to read (later)
If you ever want a small bibliography page, typical anchors include work on: - cognitive load / worked examples, - retrieval practice and spacing, - formative assessment, - motivation and expectancy–value, - classroom climate and teacher effects.

title: Motivation & goals
text: Motivation determines what people try to do, how much effort they invest, and what tradeoffs they accept. Goals don’t just guide action — they also guide attention, memory, and interpretation.

title: Motivation & goals
text:
Goal types

Approach vs avoidance

Approach: pursue desirable outcomes.
Avoidance: prevent negative outcomes.

Avoidance goals can dominate attention and produce short-horizon “relief” strategies.


Mastery vs performance

Mastery: improve competence, learn.
Performance: look competent, avoid looking bad.

Prediction pattern: performance focus increases anxiety and risk-avoidance; mastery focus increases persistence and learning.

title: Motivation & goals
text:
Intrinsic vs extrinsic motivation

Intrinsic: doing the task is rewarding.
Extrinsic: task is a means to an external reward.

Prediction pattern: heavy external control can reduce intrinsic engagement when it changes the meaning from “I choose” to “I’m being controlled.”

title: Motivation & goals
text:
Goal conflict and self-regulation
People often hold multiple goals that conflict: - study vs social media, - fairness vs self-interest, - honesty vs reputation.
Conflict resolution depends on: - salience (which goal is active), - state (stress/fatigue), - identity (what kind of person I am), - environment (friction/defaults).
Prediction pattern: making long-run goals salient at decision time improves alignment without changing values.

title: Motivation & goals
section: Motivation under uncertainty: expectancy × value (practical lens)
text:
Motivation under uncertainty: expectancy × value (practical lens)
Effort tends to rise with: - expectancy (belief that effort helps), - value (importance of the outcome).
Failures often come from: - low expectancy (“it won’t matter”), - unclear value (“why do this?”), - high immediate costs.
Intervention levers - increase expectancy via feedback and progress signals, - increase value via meaning/identity framing, - reduce immediate costs via environment design.

title: Motivation & goals
section: Social motivation: status, belonging, and norms
text:
Social motivation: status, belonging, and norms
People are motivated by: - approval and belonging, - status and respect, - avoidance of shame.
Prediction pattern: peer environments can outpower individual incentives.

title: Motivation & goals
text:
A reusable template
To explain motivated behavior, specify:

Which goal is active (approach/avoidance; mastery/performance)

Expectancy and value (why try?)

Immediate costs (effort, fear, shame, opportunity cost)

Identity and norms (who am I here?)

Prediction: what shifts if you change salience, feedback, or social audience?

title: Motivation & goals
text:
Connections

Self-control: motivation interacts with cues and commitment.
Emotion & motivation: emotions shift goal priority.
Norms & groups: identity and belonging shape goal choice.
Institutions: incentives work better when they align with identity and legitimacy.

title: Topics
text:

They sit on top of Foundations (cognition, learning, decision-making, emotion, social cognition, methods).
