title: Person perception
text:
Person perception is how we form impressions: who is trustworthy, dangerous, competent, or worth listening to. It drives hiring, friendship, conflict, stigma, authority legitimacy, and persuasion.
This page is about rapid inference under uncertainty.

title: Person perception
text:
Two core dimensions (practical, not absolute)
A lot of impressions can be summarized as: - Warmth: intent toward me/us (friend or threat?) - Competence: ability to act (capable or ineffective?)
These shape: - trust and cooperation (warmth), - deference and reliance (competence).
Prediction pattern: changing perceived intent often moves behavior more than changing perceived ability.

title: Person perception
text:
Thin slices and cue use
People infer from: - facial expression, tone, posture, - clothing, group markers, - fluency and confidence, - context (roles: “police”, “doctor”, “student”).
Thin-slice inference can be useful but error-prone.
Prediction pattern: under time pressure, people rely more on surface cues and stereotypes.

title: Person perception
text:
Attribution: intent vs constraint
Judgment often depends on: - perceived intentionality, - perceived constraints, - perceived controllability.
Prediction pattern: providing situational constraints reduces blame and moralized judgment.

title: Person perception
text:
Stereotypes as low-cost representations
Stereotypes reduce cognitive load but can become self-reinforcing: - selective attention to confirming evidence, - misinterpretation of ambiguous behavior, - avoidance reduces counter-evidence.
Prediction pattern: increasing cross-group contact under safe conditions reduces reliance on stereotypes.

title: Person perception
text:
Trust cues and credibility heuristics
People judge credibility using: - track record, expertise, institutional role, - confidence and fluency, - in-group membership.
Pitfall: fluency and confidence can be mistaken for truth.
Prediction pattern: trusted messengers outperform stronger arguments from distrusted messengers.

title: Person perception
text:
Error patterns to watch

Halo effect: one positive trait colors others.
Negativity dominance: one bad signal outweighs many good ones.
Fundamental attribution tendency: trait-blame over situation.
Out-group homogeneity: “they are all the same.”

title: Person perception
text:
A reusable template
When analyzing person perception, specify:

What cues are visible and salient

Warmth/intent inference vs competence/ability inference

Situational constraints that are ignored or unseen

Group boundaries (identity)

Prediction: what shifts with more time, more context, or different messenger?

title: Person perception
text:
Connections

Social cognition: theory of mind + attribution.
Communication: credibility, persuasion, distrust.
Norms & groups: identity shapes interpretation.
Criminology: legitimacy, threat interpretation, escalation.

title: Conceptual & historical issues
text:
Psychology has recurring debates about: - what counts as explanation, - how to connect mind, brain, and society, - how to measure invisible constructs, - how to interpret evidence and replication.
Many UG programs include “conceptual and historical issues” because it prevents two failures: - treating today’s terms as eternal truths, - mistaking methods for theories.
This page is a toolkit for thinking clearly, not a timeline quiz.

title: Conceptual & historical issues
text:
1) The “big moves” in psychology (high-level)

Introspection and early measurement
Early psychology tried to study experience directly (introspection), but found limits: - reports are biased by language, memory, and social desirability.
Lesson: self-report is informative but not a transparent window.


Behaviorism (behavior as the object)
Behaviorism emphasized: - observable behavior, - learning via reinforcement, - skepticism about unobservables.
Contribution: rigorous learning theory, experimental discipline.
Limit: struggles with representation, language, and flexible reasoning.


The cognitive revolution (representation returns)
Cognitive approaches reintroduced: - mental representations, - information processing, - attention and memory limits.
Contribution: mechanisms for thinking and perception.
Limit: risk of treating humans like disembodied computers unless emotion and social context are included.


Social and cultural turns
Social psychology emphasized: - norms, identity, roles, - institutions and group processes, - meaning and context.
Contribution: behavior is embedded in social systems.
Limit: risk of context-specific findings unless boundary conditions are made explicit.


Biological and neuroscientific integration
Biopsychology and neuroscience added: - implementation constraints (brain/body), - physiology of stress, sleep, arousal, - causal tests via lesion/perturbation.
Lesson: biology constrains and enables psychology, but does not replace it.

title: Conceptual & historical issues
text:
2) Levels of explanation (the anti-confusion framework)
A single phenomenon can be explained at multiple levels:

Functional: what problem does this solve? (e.g., detect threat)
Algorithmic: what process runs? (attention narrowing, appraisal)
Implementation: what supports it biologically? (arousal circuits, hormones)

Rule: don’t treat a lower level as “more real.” Better explanations connect levels.

title: Conceptual & historical issues
text:
3) The “construct problem”
Psychology studies unobservables (trust, anxiety, self-control). The danger is reification: - treating the label as the thing.
Rule: every construct must have: - operational definition, - measurement plan, - prediction commitments.
This links directly to your Measurement page.

title: Conceptual & historical issues
section: 4) Nature vs nurture (mostly a bad question)
text:
4) Nature vs nurture (mostly a bad question)
A better framing: - behavior arises from gene × environment × development interactions.
Most interesting questions are: - which environments amplify a vulnerability? - which experiences build resilience? - what interventions change trajectories?
Practical note: “biological” does not mean “fixed.”

title: Conceptual & historical issues
section: 5) Person vs situation (why both are true)
text:
5) Person vs situation (why both are true)
Two statements can both be true: - people differ (traits matter), - situations shape behavior strongly.
The key is: > Person × situation interactions explain when traits show up.
Strong situations (high surveillance, strong norms, high stakes) compress individual differences.

title: Conceptual & historical issues
text:
6) What is a “good” psychological theory?
A useful theory should provide: 1) clear constructs, 2) mechanism specification, 3) testable predictions, 4) boundary conditions, 5) ability to integrate with neighboring domains (bio, social, institutions).
Red flag: a theory that “explains” everything explains nothing.

title: Conceptual & historical issues
section: 7) Replication, generalization, and why psychology argues about it
text:
7) Replication, generalization, and why psychology argues about it
Modern psychology has emphasized: - replication (does the effect reproduce?), - generalization (does it hold across contexts?), - transparency (preregistration, open data, robust reporting).
You don’t need to be technical to apply the lesson: - treat single studies as suggestive, - look for converging evidence, - prioritize mechanisms and boundary conditions.
Practical rule: prefer claims that survive changes in measurement, sample, and setting.

title: Conceptual & historical issues
section: 8) Ethics and the subjectivity of participants
text:
8) Ethics and the subjectivity of participants
Psych research is unusually sensitive to: - demand characteristics, - deception and consent, - power dynamics, - stigma.
Lesson: ethics is not only moral; it affects data quality.

title: Conceptual & historical issues
section: 9) A reusable “conceptual check” for any claim
text:
9) A reusable “conceptual check” for any claim
When you read or write a claim, ask:

What is the construct? operational definition?

What is the mechanism? not just a label?

What is the evidence? and what are its limits?

What would falsify it?

Where does it generalize? and where not?

What level is this claim at? (functional/algorithmic/implementation)

What are the ethical/measurement confounds?

If you can answer these, your notes will look “university-level.”

title: Conceptual & historical issues
text:
Connections

Foundations: methods, measurement, biopsychology, cognition
Topics: biases, personality, cultural psychology (later)
Overlaps: institutions (power, legitimacy), communication (demand effects), policy design (external validity)

title: Neuroscience methods
text:
This page explains what common neuroscience methods can and cannot tell you, in a way that stays useful even if specific technologies change.
A simple rule: > Methods answer different questions: where, when, what correlates, what causes, what is necessary.
Neuro evidence is powerful when it constrains theories — not when it replaces them with “brain pictures.”

title: Neuroscience methods
section: 1) What neuro methods are for (the question map)
text:
1) What neuro methods are for (the question map)
Neuroscience methods are often used to answer:

Localization: where in the brain does activity relate to a task?
Timing: when do processes occur (early perception vs later evaluation)?
Necessity: is a region/system required for a function?
Causality: what happens when we perturb a system?
Mechanism constraints: does the brain implement your theory in a plausible way?

A good paper makes clear which of these it’s claiming.

title: Neuroscience methods
text:
2) fMRI (functional magnetic resonance imaging)

What it measures (conceptually)
fMRI measures changes related to blood oxygenation (a proxy for neural activity), with a delay.


What it is good for

spatial patterns (rough “where”)
comparing conditions (task A vs task B)
linking networks to tasks



What it is not good for

fine-grained timing (“when exactly”)
proving causality by itself
reading thoughts (in general use)

Pitfalls - reverse inference: “region X lit up, so emotion Y happened” - ignoring that many processes share the same regions
Best use: constrain competing psychological theories by showing which network patterns align with which processes.

title: Neuroscience methods
text:
3) EEG / ERP (electroencephalography / event-related potentials)

What it measures
Electrical activity at the scalp, reflecting synchronous neural activity.


What it is good for

timing (“when” processes occur)
differentiating early sensory processing vs later decision stages
studying attention and error monitoring



Limits

localization is coarse (harder to say exactly “where”)
sensitive to noise (movement, environment)

Best use: connect cognitive stages (perception → attention → evaluation) to time.

title: Neuroscience methods
text:
4) MEG (magnetoencephalography) (conceptual note)
MEG measures magnetic fields from neural activity. It is often treated as: - timing like EEG, - localization better than EEG (still not perfect).
You don’t need to emphasize it unless you later want a “methods completeness” section.

title: Neuroscience methods
text:
5) Lesion and patient studies

What they are
Study behavior after brain injury or neurological conditions.


What they are good for

necessity claims: “when this system is damaged, function F is impaired”
dissociations: one ability can break while another remains intact



Limits

lesions are rarely clean or identical across people
compensation and reorganization can occur
interpretation needs careful cognitive modeling

Best use: demonstrate constraints and dissociations that any theory must respect.

title: Neuroscience methods
text:
6) TMS / tDCS (brain stimulation and modulation)

TMS (transcranial magnetic stimulation)
Uses magnetic pulses to temporarily disrupt or alter neural activity.
Good for - causal tests: what changes when region/system is perturbed? - mapping functional roles under controlled tasks
Limits - limited depth (mostly cortex) - effects can be variable across people - “where” and “how” claims must be careful


tDCS (transcranial direct current stimulation)
Applies weak currents; effects are often smaller and more variable.
Best use: treat as “modulatory evidence,” not decisive proof.

title: Neuroscience methods
text:
7) Psychophysiology (body measures)
Includes: - heart rate variability, skin conductance, pupil dilation - hormone sampling (e.g., cortisol) - breathing patterns, startle reflex
Good for - arousal and stress responses - threat sensitivity and regulation dynamics
Limits - arousal ≠ one specific emotion - social context changes physiology strongly
Best use: connect stress/arousal to attention narrowing, habit dominance, and emotional reactivity.

title: Neuroscience methods
text:
8) Pharmacology (conceptual)
Studying behavior under substances that modulate neurotransmitter systems.
Good for - suggesting causal involvement of neurotransmitter systems - understanding mechanism plausibility
Limits - drugs have broad effects (not clean single-lever interventions) - individual differences and context matter
Best use: triangulate with behavioral and neural evidence.

title: Neuroscience methods
text:
9) Animal and comparative methods (conceptual note)
Animal models allow: - invasive measurement, - precise control, - causal circuit interventions.
But translation to human cognition: - is strongest for basic learning, reward, threat, and physiology - is weaker for language, complex social institutions, and moral reasoning.
Best use: use animal evidence to support foundational mechanisms, not to “explain society.”

title: Neuroscience methods
text:
10) What makes neuro evidence persuasive? (triangulation)
Neuroscience is most convincing when: - behavioral findings replicate, - neural evidence matches the predicted mechanism, - perturbation/lesion evidence supports necessity/causality, - results generalize across tasks and samples.
Rule: one fMRI result is rarely decisive; converging evidence is.

title: Neuroscience methods
text:
Common interpretive errors (quick list)

Reverse inference: region activation → specific mental state (too strong)
Neuro-essentialism: “because brain, it’s more real”
Overlocalization: treating networks as isolated modules
Ignoring task impurity: tasks rarely measure only one mechanism
Causality leap: correlational neural evidence treated as causal

title: Neuroscience methods
text:
A reusable method-selection template
When you want to study a psychological mechanism, write:

Mechanism hypothesis (algorithmic level)

Behavioral predictions

What would count as evidence against it

Choose method by question:

where? fMRI
when? EEG/ERP
necessary? lesions
causal perturbation? TMS
arousal/stress? physiology/hormones

Triangulate across at least two methods

title: Neuroscience methods
text:
Connections

Foundations: biopsychology, cognition, attention & memory, measurement, methods
Topics: sensation & perception, addiction & compulsion, mental health
Overlaps: policy design (interpretation caution), criminology (stress physiology, threat)

title: Beliefs, uncertainty, and confidence
text:
Beliefs are internal models of the world: what is true, how likely it is, and what causes what.
This page focuses on how beliefs form and change under limited information, limited attention, and social influence.
A key theme: > People update beliefs using evidence and psychological constraints (salience, identity, emotion, trust).

title: Beliefs, uncertainty, and confidence
text:
Three objects to track
When discussing beliefs, separate:

Level: what do I think is true?

Uncertainty: how sure am I?

Calibration: does confidence match accuracy?

Many disputes are really disputes about (2) and (3).

title: Beliefs, uncertainty, and confidence
text:
Sources of belief
Beliefs come from: - personal experience, - testimony and communication, - institutions (official reports, rules, signals), - social networks and norms, - memory (which is reconstructive).
Prediction pattern: beliefs become “sticky” when they are tied to identity or repeated through social reinforcement.

title: Beliefs, uncertainty, and confidence
section: Updating under uncertainty: why it deviates from ideal Bayesian updating
text:
Updating under uncertainty: why it deviates from ideal Bayesian updating
Even when people try to be rational, updating is constrained by:

1) Salience and availability
Evidence that is vivid, recent, or emotionally charged is overweighted.
Prediction pattern: salient events produce spikes in perceived risk that decay over time.


2) Selective attention and selective exposure
People seek information that fits goals and identity, and avoid costly dissonance.
Prediction pattern: information diets become polarized even without explicit propaganda.


3) Asymmetric skepticism
People scrutinize disconfirming evidence more harshly than confirming evidence.
Prediction pattern: mixed evidence can increase confidence rather than reduce it (biased assimilation).


4) Trust and source credibility
People treat sources as part of the data: - “Is this person competent?” - “Are they honest?” - “Are they on my side?”
Prediction pattern: same facts produce different belief change across trust groups.

title: Beliefs, uncertainty, and confidence
text:
Causal beliefs: stories beat statistics
People strongly prefer causal narratives: - “X caused Y because …” - “This type of person does …” - “This policy leads to …”
Causal learning is hard when: - multiple causes move together, - feedback is delayed, - systems adapt strategically.
Prediction pattern: people overinfer causality from small samples and salient coincidences.

title: Beliefs, uncertainty, and confidence
text:
Confidence: the underappreciated variable
Confidence drives behavior: - willingness to act, - willingness to punish, - willingness to speak, - openness to learning.
But confidence is often miscalibrated.

Overconfidence and underconfidence

Overconfidence can produce excessive risk-taking or premature commitment.
Underconfidence can produce paralysis and overreliance on authority.

Prediction pattern: reducing uncertainty (clearer feedback, better measurement) changes behavior even if belief levels don’t move much.

title: Beliefs, uncertainty, and confidence
text:
Metacognition: knowing what you know
Metacognition is the ability to monitor: - how accurate you are, - when you’re guessing, - when you need more information.
Metacognition degrades under: - stress, - time pressure, - strong emotion, - social threat.
Prediction pattern: hostile environments reduce honest uncertainty expression (“everyone must sound certain”).

title: Beliefs, uncertainty, and confidence
section: Social belief dynamics: cascades and pluralistic ignorance
text:
Social belief dynamics: cascades and pluralistic ignorance
Beliefs spread socially, sometimes creating: - information cascades: people copy others because they assume others know more. - pluralistic ignorance: people privately disagree but assume others agree, so they stay silent.
Prediction patterns - Public signals can trigger rapid belief shifts. - Small visible minorities can shape perceived norms disproportionately.

title: Beliefs, uncertainty, and confidence
text:
A reusable belief analysis template
When explaining belief formation or change, specify:

Evidence: what information exists and who sees it?

Trust: which sources are credible to whom?

Salience: what is vivid vs statistical?

Identity: what beliefs are socially rewarded?

Uncertainty: how confident are people, and is it calibrated?

Feedback: is correction fast, slow, or absent?

Prediction: what changes if you change visibility, messenger, or feedback?

title: Beliefs, uncertainty, and confidence
text:
Connections

Learning: beliefs update differently from habits; both matter.
Decision-making: confidence and uncertainty shape risk and action.
Communication overlap: trust, framing, and identity determine belief change.
Criminology overlap: perceived risk, legitimacy, and rumor dynamics drive cooperation and compliance.

title: Social cognition
text:
Social cognition studies how people perceive, interpret, and predict other people—their beliefs, intentions, emotions, and future actions. It is the psychological machinery behind coordination, conflict, trust, stigma, reputation, and norms.
A useful way to think about it:
social cognition = inference about minds + inference about situations + inference about groups.

title: Social cognition
text:
Core questions

What is this person like? (traits, character, identity)
What does this person want? (goals, incentives, motives)
What does this person know or believe? (information, ignorance, uncertainty)
What will they do next? (prediction, forecasting, response)
What do “people like us” do here? (norms, roles, scripts)

title: Social cognition
text:
Mechanisms map

1) Theory of mind (mentalizing)
Theory of mind is the capacity to represent others’ beliefs and intentions, including the possibility that others hold false beliefs.

Low mentalizing: “They see what I see.”
Higher mentalizing: “They think I think …” (recursive reasoning, but limited depth in practice).

Prediction pattern: when tasks require more steps of “I think you think,” performance drops sharply, especially under time pressure or stress.
Common pitfall: treating theory of mind as all-or-nothing. In reality it varies by context, load, familiarity, and incentives.


2) Attribution: person vs situation
When explaining behavior, people often choose between: - dispositional explanations (“that’s who they are”), and - situational explanations (“that’s what the environment made likely”).
A classic regularity: people often overweight dispositions relative to situations, especially when judging others.
Prediction pattern: providing salient situational information (constraints, incentives, background) shifts judgments and reduces moralized blame.


3) Social perception: rapid, low-data inference
Humans make fast judgments from sparse cues (face, tone, posture, labels). This can be adaptive but error-prone.
Two recurring dimensions in impressions: - Warmth (intentions: friend or threat?) - Competence (ability: can they act on intentions?)
These map naturally into many social outcomes: trust, fear, respect, pity, contempt.


4) Identity and self-categorization
People do not only think as individuals; they also think as members of groups: - “people like me” - “people like them” - “what we do”
Identity changes what is salient: - what evidence feels credible, - what behavior feels appropriate, - what costs feel worth paying.
Prediction pattern: making a shared identity salient increases cooperation; making subgroup divisions salient increases conflict and misinterpretation.


5) Norms and social scripts
A huge amount of behavior is “rule-following” without explicit deliberation. Norms specify: - what is typical (descriptive norms), - what is approved (injunctive norms).
Scripts specify “what happens next” in familiar settings (classrooms, clinics, police stops, interviews).
Prediction pattern: changing perceived descriptive norms can change behavior even when incentives do not (people follow what they think most others do).


6) Reputation and indirect reciprocity
People care about how they are seen. Reputation can substitute for direct enforcement.
Key ingredients: - observability (who sees what), - interpretability (what the action means), - memory (how long it sticks), - audience incentives (who benefits from punishing or praising).
Prediction pattern: making actions public increases pro-social behavior, but can also create performative or status-seeking distortions.

title: Social cognition
text:
Limits and distortions (important)
Social cognition is powerful but systematically constrained.

Cognitive load and stress
Under load, people: - mentalize less deeply, - rely more on stereotypes and scripts, - become more sensitive to threat cues.


Motivated reasoning
When identity, emotion, or self-image is at stake, beliefs can shift toward what is psychologically comfortable: - selective attention to confirming evidence, - asymmetric skepticism (harsh on “their” claims, lenient on “ours”), - post-hoc rationalization.


Miscalibration about others
Common misbeliefs include: - false consensus (“most people think like me”), - pluralistic ignorance (“others privately disagree but go along”), - spotlight effects (overestimating how much others notice us), - fundamental attribution tendency (over-blaming traits for others).

title: Social cognition
text:
A reusable explanation template
When you explain a social outcome, try:

Situation: what is the environment (stakes, time, observability, roles)?

Inference: what does each side think the other believes/wants?

Identity & norms: what categories and norms are active?

Emotion: what affective state is present (fear, anger, shame)?

Action: what behavior follows (cooperate, punish, withdraw, attack)?

Feedback: what is learned; what reputation update occurs?

title: Social cognition
text:
Canonical examples (stubs you can expand)

Example A: Misinterpretation cascade

A ambiguous action is interpreted as hostile.
That interpretation triggers defensive behavior.
The defensive behavior is interpreted as confirmation.
The relationship locks into conflict.

Mechanisms: attribution bias + threat sensitivity + reputation concerns.


Example B: Norm enforcement without police

People punish or shame norm violators even at personal cost.
Observers cooperate more when punishment is visible.

Mechanisms: injunctive norms + reputation + indirect reciprocity.

title: Social cognition
section: Connections to other sections on the site
text:
Connections to other sections on the site

Criminology

Legitimacy and compliance: trust in authorities depends on perceived intentions (warmth/fairness) and competence.
Reporting and cooperation: social identity, fear of retaliation, and perceived norms shape willingness to report.
Violence and escalation: misattribution plus threat sensitivity can produce rapid escalation.



Game-theory overlap (kept light here)
Social cognition supplies the psychological primitives behind strategic interaction: - depth-limited belief reasoning, - reputation and signaling, - norm-based preferences (approval, shame, guilt), - audience effects and public observability.

title: Social cognition
section: What to read next (within this notes system)
text:
What to read next (within this notes system)

Emotion & motivation (how anger, guilt, shame, and threat shape social inference)
Decision-making (how heuristics and framing distort interpersonal judgment)
Methods (how to test social cognition claims without falling into “storytelling”)

title: Sensation & perception
text:
Sensation is the detection of physical energy (light, sound, pressure).
Perception is the brain’s inference about what is out there.
A useful stance: > Perception is not recording. It is construction under uncertainty.
This page gives the core ideas commonly taught in UG psychology: bottom-up vs top-down, attention, and why perception can be systematically wrong.

title: Sensation & perception
text:
1) The perception pipeline (minimal)

Input (stimulus)
Transduction (sense organs convert energy into neural signals)
Early processing (basic features)
Integration (objects, scenes, meaning)
Interpretation (inference using context and expectations)
Action (what you do with it)

Many “errors” are predictable consequences of step (5).

title: Sensation & perception
text:
2) Bottom-up vs top-down processing

Bottom-up (data-driven)
Perception is driven by the stimulus: - contrast, edges, loudness, motion, timing.


Top-down (model-driven)
Perception is shaped by: - expectations, - goals, - context, - prior knowledge, - emotion and threat.
Prediction patterns - ambiguity increases top-down influence (people “see” what they expect). - stress and threat bias interpretation toward danger. - labels and categories change what is perceived (not only what is reported).

title: Sensation & perception
section: 3) Signal detection: sensitivity vs decision criterion (conceptual)
text:
3) Signal detection: sensitivity vs decision criterion (conceptual)
In many tasks, perception involves distinguishing signal from noise.
Two separable things: - Sensitivity: how well you can detect differences - Criterion: how willing you are to say “I detect it”
Prediction patterns - when costs of misses are high, people adopt a “liberal” criterion (report more detections, more false alarms) - when costs of false alarms are high, people adopt a “conservative” criterion (fewer reports, more misses)
This is a key bridge to: - threat detection, - eyewitness identification, - security screening, - clinical symptom reporting.

title: Sensation & perception
section: 4) Attention and perception: what you don’t attend to, you don’t perceive
text:
4) Attention and perception: what you don’t attend to, you don’t perceive
Attention selects information for deeper processing.
Prediction patterns - inattentional blindness: people miss salient events when attention is elsewhere - change blindness: large changes can go unnoticed without attention - divided attention reduces integration and increases reliance on heuristics
Design implication: if something is critical, make it salient at the moment it matters.

title: Sensation & perception
text:
5) Perceptual constancies (why perception seems stable)
The world changes (lighting, distance), but perception often remains stable: - size constancy, - color constancy, - loudness constancy.
These are achievements of inference systems that correct for context.
Prediction pattern: constancies can produce systematic illusions in unusual contexts.

title: Sensation & perception
text:
6) Illusions as diagnostics
Illusions matter because they show: - what assumptions the perceptual system is using, - when top-down inference dominates.
Takeaway: perception is optimized for typical environments, not for perfect accuracy in all cases.

title: Sensation & perception
text:
7) Multisensory integration (how senses combine)
The brain integrates signals across modalities: - vision + hearing for speech perception, - touch + vision for object inference.
Integration depends on: - timing alignment, - spatial alignment, - prior expectation that the sources belong together.
Prediction pattern: when signals conflict, perception can be dominated by the modality treated as more reliable in context.

title: Sensation & perception
text:
8) Perception, emotion, and threat
Perception is biased by affective state: - threat increases vigilance and pessimistic interpretation of ambiguity - anxiety increases attention to threat cues - anger increases perceived intentionality and hostility
Prediction pattern: safety and predictability widen attention and improve discrimination.
This is the bridge to: - stress & hot states in criminology, - institutional encounters and legitimacy, - interpersonal conflict escalation.

title: Sensation & perception
text:
A reusable perception explanation template
When analyzing a perceptual phenomenon, specify:

Stimulus ambiguity: how noisy or unclear is the input?

Goal state: what does the person want/avoid?

Context: what expectations are activated?

Attention: what is attended vs ignored?

Criterion: is the person set to detect more (false alarms) or less (misses)?

Prediction: what changes if you change costs, salience, or safety?

title: Sensation & perception
text:
Canonical examples (stubs you can expand)

Example A: Threat detection in ambiguous environments

ambiguity is high,
costs of missing threat feel huge,
criterion shifts toward “better safe than sorry.”

Mechanisms: criterion shift + top-down threat bias


Example B: Eyewitness perception under stress

high arousal narrows attention,
encoding is selective,
later recall is reconstructive.

Mechanisms: attention narrowing + memory reconstruction

title: Sensation & perception
text:
Connections

Foundations: attention & memory, cognition, social cognition (perceiving intentions), biopsychology (sensory systems), sleep & stress
Topics: biases (availability and framing start with attention), person perception
Overlaps: criminology (witnessing, threat), institutions (procedures reduce ambiguity), communication (framing changes perception)

title: Decision-making
text: Decision-making is about how people map uncertainty + preferences + constraints into choices. Psychology differs from “textbook rational choice” mainly by emphasizing: - limited attention, - limited computation, - context effects, - emotion and motivation, - social and moral preferences.

title: Decision-making
text:
Map of this topic
Use this page as the overview, and branch out when you want more detail:

Risk & uncertainty → reference points, loss sensitivity, probability weighting

Time & self-control → present focus, temptation, commitment

Judgment & heuristics → shortcuts, cue-use, framing, bounded computation

Choice architecture → defaults, friction, salience, ordering effects

Social decision-making → fairness, reciprocity, identity, norms (can live here or under Social cognition / Topics)

(Create subpages later if you want; this overview stays stable.)

title: Decision-making
text:
A minimal decomposition
A decision process can be separated into: 1) Representation: what options do I even see? 2) Evaluation: how do I assign value (including risk and time)? 3) Choice rule: how do I select (maximization vs satisficing vs habits)? 4) Learning: how do I update after feedback?
A lot of disagreement across theories is really disagreement about (1) and (3).

title: Decision-making
section: Risk: why people don’t behave like expected utility
text:
Risk: why people don’t behave like expected utility
Common psychological regularities (high-level): - Reference dependence: outcomes feel like gains/losses relative to a reference point. - Loss sensitivity: losses tend to loom larger than equally-sized gains. - Probability weighting: small probabilities may be overweighted; moderate/large may be underweighted. - Framing effects: equivalent descriptions can change choice by changing representation.
Pitfall: calling this “irrational” too early. Often it’s a mismatch between the analyst’s representation and the subject’s.

title: Decision-making
text:
Time: present bias and self-control
When decisions involve time (study now vs game now; save vs spend): - People often behave as if they put extra weight on the present. - This creates “planner vs doer” conflicts: preferences differ across time.
Prediction pattern: commitment devices can increase follow-through even without changing incentives.

title: Decision-making
section: Heuristics: not just shortcuts, but strategies
text:
Heuristics: not just shortcuts, but strategies
Heuristics are often: - fast, - robust under noise, - adapted to common environments.
Useful lens: heuristics trade off accuracy vs cost (attention, time, computation).

title: Decision-making
text:
Canonical example template (reuse later)
When you add examples, write them in this form: - Task: what is being decided? - Normative benchmark: what would a standard rational model predict? - Observed behavior: what pattern appears? - Mechanism: what cognitive/emotional/social process explains it? - Intervention: what changes the behavior (information, framing, incentives, commitment)?

title: Decision-making
section: Where this connects to the rest of the site
text:
Where this connects to the rest of the site

Social cognition: decisions depend on perceived intentions, norms, identity, and reputation.
Learning: feedback changes preferences, habits, and beliefs over time.
Criminology: risk/time preferences and self-control show up in offending, compliance, and deterrence responses.
Overlap with strategic interaction: depth limits, miscalibration about others, and social emotions change outcomes in interactive settings.

title: Attention & memory
text:
This page zooms in on two bottlenecks that explain a huge amount of behavior: - attention (what gets selected for processing), - memory (what gets stored and what gets retrieved later).
A recurring theme: > People often fail not because they “prefer” something, but because they never processed the relevant information, or can’t retrieve it when needed.

title: Attention & memory
text:
Attention: selection under scarcity
Attention is limited. It is pulled by: - goal relevance (what you’re trying to do), - novelty (what’s new), - threat (what might harm you), - emotion (what feels intense), - social cues (faces, status signals).

Selective attention
People focus on a subset of information and ignore the rest.
Prediction patterns - Making a cue visually prominent changes choices even if nothing “objective” changes. - Under time pressure, attention narrows and “second-order” considerations drop out. - When information is spread across screens/pages, integration fails.
Design lever: place the key cue at the point of action; reduce competing salience.


Inattentional blindness (practical takeaway)
People can miss obvious signals when attention is elsewhere.
Prediction pattern: adding more information can worsen outcomes if it increases clutter.


Divided attention
Multitasking reduces performance on tasks needing working memory.
Prediction pattern: errors rise sharply when tasks require integration across steps.

title: Attention & memory
section: Memory: storage and retrieval are both active processes
text:
Memory: storage and retrieval are both active processes
Memory is not a recording device. It is: - selective in encoding, - reconstructive in retrieval, - shaped by emotion and meaning.

Encoding: what gets stored
Encoding is stronger when: - attention is focused, - information is meaningful or structured, - there is repetition, - emotional salience tags it.
Prediction pattern: “I read it but forgot” often means it was never encoded well (attention/structure issue).


Retrieval: what comes to mind drives judgment
Retrieval is cue-dependent. What is easiest to retrieve feels: - more common, - more important, - more true.
This underlies availability-driven judgments.
Prediction pattern: recent or vivid events disproportionately shape perceived risk.


Reconstruction and distortion
When recalling, people fill gaps with: - schemas (“what usually happens”), - identity-consistent narratives, - emotion-consistent interpretations.
Prediction pattern: confidence in memory can be high even when details are wrong.

title: Attention & memory
section: Working memory: the small scratchpad behind reasoning
text:
Working memory: the small scratchpad behind reasoning
Working memory supports: - holding goals active, - comparing options, - multi-step reasoning (“if A then B then C”).
It is small and fragile.
Prediction patterns - As reasoning steps increase, accuracy drops quickly. - Stress, sleep loss, and threat reduce working memory capacity. - People switch to simpler heuristics when working memory is overloaded.

title: Attention & memory
text:
The “attention → memory → choice” chain
Many interventions work because they modify this chain: - attention determines what gets encoded, - memory determines what gets retrieved, - retrieved content shapes judgment and choice.
Example pattern - Reminder cues improve behavior not by changing preferences, but by changing retrieval.

title: Attention & memory
text:
A reusable analysis template
When someone “should have known better,” ask:

Attention: did they notice the relevant cue at the moment?

Encoding: was it stored in memory (repetition/meaning)?

Retrieval: was the right memory available (correct cue)?

Working memory: was the task too multi-step?

Prediction: what happens if you reduce clutter, add reminders, or simplify steps?

title: Attention & memory
text:
Connections

Cognition: this is the “detailed mechanics” layer.
Decision-making: salience and retrieval shift perceived probabilities and values.
Learning: encoding/retrieval determine what gets reinforced and generalized.
Sleep & stress: strongly modulate attention and memory.
Methods: measurement of memory and attention is sensitive to task design and demand effects.

title: Biopsychology
text:
Biopsychology (biological psychology / psychobiology) studies how brain, body, and behavior connect. It does not replace psychological explanation; it adds a second layer:
A good biopsych explanation links: > mechanism in the mind ↔︎ mechanism in the body ↔︎ observable behavior
This page is a non-technical foundation: enough to read university-level material without getting lost.

title: Biopsychology
section: The core idea: levels of explanation
text:
The core idea: levels of explanation
You can often explain the same behavior at multiple levels:

Computational / functional: what problem is being solved? (e.g., detect threat)
Algorithmic: what process implements it? (attention narrowing, habit)
Implementation: what biological system supports it? (circuits, hormones)

None of these levels alone is “the real one.” They are complementary.

title: Biopsychology
section: 1) Neurons, signals, and plasticity (what you minimally need)
text:
1) Neurons, signals, and plasticity (what you minimally need)

Neurons and communication (high-level)
Neurons communicate via: - electrical signals (spikes), - chemical signaling at synapses.
The important part for psychology: - which signals get strengthened with experience? (learning) - which systems modulate alertness, reward, and threat? (motivation/emotion)


Plasticity: how experience changes biology
Learning corresponds to changes in: - synaptic strength, - network activation patterns, - cue associations.
Prediction pattern: repeated, consistent feedback strengthens circuits supporting the repeated behavior (habit formation).

title: Biopsychology
text:
2) Brain organization (a practical map)
You do not need full neuroanatomy, but you need a working map:

Cortex (outer layer): perception, attention, planning, language, flexible reasoning

Limbic-related systems (broad umbrella): emotion, motivation, memory tagging

Basal ganglia: action selection, habit, reinforcement learning

Hippocampal system: memory for episodes and context; building “maps” of situations

Amygdala-related threat processing: rapid relevance/threat tagging (not a “fear center” only)

Brainstem/arousal systems: wakefulness, arousal, stress responses

Pitfall: “one region = one function.” Most behaviors are distributed network outcomes.

title: Biopsychology
text:
3) Neurotransmitters (conceptual, not memorization)
Neurotransmitters are chemical messengers that shape signaling patterns. For behavioral interpretation, you mostly need functional roles:

Dopamine (reward prediction and learning signals)
Often linked to: - reward learning, - motivation/approach, - updating expected value.
Prediction patterns - behaviors reinforced by unpredictable rewards become persistent (ties to compulsion/addiction loops). - dopamine-linked learning signals are sensitive to surprise (prediction error).
Pitfall: “dopamine = pleasure.” It’s better to think “dopamine supports learning and pursuit.”


Serotonin (broad regulation; caution)
Often discussed in relation to: - mood regulation, - patience/impulsivity (context-dependent), - inhibition and flexibility.
Note: serotonin is complex; avoid one-line explanations.


Norepinephrine (alertness and attention allocation)
Often linked to: - arousal, - vigilance, - shifting attention under uncertainty.
Prediction pattern: under arousal, attention becomes more selective and action becomes faster but less flexible.


GABA / glutamate (inhibition/excitation balance)
These are foundational excitatory/inhibitory systems. In notes, you can treat them as: - “stability and control of neural activity.”

title: Biopsychology
text:
4) Stress physiology (HPA axis lens, high-level)
Stress is not only “mental.” It is also physiological regulation.
A common high-level pathway: - stressor → threat appraisal → arousal + hormonal response → attention narrowing + habit dominance
Key ideas: - Acute stress can be adaptive (mobilize action). - Chronic stress can degrade sleep, control, and mood regulation.
Prediction patterns - acute threat increases vigilance and reduces deep reasoning (links to self-control and social cognition limits). - chronic stress increases short-horizon choices and avoidance loops.

title: Biopsychology
section: 5) Emotion and the body: arousal as a system parameter
text:
5) Emotion and the body: arousal as a system parameter
Arousal changes: - reaction speed, - attention breadth, - memory tagging, - aggression/avoidance readiness.
Prediction pattern: high arousal makes behavior more “scripted,” more cue-driven, and less reflective.
This is why environment design (safety, predictability) matters.

title: Biopsychology
section: 6) Sleep as biological maintenance and cognitive control support
text:
6) Sleep as biological maintenance and cognitive control support
Sleep supports: - memory consolidation, - emotion regulation, - executive control stability.
Prediction pattern: sleep loss increases impulsivity, threat sensitivity, and memory distortions (ties to your Sleep & stress page).

title: Biopsychology
text:
7) Biological constraints in social behavior
Social interaction is not disembodied. Social threat activates: - stress systems, - vigilance, - shame/anger pathways.
Prediction patterns - humiliation and status threat can produce outsized retaliation or withdrawal. - legitimacy and respect reduce threat activation and increase cooperation (bridges to institutions/criminology overlap pages).

title: Biopsychology
section: 8) Neuro methods (conceptual preview; details can be a separate page)
text:
8) Neuro methods (conceptual preview; details can be a separate page)
Different tools answer different questions:

Lesions / patient studies: what breaks when a system is damaged? (strong constraints, low control)
EEG/ERP: timing of processes (fast temporal resolution)
fMRI: where activity correlates with tasks (good spatial resolution; correlational)
TMS: perturbation to test causal roles (limited scope)
Psychophysiology: arousal and stress markers (not emotion labels)

Pitfall: treating neuro images as “proof of causality.” Most neuro measures are correlational unless combined with strong designs.

title: Biopsychology
text:
A reusable biopsych explanation template
When adding biological content, write:

Behavior: what is the phenomenon?

Psych mechanism: attention? habit? appraisal? identity?

Bio support: what system plausibly implements/modulates it (arousal, reward learning, stress)?

Prediction: what changes under sleep loss, stress, intoxication, or pharmacological modulation?

Boundary: what this does not explain alone (avoid one-region stories)

title: Biopsychology
text:
Canonical examples (stubs you can expand)

Example A: Habit under stress

stress increases arousal,
executive control decreases,
habitual routines dominate.

Psych: self-control + cue-triggered habit
Bio: arousal/stress systems modulate control networks


Example B: Addiction loop reinforcement

cue triggers craving and attention capture,
action produces reward/relief,
learning strengthens cue-action mapping.

Psych: reinforcement + negative reinforcement
Bio: reward-learning signals + stress relief mechanisms

title: Biopsychology
text:
Connections

Foundations: cognition, attention & memory, learning, emotion & motivation, sleep & stress, self-control
Topics: addiction & compulsion, mental health
Overlaps: criminology (hot states, threat), institutions (procedural justice reduces threat), policy design (mechanism-matched interventions)

title: Psychology × communication
text:
Communication is not just transmitting information. It is also: - managing impressions, - coordinating beliefs, - negotiating identity and status, - regulating emotion, - shaping norms.
This page focuses on psychological mechanisms that determine whether messages persuade, mislead, coordinate, or polarize.

title: Psychology × communication
text:
A minimal model of communication
Any message outcome depends on:

Source (who is speaking; credibility; identity)
Content (what is said; evidence; framing)
Channel (face-to-face, text, public vs private; permanence)
Receiver (goals, beliefs, attention, emotional state)
Context (stakes, norms, incentives, audiences)
Feedback (what happens after the message)

Many communication failures come from misalignment in (1), (4), or (5), not from “bad arguments.”

title: Psychology × communication
text:
Mechanism 1: Credibility and trust heuristics
People rarely verify everything. They use credibility heuristics: - expertise, - track record, - confidence signals, - group membership (“in-group messenger”), - institutional legitimacy.
Prediction patterns - The same evidence persuades more when delivered by a trusted in-group source. - Low trust environments produce “evidence-resistant” audiences. - Apparent confidence can substitute for evidence (sometimes misleadingly).
Intervention lever: credibility can be built via consistent procedure and transparency, not just rhetoric.

title: Psychology × communication
text:
Mechanism 2: Framing and representation
Frames change what the message “is about”: - gains vs losses, - moral language (“harm”, “fairness”, “betrayal”), - concrete stories vs abstract statistics, - naming and categorization (“victim” vs “suspect”, “aid” vs “handout”).
Prediction patterns - Changing labels changes perceived intent and moral judgment. - Concrete cases move emotion more than base rates (“identifiable victim effect”). - Order and salience change which reasons are remembered.
Intervention lever: align frames with the audience’s goals without distorting truth.

title: Psychology × communication
section: Mechanism 3: Motivated reasoning and identity protection
text:
Mechanism 3: Motivated reasoning and identity protection
People often treat belief as identity-relevant: - accepting some claims signals loyalty, - rejecting others signals independence or status.
Prediction patterns - Corrections can backfire when they imply “your group is wrong.” - Mixed evidence can increase polarization (biased assimilation). - People discount out-group sources even when content is strong.
Intervention levers - identity-safe framing (“this doesn’t threaten who you are”), - trusted in-group messengers, - focus on shared goals and outcomes rather than blame.

title: Psychology × communication
section: Mechanism 4: Emotion and arousal as amplifiers
text:
Mechanism 4: Emotion and arousal as amplifiers
Emotion changes: - attention, - memory, - perceived urgency, - willingness to share.
High-arousal content spreads more, but can reduce nuance.
Prediction patterns - Fear increases threat-focused interpretation and avoidance. - Anger increases perceived intentionality and punitive preferences. - Shame increases concealment and reduced disclosure.
Intervention lever: reduce threat cues if the goal is learning; increase safety and dignity if the goal is cooperation.

title: Psychology × communication
text:
Mechanism 5: Persuasion as constraint satisfaction
Many receivers ask implicitly: - “Does this fit my world model?” - “Does accepting this create social costs?” - “Does it help me act?”
A message can fail even if it is true because it: - conflicts with a stable narrative, - increases social risk, - lacks actionable implication.
Prediction patterns - Messages that offer a coherent story + actionable steps persuade more than pure data dumps. - Ambiguous evidence is absorbed into existing narratives.

title: Psychology × communication
text:
Mechanism 6: Deception and self-deception (mechanism lens)
Deception is not only strategic; it has psychological components: - impression management, - guilt/shame regulation, - motivated forgetting, - rationalization.
Receivers detect deception imperfectly because: - cognitive load limits inference, - trust heuristics dominate, - people avoid the social cost of accusing others.
Prediction patterns - Deception increases when verification is costly and accountability is weak. - Receivers are more skeptical when incentives conflict is obvious. - Public accountability reduces deception by raising reputational costs.

title: Psychology × communication
text:
Mechanism 7: Common knowledge and coordination
Some messages work by creating shared awareness: - “everyone knows that everyone knows…”
Public statements can shift behavior even without new factual content.
Prediction patterns - Public announcements change coordination more than private messages. - Ambiguous public signals can create instability (multiple interpretations).

title: Psychology × communication
text:
A reusable communication analysis template
When you analyze a message campaign or interaction, specify:

Who is speaking and what credibility cues exist

Audience identity and whether belief is identity-threatening

Frame (what is salient; what is the moral lens)

Emotional state (fear/anger/shame)

Incentives (what does each side gain by persuasion or resistance?)

Verification (how easy is fact-checking?)

Prediction (what changes if you switch messenger, frame, or channel?)

title: Psychology × communication
text:
Canonical examples (stubs you can expand)

Example A: “Facts don’t work”
Evidence fails because the listener hears: - status threat, - group attack, - identity challenge.
Mechanisms: motivated reasoning + source credibility filtering.


Example B: Rumor spread in low-trust settings

uncertainty is high,
official sources are distrusted,
vivid stories spread quickly,
corrections are ignored.

Mechanisms: availability + distrust + emotional arousal.

title: Psychology × communication
text:
Links

Foundations: cognition (attention/memory), emotion & motivation, social cognition
Topics: norms & groups, biases
Overlaps: strategic interaction (credibility), institutions (legitimacy), criminology (reporting/cooperation)

title: Psychology × criminology
text:
This page treats criminology as a domain where psychological mechanisms are unusually visible: - behavior is often high-stakes, - environments are strategic (offenders, victims, police, communities adapt), - outcomes depend on perceptions (risk, legitimacy, threat) as much as objective facts.
The goal is to link psychology to criminology in the same “mechanisms → predictions” style.

title: Psychology × criminology
text:
A compact bridge
Many criminology outcomes can be expressed as:

Opportunities (situations, routines, guardianship)
Incentives (expected benefits/costs)
Perceptions (salience, threat, legitimacy, identity)
Control (self-regulation, impulsivity, stress)
Social context (peers, norms, reputations)
Learning/adaptation (feedback loops, displacement, retaliation)

Criminology differs from “pure incentives” mainly because (3)–(6) are decisive.

title: Psychology × criminology
section: Mechanism 1: Perceived risk is not objective risk
text:
Mechanism 1: Perceived risk is not objective risk
Deterrence depends on perceived probability and severity, not just actual enforcement.
Psychological channels: - availability (recent police presence feels like higher risk), - salience (visible patrols change attention), - probability weighting (small risks can feel big or be ignored), - miscalibration (overconfidence, “it won’t happen to me”).
Prediction patterns - Highly visible enforcement changes behavior more than equally effective but invisible enforcement. - After salient events (arrests, crackdowns), risk perception spikes temporarily. - If enforcement feels arbitrary or illegitimate, it can reduce compliance through reactance.

title: Psychology × criminology
text:
Mechanism 2: Self-control, impulsivity, and “hot states”
Under stress, arousal, intoxication, or peer pressure: - attention narrows, - habit dominates deliberation, - time horizon shortens, - threat interpretation becomes more pessimistic.
Prediction patterns - Many harmful acts cluster in “hot” contexts (crowds, nightlife, conflict episodes). - Small situational changes (friction, pacing, guardianship) can reduce incidents disproportionately. - Policies that reduce acute triggers (alcohol availability, crowd management) can work even without changing long-run preferences.

title: Psychology × criminology
section: Mechanism 3: Social identity, stigma, and legitimacy
text:
Mechanism 3: Social identity, stigma, and legitimacy
People comply not only from fear of sanction but because: - rules feel legitimate, - compliance is identity-consistent, - noncompliance risks shame/exclusion, - authorities are trusted.
Legitimacy depends on: - perceived fairness, - respect and voice, - consistent procedure, - competence + benevolent intention (warmth/competence impressions).
Prediction patterns - Procedural fairness increases cooperation (reporting, testimony, compliance) even if outcomes are not favorable. - Heavy-handed enforcement can reduce trust, lowering reporting and creating measurement illusions (“crime fell” vs “reporting fell”). - Stigma increases concealment, reduces help-seeking, and can create oppositional identity (“they’re against us anyway”).

title: Psychology × criminology
text:
Mechanism 4: Peer effects and norms
Peers matter through: - imitation (what others do), - descriptive norms (what seems common), - injunctive norms (what is approved), - reputation incentives (status, toughness, loyalty).
Prediction patterns - Small changes in perceived norms can move behavior (especially in adolescence/young adulthood). - Public, visible actions (retaliation, defiance) can spread via reputational dynamics. - Networks create clustering: “hot people” and “hot places” can amplify each other.

title: Psychology × criminology
section: Mechanism 5: Conflict escalation and retaliation loops
text:
Mechanism 5: Conflict escalation and retaliation loops
Violence and conflict often follow feedback loops:

ambiguous cue → hostile attribution
anger/fear → defensive act
defensive act → interpreted as confirmation
retaliation becomes normatively justified

Prediction patterns - Interventions that reduce ambiguity and increase face-saving off-ramps reduce escalation. - Visible retaliation can shift local norms toward aggression. - Trust-building and credible dispute resolution reduce the perceived need for self-help violence.

title: Psychology × criminology
section: Mechanism 6: Learning and adaptation to enforcement
text:
Mechanism 6: Learning and adaptation to enforcement
Enforcement changes behavior, but behavior also changes enforcement conditions.
Learning channels: - reinforcement (what “worked” last time), - avoidance learning (how to evade detection), - social learning (how peers adapt), - selective feedback (you only see successful evasion).
Prediction patterns - Crackdowns can produce displacement (activity shifts) rather than pure reduction. - If enforcement targets visible behaviors, actors substitute to less visible strategies. - Early random experiences can lock in long-run distrust or deterrence sensitivity.

title: Psychology × criminology
section: A psych-first analysis template for criminology questions
text:
A psych-first analysis template for criminology questions
When reading a criminology claim, ask:

Perception: what do actors believe about risk, legitimacy, and others’ intentions?

State: are actors in “cold” or “hot” states (stress, intoxication, threat)?

Norms/networks: what do peers reward or punish?

Feedback: what gets reinforced (compliance, avoidance, retaliation)?

Measurement: are we observing true incidence or reporting/enforcement artifacts?

Prediction: what changes if you alter salience, fairness, cues, or feedback timing?

title: Psychology × criminology
text:
Canonical examples (stubs you can expand)

Example A: Deterrence with legitimacy
Two neighborhoods have equal enforcement intensity. - In one, police are trusted; reporting is high; compliance rises. - In the other, police are distrusted; reporting drops; conflicts are handled privately.
Mechanisms: legitimacy + social identity + reporting incentives.


Example B: Violence as a reputational equilibrium (psych lens)
Retaliation is not only strategic; it is emotionally and normatively reinforced: - anger supports commitment, - status norms reward toughness, - shame punishes backing down.
Mechanisms: emotion-as-commitment + norms + reputation.

text:
Links

Topics: norms & groups, biases
Criminology section: mechanisms, institutions, models, stylized facts

title: Psychology × strategic interaction
text: This page treats “game theory” as a language for interaction, and psychology as the engine of behavior. The goal is to explain how real strategic behavior differs from idealized assumptions, using psychological mechanisms.

title: Psychology × strategic interaction
section: Where psychology and game theory meet
text:
Where psychology and game theory meet
Game theory and psychology overlap whenever behaviour depends on beliefs, social perception, or bounded reasoning.





flowchart TD
    A[Game Theory] --> C[Strategic Interaction]
    B[Psychology] --> C
 
    A --> A1[Beliefs]
    A --> A2[Incentives]
    A --> A3[Equilibrium Reasoning]

    B --> B1[Preferences]

    C --> F[Belief Formation]

title: Psychology × strategic interaction
text:
The simplest bridge
Strategic interaction requires four psychological capacities:

Represent the situation (what are the options and payoffs?)
Represent other minds (what do they know, want, believe?)
Regulate emotion (threat, anger, shame, pride)
Learn from feedback (what worked, what didn’t, what others will do next)

Any breakdown in (1)–(4) changes outcomes.

title: Psychology × strategic interaction
text:
Mechanism 1: Limited depth of reasoning
Many interactions require recursive thought: - “I think you think I think…”
But depth is constrained by: - working memory, - time pressure, - stress, - familiarity.
Prediction patterns - In complex games, people often behave as if they reason only a few steps. - Simplifying the environment (fewer actions, clearer incentives) increases strategic sophistication. - Under stress, behavior becomes more habitual and less model-based.
Useful takeaway: what looks like “naive strategy” can be a cognitive-load response.

title: Psychology × strategic interaction
section: Mechanism 2: Beliefs are shaped by identity and trust
text:
Mechanism 2: Beliefs are shaped by identity and trust
In strategic settings, information is rarely neutral. People filter evidence through: - source credibility, - group identity, - prior narratives, - motivated reasoning.
Prediction patterns - Messages from in-group sources are believed more readily. - Identical evidence is discounted when it comes from distrusted sources. - Attempts at correction can backfire if they signal dominance or disrespect.
Implication: communication failures can persist even when incentives favor agreement.

title: Psychology × strategic interaction
section: Mechanism 3: Social preferences and moral motives
text:
Mechanism 3: Social preferences and moral motives
People often care about more than material payoff: - fairness and inequity, - reciprocity, - status, - guilt and shame, - norm compliance.
Prediction patterns - People punish unfairness even at personal cost. - Cooperation increases when actions are observable and reputational. - Small perceived disrespect can trigger disproportionate retaliation.
Interpretation: outcomes can look “non-equilibrium” if you assume the wrong utility function.

title: Psychology × strategic interaction
section: Mechanism 4: Emotion as commitment (and as escalation fuel)
text:
Mechanism 4: Emotion as commitment (and as escalation fuel)
Emotions can function like commitment devices: - anger makes retaliation credible, - pride makes backing down costly, - shame makes concealment likely, - guilt makes repair likely.
Prediction patterns - If retaliation is expected, deterrence can emerge without formal enforcement. - Misattribution + anger can produce escalation spirals. - Public audiences amplify commitment and reputational stakes.
Implication: credibility is not only about calculation; it’s also about affect and identity.

title: Psychology × strategic interaction
section: Mechanism 5: Learning in interactive environments is tricky
text:
Mechanism 5: Learning in interactive environments is tricky
Strategic environments generate feedback that is: - endogenous (others adapt), - selective (you see only some outcomes), - confounded (many things change at once).
Prediction patterns - People can learn the “wrong lesson” because credit assignment is hard. - Early random outcomes can lock in persistent mistrust. - Policies can create adaptation that offsets intended effects.
Bridge to criminology: enforcement and deterrence can change behavior and change the environment.

title: Psychology × strategic interaction
text:
A reusable “psych-first” analysis template
When analyzing a strategic situation, write:

Situation: what are the actions and constraints?

Beliefs: what does each side think the other will do?

Mind-reading: how well can they infer intentions/information?

Motives: beyond payoffs—fairness, status, norms, identity?

Emotion: fear/anger/shame/guilt shaping action?

Learning: what feedback occurs, and what gets reinforced?

Prediction: what changes if you alter salience, observability, identity, or feedback?

title: Psychology × strategic interaction
text:
Canonical examples (stubs you can expand)

Example A: Cooperation collapse

people start cooperative,
a few defections occur (noise or misunderstanding),
trust drops, retaliation increases,
cooperation collapses.

Mechanisms: attribution bias + negative reciprocity + learning from salient losses.


Example B: Cheap talk becomes informative

some senders value honesty or reputational integrity,
some receivers trust in-group sources more,
even costless messages can predict behavior.

Mechanisms: norms + identity + credibility heuristics.

title: Psychology × institutions
text:
Institutions (rules, procedures, organizations) shape behavior partly through incentives, but also by shaping attention, identity, emotion, and learning.
This page gives a psych-first lens for why institutions work (or fail).

title: Psychology × institutions
text:
What institutions do psychologically
Institutions don’t just change payoffs; they change: - what people notice, - what feels normal, - what feels legitimate, - what feels safe, - what actions become habitual.
A practical schema:

Rules (formal constraints and permissions)

Signals (what the institution communicates about norms and authority)

Procedures (how decisions are made and enforced)

Experiences (how people are treated)

Learning (what gets reinforced over time)

title: Psychology × institutions
text:
Mechanism 1: Salience and attention management
Institutions decide what is visible: - signage, reminders, forms, checkpoints, public metrics, dashboards.
Prediction patterns - Small, well-placed cues can change behavior more than weak penalties. - If a rule is not salient at the decision moment, compliance falls. - Overloading people with information can reduce compliance (attention collapse).
Design lever: fewer, clearer cues at the point of action.

title: Psychology × institutions
section: Mechanism 2: Defaults, friction, and choice architecture
text:
Mechanism 2: Defaults, friction, and choice architecture
Institutional design often creates defaults: - opt-in vs opt-out, - required steps, forms, waiting times, - access costs.
Prediction patterns - Defaults dominate behavior when attention is scarce. - “Hassle costs” can exclude the most vulnerable users. - Reducing friction can increase participation even without changing preferences.
Design lever: align default paths with desired behavior, but monitor fairness.

title: Psychology × institutions
text:
Mechanism 3: Legitimacy and procedural justice
People obey rules more when they believe the institution is legitimate.
Legitimacy is strongly affected by: - respectful treatment, - neutrality and consistency, - transparency and voice, - competence and good faith.
Prediction patterns - Procedural fairness increases cooperation and compliance beyond material incentives. - Harsh but inconsistent enforcement reduces legitimacy and can backfire.
Design lever: make procedures explainable and respectful; reduce arbitrary discretion.

title: Psychology × institutions
text:
Mechanism 4: Identity and role scripts
Institutions create roles: - student/teacher, patient/doctor, citizen/police, worker/manager.
Roles come with scripts: - what is expected, - what is allowed, - what is shameful or praiseworthy.
Prediction patterns - Making a prosocial identity salient increases prosocial choices. - Role ambiguity increases conflict, blame, and withdrawal. - Stigmatizing roles increase concealment and noncooperation.
Design lever: clarify roles; avoid stigmatizing classifications.

title: Psychology × institutions
section: Mechanism 5: Emotion regulation via safety and threat
text:
Mechanism 5: Emotion regulation via safety and threat
Institutions shape emotional climate: - safety, predictability, and dignity reduce threat responses, - uncertainty and humiliation increase anger and defensiveness.
Prediction patterns - Stressful institutional encounters reduce cognitive capacity and increase reactive behavior. - Fear and humiliation amplify “us vs them” dynamics.
Design lever: reduce unnecessary threat cues; create face-saving pathways.

title: Psychology × institutions
text:
Mechanism 6: Learning, feedback, and adaptation
Institutions create feedback loops: - what is rewarded/punished, - what is noticed, - what is recorded.
When feedback is noisy or delayed, people learn wrong lessons.
Prediction patterns - If compliance is rarely acknowledged but noncompliance is punished, cynicism can grow. - If enforcement is predictable, actors adapt to evade it (avoidance learning). - Early experiences can anchor long-run trust or distrust.
Design lever: provide timely, credible feedback; monitor adaptation and spillovers.

title: Psychology × institutions
text:
A psych-first institutional analysis template
For any institution (policy, organization, rule system), ask:

Attention: what does it make salient at decision time?

Friction/defaults: what is the path of least resistance?

Legitimacy: do people experience it as fair and respectful?

Identity: what roles and group boundaries does it activate?

Emotion: does it create safety or threat?

Learning: what behavior is reinforced? what adaptations emerge?

Distribution: who bears the hassle costs or enforcement burden?

title: Psychology × institutions
text:
Canonical examples (stubs you can expand)

Example A: Compliance without enforcement
A rule is followed because it is: - salient, - identity-consistent, - socially approved, - supported by respectful institutions.
Mechanisms: norms + legitimacy + reputation.


Example B: Backfire from harsh enforcement
Harsh enforcement reduces compliance over time because it: - damages legitimacy, - increases oppositional identity, - increases avoidance learning.
Mechanisms: reactance + distrust + adaptation.

title: Psychology × economics
text:
Economics and psychology overlap wherever models require assumptions about: - preferences, - beliefs, - attention and information processing, - learning and adaptation, - social motives (fairness, norms, identity).
This page keeps economics in the background and uses psychology to clarify where standard assumptions work and where they break.

title: Psychology × economics
text:
Bridge 1: Preferences vs construction
In many contexts, preferences are not fully “pre-existing.” They are constructed from: - attention and salience, - framing and reference points, - emotion and identity.
Prediction pattern: change the frame or default, and choice shifts without “preference change” in a deep sense.

title: Psychology × economics
text:
Bridge 2: Beliefs and confidence
Economic models often assume coherent belief updating. Psychology emphasizes: - trust and source filtering, - motivated reasoning, - salience and memory, - miscalibration of confidence.
Prediction pattern: interventions that increase trust and feedback quality move behavior as much as incentives do.

title: Psychology × economics
text:
Bridge 3: Time inconsistency and self-control
Present focus and cue-triggered habits create: - procrastination, - under-saving, - relapse.
Prediction pattern: commitment devices and automation are high-leverage.

title: Psychology × economics
section: Bridge 4: Social preferences and norm utility
text:
Bridge 4: Social preferences and norm utility
People care about: - fairness, - reciprocity, - shame/guilt, - status, - identity.
Prediction pattern: “pure incentives” can backfire if they signal distrust or crowd out moral motives.

title: Psychology × economics
section: Bridge 5: Learning in markets and repeated settings
text:
Bridge 5: Learning in markets and repeated settings
Learning is shaped by: - noisy feedback, - endogenous adaptation, - selective observation.
Prediction pattern: early experiences can anchor beliefs and risk-taking, even if objectively irrelevant.

title: Psychology × economics
text:
Connections

Foundations: decision-making, beliefs, learning, self-control, methods
Topics: biases, norms & groups, moral psychology
Overlaps: institutions and policy design

title: Psychology × policy design
text:
Policy design changes behavior through: - incentives and constraints, - attention and salience, - norms and identity, - legitimacy and trust, - learning and adaptation.
This page is a psych-first checklist for designing interventions that work and don’t backfire.

title: Psychology × policy design
section: Step 1: Identify the mechanism, not just the outcome
text:
Step 1: Identify the mechanism, not just the outcome
Ask: what is the bottleneck? - attention problem? - misinformation / low trust? - habit and cue problem? - emotion/threat problem? - norm and identity problem? - structural constraint (time, money, access)?
Rule: don’t use incentives to solve attention problems.

title: Psychology × policy design
section: Step 2: Choose the lever that matches the mechanism
text:
Step 2: Choose the lever that matches the mechanism

Attention/salience levers

reminders at decision time,
simpler choice sets,
clear defaults.



Habit/cue levers

friction for harmful routines,
substitution routines,
environmental redesign.



Norm/identity levers

show descriptive norms carefully,
use in-group messengers,
identity-safe framing.



Legitimacy levers

procedural fairness,
transparency and voice,
consistent enforcement.



Learning levers

timely feedback,
clear causal links,
avoid noisy or delayed signals when possible.

title: Psychology × policy design
text:
Step 3: Watch for predictable backfires

Reactance
If people feel controlled, they may resist.


Crowding out
Extrinsic incentives can reduce intrinsic or moral motives if they change meaning.


Stigma and concealment
Punitive designs can reduce truthful reporting and help-seeking.


Selection and measurement artifacts
If your measurement depends on reporting/enforcement, your “effect” may be reporting change, not behavior change.


Adaptation
People strategically adapt to predictable enforcement or rules.

title: Psychology × policy design
section: Step 4: Build evaluation into the design
text:
Step 4: Build evaluation into the design
Before deployment: - define outcomes (including spillovers), - anticipate displacement and substitution, - measure trust and legitimacy if relevant, - plan for heterogeneous effects (who benefits, who is burdened).
Rule: if you don’t measure trust/legitimacy, you may miss the main mechanism.

title: Psychology × policy design
text:
A reusable policy analysis template

Target behavior and context

Mechanism bottleneck (attention, habit, norms, legitimacy, constraints)

Lever choice and why it matches mechanism

Predicted side effects (reactance, stigma, displacement)

Measurement plan (validity, selection, invariance)

Adaptation risk and monitoring plan

Equity/distribution (who bears friction/enforcement burden?)

text:
Connections

Foundations: methods, measurement, cognition, self-control
Topics: norms & groups, biases, moral psychology

title: Psychology
text:
Psychology here is treated as a toolkit for explaining behavior: how people perceive, learn, decide, and coordinate with others.
This section is organized in three layers:

title: Psychology
text:
Design principle

Prefer mechanisms → predictions → evidence over encyclopedic summaries.
Keep every page usable as a teaching note: definitions, intuitions, common pitfalls, and one canonical example.

title: Self-control
text:
Self-control is the capacity to align behavior with goals when there is conflict: - short-run temptation vs long-run plan, - impulse vs norm, - habit vs deliberate intention.
A useful stance: > Self-control is not just “willpower.” It is a system involving attention, emotion regulation, habits, and environment design.

title: Self-control
text:
The conflict view
Many self-control failures can be framed as:

Competing motivations at different time scales
(comfort now vs outcomes later)
State-dependence
(what you want when calm differs from what you want when stressed)
Cue-triggered habits
(automatic behavior initiated before deliberation starts)

title: Self-control
text:
Mechanism 1: Executive function (the control machinery)
Executive function supports: - sustaining attention, - inhibiting responses, - switching tasks, - holding goals in working memory.
It is limited and sensitive to: - fatigue, - stress, - sleep loss, - cognitive load.
Prediction pattern: when executive load rises, people rely more on defaults and habits.

title: Self-control
text:
Mechanism 2: Temptation is often cue-driven
Temptation is not random; it is triggered by cues: - places, - people, - time of day, - emotions, - devices and notifications.
Prediction pattern: changing cues often outperforms “trying harder.”
Practical lever: remove cues or introduce friction at the cue stage.

title: Self-control
text:
Mechanism 3: Emotion regulation
Many self-control failures are attempts to regulate feelings: - anxiety → avoidance, - anger → confrontation, - sadness → withdrawal, - shame → concealment, - stress → immediate relief seeking.
Prediction pattern: improving emotion regulation reduces impulsive choices even without changing incentives.

title: Self-control
text:
Mechanism 4: Habits: the silent competitor
Habits are automatic routines learned through reinforcement. They dominate under stress and time pressure.
Prediction pattern: people can endorse a plan but still act habitually when triggered.
A useful distinction: - Goal intention: “I want to do X.” - Implementation intention: “If situation S happens, I will do X.”
Implementation intentions work by linking cues to actions.

title: Self-control
text:
Mechanism 5: Present focus (time inconsistency)
People often treat immediate outcomes as disproportionately important. This creates: - procrastination, - under-saving, - relapse dynamics.
Prediction pattern: commitment devices increase follow-through.

title: Self-control
section: Commitment devices: designing around the problem
text:
Commitment devices: designing around the problem
