Commitment is any intervention that changes future choices by altering: - access (removing temptation), - incentives (deposits, penalties), - observability (public deadlines), - defaults (pre-scheduled actions), - identity (role and norm salience).
Prediction pattern: low-cost commitments can have large effects if they operate at the cue stage.

title: Self-control
text:
A practical self-control toolkit (mechanism → lever)

If the bottleneck is attention

remove distractions, reduce choice overload,
use checklists and single-task blocks.



If the bottleneck is cues/habit

change environment, remove triggers,
substitute routine rather than “stop cold.”



If the bottleneck is emotion

reappraisal, naming emotions, time-outs,
social support and safe disclosure.



If the bottleneck is time inconsistency

pre-commit (deadlines, deposits),
automate good actions (savings, scheduling).

title: Self-control
text:
A reusable explanation template
When explaining self-control outcomes, specify:

Goal conflict: what is short-run vs long-run?

Cues: what triggers the impulsive routine?

State: stress, fatigue, sleep, social pressure?

Control capacity: executive load and attention?

Habit strength: how reinforced is the routine?

Intervention: change cues, add friction, add commitment, add support.

title: Self-control
text:
Canonical examples (stubs you can expand)

Example A: Procrastination

long-run goal is valued,
task is aversive now,
avoidance yields immediate relief.

Mechanisms: present focus + negative reinforcement (relief) + attention avoidance.


Example B: Relapse dynamics

stress increases,
cue exposure returns,
habit triggers before deliberation,
guilt/shame may worsen avoidance.

Mechanisms: cue-triggered habit + emotion regulation failure + shame loop.

title: Self-control
text:
Connections

Cognition: self-control depends on working memory and attention.
Learning: habits form through reinforcement; change requires new learning.
Emotion & motivation: many failures are regulation attempts.
Decision-making: time preferences and present focus.
Criminology: impulsivity under hot states, deterrence sensitivity, and situational triggers.

title: Cognition
text:
Cognition is how people take in information, represent it mentally, and use it to guide action. It includes perception, attention, memory, and the limited “workspace” that supports reasoning.
A useful theme for the whole site: > Many “biases” are not mysterious preferences — they are consequences of cognitive constraints.

title: Cognition
text:
The pipeline view
You can often explain behavior by locating where things break in this pipeline:

Perception (what is detected)
Attention (what is selected)
Encoding (what gets stored)
Memory & retrieval (what comes back to mind)
Working memory & reasoning (what can be manipulated)
Decision output (judgment and choice)

Different tasks fail at different stages.

title: Cognition
section: Perception: we don’t experience the world directly
text:
Perception: we don’t experience the world directly
Perception is an inference process: the mind reconstructs reality from partial input.
Key implications: - people can miss obvious signals when they are not attended to, - ambiguous stimuli are interpreted using context and expectations, - repeated exposure changes what feels “normal.”
Prediction pattern: the same event can be perceived differently depending on prior beliefs, stress, identity, and what is salient.

title: Cognition
text:
Attention: the scarce resource
Attention is limited; it is allocated based on: - novelty, - threat, - goal relevance, - emotional salience, - social relevance (faces, status cues).

Selective attention
People focus on some cues and ignore others.
Prediction pattern: changing what is salient (layout, framing, order, visual prominence) changes judgment and behavior even when information content is unchanged.


Divided attention and multitasking
Multitasking typically reduces performance and increases errors, especially for tasks requiring working memory.
Prediction pattern: under distraction, people rely more on defaults, habits, and simple heuristics.

title: Cognition
text:
Memory: storage is not recording
Memory is reconstructive. It is shaped by: - emotion (strong tagging), - repetition (availability), - meaning (schema-consistency), - recency and vividness.

Working memory vs long-term memory

Working memory: small, active “scratch space.”
Long-term memory: large but retrieval is cue-dependent.

Prediction pattern: tasks requiring multiple steps of reasoning fail when working memory load increases.


Retrieval and availability
What comes to mind easily feels more likely or more important.
Prediction pattern: vivid, recent, or emotionally salient examples dominate judgment of frequency and risk.

title: Cognition
section: Mental representations: the hidden structure behind choices
text:
Mental representations: the hidden structure behind choices
People do not store full details; they store structured representations: - categories (“type of person” / “type of situation”), - causal stories (“X causes Y”), - scripts (“what happens next here”).
Representations are useful but also create systematic errors: - you may ignore out-of-category evidence, - you may force events into familiar scripts.
Prediction pattern: changing category labels changes interpretation, even with identical behavior.

title: Cognition
text:
Reasoning: computation under constraints
Reasoning is costly and often: - stops early (satisficing), - uses shortcuts (heuristics), - depends on attention and working memory.
A practical way to write this: - depth (how many steps you can carry), - breadth (how many possibilities you can compare), - precision (how error-free your steps are).
Stress, time pressure, and fatigue reduce all three.

title: Cognition
section: Errors that look like “bias” but are cognitive mechanics
text:
Errors that look like “bias” but are cognitive mechanics
When people appear biased, check whether it could be explained by: - limited attention (missed information), - limited working memory (can’t integrate many cues), - cue-dependent retrieval (what comes to mind drives judgment), - schema-driven interpretation (story beats statistics), - default reliance (choice overload).
Rule of thumb: if an intervention that changes salience, load, or feedback changes behavior, the mechanism is likely cognitive.

title: Cognition
text:
A reusable explanation template
To explain a cognition-driven pattern, specify:

Task: what must the person compute/remember?
Bottleneck: perception, attention, memory, or working memory?
Cue structure: what cues are salient vs hidden?
Representation: what categories/scripts are activated?
Prediction: what changes if you reduce load or change salience?

title: Cognition
text:
Canonical examples (stubs you can expand)

Example A: “They had the information but didn’t use it”

info exists but is not salient,
attention is captured by another cue,
working memory is overloaded.

Mechanisms: selective attention + working memory limits.


Example B: Miscommunication in complex tasks

speaker assumes shared context,
listener lacks the same representation,
misunderstanding persists because feedback is delayed or weak.

Mechanisms: different mental models + reconstruction + weak error signals.

title: Cognition
text:
Connections to other sections

Decision-making
Many “preference anomalies” are actually representation and attention effects.


Learning
Cues and memory determine what gets reinforced and what generalizes.


Social cognition
Mentalizing depth is constrained by working memory; stereotypes are low-cost representations.


Criminology
Witness memory, stress in high-stakes encounters, and selective attention to threat cues are cognition-sensitive.


Overlaps (later)
In strategic environments, cognition limits: - depth of “I think you think…” - ability to compute contingencies, - ability to detect deception.

title: Emotion & motivation
text:
Emotion and motivation are not “noise.” They are control systems: they prioritize goals, allocate attention, trigger action tendencies, and shape what evidence feels persuasive.
A clean mental model:

title: Emotion & motivation
text:
Core functions

1) Value and priority
Emotions change the felt value of outcomes and the urgency of action. - Fear prioritizes safety and threat monitoring. - Anger prioritizes confrontation and norm enforcement. - Sadness often reduces effort and shifts attention to loss and withdrawal. - Joy can broaden attention and exploration.
Prediction pattern: same incentives can yield different behavior depending on the affective state because the objective function is effectively reweighted.


2) Attention and memory
Emotion acts like a spotlight: - it makes certain cues more salient, - it increases rehearsal and recall for emotionally tagged events, - it can narrow attention under threat.
Prediction pattern: after emotionally intense events, people remember “the gist” and key cues, but details can be distorted.


3) Action readiness
Emotions prepare the body and mind for classes of actions: - fear → avoidance / vigilance, - anger → approach / punishment, - shame → concealment / withdrawal, - guilt → repair / apology.
This makes emotions especially important in social settings.

title: Emotion & motivation
text:
Motivation: what drives goal selection

Intrinsic vs extrinsic motivation

Intrinsic: activity is rewarding itself (curiosity, mastery, meaning).
Extrinsic: activity is a means to an end (money, grades, approval).

Prediction pattern: heavy extrinsic control can sometimes reduce intrinsic engagement, especially when it shifts the meaning from “I choose” to “I’m being controlled.”


Approach vs avoidance
A useful simplification: - Approach goals: obtain valued outcomes. - Avoidance goals: prevent negative outcomes.
Avoidance motivation can be extremely powerful and can dominate attention (e.g., threat monitoring).


Self-control and conflict
Self-control problems often reflect conflicts between: - short-run drives (comfort, impulses, immediate relief), - long-run goals (health, reputation, mastery).
Prediction pattern: commitment devices (pre-commitment, removing temptation, public deadlines) increase goal-consistent behavior without “changing personality.”

title: Emotion & motivation
section: Emotion as information (and when it misleads)
text:
Emotion as information (and when it misleads)
People often use feelings as a signal: - “I feel bad about it, so it must be risky.” - “I feel good about it, so it must be right.”
This can be adaptive, but it also creates systematic errors when feelings are driven by irrelevant cues.
Pitfall: confusing arousal with evidence.

title: Emotion & motivation
section: Social emotions: the bridge to norms, institutions, and conflict
text:
Social emotions: the bridge to norms, institutions, and conflict
Some emotions are inherently social: they depend on how one is seen, judged, or related to others.

Shame vs guilt (useful distinction)

Shame: “I am bad” → conceal, withdraw, avoid exposure.
Guilt: “I did something bad” → repair, apologize, compensate.

Prediction pattern: environments emphasizing public exposure increase shame; environments emphasizing repair increase guilt-driven pro-social behavior.


Anger and punishment
Anger is strongly tied to perceived norm violation and unfairness. It supports: - deterrence via credible retaliation, - norm enforcement in groups, - escalation in conflicts when misattributions occur.
Prediction pattern: increasing perceived intentionality of harm increases anger and punitive choices.


Empathy and compassion
Empathy can increase helping, but also: - be biased toward identifiable individuals, - be stronger for in-group members, - lead to burnout without boundaries.
Prediction pattern: abstract statistics move behavior less than vivid individual stories, even with identical expected harm.

title: Emotion & motivation
text:
Threat, stress, and “narrowing”
Under threat/stress: - people rely more on habits and scripts, - mentalizing depth decreases, - attention narrows to salient cues, - ambiguity is interpreted more pessimistically.
This is a key mechanism linking environment → cognition → behavior.
Prediction pattern: time pressure and threat cues increase reliance on stereotypes and reduce careful reasoning.

title: Emotion & motivation
text:
A reusable explanation template
When you explain a behavior using emotion/motivation, specify:

Trigger/appraisal: what is the event interpreted as?
Goal relevance: what goal is threatened or advanced?
Affect: what emotion is generated (valence, arousal)?
Action tendency: approach, avoid, punish, repair, withdraw?
Regulation: reappraisal, suppression, distraction, rumination?
Outcome: choice, social response, learning, reputation update.

title: Emotion & motivation
text:
Canonical examples (stubs you can expand)

Example A: “Hot” decisions

In a calm state, a person plans to act prudently.
In a hot state (anger, arousal), they choose confrontation or risk.
Later, regret and rationalization appear.

Mechanisms: state-dependent valuation + narrowed attention + action readiness.


Example B: Compliance via legitimacy

People comply not only because of expected punishment, but because noncompliance feels wrong.
Emotions like guilt/shame and moral identity reinforce compliance.

Mechanisms: norm internalization + social emotions + identity.

title: Emotion & motivation
text:
Connections to other sections

Social cognition
Emotion shapes attribution: - anger increases intentionality judgments, - fear increases threat interpretation, - shame increases self-focused attention.


Decision-making
Emotion changes perceived risk and time: - fear increases risk aversion in some settings, - anger can increase optimism and risk-taking, - stress increases present focus.


Criminology

escalation and retaliation,
legitimacy and procedural justice,
self-control and situational triggers,
crowd dynamics, peer influence, and identity.



Overlaps (later)
This page is the psychological backbone for: - strategic commitment (anger/reputation), - punishment and deterrence, - signaling via costly emotional displays.

title: Learning
text:
Learning explains how behavior changes with experience. It is not just “updating beliefs” in a rational sense; it includes associations, habits, reinforcement, imitation, and memory distortions.
A helpful split:

title: Learning
text:
A minimal decomposition
Most learning processes can be described as:

Signal: what feedback arrives (reward, punishment, approval, outcome)?
Credit assignment: what action/cue is blamed or credited?
Update rule: how strongly do we change behavior/belief?
Generalization: do we apply the lesson to similar situations?
Persistence: do we forget, decay, or form a habit?

Many “irrational” outcomes are really failures at (2) or distortions in (4).

title: Learning
section: Reinforcement learning: behavior shaped by reward and punishment
text:
Reinforcement learning: behavior shaped by reward and punishment
In reinforcement learning, choices are strengthened by outcomes: - actions followed by reward become more likely, - actions followed by punishment become less likely.
Key feature: reinforcement can shape behavior even when people cannot fully articulate why.

Prediction patterns

Variable rewards (unpredictable rewards) can create persistent behavior (strong habit formation).
Immediate feedback produces faster learning than delayed feedback.
Sparse feedback increases superstition-like associations (“it worked once, so it must work”).



Common pitfall
Assuming punishment always reduces behavior. In many social settings punishment can also: - increase attention and status, - increase resentment and retaliation, - teach avoidance rather than compliance.

title: Learning
text:
Habit: when actions become automatic
Habits are learned action patterns triggered by cues, not by deliberation.
A useful formula: cue → routine → reward
Habits are often: - fast, - effort-saving, - stable under stress, - insensitive to new information.
Prediction pattern: people can “know better” but still repeat the behavior because the cue triggers the routine.

Changing habits
Interventions that work: - remove or change cues, - replace the routine (substitute behavior), - keep some reward (so substitution is sustainable), - reshape the environment (friction, defaults).

title: Learning
section: Belief learning: updating what you think is true
text:
Belief learning: updating what you think is true
Belief learning includes: - learning base rates and frequencies, - causal learning (what causes what), - social belief learning (what others will do / what norms are).
Belief updating is often asymmetric: - people accept confirming evidence too easily, - scrutinize disconfirming evidence too harshly, - overweight vivid experiences relative to statistics.
Prediction pattern: vivid personal experiences can dominate statistical evidence, even when objectively less informative.

title: Learning
section: Social learning: imitation, norms, and “what people like us do”
text:
Social learning: imitation, norms, and “what people like us do”
A large share of human learning comes from others: - imitation, - instruction, - conformity, - prestige-biased copying (“copy the successful/high-status person”).
Two important norm channels: - descriptive norms: what most people do - injunctive norms: what people approve/disapprove
Prediction pattern: showing that “most people comply” can increase compliance more than moral appeals, but can backfire if noncompliance is framed as common.

title: Learning
section: Learning under uncertainty: exploration vs exploitation
text:
Learning under uncertainty: exploration vs exploitation
Learners trade off: - exploitation (do what already seems best), - exploration (try alternatives to learn more).
People often explore too little when: - feedback is noisy, - losses feel especially salient, - evaluation and reputation pressure are high.
Prediction pattern: when failure is publicly punished, exploration drops and systems stagnate.

title: Learning
section: Credit assignment: the hidden driver of bad learning
text:
Credit assignment: the hidden driver of bad learning
Credit assignment asks: what exactly caused the outcome?
Failures occur when: - multiple factors change at once, - outcomes are delayed, - the environment is strategic (others respond), - feedback is selective (you only see some outcomes).
Prediction pattern: in strategic environments, naive learners can misattribute outcomes to their own action instead of to opponents’ adaptation.

title: Learning
text:
A reusable explanation template
To explain a learned behavior, write:

Environment: what feedback structure exists (immediate/delayed, noisy, sparse)?
Cues: what triggers action?
Update mechanism: reinforcement, habit, belief updating, social learning?
Bias point: where does it go wrong (credit assignment, generalization, forgetting)?
Intervention: what changes learning (feedback timing, salience, norms, friction)?

title: Learning
text:
Canonical examples (stubs you can expand)

Example A: “I keep doing it even though I know it’s bad”

behavior is cued automatically,
reward is immediate (relief, pleasure),
costs are delayed.

Mechanisms: habit + reinforcement + present focus.


Example B: Learning in social conflict

one side escalates, other side responds,
each interprets response as confirmation of hostility,
both update toward distrust.

Mechanisms: biased attribution + reinforcement of defensive routines + selective memory.

title: Learning
text:
Connections to other sections

Decision-making
Learning shapes what options feel available and what outcomes feel likely.


Social cognition
Social learning depends on identity, trust, and perceived credibility.


Emotion & motivation
Emotional arousal changes learning rates and generalization; stress strengthens habit expression.


Criminology

deterrence depends on experienced and observed consequences,
peer effects and neighborhood norms shape learning,
enforcement can teach avoidance rather than compliance.

title: Foundations
text: Foundations are the “parts list” of psychological explanation: a small set of mechanisms that, combined, generate a wide variety of behaviors.

title: Foundations
text:
What counts as an explanation?
A good psychological explanation typically specifies: 1. Input (what information/stimuli the person receives), 2. Process (what computation / association / appraisal happens), 3. Output (choice, belief, emotion, or action), 4. Constraints (limits: attention, working memory, stress, incentives), 5. Predictions (what changes when the environment changes).

title: Foundations
text:
Why “mechanisms → predictions”?
Because it forces falsifiability: - If the mechanism is correct, changing X should shift behavior in Y direction. - If it doesn’t, either the mechanism is wrong or incomplete.

title: Foundations
text:
Suggested starting order

Decision-making

Learning

Social cognition

Emotion & motivation

Cognition

Methods (keep updating as you build pages)

title: Methods
text:
Methods are the discipline’s error-correction system: how we decide whether a psychological claim is true, how big the effect is, and when it generalizes.
This page is intentionally practical: it’s a checklist for evaluating evidence while you read papers or build arguments.

title: Methods
text:
The basic problem
Psychology studies internal states (beliefs, emotions, motives) using external signals (choices, reports, physiology, behavior).
That creates two recurring challenges:

Measurement: are we measuring what we think we’re measuring?
Inference: does the evidence support causality or only association?

title: Methods
section: Study types (and what each can and can’t do)
text:
Study types (and what each can and can’t do)

1) Experiments (randomized)
Strength: best for causal inference (if implemented well).
Weakness: may be artificial; limited generalization; demand effects.
Questions to ask: - Was assignment truly random? - Was there attrition (dropout) correlated with treatment? - Was the manipulation strong and specific (not confounded)? - Are outcomes pre-specified or cherry-picked?


2) Observational studies
Strength: real-world behavior, larger samples, external validity.
Weakness: confounding, selection, reverse causality.
Questions to ask: - What could cause both X and Y? - Could Y influence X? - Are there omitted variables that change interpretation?


3) Field experiments / natural experiments
Strength: causal inference in real settings.
Weakness: messy implementation; compliance issues; spillovers.
Questions to ask: - Was treatment actually delivered (compliance)? - Were there spillovers or displacement effects? - Was the identification assumption plausible?


4) Qualitative / case-based evidence
Strength: mechanisms, context, meaning, hypothesis generation.
Weakness: hard to estimate size; risks confirmation bias.
Questions to ask: - Is the case chosen systematically or selectively? - Are rival explanations considered?

title: Methods
text:
Measurement: validity beats vibes

Construct validity
Are we measuring the intended construct (e.g., “anxiety”, “trust”, “self-control”)?

Many constructs have multiple operationalizations.
Single-item measures are fragile.
Self-reports capture self-perception and presentation, not pure internal state.

Red flags: vague constructs + weak operational definition + strong conclusions.


Reliability
Do we get similar results if we measure again (or with equivalent items)?

Low reliability attenuates effects and creates noisy findings.
If measurement is unstable, inference becomes unstable.

A practical reading rule: > If reliability is not discussed for a key measure, treat estimates as fragile.


Demand characteristics and experimenter effects
People sometimes behave the way they think the experiment “wants.”
Mitigation ideas: - deception (when ethical), - cover stories, - unobtrusive behavioral measures, - double-blind procedures.

title: Methods
section: Causal inference: the minimum you need
text:
Causal inference: the minimum you need

Confounding (omitted variables)
If a third factor drives both X and Y, the association can be misleading.
Example schema: - trait T → both X and Y
So X and Y correlate even if X does not cause Y.


Selection
People choose into conditions (schools, jobs, groups). That choice is informative.
Example schema: - motivation → program participation + later success
So participation appears to “work” even if it’s selection.


Reverse causality
Y can cause X (or they co-evolve).


Mediation vs moderation (common confusion)

Mediator: X changes M, which changes Y (mechanism pathway).
Moderator: the effect of X on Y differs by Z (heterogeneity).

Quick test:
Mediator is “how”; moderator is “when/for whom.”

title: Methods
text:
Effect sizes: “statistically significant” is not “important”
Always separate: - direction (positive/negative), - magnitude (how big), - precision (confidence interval), - practical relevance (does it matter in the real world?).
Reading habit: if a paper only reports p-values without effect sizes and uncertainty, downgrade confidence.

title: Methods
section: Replicability and generalization (the two big filters)
text:
Replicability and generalization (the two big filters)

Replication
Can the effect be reproduced in a new sample with the same procedure?
Treat “one study” as: - suggestive evidence, not a conclusion.


Generalization
Does it hold across: - populations (age, culture), - settings (lab vs field), - measurement (different instruments), - incentives/stakes?
A useful mental model: > Effects can be real but local.

title: Methods
section: Common failure modes (how to spot weak evidence)
text:
Common failure modes (how to spot weak evidence)

Many outcomes tested, only the “wins” reported (multiple comparisons).
Researcher degrees of freedom (flexible stopping rules, model choices).
Post-hoc storytelling (hypotheses invented after results are known).
Small samples with big claims.
Convenience samples presented as universal human psychology.

This does not mean “ignore everything,” but it means “calibrate confidence.”

title: Methods
section: A practical checklist for any claim
text:
A practical checklist for any claim
When you read a claim, ask:

What exactly is the construct?

How is it measured? reliable? valid?

What is the identification strategy? randomization? controls? instruments?

What are alternative explanations? confounding? selection? reverse causality?

How big is the effect? and is it meaningful?

Does it replicate?

Where does it generalize?

If a paper passes (1)–(4), it’s already unusually strong.

title: Methods
text:
Connections to other sections

Decision-making, learning, social cognition
Methods tell you which behavioral patterns are robust and which are artifacts of measurement or sampling.


Criminology
Measurement and selection issues are central (reporting bias, enforcement bias, displacement/spillovers).
A methods mindset prevents “policy conclusions” from being driven by selection.


Overlaps (later)
Many strategic-behavior claims (trust, deterrence, cooperation) hinge on whether you can distinguish: - beliefs vs preferences, - selection vs treatment, - correlation vs causality.

title: Measurement
text:
Measurement is where many psychological arguments succeed or fail.
If you want to claim “X affects Y,” you must know: - what X and Y mean operationally, - whether they are measured reliably, - whether your measure captures the construct rather than noise.
This page is deeper than Methods: it’s about how variables are built.

title: Measurement
text:
Constructs vs measures
A construct is the idea (e.g., “trust”, “self-control”, “anxiety”).
A measure is the operational tool (survey items, tasks, behavior logs).
One construct can have many measures, and one measure can mix constructs.
Rule: never argue from labels. Argue from operational definitions.

title: Measurement
section: Validity: are you measuring what you think?
text:
Validity: are you measuring what you think?

Content validity
Does the measure cover the construct’s important aspects?


Convergent / discriminant validity

Convergent: does it correlate with other measures of the same construct?
Discriminant: does it avoid correlating with unrelated constructs?



Predictive validity
Does it predict outcomes the construct should predict?
Red flag: a measure is used because it is popular, not because it is justified for the specific argument.

title: Measurement
section: Reliability: is the measure stable enough to be useful?
text:
Reliability: is the measure stable enough to be useful?

Internal consistency (for multi-item scales)
Are items measuring the same underlying thing?


Test–retest reliability
Does the measure remain similar over time (when it should)?


Inter-rater reliability
When humans rate behavior, do they agree?
Practical implication: low reliability makes effects look unstable and encourages overfitting.

title: Measurement
text:
Self-report: useful but not “direct access”
Self-report captures: - introspection, - self-image, - social desirability, - memory reconstruction.
It can be excellent for private experiences, but it also has predictable distortions.
Prediction patterns - sensitive topics are underreported in low-trust settings. - social desirability rises when anonymity is low. - current mood biases reports (“state contamination”).
Design levers - anonymity and privacy, - neutral wording, - indirect questioning when appropriate, - multiple methods (triangulation).

title: Measurement
section: Behavioral tasks: what you gain and what you risk
text:
Behavioral tasks: what you gain and what you risk
Tasks can reduce self-presentation bias but may be sensitive to: - instructions and framing, - motivation and effort, - learning during the task, - “task impurity” (multiple mechanisms affect performance).
Rule of thumb: interpret tasks as measures of performance under specific conditions, not pure traits.

title: Measurement
section: Physiological measures: strong signals, hard interpretation
text:
Physiological measures: strong signals, hard interpretation
Physiology (heart rate, skin conductance, etc.) can indicate arousal but rarely maps 1:1 to a single emotion.
Pitfall: “arousal = fear” (often false).

title: Measurement
text:
Measurement invariance (cross-group comparability)
If you compare groups (cultures, genders, age), ask: - do items mean the same thing? - do response styles differ (acquiescence, extremity, modesty)?
Prediction pattern: apparent group differences can be measurement artifacts.

title: Measurement
text:
Common measurement errors (and fixes)

Range restriction
If everyone scores near the top or bottom, correlations shrink.


Floor/ceiling effects
The measure can’t detect change.


Reactivity
Measuring behavior changes behavior (people perform for the measure).


Demand characteristics
People infer the hypothesis and comply or resist.
Fix set: pretest, blind conditions, unobtrusive outcomes, manipulate checks, and triangulate.

title: Measurement
text:
A practical checklist
Before using a variable, write:

Construct definition (one sentence)

Operationalization (exact items/task/behavior)

Reliability evidence (or why it’s acceptable without it)

Validity argument (why this measure matches the construct)

Likely biases (social desirability, reactivity, invariance)

A robustness plan (alternate measures or sensitivity tests)

title: Measurement
text:
Connections

Methods: measurement quality determines inference quality.
Mental health / stigma: self-report is especially fragile under shame/fear.
Criminology: reporting and enforcement are measurement systems with selection bias.
Institutions: procedural justice shapes willingness to report truthfully.

title: How to study psychology
text:
Psychology is a discipline about mechanisms: how minds and social systems generate behavior. To study it well, you want to avoid two traps:
This guide gives a workflow for reading, note-making, and building explanations that connect to the rest of your site.

title: How to study psychology
section: 1) The core objects psychology tries to explain
text:
1) The core objects psychology tries to explain
Most psychological explanations target one (or more) of:

Behavior: actions, choices, habits, compliance, aggression, helping
Beliefs: what people think is true; confidence; uncertainty; trust in sources
Emotion: fear, anger, shame, guilt, motivation, arousal
Cognition: attention, memory, mental models, reasoning limits
Social interaction: trust, norms, identity, reputation, conflict and repair

When reading, ask: which object is this paper actually explaining?

title: How to study psychology
text:
2) Mechanisms first: a reusable template
Write every explanation in the same skeleton:

Input: what information / stimulus / context is present?
Representation: what does the person think the situation is?
Process: what mechanism runs? (attention, habit, appraisal, attribution, etc.)
Constraint: what limits apply? (working memory, stress, incentives, identity threat)
Output: what behavior/belief/emotion results?
Prediction: what changes if you vary the input or constraints?

If a claim has no (6), it’s not yet a good explanation.

title: How to study psychology
text:
3) Evidence hierarchy (practical, not dogmatic)
Different questions need different evidence:

Experiments: strongest for causality (if design is clean)
Field / natural experiments: causality + realism (but messy)
Observational studies: broad coverage (but confounding risks)
Qualitative / case evidence: mechanisms and context (weak on magnitude)

Your default should be: start with mechanism + prediction, then ask what evidence type can test it.

title: How to study psychology
text:
4) Always separate three things
Many confusions disappear if you keep these separate:

(i) Trait vs state vs skill

Trait: stable tendency
State: temporary condition (stress, fatigue)
Skill: learned capability (reappraisal, planning)



(ii) Preference vs cognition
Is the person choosing differently because they want something different, or because they represent/compute differently (attention, memory, framing)?


(iii) Bias vs noise
Is the pattern directional and systematic (bias), or just variability (noise)?

title: How to study psychology
text:
5) A minimal reading order (the “spine”)
If you want a clean progression:

Cognition → attention, memory, working memory limits

Learning → reinforcement, habit, feedback, adaptation

Decision-making → risk, time, heuristics, choice architecture

Emotion & motivation → threat, anger, shame/guilt, goal priority

Social cognition → mentalizing, attribution, identity, norms

Methods + measurement → what counts as evidence; validity/reliability

Then branch into Topics: - biases, norms & groups, moral psychology, relationships, development, etc.

title: How to study psychology
section: 6) How to take notes that remain useful
text:
6) How to take notes that remain useful
For every page you write, include:

Definitions (short and operational)
Mechanism (what actually runs in the mind/system)
Predictions (2–5 bullets)
Failure modes (when it won’t apply)
One canonical example (worked, not vague)
Interventions (what moves behavior and why)
Links to other pages (foundations ↔︎ topics ↔︎ overlaps)

If you do this, your notes won’t become a glossary.

title: How to study psychology
section: 7) Common pitfalls (and how to avoid them)
text:
7) Common pitfalls (and how to avoid them)

“Just-so” explanations
If the explanation can fit any outcome, it explains nothing. Fix: force counterfactual predictions (what would falsify it?).


Overgeneralizing from one study
Single results are fragile. Fix: look for replications and boundary conditions.


Confusing labels with mechanisms
“Self-control” or “trust” is not an explanation. Fix: specify the process (cue-triggered habit? threat appraisal? credibility heuristic?).


Ignoring measurement and selection
Especially with self-report and institutional data. Fix: ask how the variable is constructed; what’s missing; who is unobserved.

title: How to study psychology
section: 8) How this connects to the rest of the site
text:
8) How this connects to the rest of the site

Criminology: psychology explains reporting, compliance, escalation, legitimacy, peer effects.
Strategic interaction: psychology explains depth limits, credibility, norms, and emotion-as-commitment.
Institutions & policy: psychology explains salience, defaults, legitimacy, and adaptation.

title: How to study psychology
text:
Suggested “Start here” path

Foundations: psychology/foundations/index.qmd
Then: psychology/foundations/cognition.qmd
Then: psychology/foundations/learning.qmd
Then: decision-making, emotion & motivation, social cognition
Keep methods/measurement updated as you add pages

title: Relationships
text:
Relationships are repeated interaction under uncertainty: - you infer intentions from ambiguous signals, - you learn from feedback that is noisy and emotionally charged, - you coordinate norms, roles, and expectations over time.
This page is mechanism-first: attachment + trust + conflict cycles → predictions.

title: Relationships
text:
A compact map
Relationships often hinge on four systems:

Attachment / security (how safe connection feels)

Trust and expectations (beliefs about reliability and goodwill)

Communication and repair (how errors are handled)

Conflict regulation (how threat and anger are managed)

title: Relationships
section: Mechanism 1: Attachment as a threat-regulation system (high-level)
text:
Mechanism 1: Attachment as a threat-regulation system (high-level)
Attachment can be treated as a system for managing: - closeness vs autonomy, - safety vs threat, - seeking support vs self-reliance.
When security is high: - ambiguity is interpreted more benignly, - repair is easier, - cooperation is more resilient.
When security is low: - threat interpretation increases, - reassurance-seeking or withdrawal increases, - conflict escalates faster.
Prediction pattern: increasing perceived safety reduces reactive cycles more reliably than “better arguments.”
(This is a descriptive mechanism lens, not a clinical taxonomy.)

title: Relationships
section: Mechanism 2: Trust is learned, but fragile
text:
Mechanism 2: Trust is learned, but fragile
Trust is a belief about: - competence (“can they do it?”), - goodwill (“do they intend good?”), - predictability (“will they act consistently?”).
Trust updates asymmetrically: - one betrayal can outweigh many cooperative acts (negativity dominance), - ambiguous signals are interpreted through prior trust levels.
Prediction patterns - low-trust relationships interpret ambiguity as hostile, - high-trust relationships interpret ambiguity as error/noise, - public accountability (clear commitments) stabilizes trust.

title: Relationships
text:
Mechanism 3: Expectations and scripts
Relationships create scripts: - who does what, - what counts as respect, - what “normal” conflict looks like, - what repair looks like.
Scripts reduce cognitive load, but: - mismatched scripts create chronic misunderstanding, - unspoken expectations create resentment.
Prediction pattern: making expectations explicit reduces conflict more than increasing “effort.”

title: Relationships
text:
Mechanism 4: Conflict cycles (the interaction loop)
Many conflicts follow a loop:

ambiguous cue → negative interpretation

emotion (anger/fear/shame) rises

defensive behavior (attack/withdraw)

partner responds defensively

loop confirms the negative model

Two common defensive styles: - pursue/attack (demand, criticize, escalate) - withdraw/avoid (silence, delay, disengage)
Neither is “the problem” alone; the loop is the problem.
Prediction patterns - under stress, loops intensify (less mentalizing, more habit), - small face-saving opportunities reduce escalation, - repair attempts work only if perceived as sincere and timely.

title: Relationships
section: Mechanism 5: Repair as a high-leverage move
text:
Mechanism 5: Repair as a high-leverage move
Repair includes: - acknowledgment of harm, - credible explanation (not excuse), - commitment to change, - restitution/compensation, - emotional validation.
Repair works by shifting: - beliefs (“they care / they understand”), - emotions (reduced threat), - norms (“we fix things like this”).
Prediction pattern: repair is most effective when it happens early (before narratives harden).

title: Relationships
text:
Mechanism 6: Power, dependence, and asymmetry
Dependence shapes behavior: - the more dependent partner may accommodate more, - the less dependent partner may set norms.
Power differences can distort communication: - fear of consequences reduces honesty, - disagreement becomes costly, - concealment and resentment grow.
Prediction pattern: reducing fear and increasing safe voice increases truth-telling and cooperation.

title: Relationships
text:
A reusable relationship analysis template
To analyze a relationship dynamic, specify:

Uncertainty: what is ambiguous and how is it interpreted?

Security: does the system feel safe or threatening?

Trust: competence, goodwill, predictability—where is it weak?

Scripts: what expectations are implicit vs explicit?

Cycle: what is the repeating loop (attack/withdraw, criticism/defense)?

Repair: what intervention would interrupt the loop?

title: Relationships
text:
Canonical examples (stubs you can expand)

Example A: Misinterpretation → escalation

one side interprets delay as disrespect,
responds with criticism,
other withdraws,
criticism increases.

Mechanisms: attribution + threat sensitivity + pursue/withdraw loop.


Example B: Trust stabilization via commitments

clear commitments reduce ambiguity,
follow-through produces predictable feedback,
trust increases over time.

Mechanisms: credibility + learning + norm stabilization.

title: Relationships
text:
Connections

Foundations: social cognition (intent inference), emotion & motivation (anger/shame/guilt), communication (credibility/repair), learning (trust updates), sleep & stress (amplifier)
Topics: norms & groups (relationship norms), personality (heterogeneity), biases (interpretation errors)
Overlaps: institutions (procedural fairness is “relationship repair” at scale), criminology (conflict escalation, retaliation loops)

title: Addiction & compulsion
text:
This page is a mechanism map for persistent behaviors that feel hard to stop: substance use, gambling-like reinforcement patterns, compulsive checking, and other cue-driven cycles.
It is not a diagnostic guide. The goal is to understand loops: cue → craving/urge → action → reward/relief → learning → stronger cue control.

title: Addiction & compulsion
text:
The core loop
A compact loop that explains many compulsive patterns:

Cue (place, emotion, people, device, time)

Urge/craving (state shift: attention narrows)

Action (routine)

Reward or relief (positive or negative reinforcement)

Learning (habit strengthens; cues gain power)

Aftermath (guilt/shame/stress may create new cues)

Many interventions work by breaking the loop at (1) or (2), not at (4).

title: Addiction & compulsion
text:
Mechanism 1: Reinforcement (reward and relief)
Two reinforcement channels matter:

Positive reinforcement: behavior produces pleasure/reward.
Negative reinforcement: behavior removes discomfort (stress, anxiety, withdrawal, boredom).

Negative reinforcement is often the “stickiness engine” because relief is immediate.
Prediction patterns - stress increases craving and relapse risk (more need for relief). - delayed costs are discounted; immediate relief dominates. - inconsistent rewards can create persistent repetition.

title: Addiction & compulsion
section: Mechanism 2: Cue reactivity and attentional capture
text:
Mechanism 2: Cue reactivity and attentional capture
Over time, cues become powerful: - they trigger urges automatically, - they capture attention (“tunnel vision”), - they reduce working memory available for self-control.
Prediction patterns - exposure to cues increases cravings even without conscious intent. - “willpower” fails more in cue-rich environments.

title: Addiction & compulsion
text:
Mechanism 3: Habit dominance under stress
Under stress, fatigue, and sleep loss: - executive function decreases, - habits dominate, - people revert to default routines.
Prediction pattern: relapse often follows stress spikes or depletion states, even if motivation remains high.

title: Addiction & compulsion
text:
Mechanism 4: Identity and shame loops
After repeated failure, people can form an identity narrative: - “this is who I am,” - “I can’t change,” - “people will judge me.”
Shame often increases concealment and isolation, which reduces support and increases stress.
Prediction patterns - stigma reduces help-seeking. - social support and identity-safe environments increase sustained change.

title: Addiction & compulsion
text:
Mechanism 5: Social networks and norms
Behavior is shaped by: - peer availability and models, - shared routines, - norms about use and “what counts as normal.”
Prediction pattern: changing social context can matter as much as changing individual motivation.

title: Addiction & compulsion
text:
Interventions as loop-breaking (mechanism → lever)

Break at cues (1)

remove triggers,
change routes, routines, environments,
add friction (extra steps),
block access during vulnerable times.



Break at urge (2)

urge-surfing (delay the action),
emotion regulation strategies,
alternative relief (exercise, connection, structured activity),
“if-then” implementation intentions.



Break at action-to-reward mapping (3–4)

reduce reward intensity/availability,
increase immediate costs (commitment contracts),
replace routine with a lower-harm substitute.



Break at aftermath (6)

reduce shame and isolation,
build repair scripts (“slip ≠ collapse”),
increase support and accountability.

Key principle: if an intervention relies only on motivation, it will fail in cue-rich + high-stress environments.

title: Addiction & compulsion
text:
A reusable analysis template
When analyzing a compulsive pattern, specify:

Cues: what triggers it (external + internal states)?

Reinforcement: reward or relief? immediate or delayed?

Habit strength: how automatic is the routine?

Stress/sleep: what states amplify it?

Social context: who/what environment sustains it?

Loop break: which link can realistically be weakened?

title: Addiction & compulsion
text:
Connections

Foundations: learning, self-control, sleep & stress, emotion & motivation, cognition
Topics: mental health (anxiety/stress loops), relationships (support vs conflict)
Overlaps: institutions (treatment access, stigma), criminology (substance use, enforcement, rehabilitation dynamics)

title: Health psychology
text:
Common UG elective.
Health psychology studies how psychological mechanisms shape: - health behaviors (sleep, exercise, diet, substance use), - stress and coping, - adherence to treatment, - risk perception and health communication.
A useful framing: > Many “health problems” are behavior + environment problems, mediated by attention, habit, emotion, and social norms.

title: Health psychology
section: 1) A simple model of health behavior
text:
1) A simple model of health behavior
Health behavior is shaped by:

Capabilities (skills, executive control, knowledge)
Opportunities (access, time, cost, environment cues)
Motivation (goals, identity, reward/relief)
Feedback (immediate vs delayed consequences)
Social context (norms, support, stigma)

If you ignore opportunities and feedback timing, you’ll over-blame “willpower.”

title: Health psychology
text:
2) Stress and coping
Stress changes: - attention (tunnel vision), - time horizon (short-run relief dominates), - emotion regulation (irritability, avoidance), - habit expression (defaults take over).
Coping strategies often split into: - problem-focused (change the situation), - emotion-focused (change how it feels), - avoidant (escape, short-run relief).
Prediction patterns - avoidant coping reduces distress short-run but maintains long-run problems (avoidance loops). - stable routines reduce stress reactivity over time.

title: Health psychology
text:
3) Health beliefs and risk perception
People do not perceive risk objectively. Risk perception is shaped by: - availability (vivid cases dominate), - framing (relative vs absolute risk), - trust in source, - emotion (fear/anger), - numeracy and comprehension (without blaming individuals).
Prediction patterns - narratives move behavior more than statistics when trust is low. - trust in institutions predicts compliance with guidance.
Intervention lever: improve clarity + credibility rather than only increasing information volume.

title: Health psychology
section: 4) Adherence: why people don’t follow treatment plans
text:
4) Adherence: why people don’t follow treatment plans
Non-adherence can arise from: - forgetting (attention/retrieval failure), - low expectancy (“this won’t help”), - side effects and immediate costs, - stigma and identity threat, - lack of access (structural constraint), - mistrust in providers/institutions.
Prediction patterns - reminders at the right time increase adherence even without changing beliefs. - respectful treatment and voice increase adherence through legitimacy.

title: Health psychology
section: 5) Habit and cue control (the real workhorse)
text:
5) Habit and cue control (the real workhorse)
Health behaviors are strongly cue-driven: - time-of-day routines, - location cues (kitchen, bed, phone), - emotional cues (stress → snack, anxiety → avoidance).
Prediction patterns - environment redesign outperforms motivation-only interventions. - small frictions (e.g., making unhealthy choices harder) have large effects.

title: Health psychology
text:
6) Behavior change tools (evidence-aligned, non-clinical)
Linking to your toolkit page, common high-leverage tools include:

Implementation intentions (“If it’s 10pm, I start wind-down.”)
Defaults and automation (pre-scheduling, subscriptions, medication organizers)
Commitment devices (public plans, deposits, accountability)
Self-monitoring (tracking as attention support, not moral judgment)
Social support (norms and belonging)
Choice architecture (reduce choice overload; reduce friction for desired action)

Prediction pattern: tools work best when they act at the cue stage, not at the “willpower stage.”

title: Health psychology
text:
7) Placebo, expectations, and meaning (high-level)
Expectations can change: - perceived symptoms, - pain and discomfort, - engagement and adherence.
This is not “fake”; it reflects how brain/body interpret signals under uncertainty.
Prediction pattern: credible rituals and trusted providers increase expectancy effects.

title: Health psychology
text:
8) Health inequalities (environment + stress + access)
Health outcomes correlate with: - chronic stress exposure, - neighborhood environment, - access to care, - time scarcity, - stigma and institutional trust.
Prediction pattern: interventions that ignore structural constraints may widen inequality (only the well-resourced can comply).

title: Health psychology
text:
A reusable health-psych analysis template
When analyzing a health behavior, specify:

Behavior (what exactly?)

Cue (when/where/with whom/which emotion)

Reinforcement (reward or relief; immediate vs delayed)

Constraints (time, money, access, stigma)

Beliefs (expectancy, trust, risk perception)

Social context (norms, support)

Intervention (which lever acts earliest in the loop?)

title: Health psychology
text:
Connections

Foundations: self-control, sleep & stress, learning, emotion & motivation, measurement
Topics: addiction & compulsion, mental health, therapy tools
Overlaps: institutions (trust and access), policy design (friction/defaults), criminology (substance use, stress exposure)

title: Mental health
text:
This page is a foundational, non-clinical map of mental health topics that matter for understanding behavior. It is not a diagnostic guide. The goal is to organize mechanisms and predictions in a way that is useful for study and for linking to other parts of the site (decision-making, learning, emotion, social cognition).
A helpful framing: > Mental health patterns often reflect interactions between vulnerabilities, environments, and coping strategies.

title: Mental health
text:
Core dimensions (a practical map)
Many symptoms can be grouped by a few dimensions:

Negative affect: persistent sadness, anxiety, guilt, irritability
Threat sensitivity: hypervigilance, avoidance, panic responses
Reward processing: reduced pleasure, low motivation, anhedonia
Cognitive control: attention, impulsivity, rumination, executive function
Sleep and arousal: insomnia, fatigue, agitation
Social functioning: isolation, mistrust, rejection sensitivity

Different “disorders” often share dimensions. That’s part of why comorbidity is common.

title: Mental health
section: Stress and vulnerability: a general mechanism
text:
Stress and vulnerability: a general mechanism
A broad mechanism often used is:

Vulnerability (traits, history, genetics, learned patterns)
Stressors (acute shocks, chronic strain, social conflict)
Protective factors (support, coping skills, stable routines)

Prediction pattern: the same stressor affects people differently depending on vulnerability and protection.

title: Mental health
text:
Anxiety: threat and uncertainty
Anxiety is often characterized by: - heightened threat perception, - intolerance of uncertainty, - avoidance behavior, - safety-seeking behaviors that reduce anxiety short-run but maintain it long-run.
Learning loop (common): - uncertainty → anxiety → avoidance → temporary relief → stronger avoidance habit
Prediction pattern: reducing avoidance and increasing safe exposure often weakens the loop over time (mechanism: learning + prediction error).

title: Mental health
text:
Depression: reward, energy, and self-evaluation
Depressive patterns often involve: - reduced motivation and energy, - diminished reward sensitivity (things feel less rewarding), - negative self-evaluation, - rumination (repetitive negative thinking).
Behavioral loop (common): - low mood → withdrawal → fewer rewarding experiences → lower mood
Prediction pattern: small increases in structured rewarding activity can have outsized effects because they interrupt the loop (mechanism: reinforcement and habit).

title: Mental health
section: Rumination: repetitive thought as a trap
text:
Rumination: repetitive thought as a trap
Rumination feels like problem-solving but often functions as: - attention capture, - negative memory retrieval, - threat rehearsal, - reduced action initiation.
Prediction pattern: interventions that shift attention (structured activity, reappraisal skills, sleep stabilization) reduce rumination frequency.

title: Mental health
section: Trauma-related patterns: memory, threat, and triggers
text:
Trauma-related patterns: memory, threat, and triggers
After extreme stress, some people develop: - intrusive memories, - hypervigilance, - avoidance of reminders, - emotional numbing, - sleep disruption.
Mechanism lens: emotion-tagged memory + threat system sensitization + avoidance learning.
Prediction pattern: unpredictable triggers and uncertain environments maintain hypervigilance.

title: Mental health
text:
ADHD-like patterns (non-diagnostic framing)
Common behavioral dimensions include: - inattention under low stimulation, - difficulty sustaining effort, - impulsivity (short-horizon choice), - strong sensitivity to immediate rewards.
Mechanism lens: attention regulation + reinforcement sensitivity + executive control load.
Prediction pattern: structure, feedback frequency, and reduced friction can help performance even without changing “traits.”

title: Mental health
section: Substance use and compulsive behavior (mechanism lens)
text:
Substance use and compulsive behavior (mechanism lens)
A compact mechanism view: - strong immediate reward/relief, - habit formation, - cue-triggered craving, - withdrawal/negative reinforcement, - social context and norms.
Prediction pattern: changing cue environments and social networks often matters as much as willpower.

title: Mental health
text:
Stigma and social context (often overlooked)
Mental health is shaped by: - perceived acceptance vs rejection, - shame and concealment, - access to support and care, - institutional treatment (school, workplace, legal system).
Prediction pattern: reducing stigma and increasing safe disclosure channels increases help-seeking and reduces isolation loops.

title: Mental health
text:
A reusable explanation template
When discussing a mental health-related behavior, specify:

Dimension(s) involved (threat, reward, control, sleep, social)
Loop (avoidance loop? withdrawal loop? rumination loop?)
Context (stressors, stability, social support)
Prediction (what change would interrupt the loop?)
Boundaries (what you are not claiming; avoid diagnosis)

title: Mental health
text:
Connections

Emotion & motivation: affective systems and action tendencies are central.
Learning: avoidance and reinforcement loops maintain patterns.
Cognition: attention and memory biases shape symptoms.
Norms & groups: stigma and identity can worsen or buffer outcomes.
Criminology (later link): trauma exposure, substance use, and stress can affect compliance, escalation, and institutional interactions.

title: Sleep & stress
text:
Sleep and stress modulate almost every mechanism in psychology: - attention and working memory, - emotion regulation, - threat sensitivity, - learning and habit expression, - social interpretation.
This page treats them as system-wide parameters rather than niche health topics.

title: Sleep & stress
section: Sleep: the cognitive and emotional regulator
text:
Sleep: the cognitive and emotional regulator
Sleep influences: - attention (vigilance, sustained focus), - working memory (multi-step reasoning), - emotion regulation (reactivity and recovery), - learning (consolidation of memories and skills).
Prediction patterns - sleep loss increases errors and impulsivity, - sleep loss increases negative affect and threat sensitivity, - complex reasoning and self-control degrade earlier than simple tasks.
Practical implication: if behavior looks “irrational” under sleep loss, it may be capacity limits rather than preference change.

title: Sleep & stress
text:
Stress: acute vs chronic

Acute stress
Acute stress often produces: - narrowed attention (“tunnel vision”), - faster but less flexible action, - reliance on habits and scripts, - increased threat interpretation.
Prediction pattern: under acute stress, people choose simpler strategies and show less deep mentalizing.


Chronic stress
Chronic stress often produces: - fatigue and reduced executive function, - irritability and negative affect, - reduced exploratory behavior, - stronger avoidance and withdrawal loops.
Prediction pattern: chronic stress shifts behavior toward short-run relief strategies.

title: Sleep & stress
text:
Threat sensitivity: the amplifier channel
A key pathway is threat detection: - when threat systems are activated, ambiguity is interpreted pessimistically, - social cues are read as hostile more often, - retaliation and defensiveness increase.
Prediction patterns - minor provocations escalate faster under stress, - distrust spreads more quickly in low-safety environments, - institutions that feel threatening reduce cooperation.

title: Sleep & stress
text:
Stress and learning: habit dominance
Stress often increases: - reliance on well-learned routines, - avoidance learning, - reinforcement of immediate relief behaviors.
Prediction pattern: in stressful environments, behavior becomes more habitual and less responsive to abstract information.

title: Sleep & stress
section: Stress and social cognition: attribution shifts
text:
Stress and social cognition: attribution shifts
Under stress, people: - mentalize less deeply, - rely more on stereotypes and categories, - commit more attribution errors (trait-blame vs situation).
Prediction pattern: conflict and polarization rise when stress is high and identity boundaries are salient.

title: Sleep & stress
text:
Interventions: what reliably helps (mechanism-first)

Reduce load

simplify tasks and choices,
reduce multitasking,
restructure environments to make the desired action easy.



Increase predictability and safety

clear procedures, stable rules,
respectful treatment (legitimacy),
face-saving options to reduce humiliation-driven escalation.



Improve recovery and regulation

consistent sleep routines,
downtime after conflict exposure,
supportive social ties and safe disclosure.

Note: these are not “motivational slogans”; they change cognitive capacity and emotional reactivity.

title: Sleep & stress
text:
A reusable analysis template
When sleep/stress may matter, ask:

State: acute vs chronic?

Capacity: attention/working memory reduced?

Emotion: threat sensitivity elevated?

Habit: are routines dominating?

Social inference: more hostile attribution likely?

Prediction: what changes if you reduce load or increase safety?

title: Sleep & stress
text:
Connections

Foundations: cognition, emotion & motivation, learning, self-control, social cognition
Topics: norms & groups (stress amplifies group threat dynamics)
Overlaps: institutions (procedural justice reduces threat), criminology (hot spots, escalation, legitimacy), communication (arousal-driven spread)

title: Moral psychology
text:
Moral psychology studies how people judge right and wrong, and why they enforce norms. It connects directly to: - punishment and forgiveness, - legitimacy and compliance, - polarization and “moralized” conflict.
This page uses a mechanism-first approach: moral intuitions + emotion + identity → judgments and enforcement.

title: Moral psychology
text:
Two systems (a useful simplification)
Moral judgment often reflects interaction between: - fast intuitions (emotion and gut reactions), - slower reasoning (justification, consistency checks).
Reasoning is important, but often functions as: - clarification and coherence, - persuasion, - post-hoc explanation.
Pitfall: assuming that moral disagreement is mostly about facts. Often it’s about values, identity, and perceived intent.

title: Moral psychology
text:
Key objects in moral cognition

Harm and care
People react strongly to perceived harm, especially intentional harm.
Prediction pattern: perceived intentionality increases blame and punishment.


Fairness and reciprocity
Unfairness triggers anger and punitive motivation. Reciprocity supports cooperation.
Prediction pattern: people punish unfairness even when punishment is costly.


Loyalty and group-boundaries
Group membership shapes whose suffering is salient and whose claims are credible.
Prediction pattern: moral judgments become harsher when out-groups are seen as threatening or disrespectful.


Authority and legitimacy
People often treat legitimate authority as morally relevant: - “rules exist for a reason” - “respect the process”
Prediction pattern: procedural fairness increases voluntary compliance.


Purity and contamination (where relevant)
Some moral judgments are linked to disgust and boundary maintenance.
Prediction pattern: disgust can increase harshness even when harm is unclear.

title: Moral psychology
section: Emotion as the engine of moral enforcement
text:
Emotion as the engine of moral enforcement
Moral emotions drive action: - anger → punishment and confrontation - disgust → exclusion and distancing - shame → concealment and conformity pressure - guilt → repair and apology - contempt → status downgrading and dehumanization risk
Prediction pattern: when anger is high, people over-attribute intentionality and demand harsher sanctions.

title: Moral psychology
text:
Intentions matter (often more than outcomes)
People judge harm differently based on: - intentional vs accidental, - negligent vs unavoidable, - provoked vs unprovoked, - foreseeable vs unforeseeable.
Prediction pattern: giving clear evidence of constraints reduces blame (shifts from “bad person” to “bad situation”).

title: Moral psychology
text:
Moralization: when preferences become sacred
Some issues become “moralized”: - disagreement feels like betrayal, - compromise feels dirty, - opponents feel dangerous.
Prediction patterns - moralized issues polarize more strongly than non-moral issues, - punishment and exclusion become more acceptable, - factual debate becomes less effective.
Intervention lever: de-moralize where possible by shifting from blame to shared goals and tradeoffs.

title: Moral psychology
text:
Norm enforcement: formal and informal
People enforce norms through: - gossip and reputation, - praise and shame, - exclusion, - punishment (private or public), - institutional enforcement (police, courts, HR, schools).
Prediction patterns - observability increases compliance and norm enforcement, - selective enforcement damages legitimacy, - unclear norms invite conflict over interpretation and power.

title: Moral psychology
text:
A reusable moral analysis template
When analyzing a moral conflict, specify:

What norm is at stake? (harm, fairness, loyalty, authority, purity?)

What intention is attributed? (hostile, negligent, accidental?)

What emotions are active? (anger, disgust, shame, guilt?)

What identity boundary is salient? (us vs them?)

What enforcement channel exists? (informal vs institutional)

Prediction: what changes if you change transparency, fairness, or face-saving options?

title: Moral psychology
text:
Canonical examples (stubs you can expand)

Example A: Punishment demand after perceived disrespect

small disrespect is interpreted as intentional threat,
anger rises,
punitive preference increases.

Mechanisms: threat interpretation + anger + status concern.


Example B: Legitimacy-based compliance

people comply because noncompliance feels wrong,
not just because punishment is feared.

Mechanisms: authority legitimacy + moral identity + guilt/shame.

title: Moral psychology
text:
Connections

Foundations: emotion & motivation, social cognition, communication (moral framing), methods (avoid story-driven claims)
Topics: norms & groups (in-group favoritism), relationships (repair and forgiveness), biases (intent attribution errors)
Overlaps: institutions (procedural justice), criminology (punishment, legitimacy, retaliation)

title: Tools for behavior change
text:
This page collects non-clinical, skills-based tools that reliably change behavior through mechanisms you’ve already covered: attention, learning, emotion regulation, and environment design.
It is not therapy advice or diagnosis. It’s a toolkit of methods that show up in many evidence-based approaches.

title: Tools for behavior change
text:
Tool 1: Implementation intentions (if–then plans)
Format: - “If situation S happens, then I will do action A.”
Why it works: - links cues to desired actions, - reduces working-memory demand at the moment of choice.
Prediction pattern: works best when S is specific and A is small and feasible.

title: Tools for behavior change
section: Tool 2: Behavioral activation (do first, feel later)
text:
Tool 2: Behavioral activation (do first, feel later)
When mood is low, waiting for motivation often fails. Behavioral activation: - schedules small rewarding/meaningful actions, - rebuilds reinforcement and routine.
Mechanism: learning + reward + breaking withdrawal loops.

title: Tools for behavior change
text:
Tool 3: Reappraisal (change the interpretation)
Reappraisal changes how an event is construed: - from insult → misunderstanding, - from catastrophe → challenge, - from personal failure → information.
Mechanism: emotion regulation via appraisal shifts.
Prediction pattern: reappraisal is easier before arousal peaks.

title: Tools for behavior change
text:
Tool 4: Exposure (reduce avoidance loops)
Avoidance reduces anxiety short-run but maintains it long-run. Exposure: - safely faces the cue in graded steps, - allows prediction errors (“I can tolerate this”).
Mechanism: learning under uncertainty; updating threat associations.

title: Tools for behavior change
text:
Tool 5: Friction and defaults (environment design)
If a behavior is cue-driven, modify the environment: - add friction to harmful routines, - make desired routines the default.
Mechanism: attention + habit control.

title: Tools for behavior change
text:
Tool 6: Values and identity alignment
Change sticks when behavior is identity-consistent: - “I’m the kind of person who…” - tie actions to meaning rather than only outcomes.
Mechanism: motivation + norms + self-concept.

title: Tools for behavior change
section: Tool 7: Repair scripts (for relationships and institutions)
text:
Tool 7: Repair scripts (for relationships and institutions)
Repair is structured: - acknowledge → validate → explain → commit → compensate (when appropriate)
Mechanism: reduces threat, restores trust, resets norms.

title: Tools for behavior change
text:
A reusable behavior-change plan template

Identify the cue (when/where/with whom)

Identify the loop (urge → action → reward/relief)

Pick one lever: cues, friction, substitute routine, reappraisal, exposure, support

Define one measurable micro-action

Add feedback: tracking, accountability, or public commitment

Plan for slips: “slip ≠ collapse” script

title: Tools for behavior change
text:
Connections

Self-control: cue management and commitment.
Learning: habit substitution and reinforcement.
Emotion & motivation: reappraisal and avoidance loops.
Relationships / institutions: repair and legitimacy.

title: Norms & groups
text:
Groups change psychology. People do not only act as individuals; they act as members of “us” and “them,” under shared expectations about what is normal and what is acceptable.
This page is organized as: identity + norms + social dynamics → predictions.

title: Norms & groups
text:
Core concepts

Groups and identity
A group can be defined by: - membership (formal or informal), - shared symbols (language, style, rituals), - shared fate (common outcomes), - shared narratives (“who we are”).
Identity is the psychological meaning of group membership: - it shapes attention (what matters), - it shapes belief credibility (who is trusted), - it shapes motivation (what feels worth doing), - it shapes emotion (pride, shame, anger).


Norms
Norms are shared expectations about behavior.
Two useful types: - Descriptive norms: what people actually do (“most people recycle”). - Injunctive norms: what people approve (“people should recycle”).
They can move in different directions.
Pitfall: using one as evidence for the other.

title: Norms & groups
text:
Mechanism 1: Conformity and informational reliance
People conform for at least two reasons: - Informational: “Others probably know something I don’t.” - Social: “I want approval / I want to avoid rejection.”
Prediction patterns - Conformity increases with uncertainty and ambiguity. - Conformity increases when the group is cohesive and salient. - Conformity decreases when private dissent feels safe.
Intervention levers - make independent judgment easier (private responses), - increase clarity (reduce ambiguity), - highlight diversity of behavior (break false consensus).

title: Norms & groups
section: Mechanism 2: Social identity and in-group favoritism
text:
Mechanism 2: Social identity and in-group favoritism
Once “us vs them” is salient, people often: - interpret in-group behavior more charitably, - interpret out-group behavior more suspiciously, - allocate benefits to in-group members, - enforce harsher standards on out-groups.
Prediction patterns - Shared identity salience increases cooperation inside the group. - Strong subgroup identity can increase intergroup hostility. - Threat cues amplify “us vs them” categorization.
Intervention levers - superordinate identity (“we are all part of …”), - cross-cutting ties (friendships across groups), - institutional norms that reward fairness across boundaries.

title: Norms & groups
text:
Mechanism 3: Polarization and motivated reasoning (group-based)
Group identity can shape beliefs: - People accept in-group narratives more readily. - Evidence from out-group sources is discounted. - Mixed evidence can increase confidence rather than reduce it (biased assimilation).
Prediction patterns - Polarization rises when status or moral identity is threatened. - Argument quality matters less than source identity in highly polarized contexts. - “Correcting misinformation” can backfire if it signals out-group dominance.
Intervention levers - trusted in-group messengers, - identity-safe framing (“you can believe X and still be one of us”), - shared goals that reorient attention to outcomes.

title: Norms & groups
text:
Mechanism 4: Norm enforcement and punishment
Groups often sustain norms through: - gossip, - praise/shame, - exclusion, - punishment.
This can support prosocial behavior, but it can also produce rigidity and scapegoating.
Prediction patterns - Enforcement increases when behavior is observable. - Enforcement is stronger when violations signal disrespect or threat. - If institutions are seen as illegitimate, informal enforcement rises (sometimes violently).
Intervention levers - increase procedural fairness (legitimacy), - make pro-social behavior visible, - reduce ambiguous “gray-zone” rules that invite selective punishment.

title: Norms & groups
text:
Mechanism 5: Social dilemmas (cooperation problems)
Many group outcomes involve: - individual incentives to free-ride, - collective need for cooperation, - difficulty monitoring contributions.
Prediction patterns - Cooperation increases with repeated interaction and observability. - Cooperation increases when norms are salient and shared identity is strong. - Cooperation collapses when people believe others are defecting (expectation cascades).
Intervention levers - transparency (credible monitoring), - low-cost signals of commitment, - “conditional cooperation” design (make cooperation the default once enough others do).

title: Norms & groups
text:
A reusable explanation template
To explain a group outcome, specify:

Group boundaries: who is “us” vs “them”?

Norms: what is descriptive vs injunctive?

Observability: who sees what?

Sanctions: how are norms enforced (formal vs informal)?

Threat & status: is identity/status at stake?

Prediction: what shifts if identity/norm salience changes?

title: Norms & groups
text:
Canonical examples (stubs you can expand)

Example A: False consensus / pluralistic ignorance

Many privately disagree with a norm.
Everyone believes others support it.
Public conformity persists.

Mechanisms: social fear + misperceived descriptive norms.


Example B: Escalation between groups

ambiguous act → hostile interpretation,
retaliation → confirms hostility,
norms shift toward aggression.

Mechanisms: threat sensitivity + attribution + norm enforcement.

title: Norms & groups
text:
Connections

Social cognition: identity shapes inference and trust.
Emotion & motivation: shame, pride, anger drive norm enforcement.
Criminology: legitimacy, trust, reporting, retaliation, and community enforcement all hinge on norms and group identity.
Overlap pages: strategic interaction becomes psychologically richer once identity and norms enter the utility function.

title: Fixed Points
text:
A fixed point is a point that is mapped back to itself. In game theory, fixed-point reasoning is central because an equilibrium is often a situation where each player’s strategy is consistent with everyone else’s strategy.
The basic idea is simple:
\[
x^* = f(x^*).
\]
The input and output coincide. Nothing changes after the mapping is applied.

title: Fixed Points
text:
The basic idea
Suppose there is a function
\[
f:X \to X.
\]
A point \(x^* \in X\) is a fixed point of \(f\) if
\[
f(x^*) = x^*.
\]
This means that if we start at \(x^*\) and apply the function, we end up exactly where we started.





flowchart LR
    A[Start with x] --> B[Apply mapping f]
    B --> C[Get f x]
    C --> D{Is f x equal to x?}
    D -->|Yes| E[Fixed point]
    D -->|No| F[Not fixed]






The concept is useful because many stability ideas have this structure.

title: Fixed Points
text:
Simple example
Let
\[
f(x)=\frac{x+1}{2}.
\]
A fixed point satisfies
\[
x=\frac{x+1}{2}.
\]
Multiply both sides by 2:
\[
2x=x+1.
\]
So
\[
x=1.
\]
Therefore, \(x^*=1\) is a fixed point.
Check:
\[
f(1)=\frac{1+1}{2}=1.
\]

title: Fixed Points
text:
Fixed points and equilibrium
In game theory, a Nash equilibrium can be understood as a fixed point of best-response reasoning.
Each player chooses a best response to what the others do. If everyone is already best responding to everyone else, the strategy profile is stable.





flowchart LR
    A[Strategy profile] --> B[Best-response mapping]
    B --> C[New strategy profile]
    C --> D{Same as before?}
    D -->|Yes| E[Nash equilibrium]
    D -->|No| F[Adjust again]






The formal idea is:
\[
s^* \in BR(s^*).
\]
Here \(BR\) is the best-response correspondence. A Nash equilibrium is a fixed point of the best-response correspondence.

title: Fixed Points
text:
Function versus correspondence
A function assigns exactly one output to each input.
A correspondence can assign a set of possible outputs to each input.
For example, a best response may not be unique. A player may be indifferent between several strategies. In that case, the best-response object is a correspondence rather than a function.





flowchart TD
    A[Input] --> B{Mapping type}
    B --> C[Function: one output]
    B --> D[Correspondence: set of outputs]
    D --> E[Best responses may be multiple]






This is why many equilibrium existence theorems use fixed-point theorems for correspondences.

title: Fixed Points
text:
Why fixed points matter
Fixed-point reasoning helps prove that an equilibrium exists.
In many models, we do not solve directly for the equilibrium. Instead, we show that some mapping must have a fixed point. If the mapping represents best responses, then the fixed point is an equilibrium.
The logic is:





flowchart LR
    A[Define strategy space] --> B[Define best-response mapping]
    B --> C[Check mathematical conditions]
    C --> D[Apply fixed-point theorem]
    D --> E[Equilibrium exists]






This is especially important in games with continuous strategy spaces or mixed strategies.

title: Fixed Points
text:
Brouwer fixed-point theorem
The Brouwer fixed-point theorem says, roughly:

If a continuous function maps a compact and convex set into itself, then it has at least one fixed point.

A simplified statement is:
Let \(X\) be non-empty, compact, and convex. If
\[
f:X \to X
\]
is continuous, then there exists some \(x^* \in X\) such that
\[
f(x^*)=x^*.
\]
The key conditions are:



Condition
Meaning




Non-empty
There is at least one possible point


Compact
The set is closed and bounded


Convex
Mixtures of points stay inside the set


Continuous
Small input changes do not create jumps


Maps into itself
The output remains feasible

title: Fixed Points
text:
Kakutani fixed-point theorem
Kakutani’s theorem extends the logic to correspondences.
A simplified version says:

If a correspondence maps a non-empty, compact, convex set into itself, and satisfies suitable continuity and convexity conditions, then it has a fixed point.

This is useful for game theory because best responses may be set-valued.
A fixed point of a correspondence \(F\) is a point \(x^*\) such that
\[
x^* \in F(x^*).
\]
For Nash equilibrium, this becomes:
\[
