s^* \in BR(s^*).
\]

title: Fixed Points
text:
Fixed points in mixed strategies
Finite games may fail to have a pure-strategy Nash equilibrium, but they always have a mixed-strategy Nash equilibrium.
The existence proof relies on fixed-point reasoning.
The intuition is:

each player has a set of mixed strategies;
each player has best responses to others’ mixed strategies;
the best-response correspondence maps the strategy space into itself;
under appropriate conditions, there is a fixed point;
that fixed point is a Nash equilibrium.






flowchart TD
    A[Finite game] --> B[Mixed strategy spaces]
    B --> C[Best-response correspondence]
    C --> D[Fixed-point theorem]
    D --> E[Mixed-strategy Nash equilibrium exists]






This does not tell us which equilibrium is best or unique. It only guarantees existence.

title: Fixed Points
Fixed Points
text:
Fixed point versus convergence
A fixed point is not the same as convergence.
A mapping may have a fixed point, but the process of repeatedly applying the mapping may not necessarily converge to it.
For example, a system can cycle:





flowchart LR
    A[State A] --> B[State B]
    B --> C[State C]
    C --> A






So we should separate two questions:

Does a fixed point exist?
Will a process actually reach it?

Existence is mathematical. Convergence is dynamic.

title: Fixed Points
text:
Application: best-response dynamics
In best-response dynamics, players repeatedly adjust to what others did before.





flowchart LR
    A[Initial strategies] --> B[Player 1 best responds]
    B --> C[Player 2 best responds]
    C --> D[New strategies]
    D --> E{Stable?}
    E -->|Yes| F[Equilibrium]
    E -->|No| B






If the process reaches a point where no one wants to change, it has reached a Nash equilibrium.
But best-response dynamics do not always converge. Some games cycle.

title: Fixed Points
text:
Common mistakes

1. Thinking a fixed point must be unique
A mapping may have one fixed point, many fixed points, or none.


2. Confusing fixed point with maximum
A fixed point solves \(x=f(x)\). An optimum solves a maximization or minimization problem.


3. Confusing existence with computation
A theorem may prove that an equilibrium exists without telling us how to find it.


4. Confusing existence with stability
A fixed point may exist even if a dynamic process does not converge to it.


5. Ignoring assumptions
Fixed-point theorems require conditions such as compactness, convexity, continuity, and self-mapping.

title: Fixed Points
text:
Checklist
When you see fixed-point reasoning, ask:

What is the set \(X\)?
What is the mapping \(f\) or correspondence \(F\)?
Does it map \(X\) into itself?
Is \(X\) non-empty?
Is \(X\) compact?
Is \(X\) convex?
Is the mapping continuous or suitably well-behaved?
What does the fixed point mean substantively?
Is the fixed point an equilibrium, steady state, or stable belief?
Does the argument prove existence, uniqueness, or convergence?

title: Probability
text:
Probability is the language of uncertainty. In game theory, it appears whenever players randomise, hold beliefs, observe signals, face private information, or make decisions under incomplete knowledge.
This page introduces the probability tools most often used in the notes: events, random variables, expectation, mixed strategies, conditional probability, Bayes’ rule, signals, types, and posterior beliefs.

title: Probability
section: Why probability matters in game theory
text:
Why probability matters in game theory
Game theory uses probability in two main ways.
First, probability can describe randomisation. A mixed strategy is a probability distribution over actions.
Second, probability can describe beliefs. In Bayesian games, players may be uncertain about another player’s type, payoff, information, or intention.





flowchart TD
    A[Probability in Game Theory] --> B[Randomisation]
    A --> C[Beliefs]

    B --> B1[Mixed Strategies]
    B --> B2[Expected Payoffs]
    B --> B3[Indifference Conditions]

    C --> C1[Types]
    C --> C2[Signals]
    C --> C3[Bayesian Updating]
    C --> C4[Posterior Beliefs]






The same mathematical tool therefore has two interpretations: either a player is genuinely randomising, or another player is uncertain about what is true.

title: Probability
text:
Events and probabilities
A sample space is the set of possible outcomes. An event is a subset of the sample space.
For example, if a player may be either high-cost or low-cost, the sample space is
\[
\Omega = \{H,L\}.
\]
The event that the player is high-cost is
\[
\{H\}.
\]
A probability assigns a number between 0 and 1 to each event. If
\[
\mathbb{P}(H)=0.3,
\]
then the probability of type \(H\) is 0.3.
Since there are only two types here,
\[
\mathbb{P}(L)=1-\mathbb{P}(H)=0.7.
\]

title: Probability
text:
Random variables
A random variable assigns numerical values to outcomes.
For example, suppose a player’s cost can be high or low:
\[
c(H)=10,
\qquad
c(L)=4.
\]
If the probability of type \(H\) is 0.3 and the probability of type \(L\) is 0.7, then the cost is uncertain before the type is known.
Random variables are useful because payoffs often depend on uncertain states, types, signals, or actions.

title: Probability
text:
Expectation
If a random variable \(X\) takes values \(x_k\) with probabilities \(p_k\), then
\[
\mathbb{E}[X]
=
\sum_k x_k p_k.
\]
Expectation is the probability-weighted average value of a random variable.
For example, if
\[
X =
\begin{cases}
10 & \text{with probability } 0.3,\\
4 & \text{with probability } 0.7,
\end{cases}
\]
then
\[
\mathbb{E}[X]
=
10(0.3)+4(0.7)
=
5.8.
\]
In games, expected utility uses exactly this logic: average payoffs over possible outcomes, weighted by their probabilities.

title: Probability
text:
Expected utility
Suppose a player chooses action \(a\), but the payoff depends on an uncertain state \(\theta\). If the possible states are \(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_K\), expected utility is
\[
\mathbb{E}[u(a,\theta)]
=
\sum_{k=1}^{K}
u(a,\theta_k)\mathbb{P}(\theta_k).
\]
The player chooses the action with the highest expected utility:
\[
a^*
\in
\arg\max_{a \in A}
\sum_{k=1}^{K}
u(a,\theta_k)\mathbb{P}(\theta_k).
\]
This is the bridge between probability and optimization.

title: Probability
text:
Mixed strategies
A mixed strategy is a probability distribution over pure actions.
If a player has two actions, \(A\) and \(B\), then a mixed strategy may be written as
\[
\sigma(A)=p,
\qquad
\sigma(B)=1-p,
\]
where
\[
p \in [0,1].
\]
The player chooses \(A\) with probability \(p\) and \(B\) with probability \(1-p\).
If the action set is finite,
\[
S_i = \{s_{i1},s_{i2},\ldots,s_{im}\},
\]
then a mixed strategy is a probability vector
\[
\sigma_i = (\sigma_i(s_{i1}),\ldots,\sigma_i(s_{im})),
\]
where
\[
\sigma_i(s_{ij}) \geq 0
\]
for all \(j\), and
\[
\sum_{j=1}^{m}\sigma_i(s_{ij})=1.
\]
Mixed strategies are not mystical. They are probability distributions that allow players and opponents to compute expected payoffs.

title: Probability
section: Expected payoff under a mixed strategy
text:
Expected payoff under a mixed strategy
Suppose player 1 chooses between \(A\) and \(B\), while player 2 chooses between \(L\) and \(R\).
If player 2 plays \(L\) with probability \(q\) and \(R\) with probability \(1-q\), then player 1’s expected payoff from playing \(A\) is
\[
U_1(A,q)
=
q u_1(A,L)
+
(1-q)u_1(A,R).
\]
Player 1’s expected payoff from playing \(B\) is
\[
U_1(B,q)
=
q u_1(B,L)
+
(1-q)u_1(B,R).
\]
Player 1 prefers \(A\) when
\[
U_1(A,q)>U_1(B,q).
\]
Player 1 prefers \(B\) when
\[
U_1(B,q)>U_1(A,q).
\]
Player 1 is indifferent when
\[
U_1(A,q)=U_1(B,q).
\]
This indifference condition is often used to solve mixed-strategy equilibria.

title: Probability
text:
Conditional probability
Conditional probability asks: what is the probability of event \(A\) given that event \(B\) has occurred?
It is written as
\[
\mathbb{P}(A \mid B).
\]
For events \(A\) and \(B\) with \(\mathbb{P}(B)>0\),
\[
\mathbb{P}(A\mid B)
=
\frac{\mathbb{P}(A\cap B)}{\mathbb{P}(B)}.
\]
This formula says:

among the cases where \(B\) occurs, what fraction also involve \(A\)?

Conditional probability is essential for belief updating.

title: Probability
text:
Bayes’ rule
Bayes’ rule rewrites conditional probability in a form useful for updating beliefs.
For events \(A\) and \(B\) with \(\mathbb{P}(B)>0\),
\[
\mathbb{P}(A\mid B)
=
\frac{
\mathbb{P}(B\mid A)\mathbb{P}(A)
}{
\mathbb{P}(B)
}.
\]
The terms have a standard interpretation:







Term
Meaning




\(\mathbb{P}(A)\)
prior belief


\(\mathbb{P}(B\mid A)\)
likelihood of observing evidence \(B\) if \(A\) is true


\(\mathbb{P}(B)\)
overall probability of observing evidence \(B\)


\(\mathbb{P}(A\mid B)\)
posterior belief after observing \(B\)



The intuition is:

prior belief is reweighted by how well the hypothesis predicts the evidence.

title: Probability
text:
From probability to posterior belief
This diagram shows how conditional probability and Bayes’ rule fit into belief updating.





flowchart TD
    A[Sample Space] --> B[Events]
    B --> C[Probabilities]
    C --> D[Conditional Probability]
    D --> E[Likelihood]
    E --> F[Prior Belief]
    F --> G[Bayes' Rule]
    E --> G
    G --> H[Posterior Belief]






Bayes’ rule is especially important in games with incomplete information, where players must update beliefs after observing signals, messages, or actions.

title: Probability
text:
Belief updating as a process





flowchart TD
    A[Start with a Prior] --> B[Observe Evidence or Signal]
    B --> C[Evaluate Signal Likelihood under Each State]
    C --> D[Reweight Prior Beliefs]
    D --> E[Obtain Posterior Belief]
    E --> F[Use Posterior to Make Decisions]






In words:

Start with a prior belief.
Observe a signal.
Ask how likely the signal would be under each possible state.
Reweight the prior.
Use the posterior belief to choose an action.

title: Probability
text:
Example: updating beliefs about types
A player is either type \(H\) or type \(L\). The prior beliefs are
\[
\mathbb{P}(H)=0.3,
\qquad
\mathbb{P}(L)=0.7.
\]
You observe a signal \(s\). Suppose
\[
\mathbb{P}(s\mid H)=0.8,
\qquad
\mathbb{P}(s\mid L)=0.2.
\]
First compute the overall probability of observing \(s\):
\[
\mathbb{P}(s)
=
\mathbb{P}(s\mid H)\mathbb{P}(H)
+
\mathbb{P}(s\mid L)\mathbb{P}(L).
\]
Substitute the numbers:
\[
\mathbb{P}(s)
=
0.8 \cdot 0.3
+
0.2 \cdot 0.7
=
0.24+0.14
=
0.38.
\]
Then compute the posterior probability of type \(H\):
\[
\mathbb{P}(H\mid s)
=
\frac{
\mathbb{P}(s\mid H)\mathbb{P}(H)
}{
\mathbb{P}(s)
}
=
\frac{0.8 \cdot 0.3}{0.38}
=
\frac{0.24}{0.38}
\approx
0.6316.
\]
So after observing signal \(s\), belief in type \(H\) rises from 0.3 to about 0.63.
The signal increases belief in \(H\) because it is more likely under \(H\) than under \(L\).

title: Probability
text:
Prior, likelihood, posterior
The belief-updating example can be summarised as:





flowchart LR
    A[Prior: P(H)] --> C[Posterior: P(H | s)]
    B[Likelihood: P(s | H) and P(s | L)] --> C
    C --> D[Decision after observing signal]






A posterior belief is not just the prior plus the signal. It depends on how diagnostic the signal is.
A signal is more diagnostic when its likelihood differs strongly across states.

title: Probability
text:
Signals and types
In Bayesian games, a type represents private information about a player. A type may describe:

cost
ability
patience
preference
information
intention
valuation
honesty or bias

A signal is something observed that may contain information about the type.
The basic structure is:





flowchart TD
    A[Unknown Type] --> B[Signal or Action]
    B --> C[Observer Updates Beliefs]
    C --> D[Observer Chooses Response]
    D --> E[Strategic Outcome]






This structure appears in signaling games, cheap-talk games, reputation models, screening problems, and many models of trust.

title: Probability
text:
Bayesian games
A Bayesian game includes uncertainty about types. The model normally specifies:

a set of players;
a type space for each player;
prior beliefs over types;
actions or strategies;
payoffs that may depend on types.

A player’s strategy must specify what they do for each possible type. If player \(i\) has type \(\theta_i\), a strategy can be written as
\[
s_i(\theta_i).
\]
A Bayesian Nash equilibrium requires each type to choose a best response given beliefs and the strategies of others.
In short:
\[
\text{Bayesian reasoning}
=
\text{optimization under beliefs}.
\]

title: Probability
text:
Beliefs after actions
In dynamic games, players may update beliefs after observing actions.
For example, suppose a sender chooses a message \(m\), and the receiver must infer the sender’s type \(\theta\).
The receiver’s posterior belief is
\[
\mu(\theta \mid m).
\]
Using Bayes’ rule,
\[
\mu(\theta \mid m)
=
\frac{
\mathbb{P}(m\mid \theta)\mathbb{P}(\theta)
}{
\sum_{\theta'} \mathbb{P}(m\mid \theta')\mathbb{P}(\theta')
}.
\]
This formula says that a message changes beliefs according to how likely each type would be to send that message.
This is the foundation of signaling and cheap talk.

title: Probability
text:
On-path and off-path beliefs
In dynamic games with incomplete information, some actions or messages occur with positive probability in equilibrium. These are called on-path.
Other actions or messages are not expected to occur in equilibrium. These are called off-path.
Bayes’ rule pins down beliefs after on-path observations. But after an off-path observation, Bayes’ rule may not give a unique answer because the denominator may be zero.
This is why solution concepts such as perfect Bayesian equilibrium and sequential equilibrium include belief requirements.
The key idea is:





flowchart TD
    A[Observation occurs] --> B{Positive probability in equilibrium?}
    B -->|Yes| C[Use Bayes' rule]
    B -->|No| D[Off-path belief needs extra discipline]
    C --> E[Posterior belief]
    D --> E
    E --> F[Sequentially rational action]

title: Probability
text:
Independence
Two events \(A\) and \(B\) are independent if learning that one occurred does not change the probability of the other.
Formally,
\[
\mathbb{P}(A\mid B)=\mathbb{P}(A).
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\mathbb{P}(A\cap B)
=
\mathbb{P}(A)\mathbb{P}(B).
\]
Independence is useful, but it should not be assumed automatically. In strategic settings, actions are often informative precisely because they are not independent of types or incentives.

title: Probability
text:
Common mistakes

1. Confusing prior and posterior
The prior is the belief before observing evidence. The posterior is the belief after updating on evidence.


2. Ignoring the denominator in Bayes’ rule
The denominator \(\mathbb{P}(B)\) matters because it measures how likely the evidence is overall.


3. Treating a signal as proof
A signal changes beliefs. It does not usually reveal the state with certainty.


4. Assuming independence without justification
If actions are strategically chosen, they may be correlated with private information.


5. Confusing mixed strategies with uncertainty about pure strategies
A mixed strategy is a deliberate probability distribution over actions. Uncertainty about what someone will do may arise from mixed strategies, private information, or lack of observation.


6. Forgetting off-path beliefs
In dynamic incomplete-information games, behaviour after unexpected observations may matter for equilibrium.

title: Probability
text:
Checklist for belief updating
When using Bayes’ rule in a model, ask:

What are the possible states or types?
What is the prior belief over those states?
What signal or action is observed?
How likely is that signal under each state?
What is the overall probability of the signal?
What is the posterior belief after observing it?
How does the posterior belief affect the next action?
Are we updating after an on-path or off-path observation?

title: Optimization
text:
Optimization is the language of choice. In economics and game theory, many arguments begin with a simple question:
This page collects the basic optimization tools needed for strategic reasoning: objective functions, constraints, argmax notation, first-order conditions, second-order conditions, and constrained optimization.

title: Optimization
text:
The basic structure
An optimization problem has three parts:

Choice variable: what the decision-maker controls.
Objective function: what the decision-maker wants to maximize or minimize.
Feasible set: which choices are allowed.

A simple maximization problem can be written as
\[
\max_{x \in X} f(x),
\]
where \(x\) is the choice variable, \(X\) is the feasible set, and \(f(x)\) is the objective function.
The solution is written as
\[
x^* \in \arg\max_{x \in X} f(x).
\]
This means that \(x^*\) is a choice that achieves the highest value of \(f(x)\) among all feasible choices.

title: Optimization
text:
The logic of optimization
Many problems in economics and game theory can be organised as an optimization problem.





flowchart TD
    A[Start with an objective] --> B[Define the choice variable]
    B --> C[Identify constraints]
    C --> D[Write the feasible set]
    D --> E[Check interior or boundary solution]
    E --> F[Apply FOC if differentiable]
    F --> G[Apply SOC or curvature check]
    G --> H[Obtain candidate optimum]
    H --> I[Interpret the result]






The workflow matters because many mistakes come from applying calculus before defining the feasible set.

title: Optimization
text:
Argmax notation
The notation
\[
\arg\max_{x \in X} f(x)
\]
means “the value or values of \(x\) that maximize \(f(x)\) over the set \(X\).”
This is different from
\[
\max_{x \in X} f(x).
\]
The expression \(\max f(x)\) gives the maximum value of the objective function.
The expression \(\arg\max f(x)\) gives the choice that achieves that value.
For example, suppose
\[
f(x)=2x-x^2.
\]
The maximum occurs at \(x=1\). The maximum value is
\[
f(1)=2(1)-1^2=1.
\]
So:
\[
\arg\max_x f(x)=1,
\]
but
\[
\max_x f(x)=1.
\]
In this example the argmax and the maximum value happen to be numerically the same, but conceptually they are different.

title: Optimization
text:
Interior and boundary solutions
A solution is an interior solution if it lies strictly inside the feasible set. A solution is a boundary solution if it occurs at the edge of the feasible set.
This distinction matters because first-order conditions usually identify interior candidates. Boundary solutions may not satisfy the usual condition \(f'(x)=0\).
For example, consider
\[
\max_{x \in [0,1]} x.
\]
The solution is
\[
x^*=1.
\]
But
\[
f'(x)=1,
\]
so there is no point where \(f'(x)=0\). The optimum is at the boundary.

title: Optimization
text:
First-order condition
If \(f\) is differentiable and \(x^*\) is an interior optimum, then the first-order condition is
\[
f'(x^*)=0.
\]
The intuition is that, at an interior optimum, a small movement to the left or right should not improve the objective.
For example, suppose
\[
f(x)=2x-x^2.
\]
Then
\[
f'(x)=2-2x.
\]
Set the derivative equal to zero:
\[
2-2x=0.
\]
So
\[
x^*=1.
\]
The first-order condition gives a candidate optimum.

title: Optimization
text:
Second-order condition
The first-order condition alone is not enough. It finds stationary points, but a stationary point may be a maximum, a minimum, or neither.
If \(f\) is twice differentiable, the second-order condition for a local maximum is
\[
f''(x^*)<0.
\]
For the example above,
\[
f(x)=2x-x^2,
\]
so
\[
f''(x)=-2<0.
\]
Therefore \(x^*=1\) is a local maximum.

title: Optimization
text:
Concavity
Concavity gives a stronger and cleaner way to verify a maximum.
If \(f\) is concave, then any point satisfying the first-order condition is a global maximum. If \(f\) is strictly concave, the maximum is unique.
A function is concave when it bends downward. Formally, \(f\) is concave if for all \(x,y\) and all \(\alpha \in [0,1]\),
\[
f(\alpha x+(1-\alpha)y)
\geq
\alpha f(x)+(1-\alpha)f(y).
\]
The intuition is that the value of a mixture is at least as high as the mixture of values.
Concavity is useful in economics because it often represents diminishing marginal returns.

title: Optimization
text:
Optimization and best responses
A best response in game theory is an optimization problem.
Given the strategies of other players, \(s_{-i}\), player \(i\) chooses a strategy \(s_i\) that maximizes their payoff:
\[
BR_i(s_{-i})
\in
\arg\max_{s_i \in S_i} u_i(s_i,s_{-i}).
\]
This says:

Hold everyone else’s strategies fixed, then choose the best available response.

A Nash equilibrium is a profile of strategies where everyone is already choosing a best response:
\[
s_i^* \in BR_i(s_{-i}^*)
\quad \text{for every player } i.
\]
So optimization is not separate from equilibrium analysis. It is the local decision problem inside equilibrium reasoning.





flowchart LR
    A[Other players' strategies] --> B[Player's optimization problem]
    B --> C[Best response]
    C --> D[All players best responding]
    D --> E[Nash equilibrium]

title: Optimization
section: Example: best response in a Cournot game
text:
Example: best response in a Cournot game
Suppose two firms choose quantities \(q_1\) and \(q_2\). Market price is
\[
P = a - b(q_1+q_2),
\]
and firm \(i\) has constant marginal cost \(c\).
Firm 1’s profit is
\[
\pi_1(q_1,q_2)
=
(a-b(q_1+q_2))q_1-cq_1.
\]
Simplify:
\[
\pi_1(q_1,q_2)
=
(a-c)q_1-bq_1^2-bq_1q_2.
\]
Firm 1 chooses \(q_1\) taking \(q_2\) as given:
\[
\max_{q_1 \geq 0}
(a-c)q_1-bq_1^2-bq_1q_2.
\]
The first-order condition is
\[
\frac{\partial \pi_1}{\partial q_1}
=
(a-c)-2bq_1-bq_2=0.
\]
Solving for \(q_1\) gives firm 1’s best response:
\[
q_1
=
\frac{a-c-bq_2}{2b}.
\]
With the non-negativity constraint, the best response is
\[
BR_1(q_2)
=
\max\left\{0,\frac{a-c-bq_2}{2b}\right\}.
\]
This example shows why optimization is the foundation of best-response analysis.

title: Optimization
text:
Constrained optimization
Many choices are constrained. Consumers face budgets, firms face capacity, players face strategy restrictions, and institutions face feasibility constraints.
A constrained optimization problem can be written as
\[
\max_x f(x)
\quad \text{subject to} \quad g(x)\leq 0.
\]
The objective says what the decision-maker wants.
The constraint says what the decision-maker is allowed to do.





flowchart LR
    A[Objective function] --> C[Optimization problem]
    B[Constraint set] --> C
    C --> D[Feasible choices]
    D --> E[Candidate solution]
    E --> F[Check optimality conditions]
    F --> G[Interpret trade-off]

title: Optimization
text:
Lagrangian method
For an equality-constrained problem,
\[
\max_x f(x)
\quad \text{subject to} \quad h(x)=0,
\]
the Lagrangian is
\[
\mathcal{L}(x,\lambda)=f(x)-\lambda h(x).
\]
The first-order conditions are
\[
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial x}=0
\]
and
\[
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \lambda}=0.
\]
The multiplier \(\lambda\) measures the shadow value of relaxing the constraint.
In economic terms, a shadow value tells us how much the objective would improve if the constraint became slightly less restrictive.

title: Optimization
text:
KKT conditions
For inequality constraints, use the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions.
Consider
\[
\max_x f(x)
\quad \text{subject to} \quad g_j(x)\leq 0
\quad \text{for } j=1,\ldots,m.
\]
The Lagrangian is
\[
\mathcal{L}(x,\lambda)
=
f(x)-\sum_{j=1}^m \lambda_j g_j(x),
\qquad
\lambda_j \geq 0.
\]
The KKT conditions are:

Stationarity

\[
\nabla_x \mathcal{L}(x^*,\lambda^*)=0.
\]

Primal feasibility

\[
g_j(x^*)\leq 0
\quad \text{for all } j.
\]

Dual feasibility

\[
\lambda_j^* \geq 0
\quad \text{for all } j.
\]

Complementary slackness

\[
\lambda_j^* g_j(x^*)=0
\quad \text{for all } j.
\]
The intuition is simple:

if a constraint does not bind, its multiplier is zero;
if a constraint binds, its multiplier may be positive.

title: Optimization
text:
Binding and non-binding constraints
A constraint is binding if it holds with equality at the optimum.
For example, if the constraint is
\[
x \leq 10,
\]
then it binds when
\[
x^*=10.
\]
A constraint is non-binding if it does not restrict the optimum.
In KKT terms:
\[
\lambda_j^* g_j(x^*)=0.
\]
This means either:
\[
\lambda_j^*=0,
\]
or
\[
g_j(x^*)=0.
\]
So a constraint either has no shadow value, or it binds.

title: Optimization
text:
Example: constrained optimization
Maximize
\[
f(x)=2x-x^2
\]
subject to
\[
x\geq 0.
\]
Write the constraint as
\[
g(x)=-x\leq 0.
\]
The Lagrangian is
\[
\mathcal{L}(x,\lambda)
=
2x-x^2-\lambda(-x)
=
2x-x^2+\lambda x.
\]
The KKT conditions are:
\[
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial x}
=
2-2x+\lambda=0,
\]
\[
x\geq 0,
\]
\[
\lambda \geq 0,
\]
and
\[
\lambda x=0.
\]
From stationarity,
\[
2-2x+\lambda=0.
\]
So
\[
x=1+\frac{\lambda}{2}.
\]
If \(x>0\), then complementary slackness implies
\[
\lambda=0.
\]
Therefore
\[
x^*=1.
\]
This is feasible, so the solution is
\[
x^*=1.
\]
The constraint does not bind.

title: Optimization
text:
Boundary example
Now consider
\[
\max_{x\geq 0} -x.
\]
The unconstrained objective is decreasing, so the best feasible choice is
\[
x^*=0.
\]
Here the constraint binds. The decision-maker would like to choose a lower value of \(x\), but the feasible set does not allow it.
This kind of example is important because not every optimum is found by setting the derivative equal to zero.

title: Optimization
text:
Comparative statics
Comparative statics asks how the solution changes when a parameter changes.
Suppose the optimal choice is
\[
x^*(a).
\]
A comparative static asks:
\[
\frac{d x^*(a)}{d a}.
\]
In words:

When the parameter \(a\) changes, how does the optimal choice change?

In game theory, comparative statics often ask how equilibrium strategies change when costs, benefits, information, discount factors, or enforcement probabilities change.
For example:

How does a firm’s quantity change when marginal cost rises?
How does crime change when the probability of detection rises?
How does cooperation change when players become more patient?
How does communication change when preferences become more aligned?

title: Optimization
text:
Optimization versus equilibrium
Optimization is individual. Equilibrium is collective.
An individual optimization problem asks:
\[
\max_{s_i \in S_i} u_i(s_i,s_{-i}).
\]
An equilibrium asks whether every player is solving their own optimization problem at the same time:
\[
s_i^* \in \arg\max_{s_i \in S_i} u_i(s_i,s_{-i}^*)
\quad
\text{for every } i.
\]
This is the bridge from calculus to game theory.





flowchart TD
    A[Individual choice problem] --> B[Best response]
    B --> C[Best-response system]
    C --> D[Fixed point]
    D --> E[Equilibrium]

title: Optimization
text:
Common mistakes

1. Confusing max and argmax
The maximum is the value of the objective. The argmax is the choice that achieves it.


2. Ignoring the feasible set
An unconstrained optimum may be infeasible. Always check constraints.


3. Applying FOC to boundary solutions
The first-order condition is necessary for interior optima, not for all optima.


4. Forgetting the second-order condition
A stationary point may be a maximum, minimum, or saddle point.


5. Treating best responses as fixed numbers
Best responses usually depend on other players’ strategies. A best response is often a function, not just a single value.


6. Forgetting interpretation
Solving the math is only part of the work. The final step is explaining what the result means in the model.

title: Optimization
section: Checklist for solving an optimization problem
text:
Checklist for solving an optimization problem
Use this checklist before moving to equilibrium analysis:

What is the choice variable?
What is the objective function?
What is the feasible set?
Is the problem constrained or unconstrained?
Is the solution interior or on the boundary?
Can FOC be used?
Does SOC or concavity confirm a maximum?
What does the solution mean economically?
How does the solution change when parameters change?
If this is a game, how does this become a best response?

title: Dynamic Reasoning
text:
Dynamic reasoning studies decisions that unfold over time. In a static problem, a player chooses once. In a dynamic problem, players act after histories, observe earlier moves, form expectations about later moves, and ask whether threats or promises are credible.
This page introduces the logic behind backward induction, sequential rationality, credibility, continuation payoffs, and dynamic equilibrium.

title: Dynamic Reasoning
Dynamic Reasoning
text:
Histories and continuation
A history is a sequence of actions that has occurred so far.
For example, in a simple two-stage game:

Player 1 chooses \(A\) or \(B\).
Player 2 observes Player 1’s action.
Player 2 chooses \(L\) or \(R\).

After Player 1 chooses \(A\), the history is
\[
h = A.
\]
After Player 1 chooses \(B\), the history is
\[
h = B.
\]
Player 2 may choose differently after different histories. This is why a strategy in a dynamic game must specify what a player would do after every relevant history.

title: Dynamic Reasoning
text:
Strategies in dynamic games
In a static game, a strategy can often be thought of as one action.
In a dynamic game, a strategy is a complete contingent plan. It says what the player will do at every decision point where they may be called to move.
For example, if Player 2 moves after either \(A\) or \(B\), then a strategy for Player 2 must specify:
\[
s_2(A)
\]
and
\[
s_2(B).
\]
A complete strategy might be:
\[
s_2 = (L \text{ after } A,\ R \text{ after } B).
\]
This matters because equilibrium requires optimality not only along the path that actually occurs, but also after possible histories that might not occur.

title: Dynamic Reasoning
text:
The logic of backward induction
Backward induction solves a finite dynamic game by starting from the final decision nodes and moving backward to the beginning.





flowchart TD
    A[Start at terminal decision nodes] --> B[Find the last mover's optimal action]
    B --> C[Replace the continuation with resulting payoffs]
    C --> D[Move to the previous decision node]
    D --> E[Find that player's optimal action]
    E --> F[Repeat the process]
    F --> G[Reach the initial node]
    G --> H[Obtain the predicted path]






The key idea is simple:

To know what a player should do now, first determine what later players would rationally do.

Backward induction is therefore reasoning from the future back to the present.

title: Dynamic Reasoning
text:
A small example
Suppose Player 1 chooses whether to Enter or Stay Out.
If Player 1 stays out, the game ends. If Player 1 enters, Player 2 chooses whether to Fight or Accommodate.
The game has this structure:





flowchart TD
    A[Player 1: Enter or Stay Out] --> B[Stay Out]
    A --> C[Enter]
    C --> D[Player 2: Fight or Accommodate]
    D --> E[Fight]
    D --> F[Accommodate]






To solve this game, do not start by asking whether Player 1 should enter. Start at Player 2’s decision node.
If Player 2 would prefer to accommodate rather than fight after entry, then Player 1 anticipates accommodation. Player 1’s entry decision should be evaluated against that expected response.
If Player 2 would prefer to fight after entry, then Player 1 anticipates fighting. Player 1’s entry decision may change.
The first move depends on the credible second move.

title: Dynamic Reasoning
text:
Credibility
A threat is credible if the player would actually want to carry it out when the time comes.
A promise is credible if the player would actually want to honour it when the time comes.
In dynamic games, announcements alone are not enough. What matters is whether the announced behaviour is sequentially optimal.





flowchart LR
    A[Threat or promise] --> B{Would the player carry it out later?}
    B -->|Yes| C[Credible]
    B -->|No| D[Not credible]
    C --> E[Affects current behaviour]
    D --> F[Should be ignored in equilibrium]






This is one of the most important lessons of dynamic reasoning: future behaviour must be optimal when the future arrives.

title: Dynamic Reasoning
text:
Sequential rationality
A strategy is sequentially rational if it prescribes optimal behaviour at every decision point, given the player’s beliefs and continuation payoffs.
This is stronger than simply being optimal at the start of the game.
For example, a player may announce:

“If you enter, I will fight.”

But if fighting is costly and accommodation is better after entry occurs, then fighting is not sequentially rational. The threat is not credible.
Sequential rationality asks:

At each point in the game, given the history so far, is this action optimal from that point onward?

title: Dynamic Reasoning
text:
Subgames
A subgame is a part of a dynamic game that begins at a decision node and includes all later actions and payoffs from that node onward.
A strategy profile is a subgame perfect equilibrium if it induces a Nash equilibrium in every subgame.
The intuition is:

A dynamic equilibrium should remain rational after every possible history.

This rules out equilibria supported by non-credible threats.





flowchart TD
    A[Dynamic Game] --> B[Subgame 1]
    A --> C[Subgame 2]
    A --> D[Subgame 3]
    B --> E[Optimal continuation]
    C --> F[Optimal continuation]
    D --> G[Optimal continuation]
    E --> H[Subgame Perfect Equilibrium]
    F --> H
    G --> H

title: Dynamic Reasoning
text:
Backward induction and subgame perfection
In finite games with perfect information, backward induction produces a subgame perfect equilibrium.
The relationship is:





flowchart LR
    A[Finite dynamic game] --> B[Perfect information]
    B --> C[Backward induction]
    C --> D[Optimal action in every subgame]
    D --> E[Subgame perfect equilibrium]






Backward induction is a procedure.
Subgame perfection is a solution concept.
They are related, but not identical.

title: Dynamic Reasoning
text:
Perfect information and imperfect information
A game has perfect information if every player observes all previous actions before choosing.
A game has imperfect information if some player does not observe some earlier action, or if decision nodes are grouped into information sets.
Perfect-information games can often be solved by backward induction. Imperfect-information games may require beliefs.





flowchart TD
    A[Dynamic Game] --> B{Does each player observe all previous actions?}
    B -->|Yes| C[Perfect Information]
    B -->|No| D[Imperfect Information]
    C --> E[Backward Induction]
    D --> F[Beliefs and information sets]
    F --> G[Perfect Bayesian or sequential equilibrium]






When players do not know exactly where they are in the game, dynamic reasoning becomes belief-based.

title: Dynamic Reasoning
text:
Continuation payoffs
A continuation payoff is the payoff a player expects from a point in the game onward.
Dynamic reasoning often compares current actions by asking how they change future continuation payoffs.
For example, in a repeated relationship, cheating today may give a current benefit but reduce future continuation value.
The basic comparison is:
\[
\text{current payoff} + \text{future continuation payoff}.
\]
If a player discounts the future by \(\delta \in (0,1)\), then the value of a stream of future payoffs may be written as
\[
U
=
u_0
+
\delta u_1
+
\delta^2 u_2
+
\cdots.
\]
The discount factor \(\delta\) measures patience. A higher \(\delta\) means the player cares more about future payoffs.

title: Dynamic Reasoning
Dynamic Reasoning
text:
Repeated games
Repeated games are dynamic games where the same stage game is played more than once.
Repetition can support cooperation because players can reward or punish one another across time.
For example, suppose cooperation gives long-run benefits but defection gives a short-run gain. Cooperation may be sustained if the future loss from punishment is larger than the current gain from defection.
A typical incentive condition has the form:
\[
\text{gain from deviation}
\leq
\text{future loss from punishment}.
\]
This is one of the central ideas behind repeated-game cooperation.

title: Dynamic Reasoning
text:
Commitment
Commitment changes dynamic reasoning by changing what future actions are available or attractive.
A player has commitment power if they can bind themselves to a future action.
Without commitment, a promise may fail because the player will later want to break it.
With commitment, the same promise may become credible.





flowchart TD
    A[Future action] --> B{Can the player commit?}
    B -->|No| C[Future self may revise action]
    B -->|Yes| D[Future action becomes fixed or costly to change]
    C --> E[Credibility problem]
    D --> F[Credibility strengthened]






Commitment is important in contracts, bargaining, monetary policy, deterrence, and institutional design.

title: Dynamic Reasoning
text:
Dynamic reasoning in Bayesian settings
When dynamic games include incomplete information, players must reason about both future actions and beliefs.
For example, if a sender sends a message, the receiver may update beliefs about the sender’s type. The receiver then chooses a response. The sender anticipates this response when choosing the message.
The reasoning chain is:





flowchart TD
    A[Sender has type] --> B[Sender chooses message or action]
    B --> C[Receiver observes signal]
    C --> D[Receiver updates belief]
    D --> E[Receiver chooses response]
    E --> F[Sender anticipates this when choosing]






This is the logic behind signaling, cheap talk, reputation, and perfect Bayesian equilibrium.

title: Dynamic Reasoning
text:
Common mistakes

1. Solving from the beginning
In finite perfect-information games, solve from the end first. The first move depends on later credible responses.


2. Confusing actions and strategies
In dynamic games, a strategy is a complete plan for every relevant decision point.


3. Ignoring off-path behaviour
Equilibrium may require specifying what players would do after histories that do not occur on the equilibrium path.


4. Treating threats as automatically credible
A threat affects behaviour only if it is optimal to carry out when the time comes.


5. Forgetting beliefs
In dynamic games with incomplete information, players must update beliefs after observations.


6. Confusing backward induction with equilibrium
Backward induction is a method. Subgame perfect equilibrium is a solution concept.

title: Dynamic Reasoning
text:
Checklist for dynamic games
When analysing a dynamic game, ask:

Who moves first?
Who moves later?
What does each player observe before choosing?
What are the possible histories?
What is each player’s complete strategy?
What happens at the final decision nodes?
Which threats or promises are credible?
Are actions optimal in every subgame?
Are beliefs needed?
What is the equilibrium path?

title: About
text:
Margins of Rationality is a personal academic notes site about strategic reasoning, rationality, institutions, crime, psychology, and the mathematical tools used to study them.
The site is built as a working notebook rather than a finished textbook. Some pages are conceptual maps. Some are technical notes. Some are short guides for reading formal models. The common theme is the boundary between rational structure and real behaviour.

title: About
text:
Main idea
Rationality is rarely simple.
People choose under uncertainty. They respond to incentives, beliefs, institutions, emotions, histories, norms, and other people. A model can clarify this structure, but it can also hide assumptions if used carelessly.
This site tries to keep both sides visible:

the formal structure of models;
the behavioural and institutional limits of those models.

title: About
About
About
text:
Why “Margins of Rationality”?
The title points to the edges of rational-choice reasoning.
At the centre are clean models: players, strategies, beliefs, payoffs, and equilibrium.
At the margins are the complications that make human behaviour interesting: uncertainty, misperception, self-control, identity, trust, institutions, social norms, stigma, emotion, and bounded reasoning.
The site studies both the centre and the margins.

title: About
text:
Current status
This is a living site. Pages may be expanded, reorganized, or rewritten over time. Some pages are full notes; others are maps or placeholders for future development.
The long-term goal is to build a coherent set of notes that can be read across fields rather than only within one discipline.

title: Bayesian Nash Equilibrium
text:
Bayesian Nash equilibrium is the basic equilibrium concept for static games with incomplete information. It requires every type of every player to choose a best response, given beliefs about other players’ types and strategies.
The central idea is:

title: Bayesian Nash Equilibrium
text:
From Nash to Bayesian Nash
In a complete-information game, Nash equilibrium requires each player to best respond to others’ strategies.
In a Bayesian game, each player may have different possible types. Therefore, equilibrium must specify what each type does.





flowchart LR
    A[Nash equilibrium] --> B[Each player best responds]
    C[Bayesian Nash equilibrium] --> D[Each type of each player best responds]






The difference is that strategies are type-contingent.

title: Bayesian Nash Equilibrium
text:
Basic setup
A Bayesian game includes:



Object
Meaning




\(N\)
players


\(\Theta_i\)
type space of player \(i\)


\(A_i\)
action set of player \(i\)


\(p(\theta)\)
prior over type profiles


\(u_i(a,\theta)\)
payoff of player \(i\)



A strategy for player \(i\) is a function:
\[
s_i:\Theta_i \to A_i.
\]
This means that the strategy assigns an action to every type.

title: Bayesian Nash Equilibrium
text:
Expected payoff
If player \(i\) has type \(\theta_i\), then the player forms beliefs about other players’ types \(\theta_{-i}\).
Given a strategy profile \(s\), the expected payoff from choosing action \(a_i\) is:
\[
\sum_{\theta_{-i}}
u_i(a_i,s_{-i}(\theta_{-i}),\theta_i,\theta_{-i})
\Pr(\theta_{-i}\mid \theta_i).
\]
The type \(\theta_i\) chooses the action that maximizes this expected payoff.

title: Bayesian Nash Equilibrium
text:
Definition
A strategy profile
\[
s^*=(s_1^*,\ldots,s_n^*)
\]
is a Bayesian Nash equilibrium if, for every player \(i\) and every type \(\theta_i \in \Theta_i\),
\[
s_i^*(\theta_i)
\in
\arg\max_{a_i\in A_i}
\sum_{\theta_{-i}}
u_i(a_i,s_{-i}^*(\theta_{-i}),\theta_i,\theta_{-i})
\Pr(\theta_{-i}\mid \theta_i).
\]
In words:

each type chooses a best response to the type-contingent strategies of others.

title: Bayesian Nash Equilibrium
text:
The logic





flowchart TD
    A[Player observes own type] --> B[Forms belief about others' types]
    B --> C[Predicts others' type-contingent strategies]
    C --> D[Computes expected payoff]
    D --> E[Chooses best response]
    E --> F[Bayesian Nash equilibrium if all types do this]






This is the core of Bayesian Nash equilibrium.

title: Bayesian Nash Equilibrium
text:
Example: two types
Suppose player 1 can be type \(H\) or type \(L\).
A strategy for player 1 is not just one action. It must specify:
\[
s_1(H)
\]
and
\[
s_1(L).
\]
For example:
\[
s_1(H)=A,
\qquad
s_1(L)=B.
\]
This means the high type chooses \(A\), while the low type chooses \(B\).
The opponent may not observe the type, but forms beliefs about which type is being faced.

title: Bayesian Nash Equilibrium
text:
Type-contingent best response
Suppose type \(H\) and type \(L\) have different payoffs.
Then the same action may be optimal for one type but not for the other.





flowchart TD
    A[Type H] --> B[Payoff function for H]
    B --> C[Best response for H]

    D[Type L] --> E[Payoff function for L]
    E --> F[Best response for L]

    C --> G[Type-contingent strategy]
    F --> G






Bayesian Nash equilibrium requires both type-specific choices to be optimal.

title: Bayesian Nash Equilibrium
text:
Pure and mixed Bayesian strategies
A pure Bayesian strategy maps each type to a pure action.
A mixed Bayesian strategy maps each type to a probability distribution over actions.
For example:
\[
\sigma_i(\theta_i)(a_i)
\]
is the probability that type \(\theta_i\) of player \(i\) chooses action \(a_i\).
This allows different types to randomize differently.

title: Bayesian Nash Equilibrium
text:
Interim perspective
Bayesian Nash equilibrium is usually defined from the interim perspective.
This means each player has already learned their own type but remains uncertain about others’ types.
The stages are:





flowchart LR
    A[Ex ante: before types] --> B[Interim: after own type]
    B --> C[Action choice]
    C --> D[Ex post: after types and actions]






BNE asks whether each type is optimal at the interim stage.

title: Bayesian Nash Equilibrium
text:
Bayesian Nash and Bayes’ rule
In static Bayesian games, beliefs are usually derived from the common prior and the player’s own type.
If types are independent, then learning your own type may not change beliefs about others.
If types are correlated, then learning your own type may provide information about others.
Bayes’ rule gives:
\[
\Pr(\theta_{-i}\mid \theta_i)
=
\frac{
\Pr(\theta_i,\theta_{-i})
}{
\Pr(\theta_i)
}.
\]
This conditional belief is used in the expected payoff calculation.

title: Bayesian Nash Equilibrium
text:
Relation to Harsanyi transformation
Bayesian Nash equilibrium can be understood as Nash equilibrium in the Harsanyi-transformed game.
The transformed game has:

nature draws types;
each player observes own type;
each player chooses an action according to a type-contingent strategy.






flowchart TD
    A[Bayesian game] --> B[Harsanyi transformation]
    B --> C[Game with nature's move]
    C --> D[Nash equilibrium in type-contingent strategies]
    D --> E[Bayesian Nash equilibrium]






This is why Bayesian Nash equilibrium is a natural extension of Nash equilibrium.

title: Bayesian Nash Equilibrium
text:
Example structure: first-price auction
In a first-price sealed-bid auction, each bidder knows their own valuation but not others’ valuations.
A bidder’s type is their valuation:
\[
\theta_i = v_i.
\]
A strategy maps valuation into bid:
\[
b_i(v_i).
\]
A Bayesian Nash equilibrium is a bidding function where every valuation type bids optimally given beliefs about other bidders’ valuations and bidding strategies.
This shows why BNE is useful in auctions.

title: Bayesian Nash Equilibrium
section: Example structure: entry with unknown cost
text:
Example structure: entry with unknown cost
Suppose a firm may be high-cost or low-cost. A rival does not observe the cost type.
The firm’s strategy specifies what each cost type does:
\[
s(H), \quad s(L).
\]
The rival’s strategy is based on expected payoff under beliefs about whether the firm is high-cost or low-cost.
The equilibrium requires:

high-cost type best responds;
low-cost type best responds;
rival best responds to its beliefs.

title: Bayesian Nash Equilibrium
text:
BNE versus PBE
Bayesian Nash equilibrium is mainly for static incomplete-information games.
Perfect Bayesian equilibrium is for dynamic incomplete-information games.








Concept
Used for
Requires




Bayesian Nash equilibrium
static incomplete information
type-contingent best responses


Perfect Bayesian equilibrium
dynamic incomplete information
sequential rationality and beliefs


Sequential equilibrium
dynamic incomplete information
stronger belief consistency



If actions reveal information over time, BNE may not be enough.

title: Bayesian Nash Equilibrium
text:
Common mistakes

1. Solving only for one type
Every possible type must be optimizing.


2. Forgetting that strategy is a function
A Bayesian strategy maps types to actions.


3. Confusing type and belief
A type is private information. A belief is a probability over unknown types or states.


4. Ignoring expected payoff
Players choose based on expected payoff over uncertain types.


5. Applying BNE to dynamic signaling without beliefs after actions
Dynamic signaling games usually need PBE or sequential equilibrium.


6. Forgetting type correlation
If types are correlated, observing your own type can change beliefs about others.

title: Bayesian Nash Equilibrium
text:
Checklist
When checking Bayesian Nash equilibrium, ask:

What are the players?
What are the type spaces?
What does each player observe?
What is the prior distribution?
Are types independent or correlated?
What is each player’s action set?
What is each type’s strategy?
What belief does each type hold about others?
What expected payoff does each type maximize?
Is every type choosing a best response?

title: Trembling-hand perfect equilibrium
text:
A trembling-hand perfect equilibrium (perfect equilibrium) is a Nash equilibrium that remains optimal when every player might make tiny mistakes (“trembles”).
Formally (intuition-level): a strategy profile is perfect if it is the limit of a sequence of fully mixed strategy profiles (every action played with positive probability) where each player’s strategy is a best response to the others in that sequence.

title: Trembling-hand perfect equilibrium
text:
A trembling-hand perfect equilibrium (perfect equilibrium) is a Nash equilibrium that remains optimal when every player might make tiny mistakes (“trembles”).
Formally (intuition-level): a strategy profile is perfect if it is the limit of a sequence of fully mixed strategy profiles (every action played with positive probability) where each player’s strategy is a best response to the others in that sequence.

title: Trembling-hand perfect equilibrium
text:
Where it shows up

Normal-form games where Nash equilibria include weakly dominated or non-robust behavior
Refinement arguments: “Would this equilibrium survive small mistakes?”
Often discussed alongside proper equilibrium and sequential equilibrium

title: Trembling-hand perfect equilibrium
text:
Why it exists (intuition)
If an equilibrium relies on assigning zero probability to “unlikely” actions, trembles force you to confront those actions. Strategies that are only optimal because some opponent action is assumed impossible may fail perfection.

title: Trembling-hand perfect equilibrium
text:
How to solve (recipe)

Find Nash equilibria.
Check whether an equilibrium uses weakly dominated strategies or fragile best responses.
Consider small trembles: assume each player plays every action with tiny probability.
Ask: is the equilibrium strategy still a best response when opponents sometimes tremble?
If yes (as a limit), it’s perfect.

title: Trembling-hand perfect equilibrium
section: Solved example (eliminating a weakly dominated equilibrium)
text:
Solved example (eliminating a weakly dominated equilibrium)

Problem (context + question)
Consider this 2×2 game (payoffs shown as (player 1, player 2)):
\[
\begin{array}{c|cc}
& L & R\\ \hline
U & (1,1) & (0,1)\\
D & (1,0) & (0,0)
\end{array}
\]
Question: (i) Find all Nash equilibria. (ii) Which are trembling-hand perfect?


Solution
Step 1: Best responses - Player 1: - If player 2 plays \(L\): payoff from \(U\) is 1, from \(D\) is 1 → both \(U\) and \(D\) are best responses. - If player 2 plays \(R\): payoff from \(U\) is 0, from \(D\) is 0 → both are best responses. - Player 2: - If player 1 plays \(U\): payoffs are 1 from \(L\) and 1 from \(R\) → both best responses. - If player 1 plays \(D\): payoffs are 0 from \(L\) and 0 from \(R\) → both best responses.
So every pure profile is a Nash equilibrium (players are indifferent everywhere).
Step 2: Add trembles Suppose player 2 trembles: plays \(L\) with probability \(1-\varepsilon\) and \(R\) with probability \(\varepsilon>0\).
Player 1’s expected payoff from: - \(U\): \((1-\varepsilon)\cdot 1 + \varepsilon\cdot 0 = 1-\varepsilon\) - \(D\): \((1-\varepsilon)\cdot 1 + \varepsilon\cdot 0 = 1-\varepsilon\)
Still indifferent. So trembles do not break player 1’s indifference.
Now suppose player 1 trembles: plays \(U\) with probability \(1-\delta\) and \(D\) with probability \(\delta>0\).
Player 2’s expected payoff from: - \(L\): \((1-\delta)\cdot 1 + \delta\cdot 0 = 1-\delta\) - \(R\): \((1-\delta)\cdot 1 + \delta\cdot 0 = 1-\delta\)
Still indifferent.
Result: In this particular game, trembles do not select: equilibria are robust because payoffs create genuine indifference.


Takeaway
Perfection rules out equilibria that only work by assuming “impossible” actions never happen. But if the game truly makes players indifferent, perfection won’t refine further.

title: Trembling-hand perfect equilibrium
text:
Later-on analysis

Proper equilibrium strengthens perfection by making “worse mistakes” exponentially less likely.
In extensive-form games, sequential equilibrium is the tremble-based refinement with beliefs.
In many applied models, perfection is used to exclude equilibria involving weakly dominated actions.

title: Equilibrium cheat sheet
text:
Simultaneous move, complete info → NE (and refinements if needed)
Sequential, perfect information → SPE (backward induction)
Incomplete information, static → BNE
Dynamic + beliefs needed (signaling/screening) → PBE
Off-path beliefs feel arbitrary → Sequential equilibrium (trembles discipline beliefs)
Cheap talk baseline → Babbling equilibrium always exists
Need “robust to mistakes” → Trembling-hand perfect / proper
Want coordination via signals → Correlated equilibrium
Want weak prediction set → Rationalizability

title: Equilibrium cheat sheet
text:
Simultaneous move, complete info → NE (and refinements if needed)
Sequential, perfect information → SPE (backward induction)
Incomplete information, static → BNE
Dynamic + beliefs needed (signaling/screening) → PBE
Off-path beliefs feel arbitrary → Sequential equilibrium (trembles discipline beliefs)
Cheap talk baseline → Babbling equilibrium always exists
Need “robust to mistakes” → Trembling-hand perfect / proper
Want coordination via signals → Correlated equilibrium
Want weak prediction set → Rationalizability

title: Equilibrium cheat sheet
text:
Recipe card: Nash equilibrium (NE)

Pure NE

(Optional) Remove strictly dominated actions.
Compute best responses.
Intersections of best responses = pure NE.



Mixed NE (quick 2×2 method)
Let player 1 mix \(p\) on \(U\) (and \(1-p\) on \(D\)). Let player 2 mix \(q\) on \(L\) (and \(1-q\) on \(R\)). 1) Make player 1 indifferent between \(U\) and \(D\) → solve for \(q\). 2) Make player 2 indifferent between \(L\) and \(R\) → solve for \(p\). 3) Check \(p,q\in[0,1]\) and supports are consistent.
Common pitfall: mixing is only required when the opponent is indifferent among the actions in their support.

title: Equilibrium cheat sheet
text:
Recipe card: Subgame perfect equilibrium (SPE)

Backward induction (finite perfect-information trees)

Start at the last decision nodes.
Choose optimal action there.
Replace that subgame with its continuation payoff.
Move backward until the root.

Common pitfall: using non-credible threats (actions that wouldn’t be optimal if reached).

title: Equilibrium cheat sheet
text:
Recipe card: Bayesian Nash equilibrium (BNE)

Write types and prior \(\Pr(\theta)\).
Strategy is type-contingent: \(a_i=s_i(\theta_i)\).
For each type, compute expected payoff for each action.
Choose best responses for each type; verify consistency across players.

Common pitfall: forgetting strategies are functions of type, not single actions.

title: Equilibrium cheat sheet
text:
Recipe card: Perfect Bayesian equilibrium (PBE)
A PBE is (strategies, beliefs) satisfying: - Sequential rationality: actions optimal at every information set. - Bayes consistency on-path: update beliefs using Bayes’ rule where possible.

Standard workflow (signaling/screening)

Guess form: separating / pooling / semi-separating.
Propose strategies for sender types + receiver actions.
Compute on-path posteriors via Bayes.
Check receiver best responses given beliefs.
Check each sender type’s incentive constraints (no profitable deviations).
Specify off-path beliefs (carefully) and re-check deviations.

Common pitfall: not stating off-path beliefs, or using off-path beliefs that “magically” punish deviations without justification (sequential equilibrium addresses this).

title: Equilibrium cheat sheet
text:
Recipe card: Sequential equilibrium (SE)
Sequential equilibrium is PBE + a discipline on beliefs: - Beliefs must be limits of Bayes-updated beliefs from fully mixed trembles.

Practical use
If your PBE relies heavily on off-path beliefs: 1) Add tiny tremble probabilities to every action. 2) Compute implied posteriors. 3) Take limits → see which beliefs are justifiable. 4) Re-check optimality.
Common pitfall: treating off-path beliefs as completely free.

title: Equilibrium cheat sheet
text:
Recipe card: Babbling equilibrium (cheap talk)

Receiver ignores message: same action after every message.
Beliefs stay at the prior (or any belief consistent with ignoring).
Sender is indifferent over messages because messages don’t affect actions.

Use: baseline; compare informative equilibria against it.

title: Equilibrium cheat sheet
text:
Recipe card: Trembling-hand perfect equilibrium

Start from a Nash equilibrium.
Ask whether it survives when opponents sometimes make small mistakes.
Equilibria relying on “impossible” actions not happening can fail.

Heuristic: if an equilibrium uses weakly dominated actions or fragile indifference, perfection may eliminate it.

title: Equilibrium cheat sheet
text:
Recipe card: Proper equilibrium
Like perfect equilibrium, but: - very bad mistakes are much less likely than slightly bad mistakes.
Use: sharper selection when perfection is not selective enough.

title: Equilibrium cheat sheet
text:
Recipe card: Correlated equilibrium (CE)

Specify a distribution over action profiles (recommendations).
For each player and each recommendation, write obedience constraints: following ≥ deviating.
If all constraints hold, it’s a CE.

Memory aid: “Follow the recommendation because conditional on it, deviating doesn’t help.”

title: Equilibrium cheat sheet
text:
Recipe card: Rationalizability

Iteratively delete strictly dominated actions.
Repeat in the reduced game until no more deletions.
Remaining actions are rationalizable.

Common pitfall: weak dominance deletion can be order-dependent (start with strict).

title: Equilibrium cheat sheet
text:
Mini glossary (quick)

NE: best response to best response.
SPE: NE in every subgame (credible).
BNE: NE with types; best response in expectation.
PBE: strategies + beliefs; Bayes on-path; sequentially rational.
SE: PBE + tremble-consistent beliefs.
CE: equilibrium over distributions; “obey the signal.”
Rationalizability: what survives iterated strict dominance.

title: Babbling Equilibrium
text:
A babbling equilibrium is a cheap-talk equilibrium in which messages carry no information. The sender may still send messages, but the receiver ignores them.
The central idea is:
Babbling is important because it shows that costless communication is not automatically informative.

title: Babbling Equilibrium
text:
Basic structure
In a cheap-talk game:

the sender observes private information;
the sender sends a message;
the receiver observes the message;
the receiver chooses an action.

In a babbling equilibrium, the receiver’s action does not depend on the message.





flowchart LR
    A[Sender observes information] --> B[Sender sends message]
    B --> C[Receiver hears message]
    C --> D[Receiver ignores message]
    D --> E[Receiver acts on prior]






The message is strategically irrelevant.

title: Babbling Equilibrium
Babbling Equilibrium
text:
Why babbling is an equilibrium
Babbling is self-confirming.





flowchart TD
    A[Receiver expects messages to be uninformative] --> B[Receiver ignores messages]
    B --> C[Messages do not affect action]
    C --> D[Sender has no incentive to choose informative messages]
    D --> A






Because the receiver does not respond to messages, the sender cannot benefit from carefully choosing a message. Since the sender does not choose messages informatively, the receiver is right to ignore them.

title: Babbling Equilibrium
text:
Prior-based action
If the receiver ignores the message, the receiver chooses the action that maximizes expected payoff under the prior belief.
If the state is \(\theta\), and the receiver chooses action \(a\), then the receiver solves:
\[
a^*
\in
\arg\max_{a\in A}
\sum_{\theta}
u_R(a,\theta)\Pr(\theta).
\]
The message does not enter the receiver’s decision.

title: Babbling Equilibrium
text:
Beliefs
In a babbling equilibrium, on-path messages do not change beliefs.
For message \(m\):
\[
\mu(\theta\mid m)=\Pr(\theta).
\]
The posterior equals the prior.
This is what it means for the message to carry no information.

title: Babbling Equilibrium
text:
Example intuition
Suppose an expert knows whether a project is good or bad. The decision-maker must decide whether to approve it.
If the expert always wants approval, regardless of the true project quality, then the expert may always say:
The project is good.
The decision-maker anticipates this and ignores the message.
The message becomes babble.

title: Babbling Equilibrium
text:
Babbling and pooling
Babbling is related to pooling, but they are not identical.
In a pooling equilibrium, multiple types send the same message.
In a babbling equilibrium, the receiver’s action does not depend on the message.



Concept
Meaning




Pooling
different types choose the same message or signal


Babbling
messages do not affect beliefs or actions



A pooling equilibrium can be informative if the pooled group still changes beliefs relative to some other message. Babbling is fully uninformative.

title: Babbling Equilibrium
text:
Babbling and cheap talk
Babbling is especially common in cheap-talk games because messages are costless and non-binding.
If sender and receiver preferences are too misaligned, informative communication may fail. The receiver ignores messages, and the sender cannot credibly transmit information.





flowchart LR
    A[Preference conflict] --> B[Receiver distrusts message]
    B --> C[Message ignored]
    C --> D[Babbling equilibrium]

title: Babbling Equilibrium
Babbling Equilibrium
text:
Babbling versus informative equilibrium



Feature
Babbling
Informative communication




Message changes belief?
no
yes


Message changes action?
no
yes


Sender strategy depends on type?
not meaningfully
yes


Receiver learns from message?
no
partly or fully


Requires aligned interests?
no
usually some alignment



Babbling is the baseline. Informative communication requires additional incentive structure.

title: Babbling Equilibrium
text:
Off-path messages
Off-path messages are messages that are not expected in equilibrium.
In babbling equilibria, off-path beliefs can matter if a receiver might react strongly to an unexpected message.
A proposed babbling equilibrium should specify:

what beliefs the receiver holds after each message;
what action the receiver takes after each message;
why the sender does not want to deviate.

title: Babbling Equilibrium
Babbling Equilibrium
text:
Common mistakes

1. Thinking babbling means no message is sent
Messages may be sent. They are just ignored.


2. Thinking babbling means irrationality
Babbling can be fully rational in equilibrium.


3. Confusing babbling with lying
Babbling is about informativeness, not necessarily truth or falsehood.


4. Ignoring receiver action
Babbling requires the receiver’s action not to depend on the message.


5. Assuming babbling is the only possible cheap-talk equilibrium
Informative cheap-talk equilibria may exist under sufficient preference alignment.

title: Babbling Equilibrium
text:
Checklist
When checking a babbling equilibrium, ask:

What information does the sender observe?
What messages are available?
Does the receiver’s belief change after messages?
Does the receiver’s action change after messages?
Is the receiver’s action optimal under the prior?
Is the sender indifferent among messages?
Could any message profitably change the receiver’s action?
Are off-path beliefs specified?
Are there possible informative equilibria too?
What does babbling mean substantively in this case?

title: Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium
text:
Perfect Bayesian equilibrium is a solution concept for dynamic games with incomplete information. It combines sequential rationality with beliefs.
The central idea is:
Perfect Bayesian equilibrium is especially important for signaling games, cheap-talk games, reputation models, and dynamic Bayesian games.

title: Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium
text:
Why PBE is needed
Bayesian Nash equilibrium handles incomplete information, but it is not enough for dynamic games where players observe actions and update beliefs over time.
Subgame perfect equilibrium handles dynamic games, but it may not fully discipline beliefs after observed actions.
Perfect Bayesian equilibrium combines both concerns.





flowchart TD
    A[Dynamic game] --> B[Need sequential rationality]
    C[Incomplete information] --> D[Need beliefs]
    B --> E[Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium]
    D --> E

title: Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium
text:
Main components
A perfect Bayesian equilibrium includes:

strategies for all players;
beliefs at information sets;
sequential rationality;
belief consistency using Bayes’ rule wherever possible.






flowchart LR
    A[Strategies] --> C[PBE]
    B[Beliefs] --> C
    C --> D[Sequential rationality]
    C --> E[Bayesian updating]






Strategies say what players do.
Beliefs say what players think has happened or what type they face.

title: Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium
text:
Sequential rationality
Sequential rationality means that at every information set, each player’s strategy must be optimal given their belief and the continuation strategies.
In words:

whenever a player is called to move, the prescribed action must maximize expected payoff from that point onward.

This requirement applies both on and off the equilibrium path.

title: Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium
text:
Beliefs
Beliefs describe the probability a player assigns to possible nodes, states, or types at an information set.
For example, after observing message \(m\), a receiver may believe:
\[
\mu(H\mid m)=0.7.
\]
This means the receiver assigns probability 0.7 to the sender being high type after observing message \(m\).
The receiver then chooses an action that maximizes expected payoff under this belief.

title: Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium
text:
Bayes’ rule on path
If an information set is reached with positive probability in equilibrium, beliefs must be updated by Bayes’ rule.
For a message \(m\):
\[
\mu(\theta\mid m)
=
\frac{
\Pr(m\mid \theta)\Pr(\theta)
}{
\sum_{\theta'}\Pr(m\mid \theta')\Pr(\theta')
}.
\]





flowchart LR
    A[Prior belief] --> B[Observed action or message]
    B --> C[Bayes' rule]
    C --> D[Posterior belief]
    D --> E[Sequentially rational response]

title: Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium
text:
Off-path beliefs
If an information set is reached with zero probability in equilibrium, Bayes’ rule may not pin down beliefs.
These are off-path beliefs.
PBE allows some freedom in off-path beliefs, but the beliefs still influence whether the equilibrium is plausible.





flowchart TD
    A[Observation] --> B{Positive probability in equilibrium?}
    B -->|Yes| C[Beliefs pinned down by Bayes' rule]
    B -->|No| D[Off-path beliefs not fully pinned down]
    C --> E[Receiver response]
    D --> E






This is one reason sequential equilibrium is sometimes preferred: it imposes stronger consistency requirements.

title: Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium
text:
PBE in signaling games
In a signaling game, a PBE specifies:

sender signal choice for each type;
receiver belief after each signal;
receiver action after each signal;
optimality for sender and receiver;
Bayes-consistent beliefs on path.






flowchart LR
    A[Sender type] --> B[Signal strategy]
    B --> C[Receiver belief]
    C --> D[Receiver action]
    D --> E[Sender incentive compatibility]






A separating PBE has different types sending different signals.
A pooling PBE has different types sending the same signal.

title: Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium
text:
Separating PBE
In a separating PBE:
\[
s(H) \neq s(L).
\]
The receiver can infer type from signal.
For example:
\[
\mu(H\mid s_H)=1,
\]
and
\[
\mu(L\mid s_L)=1.
\]
The sender types must prefer their assigned signals, and the receiver must best respond to the inferred type.

title: Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium
text:
Pooling PBE
In a pooling PBE:
\[
s(H)=s(L).
\]
Both types send the same signal.
The receiver cannot infer the type from the pooled signal and uses the prior belief after observing it.
Off-path beliefs after unexpected signals can be important for sustaining the pooling equilibrium.

title: Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium
text:
Cheap talk and PBE
Cheap-talk games are often solved using PBE.
A cheap-talk PBE requires:

sender messages are optimal given expected receiver responses;
receiver actions are optimal given beliefs after messages;
beliefs are updated by Bayes’ rule when possible.

Babbling equilibria are PBE in many cheap-talk games.

title: Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium
text:
PBE versus SPE








Concept
Used for
Main requirement




SPE
dynamic complete-information games
Nash equilibrium in every subgame


PBE
dynamic incomplete-information games
sequential rationality plus beliefs


Sequential equilibrium
dynamic incomplete-information games
stronger belief consistency



PBE is more general than SPE for games where beliefs matter.

title: Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium
text:
Common mistakes

1. Giving strategies but no beliefs
A PBE requires both strategies and beliefs.


2. Checking only on-path optimality
Sequential rationality must hold at every information set.


3. Ignoring Bayes’ rule
On-path beliefs must be consistent with Bayes’ rule.


4. Treating off-path beliefs as irrelevant
Off-path beliefs can support or destroy candidate equilibria.


5. Using BNE when actions reveal information over time
Dynamic updating usually requires PBE or sequential equilibrium.

title: Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium
text:
Checklist
When checking PBE, ask:

What are the players and types?
What are the histories and information sets?
What strategy is assigned to each player or type?
What beliefs are assigned at each information set?
Are beliefs on path derived by Bayes’ rule?
Is each player sequentially rational given beliefs?
Are sender incentive constraints satisfied?
Are receiver responses optimal?
What happens after off-path actions?
Is a stronger refinement needed?

title: Subgame Perfect Equilibrium
text:
Subgame perfect equilibrium is a refinement of Nash equilibrium for dynamic games. It rules out equilibria that rely on non-credible threats or promises.
The central idea is:

title: Subgame Perfect Equilibrium
section: Why Nash equilibrium is not enough
text:
Why Nash equilibrium is not enough
Nash equilibrium checks whether players want to deviate from their complete strategies.
In dynamic games, this can allow threats that would not actually be carried out if the relevant history occurred.





flowchart LR
    A[Nash equilibrium] --> B[Mutual best responses]
    B --> C[May include non-credible threats]
    C --> D[Need stronger concept]
    D --> E[Subgame perfect equilibrium]






Subgame perfection adds credibility.

title: Subgame Perfect Equilibrium
text:
Definition
A strategy profile is a subgame perfect equilibrium if it induces a Nash equilibrium in every subgame.
In words:

after every history that begins a subgame, the continuation strategies must form a Nash equilibrium of that subgame.

This means players must behave optimally not only along the equilibrium path, but also after possible deviations.

title: Subgame Perfect Equilibrium
text:
Subgames
A subgame is a part of an extensive-form game that:

begins at a decision node;
includes all future nodes and actions from that node;
does not cut across an information set.






flowchart TD
    A[Whole game] --> B[Decision node]
    B --> C[Subgame from that node]
    C --> D[All future actions]
    C --> E[All terminal payoffs]






A subgame is like a smaller game inside the larger game.

title: Subgame Perfect Equilibrium
text:
Basic logic
Subgame perfect equilibrium asks:





flowchart TD
    A[Choose strategy profile] --> B[Look at each subgame]
    B --> C{Are continuation strategies Nash equilibria?}
    C -->|Yes| D[Subgame perfect]
    C -->|No| E[Not subgame perfect]






The key test is whether the strategy profile remains rational inside every subgame.

title: Subgame Perfect Equilibrium
text:
Backward induction
In finite games with perfect information, backward induction finds a subgame perfect equilibrium.





flowchart LR
    A[Finite perfect-information game] --> B[Backward induction]
    B --> C[Optimal action in final subgames]
    C --> D[Move backward]
    D --> E[Optimal action in every subgame]
    E --> F[Subgame perfect equilibrium]






Backward induction is the procedure. Subgame perfect equilibrium is the solution concept.

title: Subgame Perfect Equilibrium
text:
Example: entry deterrence
Consider the following game.





flowchart TD
    A[Entrant] -->|Stay Out| B[0,2]
    A -->|Enter| C[Incumbent]
    C -->|Fight| D[-1,-1]
    C -->|Accommodate| E[2,1]






If the entrant enters, the incumbent chooses between Fight and Accommodate.
The incumbent prefers Accommodate because:
\[
1>-1.
\]
So Fight is not credible.
The entrant anticipates Accommodate and chooses Enter because:
\[
2>0.
\]
The subgame perfect outcome is:
\[
(\text{Enter},\text{Accommodate}).
\]

title: Subgame Perfect Equilibrium
text:
Non-credible threat
The incumbent may want to threaten:

If you enter, I will fight.

But after entry occurs, fighting gives the incumbent a lower payoff. Therefore the threat is not credible.





flowchart LR
    A[Threat to fight] --> B[Entry occurs]
    B --> C{Is fighting optimal?}
    C -->|No| D[Threat not credible]
    D --> E[Ruled out by SPE]






Subgame perfection removes equilibria supported by this kind of threat.

title: Subgame Perfect Equilibrium
text:
Strategy profiles and paths
In dynamic games, an equilibrium strategy profile specifies:

what happens on the equilibrium path;
what would happen after off-path histories.

The equilibrium path is the sequence of actions that actually occurs if everyone follows the equilibrium strategies.
Off-path behaviour describes what players would do after deviations.
Subgame perfection requires off-path behaviour to be optimal in every subgame.

title: Subgame Perfect Equilibrium
text:
Sequential rationality
Subgame perfection is closely related to sequential rationality.
Sequential rationality means that at every point where a player acts, the prescribed action is optimal given the continuation game.
In perfect-information games, subgame perfection captures this idea well.
In imperfect-information games, we often need belief-based refinements such as perfect Bayesian equilibrium or sequential equilibrium.

title: Subgame Perfect Equilibrium
text:
SPE versus Nash equilibrium








Concept
Requirement
Problem addressed




Nash equilibrium
no profitable unilateral deviation from complete strategy
strategic stability


Subgame perfect equilibrium
Nash equilibrium in every subgame
credibility


Perfect Bayesian equilibrium
sequential rationality plus beliefs
dynamic incomplete information



Every subgame perfect equilibrium is a Nash equilibrium. But not every Nash equilibrium is subgame perfect.

title: Subgame Perfect Equilibrium
text:
Finite-horizon repeated games
Subgame perfection explains unraveling in finitely repeated prisoners’ dilemma games.
If the final period is known, players defect in the final period. Knowing that, they defect in the previous period, and so on.





flowchart LR
    A[Final period] --> B[No future punishment]
    B --> C[Defection]
    C --> D[Previous period loses future discipline]
    D --> E[Backward unraveling]






This is a classic application of backward induction.

title: Subgame Perfect Equilibrium
text:
One-deviation principle
In many dynamic games, the one-deviation principle can simplify checking subgame perfection.
The idea is:

a strategy profile is subgame perfect if no player can gain by deviating once and then returning to the strategy.

This works under particular conditions, especially in many finite or discounted dynamic games.
It is useful because checking every possible deviation can be hard.

title: Subgame Perfect Equilibrium
text:
Common mistakes

1. Thinking SPE is only about the equilibrium path
SPE also requires optimal behaviour after off-path histories.


2. Treating threats as credible because they are announced
A threat is credible only if it is optimal to carry out.


3. Confusing backward induction with SPE
Backward induction is a method; SPE is a solution concept.


4. Applying subgame perfection where there are no proper subgames
In some imperfect-information games, subgame perfection may add little beyond Nash equilibrium.


5. Cutting through information sets
A subgame cannot begin in the middle of an information set.

title: Subgame Perfect Equilibrium
text:
Checklist
When checking subgame perfection, ask:

What is the extensive-form game?
What are the proper subgames?
What strategy profile is proposed?
Does the profile induce a Nash equilibrium in the whole game?
Does it induce a Nash equilibrium in every subgame?
Are threats credible?
Are promises credible?
What is the equilibrium path?
What happens off path?
Would backward induction give the same result in a finite perfect-information game?
