title: Repeated Games
text:
Repeated games study what happens when the same strategic interaction occurs more than once. Repetition changes incentives because current actions can affect future behaviour.
A player may cooperate today not because cooperation is immediately best, but because defection today may trigger punishment tomorrow.

title: Repeated Games
text:
The basic idea
A repeated game begins with a stage game. The stage game is played multiple times.





flowchart LR
    A[Stage game] --> B[Period 1]
    B --> C[Period 2]
    C --> D[Period 3]
    D --> E[Future periods]






The key difference from a one-shot game is that history matters.
Players can condition current actions on past behaviour.

title: Repeated Games
text:
Why repetition matters
In a one-shot prisoners’ dilemma, defection may be the dominant strategy.
In a repeated prisoners’ dilemma, cooperation may be possible because defection can be punished in future periods.





flowchart LR
    A[Cooperate today] --> B[Good future relationship]
    C[Defect today] --> D[Short-run gain]
    D --> E[Future punishment]
    E --> F[Lower continuation payoff]






The comparison is:
\[
\text{short-run gain from defection}
\leq
\text{future loss from punishment}.
\]
If this condition holds, cooperation can be sustained.

title: Repeated Games
text:
Histories
A history is the sequence of actions observed so far.
After \(t\) periods, a history may be written as:
\[
h^t = (a^0,a^1,\ldots,a^{t-1}).
\]
A repeated-game strategy maps histories into current actions:
\[
s_i(h^t) \in A_i.
\]
This means a player’s action today may depend on what happened before.

title: Repeated Games
text:
Discounting
Future payoffs are usually discounted.
Let \(\delta \in (0,1)\) be the discount factor. A player’s total payoff may be written as:
\[
U_i
=
u_i^0
+
\delta u_i^1
+
\delta^2 u_i^2
+
\cdots.
\]
A higher \(\delta\) means the player is more patient.
If \(\delta\) is close to 1, future payoffs matter a lot. If \(\delta\) is close to 0, the player is impatient and mostly cares about the present.

title: Repeated Games
section: Present value of a constant payoff
text:
Present value of a constant payoff
If a player receives payoff \(x\) every period forever, the discounted value is:
\[
x+\delta x+\delta^2 x+\cdots
=
\frac{x}{1-\delta}.
\]
This formula is used constantly in repeated games.

title: Repeated Games
text:
Trigger strategies
A trigger strategy begins by cooperating and then punishes if the other player defects.
One simple version is grim trigger:

cooperate as long as no one has defected;
if anyone defects, punish forever.






flowchart TD
    A[Start by cooperating] --> B{Has anyone defected?}
    B -->|No| C[Continue cooperating]
    B -->|Yes| D[Punish forever]
    C --> B






Grim trigger is severe, but analytically simple.

title: Repeated Games
text:
Tit-for-tat
Tit-for-tat is another common strategy:

cooperate in the first period;
after that, copy the other player’s previous action.






flowchart TD
    A[First period: cooperate] --> B[Observe opponent's last action]
    B --> C[Choose same action this period]
    C --> B






Tit-for-tat is less severe than grim trigger because cooperation can resume after punishment.

title: Repeated Games
text:
Repeated prisoners’ dilemma
In the one-shot prisoners’ dilemma, defection is individually optimal.
But in an infinitely repeated game, cooperation can be supported if players are sufficiently patient.
Suppose:



Outcome
Payoff




mutual cooperation
\(R\)


defect while other cooperates
\(T\)


mutual defection
\(P\)


cooperate while other defects
\(S\)



where:
\[
T>R>P>S.
\]
If both cooperate forever, the value is:
\[
\frac{R}{1-\delta}.
\]
If one player defects today and is punished forever after, the value is:
\[
T+\delta\frac{P}{1-\delta}.
\]
Cooperation is sustainable if:
\[
\frac{R}{1-\delta}
\geq
T+\delta\frac{P}{1-\delta}.
\]
This condition says that the value of continued cooperation must be at least as large as the value of cheating once and then being punished.

title: Repeated Games
text:
Solving the incentive condition
Start with:
\[
\frac{R}{1-\delta}
\geq
T+\delta\frac{P}{1-\delta}.
\]
Multiply both sides by \(1-\delta\):
\[
R \geq T(1-\delta)+\delta P.
\]
Expand:
\[
R \geq T-\delta T+\delta P.
\]
Rearrange:
\[
\delta(T-P) \geq T-R.
\]
So:
\[
\delta \geq \frac{T-R}{T-P}.
\]
Cooperation is easier to sustain when:

the temptation payoff \(T-R\) is small;
the punishment gap \(T-P\) is large;
players are patient.

title: Repeated Games
text:
Finite versus infinite repetition
Finite and infinite repeated games behave differently.
If the game has a known final period, backward induction can unravel cooperation.
In the final period, there is no future punishment, so players may defect. Knowing this, cooperation may unravel in the previous period, and so on.





flowchart LR
    A[Known final period] --> B[No future punishment]
    B --> C[Defection in final period]
    C --> D[Previous period unravels]
    D --> E[Cooperation may collapse]






Infinite repetition avoids a known last period.

title: Repeated Games
text:
Folk theorem intuition
The folk theorem says, roughly, that if players are sufficiently patient, many feasible and individually rational payoff profiles can be sustained as equilibria in infinitely repeated games.
The intuition is:

patient players can use future rewards and punishments to support many forms of cooperation.

This is powerful but also creates multiplicity. Repeated games may have many equilibria.

title: Repeated Games
text:
Reputation
Repeated interaction can create reputation.
A player may act cooperatively today to influence how others treat them tomorrow.





flowchart LR
    A[Current action] --> B[Observed by others]
    B --> C[Belief about type or reliability]
    C --> D[Future treatment]
    D --> E[Current incentive]






Reputation is especially important when players are uncertain about each other’s types.

title: Repeated Games
Repeated Games
text:
Common mistakes

1. Treating repeated play as just many one-shot games
History changes incentives.


2. Forgetting discounting
Future punishment matters only if players care about the future.


3. Assuming cooperation always occurs
Repetition can support cooperation, but only under incentive conditions.


4. Ignoring finite-horizon unraveling
A known final period can destroy cooperation through backward induction.


5. Treating punishment as costless
Punishment may reduce the punisher’s payoff too.


6. Ignoring multiple equilibria
Repeated games often have many possible equilibria.

title: Repeated Games
text:
Checklist
When analysing a repeated game, ask:

What is the stage game?
Is the game repeated finitely or infinitely?
What does each player observe after each period?
What is the discount factor?
What strategies are available?
What history triggers punishment?
What is the gain from deviation?
What is the future loss from punishment?
Is cooperation sustainable?
Are there multiple equilibria?

title: Auctions
text: Auctions allocate an item based on bids. Models differ by: - format (first-price, second-price, English, Dutch), - values (private values vs common values), - information (signals, asymmetries).

title: Auctions
text: Auctions allocate an item based on bids. Models differ by: - format (first-price, second-price, English, Dutch), - values (private values vs common values), - information (signals, asymmetries).

title: Auctions
text:
What’s special

Bidding strategies trade off winning probability vs payment.
In private values with risk-neutral bidders, many formats have linked outcomes (revenue equivalence under conditions).
In common-value settings, bidders fear the winner’s curse.

title: Auctions
text:
One example (second-price auction, private values)
Each bidder has value \(v_i\) for the item. In a second-price (Vickrey) auction, the highest bidder wins and pays the second-highest bid.
A dominant strategy is: \[
b_i = v_i.
\]
Intuition: your bid only affects whether you win, not what you pay conditional on winning. Overbidding risks winning at a price above your value; underbidding risks losing when you would have profited.

title: Auctions
text:
Story
A tutor releases one Saturday slot. Many students bid; each has private urgency. The rule for who pays what shapes bidding incentives.

title: Auctions
text:
Model

Bidders \(i=1,\dots,n\)
Private values \(v_i\)
Bids \(b_i\)
Auction format determines allocation and payment

title: Auctions
text:
Equilibrium (second-price auction)
In a second-price auction, the highest bidder wins and pays the second-highest bid. A dominant strategy is: \[
b_i=v_i.
\]
Reason (one-line): your bid affects winning, but the price conditional on winning is the opponent’s bid, not yours.

title: Auctions
text:
Later-on analysis

First-price auctions: equilibrium involves bid shading; risk aversion matters.
Common values: winner’s curse and information aggregation dominate.
Reserve prices and optimal design: mechanism design connects auctions to revenue maximization.

title: Normal-form Games
text:
A normal-form game represents a strategic situation in which players choose strategies and receive payoffs from the resulting strategy profile. It is the standard representation for simultaneous-move games and the natural starting point for Nash equilibrium.
The normal form is useful because it makes the basic ingredients of a game explicit: players, strategies, and payoffs.

title: Normal-form Games
text:
Basic structure
A normal-form game can be written as
\[
G=\langle N,(S_i)_{i\in N},(u_i)_{i\in N}\rangle.
\]
Here:



Object
Meaning




\(N\)
set of players


\(S_i\)
strategy set of player \(i\)


\(u_i\)
payoff function of player \(i\)



A strategy profile is
\[
s=(s_1,\ldots,s_n).
\]
Player \(i\)’s payoff is
\[
u_i(s_i,s_{-i}),
\]
where \(s_{-i}\) denotes the strategies of all players other than \(i\).

title: Normal-form Games
text:
Why normal form matters
Normal form gives the cleanest setting for best-response reasoning.





flowchart LR
    A[Players] --> D[Normal-form game]
    B[Strategies] --> D
    C[Payoffs] --> D
    D --> E[Best responses]
    E --> F[Nash equilibrium]






Once the normal-form game is defined, the main question is:

Which strategies are best responses to which other strategies?

title: Normal-form Games
text:
Payoff matrix
For two-player finite games, the normal form is often shown as a payoff matrix.
For example:




Player 2: L
Player 2: R




Player 1: U
\((2,2)\)
\((0,3)\)


Player 1: D
\((3,0)\)
\((1,1)\)



Each cell gives payoffs in the form:
\[
(\text{Player 1 payoff}, \text{Player 2 payoff}).
\]
If Player 1 chooses \(U\) and Player 2 chooses \(L\), the outcome is \((2,2)\).

title: Normal-form Games
section: Simultaneous does not always mean literal same time

title: Normal-form Games
text:
Best responses
A best response is a strategy that maximizes a player’s payoff given the strategies of others.
For player \(i\),
\[
BR_i(s_{-i})
\in
\arg\max_{s_i\in S_i}
u_i(s_i,s_{-i}).
\]
This says:

hold the other players’ strategies fixed, then choose the strategy that gives the highest payoff.






flowchart LR
    A[Others' strategies] --> B[Player i compares payoffs]
    B --> C[Choose highest payoff strategy]
    C --> D[Best response]






Best-response analysis is the core method for solving normal-form games.

title: Normal-form Games
text:
Nash equilibrium
A Nash equilibrium is a strategy profile where every player is choosing a best response to the others.
Formally, \(s^*\) is a Nash equilibrium if, for every player \(i\),
\[
u_i(s_i^*,s_{-i}^*)
\geq
u_i(s_i,s_{-i}^*)
\quad
\text{for all } s_i\in S_i.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
s_i^* \in BR_i(s_{-i}^*)
\quad
\text{for every } i.
\]

title: Normal-form Games
text:
Solving a 2-by-2 game
For a two-player, two-action game, use this workflow:





flowchart TD
    A[Write payoff matrix] --> B[Find Player 1's best response to each Player 2 action]
    B --> C[Find Player 2's best response to each Player 1 action]
    C --> D[Mark mutual best responses]
    D --> E[Nash equilibria]
    E --> F[Interpret result]






A cell is a pure-strategy Nash equilibrium if both players’ strategies are best responses in that cell.

title: Normal-form Games
text:
Dominant strategies
A strategy is strictly dominant if it gives a player a higher payoff than every other strategy, no matter what the other players do.
For player \(i\), strategy \(s_i\) strictly dominates \(s_i'\) if
\[
u_i(s_i,s_{-i})
>
u_i(s_i',s_{-i})
\]
for all \(s_{-i}\).
A weakly dominant strategy gives at least as high a payoff in every case and a strictly higher payoff in at least one case.
Dominant strategies are powerful because they do not depend on beliefs about what others do.

title: Normal-form Games
text:
Dominated strategies
A strategy is dominated if another strategy always performs better.
Dominated strategies are often removed through iterative elimination.





flowchart TD
    A[Start with full game] --> B[Find dominated strategies]
    B --> C[Remove dominated strategies]
    C --> D[Reduced game]
    D --> E{More dominated strategies?}
    E -->|Yes| B
    E -->|No| F[Remaining strategies]






This process is useful, but it is not the same as finding all Nash equilibria.

title: Normal-form Games
text:
Coordination games
A coordination game has multiple equilibria, and players prefer to match each other’s actions.
Example:




L
R




U
\((2,2)\)
\((0,0)\)


D
\((0,0)\)
\((1,1)\)



There are two Nash equilibria:
\[
(U,L)
\]
and
\[
(D,R).
\]
The problem is not conflict alone. The problem is selecting the same equilibrium.

title: Normal-form Games
text:
Prisoners’ dilemma
The prisoners’ dilemma shows how individually rational behaviour can lead to a collectively worse outcome.
The usual structure is:




Cooperate
Defect




Cooperate
good for both
sucker payoff


Defect
temptation payoff
bad for both



Each player has an incentive to defect, but mutual defection is worse than mutual cooperation.
This is why Nash equilibrium should not be confused with social optimality.

title: Normal-form Games
text:
Mixed strategies
A mixed strategy is a probability distribution over pure strategies.
If Player 1 chooses \(U\) with probability \(p\) and \(D\) with probability \(1-p\), then Player 1’s mixed strategy is
\[
\sigma_1=(p,1-p).
\]
Mixed strategies are useful when no pure-strategy equilibrium exists or when players need to keep opponents indifferent.
A mixed-strategy equilibrium requires each player to be willing to randomize among the strategies used with positive probability.

title: Normal-form Games
text:
Expected payoff
If Player 2 plays \(L\) with probability \(q\) and \(R\) with probability \(1-q\), Player 1’s expected payoff from \(U\) is
\[
U_1(U,q)
=
q u_1(U,L)+(1-q)u_1(U,R).
\]
Player 1’s expected payoff from \(D\) is
\[
U_1(D,q)
=
q u_1(D,L)+(1-q)u_1(D,R).
\]
If Player 1 mixes between \(U\) and \(D\), then they must be indifferent:
\[
U_1(U,q)=U_1(D,q).
\]
This condition is often used to solve mixed equilibria.

title: Normal-form Games
text:
Normal form and extensive form
A dynamic game can often be converted into normal form by listing each player’s complete strategies.
However, the normal form may hide timing and credibility.








Representation
Strength
Weakness




Normal form
clear strategy-payoff structure
hides timing


Extensive form
shows sequence and information
can be larger and more complex



For sequential games, the extensive form is usually better for reasoning about credibility and subgame perfection.

title: Normal-form Games
text:
Common mistakes

1. Confusing actions with strategies
In static games, an action and strategy may look similar. In dynamic games, a strategy is a complete plan.


2. Reading payoffs in the wrong order
In a payoff pair \((a,b)\), the first number usually belongs to Player 1 and the second to Player 2.


3. Treating Nash equilibrium as the best social outcome
A Nash equilibrium may be inefficient.


4. Removing strategies incorrectly
Only dominated strategies should be removed under dominance reasoning.


5. Ignoring mixed strategies
A game may have no pure equilibrium but still have a mixed equilibrium.

title: Normal-form Games
text:
Checklist
When analysing a normal-form game, ask:

Who are the players?
What are their strategies?
What are the payoffs?
What is each player’s best response to each opponent strategy?
Are there dominant or dominated strategies?
Are there mutual best responses?
Are there multiple equilibria?
Is there a mixed equilibrium?
Is the equilibrium efficient?
What does the result mean substantively?

title: Game Types
text:
Game types describe the strategic environment before we choose an equilibrium concept. They answer questions such as: Do players move at the same time or in sequence? Do they know each other’s payoffs? Is the game played once or repeatedly? Can players communicate? Are they connected through a network?
This page gives a map of the main game forms used across the notes.

title: Game Types
text:
The basic classification
A game can often be classified by four modelling choices:

Timing: simultaneous or sequential.
Information: complete or incomplete.
Frequency: one-shot or repeated.
Communication and structure: messages, signals, networks, bargaining, auctions, or learning.






flowchart TD
    A[Game Types] --> B[Timing]
    A --> C[Information]
    A --> D[Repetition]
    A --> E[Communication]
    A --> F[Market and social structure]

    B --> B1[Static Games]
    B --> B2[Dynamic Games]

    C --> C1[Complete Information]
    C --> C2[Incomplete Information]

    D --> D1[One-shot Games]
    D --> D2[Repeated Games]

    E --> E1[Cheap Talk]
    E --> E2[Signaling]
    E --> E3[Screening]

    F --> F1[Bargaining]
    F --> F2[Auctions]
    F --> F3[Network Games]
    F --> F4[Evolutionary and Learning Models]






The categories overlap. For example, a signaling game is usually dynamic, incomplete-information, and communicative. A repeated game may also include incomplete information and reputation. The classification is useful because it tells us what kind of reasoning the model requires.

title: Game Types
text:
Main families of games



Normal-form games
Static games in which players choose strategies without observing current actions by others. Useful for simultaneous-move interaction, coordination, conflict, and basic Nash equilibrium analysis.
Open →




Extensive-form games
Dynamic games represented by decision nodes, branches, information sets, and terminal payoffs. Useful for sequential reasoning, credibility, and backward induction.
Open →




Bayesian games
Games with incomplete information, where players may have private types and beliefs about others.
Open →




Repeated games
Games in which the same strategic situation occurs more than once. Useful for cooperation, punishment, reputation, and long-run incentives.
Open →

title: Game Types
text:
Communication and information design



Cheap talk
A sender sends a costless, non-binding message to a receiver. The key question is whether information can be transmitted without commitment.
Open →




Signaling
An informed player takes an action that may reveal private information. The signal can be informative because it is costly or strategically separating.
Open →




Screening and mechanism design
The uninformed side designs choices, contracts, or mechanisms to induce information revelation or desired behaviour.
Open →

title: Game Types
text:
Economic and social applications



Bargaining
Players negotiate over surplus division, agreement, delay, outside options, and commitment.
Open →




Auctions
Bidders compete under rules that determine allocation and payment. Auctions connect incentives, information, and mechanism design.
Open →




Global games
Small uncertainty about fundamentals can select among multiple equilibria and explain coordination under incomplete information.
Open →




Evolutionary games and learning
Behaviour changes through adaptation, imitation, reinforcement, or population dynamics rather than full rational calculation.
Open →




Network games
Players interact through social, economic, or institutional networks. The structure of connections affects incentives and outcomes.
Open →

title: Game Types
section: How to choose a game type
text:
How to choose a game type
The following decision tree gives a practical way to choose a modelling form.





flowchart TD
    A[What is the strategic situation?] --> B{Do players move simultaneously?}

    B -->|Yes| C[Normal-form game]
    B -->|No, sequence matters| D[Extensive-form game]

    C --> E{Is there private information?}
    D --> F{Is there private information?}

    E -->|No| G[Complete-information static game]
    E -->|Yes| H[Bayesian game]

    F -->|No| I[Dynamic complete-information game]
    F -->|Yes| J[Dynamic incomplete-information game]

    G --> K[Nash equilibrium]
    H --> L[Bayesian Nash equilibrium]
    I --> M[Backward induction or SPE]
    J --> N[PBE or sequential equilibrium]

    A --> O{Is the interaction repeated?}
    O -->|Yes| P[Repeated game]
    P --> Q[Reputation, punishment, cooperation]

    A --> R{Is communication central?}
    R -->|Costless messages| S[Cheap talk]
    R -->|Costly or informative actions| T[Signaling]
    R -->|Menu or contract design| U[Screening or mechanism design]






This tree is not meant to be mechanical. It is a way to prevent confusion between the strategic environment and the solution concept.

title: Game Types
text:
Timing: static versus dynamic games
The first distinction is timing.
In a static game, players make choices without observing the current choices of others. This does not always mean the game literally happens at the same instant. It means that no player can condition their current action on the current action of another player.
In a dynamic game, at least one player moves after observing something about earlier play. Dynamic games require attention to histories, information sets, and credibility.








Question
Static game
Dynamic game




How are choices made?
Simultaneously or without observation
Sequentially or over time


Standard representation
Normal form
Extensive form


Main object
Strategy profile
Strategy profile over histories


Main issue
Mutual best response
Credibility and continuation behaviour


Typical solution
Nash equilibrium
Backward induction or subgame perfection

title: Game Types
text:
Information: complete versus incomplete information
A game has complete information when the relevant payoffs, players, strategies, and structure of the game are commonly known.
A game has incomplete information when at least one player is uncertain about another player’s type, payoff, cost, ability, preference, or intention.
Incomplete information changes the model because players must reason with beliefs.





flowchart LR
    A[Incomplete Information] --> B[Private Types]
    B --> C[Beliefs]
    C --> D[Type-contingent Strategies]
    D --> E[Bayesian Equilibrium]






This is the bridge between game theory and probability. In Bayesian games, a strategy is not just an action. It is a plan that specifies what each type would do.

title: Game Types
text:
Repetition and reputation
Repetition changes incentives because actions today affect future responses.
A player may cooperate today not because cooperation is immediately optimal, but because defection would damage future payoffs. This logic appears in repeated trade, collusion, social norms, trust, and informal enforcement.





flowchart LR
    A[Current behaviour] --> B[Observed by others]
    B --> C[Beliefs updated]
    C --> D[Future treatment changes]
    D --> E[Current incentive changes]






Repeated games therefore connect equilibrium reasoning to reputation and history.

title: Game Types
text:
Communication games
Communication games ask whether messages, signals, or contracts can transmit information.








Game type
Who has information?
Main question




Cheap talk
Sender
Can costless messages be informative?


Signaling
Sender
Can costly actions reveal type?


Screening
Receiver or designer
Can menus induce self-selection?


Mechanism design
Designer
Can rules align incentives with desired outcomes?



Communication is strategically interesting because messages are not automatically believed. A message matters only when it changes beliefs and the sender has an incentive to send it.

title: Game Types
text:
Structure: markets, networks, and learning
Not all strategic interaction is best represented as a small two-player game. Some models focus on structure.
Auctions study allocation under bidding rules.
Bargaining studies surplus division and agreement.
Network games study how links among agents shape incentives.
Evolutionary games study how behaviour changes across populations or time.
Global games study equilibrium selection when players face noisy information about fundamentals.
These models are useful when the environment itself is doing important explanatory work.

title: Game Types
text:
Suggested reading paths

If you are starting from basic game theory

If you are interested in information

Cheap talk

If you are interested in applications

Bargaining

title: Game Types
text:
Common mistakes

1. Confusing game type with equilibrium concept
“Bayesian game” is a type of game. “Bayesian Nash equilibrium” is a solution concept for that type of game.


2. Thinking static means unchanging
A static game means choices are not conditioned on current observation of others’ actions. It does not mean the real-world situation has no time dimension.


3. Forgetting that strategies are complete plans
In dynamic games, a strategy must specify what a player would do after every relevant history, not only along the equilibrium path.


4. Treating communication as automatically informative
Messages are informative only when incentives support truthful or partially informative communication.


5. Ignoring information structure
Many models differ only in what players know. Changing the information structure can change the equilibrium completely.

title: Network games
text: In network games, each agent’s payoff depends on their action and the actions of their neighbors in a graph.

title: Network games
text: In network games, each agent’s payoff depends on their action and the actions of their neighbors in a graph.

title: Network games
text:
What’s special

Local interactions can produce global patterns (cascades, clusters).
Strategic complements/substitutes on a graph lead to amplification or dampening.
Network position (centrality) can predict influence and equilibrium actions.

title: Network games
text:
One example (linear-quadratic network game)
Let \(G\) be an adjacency matrix and actions \(a\in\mathbb{R}^n\). A common form is:
\[
u_i(a)=\alpha a_i - \frac12 a_i^2 + \beta \sum_j G_{ij} a_i a_j.
\]
FOC for each \(i\) gives: \[
a_i = \alpha + \beta \sum_j G_{ij} a_j.
\]
In vector form: \[
a = \alpha \mathbf{1} + \beta G a
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
a = (I-\beta G)^{-1}\alpha \mathbf{1},
\] when \((I-\beta G)\) is invertible.
Intuition: your action responds to neighbors; the network structure shapes equilibrium via the matrix inverse.

title: Network games
text:
Story
Study effort spreads through friendships: when your neighbors study more, you feel pressure and motivation. Your best response depends on your local network, and the network structure shapes the overall pattern.

title: Network games
text:
Model

Players are nodes in a graph with adjacency matrix \(G\)
Each chooses action \(a_i\)
Payoff has spillovers with neighbors

title: Network games
text:
Equilibrium (linear-quadratic network game)
Utility: \[
u_i(a)=\alpha a_i-\frac12 a_i^2+\beta\sum_j G_{ij}a_i a_j.
\]
FOC: \[
a_i=\alpha+\beta\sum_j G_{ij}a_j.
\]
Vector form: \[
a=\alpha\mathbf 1+\beta G a
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
a=(I-\beta G)^{-1}\alpha\mathbf 1,
\] provided \((I-\beta G)\) is invertible (a common sufficient condition is \(|\beta|<1/\rho(G)\) where \(\rho(G)\) is the spectral radius).

title: Network games
text:
Later-on analysis

Complements vs substitutes: sign of \(\beta\) changes amplification vs dampening.
Centrality: equilibrium actions often correlate with network centrality.
Interventions: targeted subsidies/penalties can propagate through the network.

title: Bayesian Games
text:
Bayesian games study strategic interaction under incomplete information. Players may be uncertain about other players’ preferences, payoffs, costs, abilities, intentions, information, or types.
The key idea is that players do not simply choose actions. They choose actions while holding beliefs about what kind of opponents they are facing.

title: Bayesian Games
text:
Complete versus incomplete information
A game has complete information if the structure of the game, including payoffs and types, is commonly known.
A game has incomplete information if at least one player is uncertain about another player’s type or payoff-relevant characteristic.





flowchart TD
    A[Strategic interaction] --> B[Complete information]
    A --> C[Incomplete information]
    B --> D[Players know payoffs and types]
    C --> E[Players hold beliefs over types]
    E --> F[Bayesian game]






Incomplete information does not mean players know nothing. It means they reason with probability.

title: Bayesian Games
Bayesian Games
text:
Type spaces
Each player has a type space.
For player \(i\), the type space is written as
\[
\Theta_i.
\]
A type is an element:
\[
\theta_i \in \Theta_i.
\]
A profile of types is
\[
\theta = (\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_n).
\]
The types of everyone except player \(i\) are written as
\[
\theta_{-i}.
\]

title: Bayesian Games
text:
Beliefs
Players hold beliefs over types.
If player 2 may be high-cost or low-cost, player 1 may believe:
\[
\Pr(\theta_2=H)=p,
\]
and
\[
\Pr(\theta_2=L)=1-p.
\]
Beliefs are central because players choose actions based on expected payoffs.





flowchart LR
    A[Unknown type] --> B[Belief over types]
    B --> C[Expected payoff]
    C --> D[Optimal action]

title: Bayesian Games
text:
Nature
A Bayesian game is often represented as a game where nature first draws types.





flowchart TD
    A[Nature draws types] --> B[Each player observes own type]
    B --> C[Players choose actions]
    C --> D[Payoffs depend on actions and types]






This converts incomplete information into imperfect information about nature’s move.

title: Bayesian Games
text:
Strategy in a Bayesian game
A strategy in a Bayesian game is a type-contingent plan.
Player \(i\)’s strategy maps types into actions:
\[
s_i:\Theta_i \to A_i.
\]
This means each type of player \(i\) may choose a different action.
For example:
\[
s_i(H)=a_H,
\]
and
\[
s_i(L)=a_L.
\]
A strategy must specify what every possible type would do.

title: Bayesian Games
text:
Expected payoff
Suppose player \(i\) has type \(\theta_i\) and chooses action \(a_i\). The player is uncertain about others’ types.
The expected payoff is:
\[
\mathbb{E}_{\theta_{-i}}
[
u_i(a_i,a_{-i},\theta_i,\theta_{-i})
].
\]
With finitely many types, this can be written as:
\[
\sum_{\theta_{-i}}
u_i(a_i,a_{-i},\theta_i,\theta_{-i})
\Pr(\theta_{-i}\mid \theta_i).
\]
The player chooses an action that maximizes expected payoff.

title: Bayesian Games
text:
Bayesian Nash equilibrium
A Bayesian Nash equilibrium is a strategy profile where every type of every player chooses a best response given beliefs and the type-contingent strategies of others.





flowchart TD
    A[Each player has a type] --> B[Each type has beliefs]
    B --> C[Each type chooses best response]
    C --> D[Strategies are type-contingent]
    D --> E[Bayesian Nash equilibrium]






The important phrase is:

every type of every player.

A Bayesian equilibrium is not just one optimal action per player. It is optimal behaviour for each possible type.

title: Bayesian Games
text:
Example: high-cost and low-cost firm
Suppose a firm may be high-cost or low-cost.
A rival does not observe the firm’s cost type. The rival only has a prior belief:
\[
\Pr(L)=p.
\]
The low-cost firm may be more willing to set a low price. Observing a low price may make the rival think the firm is more likely to be low-cost.
This is the beginning of signaling logic.





flowchart LR
    A[Private cost type] --> B[Price choice]
    B --> C[Opponent updates belief]
    C --> D[Opponent chooses response]






Bayesian games therefore connect naturally to signaling games.

title: Bayesian Games
text:
Harsanyi transformation
The Harsanyi transformation converts incomplete information into imperfect information.
The steps are:

nature chooses types according to a commonly known prior;
each player observes their own type;
players choose strategies;
payoffs depend on actions and types.






flowchart TD
    A[Incomplete information problem] --> B[Nature draws types]
    B --> C[Players observe own types]
    C --> D[Players choose actions]
    D --> E[Payoffs realized]






This allows incomplete-information games to be analysed using standard game-theoretic tools.

title: Bayesian Games
text:
Common prior
A common prior means that players begin from the same probability distribution over types.
They may hold different beliefs after observing different private information, but those beliefs come from the same underlying prior.
The common prior assumption is powerful but restrictive. It rules out some forms of disagreement.

title: Bayesian Games
text:
Bayesian games and mixed strategies
Bayesian games and mixed strategies both use probability, but they are different.



Concept
Probability describes




Mixed strategy
randomization over actions


Bayesian type
uncertainty about payoff-relevant characteristics


Belief
subjective probability over states or types



A player may use a pure strategy in a Bayesian game. The uncertainty comes from not knowing the type.
A player may also mix within each type.

title: Bayesian Games
text:
Incomplete information versus imperfect information
These terms are related but not identical.







Term
Meaning




Incomplete information
uncertainty about payoffs, types, or characteristics


Imperfect information
uncertainty about previous moves or current node


Bayesian game
standard model of incomplete information



The Harsanyi transformation turns incomplete information into imperfect information about nature’s move.

title: Bayesian Games
Bayesian Games
text:
Common mistakes

1. Treating type as action
A type is private information. An action is chosen by the player.


2. Forgetting type-contingent strategies
A strategy must say what each type would do.


3. Ignoring beliefs
Bayesian games require beliefs over types.


4. Confusing mixed strategies with incomplete information
Randomizing over actions is not the same as being uncertain about types.


5. Forgetting the common prior
Many Bayesian games assume a commonly known prior distribution over types.


6. Solving only for one type
Bayesian Nash equilibrium requires optimality for every type.

title: Bayesian Games
text:
Checklist
When analysing a Bayesian game, ask:

Who are the players?
What are the possible types?
Who observes which type?
What is the prior belief over types?
What actions are available?
How do payoffs depend on types?
What is each type’s strategy?
What expected payoff does each type maximize?
What are the best responses?
Is the strategy profile a Bayesian Nash equilibrium?

How to use these notes
Game theory is easiest to learn when every page is read with four questions in mind:

Who are the players?
What can they do?
What do they know?
Why is the proposed behaviour stable?

Most mistakes in game-theoretic reasoning come from skipping one of these questions. A model may look formal, but if the players, strategies, information, or payoffs are unclear, the equilibrium result will also be unclear.





flowchart LR
    A[Players] --> E[Game]
    B[Strategies] --> E
    C[Information] --> E
    D[Payoffs] --> E
    E --> F[Solution Concept]
    F --> G[Equilibrium]
    G --> H[Interpretation]

title: Metrics
text:
Metrics are tools for making comparisons precise. They turn concepts into quantities, but they also introduce assumptions. A metric is useful only when we understand what it measures, what it leaves out, and how it can be misread.
This page collects basic measurement ideas used across the site.

title: Metrics
text:
Why metrics matter
Many arguments depend on measurement.
In game theory, we compare payoffs, beliefs, welfare, strategies, and equilibrium outcomes.
In criminology, we compare crime counts, rates, reporting, risk, harm, institutional outcomes, and policy effects.
In psychology, we compare behaviour, beliefs, symptoms, responses, and decision patterns.





flowchart LR
    A[Concept] --> B[Metric]
    B --> C[Comparison]
    C --> D[Interpretation]
    D --> E[Decision or argument]






The danger is that the metric may look precise while the underlying concept remains unclear.

title: Metrics
text:
Count and rate
A count records the number of events.
A rate normalizes the count by a relevant denominator.
For example:
\[
\text{Crime rate}
=
\frac{\text{Number of crimes}}{\text{Population}}
\times 100{,}000.
\]
Counts are useful for scale. Rates are useful for comparison.
If City A has more crimes than City B, it may simply have a larger population. A rate adjusts for this.

title: Metrics
Metrics
text:
Stock and flow
A stock is measured at a point in time.
A flow is measured over an interval.
Examples:








Concept
Stock
Flow




prison population
people in prison on a date
admissions or releases per year


unemployment
people unemployed now
people entering unemployment


cases
pending cases
new filings


beliefs
current probability belief
belief update after signal



Stock-flow confusion is common. A system can have a high stock because inflow is high, outflow is low, or duration is long.

title: Metrics
text:
Prevalence and incidence
Prevalence asks how widespread something is in a population.
Incidence asks how many new events occur over a period.
For example:
prevalence: share of people victimized this year
incidence: number of victimization events this year
If the same person is victimized multiple times, incidence may be high even when prevalence is lower.

title: Metrics
text:
Risk and probability
A risk is often represented as a probability.
For example:
\[
\Pr(\text{victimization})
\]
or
\[
\Pr(\text{detection} \mid \text{offending}).
\]
Conditional probabilities are especially important.
For example:
\[
\Pr(\text{recorded} \mid \text{reported})
\]
is different from
\[
\Pr(\text{reported} \mid \text{crime occurred}).
\]





flowchart TD
    A[Crime occurs] --> B{Reported?}
    B -->|Yes| C{Recorded?}
    B -->|No| D[Hidden]
    C -->|Yes| E[Recorded crime]
    C -->|No| F[Reported but unrecorded]






Each transition has its own probability.

title: Metrics
text:
Expected value
Expected value is a probability-weighted average.
If outcome \(x_k\) occurs with probability \(p_k\), then
\[
\mathbb{E}[X]
=
\sum_k p_k x_k.
\]
Expected value is central to decision theory, deterrence, and game theory.
For example, expected punishment can be written as:
\[
\mathbb{E}[\text{punishment}]
=
\Pr(\text{caught}) \times \text{sanction}.
\]
This simple expression is useful, but incomplete. It assumes the actor perceives the probability and sanction, and that they are responsive to expected future costs.

title: Metrics
text:
Accuracy, precision, and bias
A metric can fail in different ways.



Term
Meaning




Accuracy
closeness to the true value


Precision
consistency or narrowness of measurement


Bias
systematic error


Noise
random variation


Validity
whether the measure captures the intended concept


Reliability
whether measurement is consistent



A measure can be precise but biased. It can be reliable but invalid.
For example, recorded crime can be measured consistently but still fail to capture true crime if reporting is low.

title: Metrics
text:
Proxy measures
A proxy is a measurable variable used to approximate a harder-to-measure concept.
Examples:



Concept
Possible proxy




trust in police
survey response or reporting behaviour


offending
arrest, conviction, self-report, victimization data


social disorder
calls for service, complaints, observation


deterrence
perceived detection risk


harm
injury, loss, trauma, cost


ability
test score or qualification



A proxy should never be treated as identical to the concept.

title: Metrics
Metrics
Metrics
text:
Payoff comparison
Game theory often compares payoffs across actions.
Player \(i\) prefers action \(a\) over action \(b\) when
\[
u_i(a) > u_i(b).
\]
In strategic settings, payoffs depend on what others do:
\[
u_i(a_i,a_{-i}).
\]
Payoff comparisons become best-response comparisons:
\[
a_i^*
\in
\arg\max_{a_i}
u_i(a_i,a_{-i}).
\]
The metric here is not necessarily money. It is an ordering of outcomes.

title: Metrics
Metrics
text:
Rates over time
When comparing rates over time, ask:

Did the numerator change?
Did the denominator change?
Did measurement practice change?
Did reporting change?
Did the population at risk change?
Did the category definition change?






flowchart LR
    A[Observed rate change] --> B[Numerator change]
    A --> C[Denominator change]
    A --> D[Measurement change]
    A --> E[Reporting change]
    A --> F[Real behavioural change]






A trend is not automatically an explanation.

title: Metrics
text:
Common mistakes

1. Comparing counts when rates are needed
A larger place may have more events simply because it has more people or opportunities.


2. Using the wrong denominator
The denominator should match the population at risk.


3. Treating proxy as concept
A proxy is evidence about a concept, not the concept itself.


4. Ignoring measurement process
Metrics are produced through institutions, surveys, instruments, or coding rules.


5. Confusing prediction with explanation
A variable may predict an outcome without causing it.


6. Ignoring uncertainty
Point estimates should be interpreted with uncertainty, variation, and possible error in mind.

title: Metrics
text:
Checklist for using a metric

What concept is being measured?
What is the exact metric?
What is the numerator?
What is the denominator?
What is the unit of analysis?
Is it a count, rate, stock, flow, prevalence, or incidence?
Is the measure a direct measure or proxy?
What measurement process produced it?
What bias or missingness may exist?
What comparison is being made?
What interpretation is justified?
What interpretation would be too strong?

title: Criminology
text:
Criminology studies crime, victimization, and social control: why harmful/illegal acts occur, how they concentrate across people and places, and how institutions (police, courts, corrections) shape incentives, behavior, and legitimacy.
This section is theory-first. Empirical findings appear mainly as stylized facts and as motivation for mechanisms and models.

title: Criminology
section: How the subject is studied (academic map)
text:
How the subject is studied (academic map)
Criminology is typically organized around three kinds of questions:

Descriptive: What patterns exist? (who/where/when crime occurs; concentration; trends)

Explanatory / causal: Why do these patterns arise? (mechanisms; incentives; social interactions; opportunity)

Evaluative / policy: What interventions change outcomes? (deterrence, prevention, rehabilitation, legitimacy)

Across these questions, research commonly moves between: - Mechanisms (theory) → clear behavioral or social channels - Evidence (empirics) → measurement, identification, evaluation - Institutions (policy context) → how rules and enforcement operate in practice

title: Corrections (incarceration, supervision, reentry)
text:
Corrections includes incarceration, probation/parole, and reentry.
Academic analysis separates three channels:

incapacitation (reduces opportunity to offend),
deterrence (incentives via expected punishment),
rehabilitation / dynamic effects (future states: skills, stigma, networks).

title: Corrections (incarceration, supervision, reentry)
text:
Corrections includes incarceration, probation/parole, and reentry.
Academic analysis separates three channels:

incapacitation (reduces opportunity to offend),
deterrence (incentives via expected punishment),

title: Corrections (incarceration, supervision, reentry)
text:
Core research questions

What are short-run vs long-run effects of incarceration?
How do supervision intensity and conditions affect compliance?
How do reentry constraints (employment, housing, stigma) shape recidivism?

title: Corrections (incarceration, supervision, reentry)
text:
Institutional primitives (what to model)

A) Dynamic states
Let a person’s state include employability, stigma/record, network exposure, addiction constraints.
Punishment can shift these states (positively or negatively).


B) Supervision as monitoring
Probation/parole can be modeled as: - monitoring probability, - rule system (violations), - sanctions for violation.


C) Capacity constraints
Crowding, budgets, and staff ratios matter for rehabilitation quality and supervision.

text:

text:

Corrections is where static deterrence becomes dynamic: policies can reduce crime today yet worsen (or improve) future states.

title: Courts (charging, plea bargaining, sentencing)
text:
Courts convert suspected offending into formal outcomes: charges, pleas/trials, and sentences.
Academic analysis emphasizes information, bargaining, discretion, incentives, and selection.

title: Courts (charging, plea bargaining, sentencing)
text:
Courts convert suspected offending into formal outcomes: charges, pleas/trials, and sentences.
Academic analysis emphasizes information, bargaining, discretion, incentives, and selection.

title: Courts (charging, plea bargaining, sentencing)
text:
Core research questions

How do prosecutors and defendants bargain under asymmetric information?
How do plea offers trade off certainty vs severity (and trial costs)?
Where do disparities arise (discretion, bargaining power, information gaps)?

title: Courts (charging, plea bargaining, sentencing)
text:
Institutional primitives (what to model)

A) Actors and payoffs

Prosecutor: sentencing/conviction objectives, workload, trial cost.
Defendant: expected sentence, risk attitudes, legal costs, collateral consequences.



B) Information

Strength of evidence, conviction probability, defendant type (risk, priors).
Observability differs across parties → asymmetric information.



C) Process
Charging → plea offer(s) → accept/reject → trial → sentencing.

title: Courts (charging, plea bargaining, sentencing)
text:
Canonical theoretical lenses

Bargaining (Nash/Rubinstein variants)

Screening/signaling (plea offers as screening devices)

Mechanism design (rules shaping incentives and revelation)

Selection into trial (observed trials are endogenously chosen)

title: Courts (charging, plea bargaining, sentencing)
text:
Key conceptual distinctions

Case strength vs outcomes: plea rates reflect bargaining under uncertainty, not only guilt.
Selection into trial: trials are not random; they are selected.
Severity vs certainty: deterrence can operate through either margin.

title: Courts (charging, plea bargaining, sentencing)
text:
Later-on analysis
A clean theory-first approach embeds the court stage inside a broader system: bargaining affects expected punishment, which affects offending, reporting, and enforcement incentives.

title: Opportunity & routine activity
text:
NoteStylized facts this mechanism aims to match




Crime is concentrated in places (hotspots) and changes with routine patterns and guardianship.
Some interventions reduce crime by reducing opportunity rather than changing preferences.

title: Opportunity & routine activity
text:
NoteStylized facts this mechanism aims to match




Crime is concentrated in places (hotspots) and changes with routine patterns and guardianship.
Some interventions reduce crime by reducing opportunity rather than changing preferences.

title: Opportunity & routine activity
text:
Mechanism
The opportunity perspective treats crime as requiring: - a motivated offender, - a suitable target, - absence of capable guardianship.
Academic implication: you can reduce crime by changing the environment of opportunity (visibility, access, guardianship), even holding preferences fixed.

title: Opportunity & routine activity
text:
Canonical modeling primitives

offenders choose where/when to search (location choice)
guardianship shifts detection risk
targets differ in attractiveness
displacement is possible (crime moves rather than disappears)

title: Opportunity & routine activity
text:
Predictions (qualitative)

increasing guardianship in a place reduces expected returns and shifts activity elsewhere unless there are frictions
policies can change measured crime mechanically through visibility/reporting changes
hotspot concentration can arise from heterogeneity in target density and guardianship

title: Opportunity & routine activity
text:
Later-on analysis

combine with deterrence: opportunity changes the benefit side (\(b\)) and/or detection probability (\(q\))
add spatial equilibrium: offenders allocate across locations until expected payoffs equalize (with frictions)

title: Mechanisms
text:
Mechanism pages explain how crime, compliance, reporting, punishment, and desistance are produced. Instead of treating theories as labels, this section treats them as channels: each mechanism describes a process linking context to behaviour.
A useful mechanism should answer:

title: Mechanisms
text:
Mechanism-first criminology
A theory becomes analytically useful when it identifies a mechanism.





flowchart LR
    A[Context or condition] --> B[Mechanism]
    B --> C[Behavioural response]
    C --> D[Observed pattern]
    D --> E[Evidence or policy implication]






For example, deterrence is not just the claim that punishment reduces crime. The mechanism is that perceived sanction risk changes expected costs. If people do not perceive the risk, or if they are not responsive to future consequences, the mechanism may be weak.

title: Mechanisms
text:
Map of core mechanisms





flowchart TD
    A[Crime and Compliance Mechanisms] --> B[Incentives and Deterrence]
    A --> C[Opportunity and Routine Activity]
    A --> D[Self-Control and Present Bias]
    A --> E[Social Interactions and Networks]
    A --> F[Legitimacy and Compliance]
    A --> G[Labeling and Stigma]
    A --> H[Life-Course Dynamics]
    A --> I[Inequality and Trust]

    B --> B1[Expected costs]
    B --> B2[Sanction risk]
    B --> B3[Perceived deterrence]

    C --> C1[Suitable targets]
    C --> C2[Guardianship]
    C --> C3[Opportunity structure]

    D --> D1[Impulsivity]
    D --> D2[Short-run rewards]
    D --> D3[Weak future weighting]

    E --> E1[Peer effects]
    E --> E2[Learning]
    E --> E3[Diffusion]

    F --> F1[Fairness]
    F --> F2[Trust]

These mechanisms can combine. A single crime pattern may involve opportunity, peer influence, weak guardianship, low trust, and institutional response at the same time.

title: Mechanisms
text:
A simple mechanism template
Each mechanism page should ideally answer the same basic questions.





flowchart TD
    A[Starting condition] --> B[Actor or group affected]
    B --> C[Perception or constraint changes]
    C --> D[Incentive or identity changes]
    D --> E[Behaviour changes]
    E --> F[Aggregate pattern]
    F --> G[Measurement issue]
    G --> H[Policy implication]






This template helps avoid vague explanations. It forces the page to specify the pathway from cause to outcome.

title: Mechanisms
text:
Mechanisms and evidence
A mechanism should generate observable implications.
For example:







Mechanism
Expected observable pattern




Deterrence
Offending falls when perceived detection risk rises


Routine activity
Crime clusters where targets and weak guardianship coincide


Peer effects
Behaviour spreads through social ties or group settings


Legitimacy
Cooperation increases when authorities are seen as fair


Labeling
Formal contact may increase future exclusion or offending risk


Life-course
Turning points alter offending trajectories


Self-control
Immediate rewards weigh more heavily than delayed costs



Evidence does not need to be purely quantitative. Mechanisms can be studied through interviews, ethnography, administrative data, experiments, quasi-experiments, case studies, and formal modelling.

title: Mechanisms
text:
Mechanisms and models
Mechanisms can often be translated into simple models.





flowchart LR
    A[Mechanism] --> B[Actors]
    B --> C[Choices]
    C --> D[Information]
    D --> E[Payoffs or constraints]
    E --> F[Prediction]
    F --> G[Evidence]






For example:

deterrence can become an inspection game;
reporting can become a trust and cooperation game;
co-offending can become a coordination game;
social diffusion can become a network model;
plea bargaining can become an asymmetric-information model.

This is why the mechanism section connects directly to the models section.

title: Mechanisms
text:
Mechanisms and policy
Policy works through mechanisms. A policy intervention does not simply “reduce crime” in the abstract. It changes incentives, opportunities, beliefs, constraints, or institutional behaviour.
Examples:







Policy type
Mechanism it may target




More patrols
Detection risk and guardianship


CCTV
Visibility, deterrence, evidence generation


Youth programmes
Peer networks, opportunity, self-control


Procedural justice training
Legitimacy and trust


Rehabilitation
skills, constraints, identity, and future orientation


Record expungement
stigma and opportunity after system contact


Hotspot policing
spatial concentration and resource allocation



A good policy analysis should ask which mechanism the policy is supposed to activate.

title: Mechanisms
text:
Common mistakes

1. Naming a theory instead of explaining it
Saying “this is deterrence” is not enough. Explain how perceived cost changes behaviour.


2. Assuming one mechanism explains everything
Most crime patterns are multi-mechanism. Violence, for example, may involve peers, alcohol, retaliation, opportunity, and low guardianship.


3. Ignoring measurement
If the outcome is recorded crime, the mechanism may affect reporting or detection rather than actual offending.


4. Treating policy as direct cause
Policy effects depend on institutional implementation and behavioural response.


5. Ignoring time
Some mechanisms are immediate, while others unfold across years.


6. Confusing individual and aggregate mechanisms
Individual-level explanations do not automatically explain area-level crime rates.

NoteStylized facts this mechanism aims to match




System contact (arrest, conviction, incarceration) can change future outcomes beyond the immediate punishment.

title: Labeling, stigma & system contact
text:
NoteStylized facts this mechanism aims to match




System contact (arrest, conviction, incarceration) can change future outcomes beyond the immediate punishment.
Stigma can alter employment, schooling, social ties, and incentives.

title: Labeling, stigma & system contact
text:
Mechanism (core idea)
Labeling theories emphasize that formal control can produce secondary effects: - stigma changes opportunities (labor-market access, housing), - social identity and peer grouping can shift, - repeated contact can become self-reinforcing.
In a theory-first framework, stigma is modeled as a state that affects payoffs and constraints going forward.

title: Labeling, stigma & system contact
text:
Canonical modeling primitives

stigma state \(z\in\{0,1\}\) (or continuous) that increases after system contact
stigma reduces legal option \(w(z)\) and/or increases network exposure to crime
feedback loop: stigma → lower \(w\) → higher crime incentives → more contact → more stigma

title: Labeling, stigma & system contact
text:
Predictions (qualitative)

Policies increasing detection/arrest can reduce crime short-run but may increase long-run crime if stigma harms future legal options.
Diversion programs and record-sealing can improve long-run outcomes by weakening the stigma transition.
The effect depends on who is marginally affected: high-risk vs low-risk populations.

title: Labeling, stigma & system contact
text:
What would count as evidence? (conceptual)
Empirical work often tries to separate: - selection into system contact vs causal impact of contact on later employment/offending, - short-run deterrence/incapacitation vs long-run stigma effects.

title: Labeling, stigma & system contact
text:
Later-on analysis (model links)

Fits naturally inside life-course dynamics and dynamic choice.
Links to courts/corrections: sentencing policies determine stigma transitions.
Provides a theory channel for observed persistence beyond stable “types.”

NoteStylized facts this mechanism aims to match




Reporting and cooperation vary with trust in institutions.
Enforcement can backfire if it reduces perceived legitimacy (lower cooperation).

title: Legitimacy, trust & compliance
text:
NoteStylized facts this mechanism aims to match




Reporting and cooperation vary with trust in institutions.

title: Legitimacy, trust & compliance
text:
Mechanism
Legitimacy affects: - willingness to report victimization, - willingness to cooperate as witness, - voluntary compliance with rules.
This can be modeled as: - a participation constraint (report/cooperate only if expected benefit exceeds cost), - a utility component (disutility from cooperating with an illegitimate authority), - or a belief channel (expectations of fair treatment).

title: Legitimacy, trust & compliance
text:
Canonical modeling primitives

reporting stage: victim decides to report; police decide effort; offender anticipates
informational asymmetry: police need community cooperation to identify offenders
dynamic trust: policies today affect future cooperation

title: Legitimacy, trust & compliance
text:
Predictions (qualitative)

higher legitimacy increases reporting and clearance rates (even holding incidence fixed)
aggressive policies can reduce cooperation, lowering detection and potentially increasing incidence in the long run
measured crime can rise when trust improves (more reporting), even if incidence falls

title: Legitimacy, trust & compliance
text:
Later-on analysis

links naturally to signaling and dynamic games (reputation of institutions)
connects to “recorded vs incidence” measurement: reporting is endogenous

title: Inspection games (deterrence & monitoring)
text:
Inspection games model strategic interaction between: - an agent who may violate (offend), and - an enforcer who can monitor/inspect at a cost.
They formalize deterrence under scarce enforcement resources.

title: Inspection games (deterrence & monitoring)
text:
Inspection games model strategic interaction between: - an agent who may violate (offend), and - an enforcer who can monitor/inspect at a cost.
They formalize deterrence under scarce enforcement resources.

title: Inspection games (deterrence & monitoring)
text:
Canonical setup
Offender chooses \(C\) (crime) or \(N\) (no crime).
Enforcer chooses \(I\) (inspect) or \(\bar I\) (not inspect).
Parameters: - illegal gain if successful: \(b>0\) - sanction if caught: \(s>0\) - harm to enforcer if crime succeeds: \(h>0\) - inspection cost: \(k>0\)
Payoffs: - If \(N\): offender \(0\); enforcer pays \(-k\) if inspecting, \(0\) otherwise. - If \(C\) and \(I\): offender caught \(\to -s\); enforcer pays \(-k\). - If \(C\) and \(\bar I\): offender succeeds \(\to b\); enforcer suffers \(-h\).

title: Inspection games (deterrence & monitoring)
text:
Solved equilibrium (mixed strategies)
Let enforcer inspect with probability \(q\) and offender commit crime with probability \(p\).

Step 1: offender indifference
\[
\mathbb{E}[u_O(C)] = q(-s) + (1-q)b = b - q(b+s).
\] Indifference with \(N\) (payoff 0) gives: \[
q^*=\frac{b}{b+s}.
\]


Step 2: enforcer indifference
Enforcer payoff from inspecting: \[
\mathbb{E}[u_E(I)] = -k
\] Enforcer payoff from not inspecting: \[
\mathbb{E}[u_E(\bar I)] = -ph.
\] Indifference yields: \[
p^*=\frac{k}{h}.
\]
Interior mixing requires \(0<k<h\).

title: Inspection games (deterrence & monitoring)
text:
Predictions (comparative statics)

\(q^*\) decreases in \(s\) and increases in \(b\).
\(p^*\) increases in \(k\) and decreases in \(h\).

title: Allocation dynamics (hotspots and resource allocation)
text: Allocation models study how an enforcer distributes scarce resources across space and time, under uncertainty and strategic response.

title: Allocation dynamics (hotspots and resource allocation)
text: Allocation models study how an enforcer distributes scarce resources across space and time, under uncertainty and strategic response.

title: Allocation dynamics (hotspots and resource allocation)
text:
Canonical two-location baseline
Allocate effort \(e_A,e_B\ge 0\) with: \[
e_A + e_B \le E.
\] Crime intensity in location \(\ell\) decreases in effort: \(\lambda_\ell(e_\ell)\downarrow\), but offenders may substitute across locations.

title: Allocation dynamics (hotspots and resource allocation)
text:
Why dynamics matters
In practice: - the enforcer learns where problems are (updating beliefs), - offenders adapt to allocation patterns, - recorded crime reflects both incidence and reporting.
Dynamic primitives: - belief state about each location, - learning/updating, - offender adaptation, - objective function (harm vs recorded metrics).

title: Allocation dynamics (hotspots and resource allocation)
text:
Predictions (qualitative)

allocate to high marginal return hotspots, but displacement can occur when substitution is easy
exploration–exploitation arises when learning is valuable
metrics can distort allocation if they reward recorded outcomes

title: Reporting & trust (legitimacy and cooperation)
text:
Many outcomes depend on whether victims/witnesses: - report incidents, - cooperate with investigation.
Legitimacy and trust affect reporting, which affects detection and deterrence.

title: Reporting & trust (legitimacy and cooperation)
text:
Many outcomes depend on whether victims/witnesses: - report incidents, - cooperate with investigation.
Legitimacy and trust affect reporting, which affects detection and deterrence.

title: Reporting & trust (legitimacy and cooperation)
text:
Canonical three-stage setup

Offender chooses \(C\) or \(N\).
If \(C\), victim chooses report \(R\) or not \(\bar R\).
If report, police choose effort \(e\in\{0,1\}\) and detection probability is: \[
q = q_0 + \alpha e,\quad q\le 1,
\] with \(q_0\in(0,1)\) and \(\alpha>0\).

Reporting cost: \(c_R>0\).
Victim benefit from detection: \(B(L)=B_0+\lambda L\) with \(\lambda>0\).
Victim reports iff: \[
(q_0+\alpha e)B(L) \ge c_R.
\]
Threshold: \[
L \ge \frac{c_R}{\lambda(q_0+\alpha e)} - \frac{B_0}{\lambda}.
\]

title: Reporting & trust (legitimacy and cooperation)
text:
Interpretation

Higher legitimacy increases reporting.
Reporting can increase recorded crime even if incidence is unchanged.
Deterrence can strengthen via higher anticipated detection.

title: Co-offending games (coordination and betrayal)
text: Co-offending can be modeled as a coordination/trust problem: - group action increases returns or reduces risk, - but creates betrayal and coordination failure risks.

title: Co-offending games (coordination and betrayal)
text: Co-offending can be modeled as a coordination/trust problem: - group action increases returns or reduces risk, - but creates betrayal and coordination failure risks.

title: Co-offending games (coordination and betrayal)
text:
Canonical stag-hunt setup
Two agents choose Join (\(J\)) or Stay out (\(O\)).

If both join: \((J,J)\) yields \(G>0\) each.
If one joins alone: joiner gets \(-d<0\), other gets \(0\).
If both stay out: \((0,0)\).

title: Co-offending games (coordination and betrayal)
text:
Equilibria
Two pure Nash equilibria: - \((J,J)\) (high-participation) - \((O,O)\) (low-participation)
Interpretation: co-offending can be self-reinforcing; small shifts in risk/coordination can change equilibrium selection.

title: Units of analysis
text:
Criminology claims look different depending on whether you study: - persons, places, networks, institutions, or time.
A good academic note states its unit explicitly.

title: Units of analysis
text:
Criminology claims look different depending on whether you study: - persons, places, networks, institutions, or time.
A good academic note states its unit explicitly.

title: Units of analysis
text:
Person-level (micro)
Typical questions: - Why do some individuals offend repeatedly? - What predicts onset/desistance?
Model primitives: - types, constraints, dynamic states (employment, stigma), discounting/self-control.
Pitfall: - selection into arrest/conviction is not identical to selection into offending.

title: Units of analysis
text:
Place-level (spatial)
Typical questions: - Why do hotspots exist? - Do interventions displace crime?
Model primitives: - opportunity/guardianship, spatial choice, congestion, displacement.
Pitfall: - shifting crime across blocks can look like “success” locally but not globally.

title: Units of analysis
text:
Network-level (social)
Typical questions: - Why co-offending clusters? - How do tactics diffuse?
Model primitives: - strategic complements, learning, partner choice, trust/betrayal, diffusion.
Pitfall: - peer effects vs sorting (who befriends whom) are easy to confuse empirically.

title: Units of analysis
text:
Institutional level (police/courts/corrections)
Typical questions: - How do agencies allocate scarce resources? - How do discretion and incentives shape outcomes?
Model primitives: - objectives, constraints, information, capacity, performance measures.
Pitfall: - “crime falls after more policing” can reflect recording/classification changes too.

title: Units of analysis
text:
Time / dynamics
Typical questions: - When does policy have short-run vs long-run effects? - How do offenders adapt?
Model primitives: - dynamic games, Markov states, learning, reputation, equilibrium adjustment.
Pitfall: - ignoring adaptation can overstate policy impact.

title: Units of analysis
text:
Practical rule
If your theory prediction is about behavior, say so.
If your prediction is about recorded outcomes, say which stage (reporting, recording, clearance, conviction) is affected.

title: Key definitions
text: This page fixes terminology so later theory is precise. Many disputes in criminology are partly about what is being measured.

title: Key definitions
text: This page fixes terminology so later theory is precise. Many disputes in criminology are partly about what is being measured.

title: Key definitions
text:
Crime, harm, and illegality

Crime: an act defined as illegal by law (jurisdiction-specific and time-varying).
Harm: a broader concept including non-criminal harms (e.g., some corporate/environmental harms).
Academic work often distinguishes: legal definitions (crime) vs normative/social definitions (harm).

Implication for theory: specify whether your model targets illegal behavior or harmful behavior more broadly.

title: Key definitions
text:
Incidence vs recorded crime

Incidence: underlying events that occur (often unobserved).
Recorded crime: events that appear in administrative data.

A stylized decomposition is:

Incidence occurs

Victim/witness chooses to report (or not)

Agency chooses to record/classify and may clear a case

Courts/corrections outcomes follow

Implication: changes in policing or trust can change recorded crime even if incidence changes less (or differently).

title: Key definitions
text:
Offending, victimization, and events

Offending: the behavior of potential offenders.
Victimization: the experience of victims (often measured via victimization surveys).
Event: a single incident; may involve multiple offenders/victims.

Implication: your unit of analysis matters (person vs event vs place).

title: Key definitions
text:
Deterrence, incapacitation, rehabilitation
Three distinct channels by which punishment/policy can reduce harm: - Deterrence: changes incentives (expected costs/benefits). - Incapacitation: reduces ability to offend (e.g., incarceration). - Rehabilitation: changes future preferences/skills/constraints (dynamic effects).
Implication: don’t conflate them—models usually represent one channel at a time.

title: Key definitions
text:
Compliance and legitimacy

Compliance: following rules/law.
Legitimacy: perceived rightfulness of authorities; affects cooperation, reporting, and voluntary compliance.

Implication: legitimacy can be modeled as shifting participation constraints (reporting/cooperation) or utility from compliance.

title: Key definitions
text:
A minimal “data caution” note
Administrative outcomes (arrests, convictions) combine: - behavior, - reporting decisions, - enforcement allocation, - legal processing rules.
When you interpret facts, always ask: “Is this about incidence, recording, or processing?”

title: White-Collar Crime
text:
White-collar crime refers to illegal or harmful conduct carried out through professional, corporate, financial, bureaucratic, or organizational roles. Examples include fraud, insider trading, corruption, false accounting, regulatory violations, wage theft, bribery, tax evasion, and unsafe corporate practices.
The key feature is not simply that the offender is wealthy. The key feature is that the offence is enabled by legitimate roles, organizations, expertise, trust, and access.

title: White-Collar Crime
text:
Basic mechanism map





flowchart TD
    A[White-Collar Crime] --> B[Organizational access]
    A --> C[Information advantage]
    A --> D[Weak monitoring]
    A --> E[Incentive pressure]
    A --> F[Neutralization]

    B --> B1[Role-based authority]
    B --> B2[Control over records]

    C --> C1[Complex products]
    C --> C2[Asymmetric information]

    D --> D1[Audit limits]
    D --> D2[Regulatory gaps]

    E --> E1[Profit targets]
    E --> E2[Career rewards]

    F --> F1[Everyone does it]
    F --> F2[No direct victim]
    F --> F3[Only bending rules]






White-collar crime often depends on the gap between formal rules and actual organizational incentives.

title: White-Collar Crime
text:
Core mechanisms

Agency problems
An agent may act against the interests of a principal. Managers, employees, advisers, or contractors may exploit their role for private benefit.


Information asymmetry
White-collar crime often involves one side knowing more than another. This can make fraud, concealment, manipulation, or misreporting easier.


Weak monitoring
Complex organizations are difficult to monitor. Auditors, regulators, customers, and shareholders may not observe misconduct until much later.


Incentive pressure
Targets, bonuses, competition, and organizational culture can reward risky or illegal conduct.


Neutralization
Offenders may justify misconduct by denying harm, blaming the system, or reframing violations as normal business practice.

title: White-Collar Crime
text:
Measurement issues
White-collar crime is difficult to measure.







Issue
Why it matters




Low visibility
victims may not know they were harmed


Complex evidence
misconduct may require expert investigation


Regulatory dependence
detection depends on audit and enforcement


Organizational concealment
records may be manipulated


Ambiguous harm
harm may be delayed, diffuse, or collective


Civil/criminal boundary
cases may be handled administratively rather than criminally



Recorded white-collar crime is often closer to detected white-collar crime than true white-collar crime.

title: White-Collar Crime
text:
Principal-agent model
A simple model treats misconduct as an agency problem.





flowchart LR
    A[Principal delegates task] --> B[Agent controls information or action]
    B --> C{Monitor effectively?}
    C -->|Yes| D[Compliance more likely]
    C -->|No| E[Opportunity for misconduct]
    E --> F[Private gain]
    F --> G[Possible detection and sanction]






The central problem is that the agent has both opportunity and private information.

title: White-Collar Crime
text:
Audit logic
A regulator or firm may audit only some cases because monitoring is costly.





flowchart LR
    A[Possible violation] --> B{Audit?}
    B -->|No| C[Violation may remain hidden]
    B -->|Yes| D{Detected?}
    D -->|No| E[No sanction]
    D -->|Yes| F[Penalty or correction]






This connects white-collar crime to inspection games.

title: White-Collar Crime
text:
Policy trade-offs








Policy
Mechanism
Possible limitation




More audits
raises detection risk
costly and selective


Whistleblower protection
increases internal reporting
retaliation and credibility issues


Compliance systems
improves monitoring
may become symbolic


Stronger penalties
increases expected cost
only if detection is plausible


Transparency rules
reduces information asymmetry
may overload users with information


Individual liability
targets decision-makers
difficult to prove intent

title: White-Collar Crime
text:
Compliance theatre
A special problem in white-collar crime is compliance theatre: organizations create formal compliance structures that look good externally but do not change internal incentives.





flowchart TD
    A[Formal compliance rule] --> B[Box-ticking]
    B --> C[Appearance of control]
    C --> D[Weak behavioural change]
    D --> E[Misconduct risk remains]






This is why policy must examine implementation, not only formal rules.

title: White-Collar Crime
text:
Common mistakes

1. Treating white-collar crime as victimless
Harm can be diffuse, delayed, financial, physical, environmental, or institutional.


2. Focusing only on individual greed
Organizational incentives and culture may matter as much as individual motive.


3. Treating compliance programmes as proof of compliance
Formal systems may exist without meaningful enforcement.


4. Ignoring detection bias
Observed cases are shaped by audit, regulation, whistleblowing, and investigation.


5. Ignoring civil and administrative enforcement
Many white-collar harms are handled outside criminal prosecution.

title: White-Collar Crime
text:
Checklist for analysing white-collar crime

What role or organization enabled the misconduct?
Who had information advantage?
Who was supposed to monitor?
What incentive pressure existed?
Who was harmed, and how?
Was the harm direct, diffuse, delayed, or hidden?
How was the misconduct detected?
Was enforcement criminal, civil, administrative, or internal?
Did compliance systems actually affect behaviour?
What reform targets the mechanism?

title: Topics
text:
Topic pages apply criminological mechanisms, institutional analysis, and models to substantive crime areas. They are not meant to be isolated summaries. Each topic should connect crime type, mechanism, measurement, evidence, and policy.
The goal is to ask: what kind of behaviour is being studied, why does it occur, how is it measured, and what does intervention change?

text:
Comparing topic areas








Topic
Central mechanisms

Violent crime
conflict, retaliation, emotion, peer norms, weapons

title: Topics
text:
From topic to mechanism
A substantive topic is not yet an explanation. To explain a crime pattern, we need a mechanism.
For example:
property crime
→ opportunity and weak guardianship
→ target selection
→ spatial concentration
or:
violent crime
→ conflict plus peer audience
→ status threat
→ retaliation
or:
white-collar crime
→ agency problem plus weak monitoring
→ rule violation
→ delayed detection
The move from topic to mechanism is the move from description to explanation.

title: Topics
text:
From topic to model
Topic pages also connect to models.



Topic
Possible model




Violent crime
repeated conflict or retaliation game


Property crime
target-selection or inspection game


Organized crime
repeated enforcement and reputation model


White-collar crime
principal-agent or audit game


Cybercrime
attacker-defender game


Drug markets
illicit market equilibrium or network model



The model should be chosen because it clarifies a mechanism.

title: Topics
text:
Policy comparison
Different topics create different policy problems.





flowchart LR
    A[Crime topic] --> B[Mechanism]
    B --> C[Institutional response]
    C --> D[Behavioural adaptation]
    D --> E[Policy outcome]
    E --> F[Unintended effects]






For example, enforcement against drug markets may reduce visible dealing in one place while shifting activity elsewhere. Cybercrime enforcement may remove one platform while offenders migrate to another. White-collar regulation may reduce some misconduct while creating compliance theatre.

title: Topics
text:
Common mistakes

1. Treating a topic as a mechanism
“Cybercrime” is not a mechanism. It is a domain. The mechanism may be anonymity, automation, deception, or weak enforcement.


2. Treating official data as complete
Many topic areas are heavily underreported or dependent on detection.


3. Assuming one policy fits all crime types
Violent crime, cybercrime, fraud, and drug markets respond to different mechanisms.


4. Ignoring adaptation
Offenders, institutions, and markets adapt to interventions.


5. Ignoring harm variation
The same legal category may contain events with very different harms.

text:
Suggested reading order
