title: Drug Markets
text:
Drug markets involve the production, distribution, sale, purchase, and consumption of prohibited or regulated substances. They combine demand, dependence, illicit exchange, enforcement risk, violence, public health, stigma, and institutional response.
Drug markets are useful for studying how policy changes market structure rather than simply turning behaviour on or off.

title: Drug Markets
text:
Basic mechanism map





flowchart TD
    A[Drug Markets] --> B[Demand]
    A --> C[Supply and distribution]
    A --> D[Enforcement risk]
    A --> E[Violence and governance]
    A --> F[Health and harm]

    B --> B1[Dependence]
    B --> B2[Recreation]
    B --> B3[Social context]

    C --> C1[Dealers]
    C --> C2[Networks]
    C --> C3[Territory]

    D --> D1[Detection]
    D --> D2[Sanction]
    D --> D3[Risk premium]

    E --> E1[Dispute resolution]
    E --> E2[Retaliation]
    E --> E3[Market control]

    F --> F1[Overdose]
    F --> F2[Contamination]
    F --> F3[Treatment access]






The key feature of illicit drug markets is that demand and supply persist under legal risk, but the form of the market changes.

title: Drug Markets
text:
Core mechanisms

Demand persistence
Demand may persist because of dependence, recreation, pain, social environment, or economic opportunity. Enforcement alone may not remove demand.


Risk premium
Illegality raises costs and risks. Sellers may require higher returns to compensate for punishment risk, seizure, violence, and uncertainty.


Non-contractibility
Illegal market participants cannot rely on courts. This increases the importance of reputation, violence, trust, and repeated exchange.


Enforcement displacement
Enforcement may move markets across places, platforms, methods, or substances.


Public health harm
Drug policy affects not only crime, but also overdose, contamination, treatment access, stigma, and willingness to seek help.

title: Drug Markets
text:
Measurement issues
Drug markets are partly hidden and enforcement-dependent.







Issue
Why it matters




Arrest data
reflects enforcement intensity as well as behaviour


Seizure data
reflects detection and policing strategy


Self-report data
may understate stigmatized behaviour


Health data
captures harm but not full market activity


Price and purity
may indicate market pressure but are hard to measure


Open-air visibility
visible markets are easier to police and count



A rise in drug arrests may mean more drug activity, more enforcement, or changed policing priorities.

title: Drug Markets
text:
Illicit market logic
A simple market view begins with supply and demand, but illegality adds enforcement risk.





flowchart LR
    A[Demand] --> C[Illicit exchange]
    B[Supply] --> C
    D[Enforcement risk] --> E[Risk premium]
    E --> C
    C --> F[Price, purity, availability]
    F --> G[Consumption and harm]






Enforcement can raise costs, but the effect depends on market adaptation and demand elasticity.

title: Drug Markets
text:
Violence in drug markets
Violence may arise because illegal market participants cannot use legal institutions to resolve disputes.





flowchart TD
    A[Illicit transaction] --> B{Dispute or betrayal?}
    B -->|No| C[Exchange continues]
    B -->|Yes| D{Legal enforcement available?}
    D -->|No| E[Self-help enforcement]
    E --> F[Threats or violence]
    D -->|Yes| G[Formal dispute resolution]






Violence is therefore connected to governance, trust, and market structure.

title: Drug Markets
text:
Enforcement and adaptation
Drug markets often adapt to enforcement.





flowchart LR
    A[Enforcement pressure] --> B[Higher risk]
    B --> C[Market adaptation]
    C --> D[New location]
    C --> E[New method]
    C --> F[New substance]
    C --> G[More hidden transactions]






This means policy analysis should look beyond immediate arrests.

title: Drug Markets
Drug Markets
text:
Policy trade-offs








Policy
Intended mechanism
Possible risk




Supply enforcement
raises cost and risk
displacement, violence, hidden markets


Demand reduction
lowers consumption
slow and support-dependent


Treatment
reduces dependence-related demand
access and retention challenges


Harm reduction
reduces death and injury
political resistance


Decriminalization
reduces justice-system harm
depends on health infrastructure


Market regulation
reduces illicit control
design and compliance challenges

title: Drug Markets
text:
Common mistakes

1. Treating drug markets as simple supply problems
Demand, dependence, substitution, and social context matter.


2. Using arrests as direct evidence of market size
Arrests are strongly shaped by enforcement.


3. Ignoring public health outcomes
Policy may reduce visible dealing but increase overdose or contamination risk.


4. Ignoring displacement
Markets can move across space, method, or substance.


5. Treating all substances as the same
Different drugs have different markets, harms, users, and enforcement dynamics.

title: Drug Markets
text:
Checklist for analysing drug markets

Which substance or market is being studied?
What drives demand?
How is supply organized?
How does enforcement affect risk and price?
What role does violence play?
What data source is being used?
Does the measure reflect behaviour or enforcement?
Is displacement likely?
What public health outcomes matter?
What policy trade-off is involved?

title: How criminology is studied
text:
Criminology is not only “crime statistics.” As an academic field, it combines: - Concepts and measurement (what is counted as crime; why measurement is difficult) - Theories of mechanism (why behavior occurs; how social structure matters) - Institutional analysis (police/courts/corrections; legitimacy and compliance) - Evaluation and identification (what changes outcomes; how we infer causality)
This page provides a discipline map so readers can locate a topic within the broader research program.

title: How criminology is studied
text:
Criminology is not only “crime statistics.” As an academic field, it combines: - Concepts and measurement (what is counted as crime; why measurement is difficult) - Theories of mechanism (why behavior occurs; how social structure matters) - Institutional analysis (police/courts/corrections; legitimacy and compliance) - Evaluation and identification (what changes outcomes; how we infer causality)
This page provides a discipline map so readers can locate a topic within the broader research program.

title: How criminology is studied
text:
Core question types

1) Descriptive (pattern-finding)
Typical objects: - concentration by person (repeat offending/victimization), - concentration by place (hotspots), - temporal patterns (seasonality, routine changes), - network clustering (co-offending, gangs).
The descriptive layer also flags the measurement problem: recorded crime depends on reporting and enforcement.


2) Explanatory / causal (mechanism)
Mechanism-based questions: - How do incentives and detection risk affect offending? - When does opportunity/guardianship reduce crime without displacement? - How do peer effects and networks amplify or dampen crime? - How does legitimacy affect reporting and compliance?


3) Evaluative / policy (interventions)
Interventions include: - policing strategies (hotspots, visibility, patrol allocation), - sanctions and sentencing policies, - prevention programs, - rehabilitation and reentry policies, - institutional reforms targeting trust and cooperation.

title: How criminology is studied
section: Levels of analysis (what unit the theory “lives on”)
text:
Levels of analysis (what unit the theory “lives on”)
Criminological explanations often differ by unit:

Individual: preferences, beliefs, constraints, self-control, human capital

Interaction / network: strategic complements, trust, co-offending, diffusion

Place: opportunities, guardianship, environmental design, spatial displacement

Institution: rules, legitimacy, capacity, incentives within organizations

A good academic write-up states its unit explicitly and clarifies what is taken as primitive.

title: How criminology is studied
text:
Evidence types (what “counts” in the literature)
Even if you focus on theory, it helps to know what kinds of evidence usually support claims:

Administrative data: police incidents, arrests, court records, corrections

Surveys / self-reports: victimization surveys, self-reported offending

Field experiments / RCTs: randomized patrol or program assignment

Quasi-experiments: policy changes, discontinuities, natural experiments

Qualitative: interviews, ethnography, case studies (mechanism discovery)

title: How criminology is studied
section: Common threats to inference (why crime data is hard)
text:
Common threats to inference (why crime data is hard)
These issues appear repeatedly in criminology papers:

Underreporting (many crimes never enter official data)

Enforcement selection (arrests reflect policing choices)

Simultaneity (police respond to crime; crime responds to police)

Displacement (crime moves across space/time/type)

Equilibrium adaptation (offenders change tactics when policy changes)

For theory, these threats matter because they influence what is “observable” and how one interprets patterns.

title: How criminology is studied
text:
Theory families (mechanism organizers)
A practical academic taxonomy:

Incentives / deterrence

Opportunity / routine activity

Social interactions and networks

Legitimacy, trust, and compliance

Inequality, deprivation, and social capital

Life-course dynamics and stigma

Behavioral microfoundations (present bias, impulsivity; optional)

These map cleanly into models: inspection games, bargaining, dynamic choice, network games.

title: How criminology is studied
section: How to read a criminology paper (fast checklist)
text:
How to read a criminology paper (fast checklist)
When skimming: 1) What is the unit of analysis? (person/place/network/institution)
2) What outcome is used? (incidence vs recorded vs victimization)
3) What mechanism is proposed?
4) What is the identification strategy (if empirical)?
5) What equilibrium or adaptation effects could offset the policy?
6) What predictions are robust across plausible measurement choices?

title: How criminology is studied
text:
Where these notes fit
This site leans toward: - explicit mechanisms, - model-based clarity (players, information, incentives), - and “what would the model predict if parameter X increases?”
Empirical content is used selectively as stylized facts and as constraints on theory.

title: Glossary
text: This glossary defines recurring terms used across the criminology notes. The definitions are intentionally compact. They are meant to support reading, not replace full theory pages.

title: Glossary
text:
Core concepts

Crime
Behaviour prohibited by criminal law and subject to formal sanction.


Deviance
Behaviour that violates social norms. Deviance is not always criminal, and crime is not always treated as equally deviant.


Harm
Damage or injury to persons, groups, communities, institutions, or social relations. Some harmful acts are not criminalized.


Criminalization
The process through which behaviour becomes defined and treated as criminal.


Social control
Formal or informal processes that regulate behaviour. Formal social control includes police, courts, and law. Informal social control includes family, peers, communities, and norms.


Victimization
The experience of being harmed by crime or deviant behaviour.


Offending
Engaging in behaviour defined as criminal or rule-breaking.


Desistance
The process through which a person stops offending over time.

title: Glossary
text:
Measurement terms

True crime
The actual amount of crime that occurs, whether or not it is reported or recorded.


Recorded crime
Crime that appears in official records.


Hidden crime
Crime that occurs but does not appear in official statistics.


Reporting
The process by which a victim, witness, or institution communicates an event to authorities.


Detection
The process by which authorities discover an offence.


Recording
The institutional classification and entry of an event into official data.


Prevalence
The proportion of a population experiencing or engaging in an event during a period.


Incidence
The number of events occurring during a period.


Rate
A count normalized by population, exposure, time, or opportunity.


Clearance
A case outcome indicating that an offence has been resolved or attributed according to official criteria. Clearance does not always mean conviction.

title: Glossary
text:
Mechanism terms

Deterrence
The idea that expected punishment can reduce offending by increasing expected costs.


Certainty
The perceived or actual probability of punishment.


Severity
The harshness of punishment if imposed.


Celerity
The speed with which punishment follows the offence.


Incapacitation
Crime reduction by physically preventing a person from offending, often through custody or restriction.


Rehabilitation
Intervention aimed at changing skills, constraints, behaviour, or circumstances associated with offending.


Routine activity
The idea that crime occurs when a motivated offender, suitable target, and lack of capable guardianship converge.


Guardianship
Presence of people, institutions, technologies, or conditions that reduce opportunity for crime.


Opportunity
A situational condition that makes offending easier, more attractive, or less risky.


Self-control
Capacity to regulate impulses, delay gratification, and consider longer-term consequences.


Present bias
Overweighting immediate rewards or costs relative to future consequences.


Peer effect
Influence of peers on behaviour through learning, pressure, imitation, approval, or opportunity.


Social learning
Learning behaviour, motives, techniques, or justifications through interaction with others.


Labeling
The process by which official or social reaction changes identity, status, opportunity, or future behaviour.


Stigma
Negative social marking that can reduce opportunity, trust, and social standing.


Legitimacy
The perceived rightfulness of an authority, law, or institution.


Procedural justice
Fairness of decision-making processes, including voice, neutrality, respect, and trustworthy motives.


Compliance
Behaviour that follows rules, laws, or institutional expectations.

title: Glossary
text:
Institution terms

Police discretion
The room police have to decide whether and how to intervene, record, warn, arrest, or escalate.


Prosecution
The legal process of bringing charges against a defendant.


Plea bargaining
Negotiation in which a defendant may plead guilty in exchange for concessions, reduced charges, or sentencing expectations.


Conviction
A formal legal finding of guilt.


Sentencing
The formal assignment of punishment or legal consequence after conviction.


Probation
Community-based supervision, usually imposed instead of or after custody.


Parole
Conditional release from custody under supervision.


Reentry
The process of returning to community life after incarceration.


Recidivism
Reoffending after prior contact with the criminal justice system.

title: Glossary
text:
Model terms

Actor
A person, institution, group, or organization that makes choices in a model.


Choice
An action available to an actor.


Information
What an actor knows or observes when choosing.


Payoff
What an actor gains, loses, values, or avoids.


Strategy
A complete plan of action, especially in strategic settings.


Equilibrium
A stable pattern of behaviour in which actors have no relevant incentive to deviate, given the model.


Inspection game
A model in which one actor may violate a rule and another actor may inspect or monitor.


Reporting game
A model in which a victim or witness decides whether to report, often depending on trust, cost, and expected response.


Network model
A model where relationships among actors affect behaviour, diffusion, opportunity, or enforcement.


Displacement
A change in crime location, time, target, method, or type after an intervention.


Diffusion of benefits
A reduction in crime beyond the directly targeted area or group.

title: Methods Map
text:
A method should match the research question. Criminology uses many kinds of evidence because crime is partly hidden, institutionally recorded, socially interpreted, and unevenly distributed.
This page maps common research questions to suitable methods.

title: Methods Map
text:
The basic decision
The first question is not “Which method should I use?” but:

What kind of question am I asking?






flowchart TD
    A[Research question] --> B[Describe patterns]
    A --> C[Explain mechanisms]
    A --> D[Estimate causal effects]
    A --> E[Predict risk or outcomes]
    A --> F[Interpret meaning or experience]
    A --> G[Evaluate institutions or policy]

    B --> B1[Descriptive statistics]
    B --> B2[Maps and trend plots]

    C --> C1[Theory building]
    C --> C2[Process tracing]
    C --> C3[Qualitative evidence]

    D --> D1[Experiments]
    D --> D2[Quasi-experiments]
    D --> D3[Difference-in-differences]
    D --> D4[Regression discontinuity]
    D --> D5[Instrumental variables]

    E --> E1[Prediction models]
    E --> E2[Validation]
    E --> E3[Calibration]

    F --> F1[Interviews]
    F --> F2[Ethnography]
    F --> F3[Discourse or document analysis]

    G --> G1[Process evaluation]
    G --> G2[Outcome evaluation]
    G --> G3[Cost-benefit analysis]

title: Methods Map
Methods Map
text:
Mechanism questions
Mechanism questions ask:

How or why does this pattern arise?

Examples:

Why might victims choose not to report?
How do peer groups shape offending?
How does labeling affect future opportunity?
Why might aggressive enforcement reduce trust?

Useful methods include:

qualitative interviews;
ethnography;
case studies;
process tracing;
formal modelling;
theory-guided empirical analysis;
mixed-method designs.

Mechanism evidence often needs more than one source.





flowchart LR
    A[Observed pattern] --> B[Possible mechanism]
    B --> C[Observable implication]
    C --> D[Evidence]
    D --> E[Revised explanation]

Methods Map
Methods Map

text:
Data sources
Criminology uses multiple data sources.








Data source
Strength
Limitation




Police records
detailed official events
affected by reporting and recording


Court records
legal process and outcomes
only includes cases entering courts


Prison/probation records
correctional contact
selected population


Victimization surveys
captures unreported victimization
recall and survey design issues


Self-report surveys
captures hidden offending
honesty and sample issues


Interviews
meaning and mechanism
limited generalizability


Ethnography
deep contextual insight
time-intensive and local


Spatial data
place concentration
boundary and exposure issues


Network data
relational structure
missing ties and privacy constraints


Digital trace data
scale and behaviour logs
platform bias and access limits



No data source is perfect. The method should acknowledge what the data can and cannot show.

title: Methods Map
text:
Matching table








Question type
Example question
Suitable methods




Descriptive

maps, rates, trend plots


Mechanism

Causal

experiment, DiD, RD, IV

machine learning, validation, calibration

interviews, ethnography


Institutional

administrative data, process evaluation


Network
How does crime diffuse?
network analysis, diffusion models

title: Methods Map
text:
Common mistakes

1. Using a causal language with descriptive evidence
A correlation or trend does not automatically identify an effect.


2. Treating prediction as explanation
A predictive variable is not necessarily a causal mechanism.


3. Ignoring measurement process
Crime data are produced through reporting, detection, and recording.


4. Choosing method before question
The research question should determine the method.


5. Ignoring implementation
A policy cannot work as designed if it was not implemented as designed.


6. Overgeneralizing from one data source
Different sources capture different parts of the crime process.

title: Methods Map
text:
Method-selection checklist

What is the research question?
Is it descriptive, causal, predictive, interpretive, institutional, or mechanism-focused?
What is the unit of analysis?
What is the outcome?
Is the outcome true crime, recorded crime, reporting, detection, or institutional response?
What comparison is needed?
What data source is available?
What does the data miss?
What alternative explanations remain?
What kind of claim can the method support?
